body.text: Bāṇa: Harṣacarita
body.translated_text: <s>Bāṇa</s>: <s>Harṣacarita</s>

body.text: prathama ucchvāsaḥ
body.translated_text: First Chapter (<s>Ucchvāsa</s>)

children.text: namas tuṅga-śiraś-cumbi-candra-cāmara-cārave /
children.translated_text: Homage to the one whose lofty head kisses the moon, beautiful as a <s>cāmara</s> (flywhisk),

children.text: trailokya-nagarârambha-mūla-stambhāya Śambhave // 1.1 //
children.translated_text: to <s>Śambhu</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), who is the foundation-pillar of the edifice of the three worlds. ||1.1||

children.text: Hara-kaṇṭha-grahânanda-mīlitâkṣīṃ namāmy Umām /
children.translated_text: I bow to <s>Umā</s>, whose eyes are closed in the bliss of embracing <s>Hara</s>'s neck,

children.text: kāla-kūṭa-viṣa-sparśa-jāta-mūrcchâgamām iva // 1.2 //
children.translated_text: as if she had fainted from the touch of the <s>kālakūṭa</s> poison. ||1.2||

children.text: namaḥ sarva-vide tasmai Vyāsāya kavi-vedhase /
children.translated_text: Homage to the omniscient <s>Vyāsa</s>, the creator-poet,

children.text: cakre puṇyaṃ Sarasvatyā yo varṣam iva Bhāratam // 1.3 //
children.translated_text: who made the <s>Bhārata</s>, a holy rain-cloud, as it were, of <s>Sarasvatī</s> (Learning). ||1.3||

children.text: prāyaḥ ku-kavayo loke rāgâdhiṣṭhita-dṛṣṭayaḥ /
children.translated_text: For the most part, bad poets in this world, their vision governed by passion,

children.text: kokilā iva jāyante vācâlāḥ kāma-kāriṇaḥ // 1.4 //
children.translated_text: are born like cuckoos—noisy and wanton. ||1.4||

children.text: santi śvāna ivâsaṃkhyā jāti-bhājo gṛhe-gṛhe /
children.translated_text: As innumerable as dogs, marked [merely] by their birth, are found in every house;

children.text: utpādakā na bahavaḥ kavayaḥ śarabhā iva // 1.5 //
children.translated_text: but original poets are rare, like the <s>śarabha</s> (mythical eight-legged beast). ||1.5||

children.text: anya-varṇa-parāvṛttyā bandha-cihna-nigūhanaiḥ /
children.translated_text: By turning another's words [into his own] and concealing the marks of [verbal] bondage,

children.text: an-ākhyātāḥ satāṃ madhye kaviś cauro vibhāvyate // 1.6 //
children.translated_text: among the good, an unidentified poet is recognized as a thief. ||1.6||

children.text: śleṣa-prāyam udīcyeṣu pratīcyeṣv artha-mātrakam /
children.translated_text: Among the northerners, [poetry is] mostly <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning); among the westerners, mere sense;

children.text: utprekṣā dākṣiṇātyeṣu Gauḍeṣv akṣara-ḍambaram // 1.7 //
children.translated_text: among the southerners, <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy); and among the <s>Gauḍas</s>, pomposity of syllables. ||1.7||

children.text: navo 'rtho jātir a-grāmyā śleṣo 'kliṣṭaḥ sphuṭo rasaḥ /
children.translated_text: Novel meaning, unvulgar diction, effortless <s>śleṣa</s> (double meaning), vivid <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion),

children.text: vikaṭâkṣara-bandhaś ca kṛtsnam ekatra duṣkaram // 1.8 //
children.translated_text: and intricate composition of syllables—all these together in one work is difficult to achieve. ||1.8||

body.text: kiṃ kaves tasya kāvyena sarva-vṛttânta-gāminī /

children.text: kathêva bhāratī yasya na vyāpnoti jagat-trayam // 1.9 //
children.translated_text: like a narrative, encompassing all events, does not pervade the three worlds? ||1.9||

body.translated_text: What need has that poet of poetry, whose <s>Bhāratī</s> (speech),

children.text: ucchvāsânte 'py a-khinnās te yeṣāṃ vaktre Sarasvatī /
children.translated_text: Unwearied even at the end of a chapter, those in whose mouths <s>Sarasvatī</s> dwells—

children.text: katham ākhyāyikâkārā na te vandyāḥ kavîśvarāḥ // 1.10 //
children.translated_text: how can those lords of poets, the composers of <s>ākhyāyikā</s> (historical romances), not be revered? ||1.10||

children.text: kavīnām agalad darpo nūnaṃ Vāsavadattayā /
children.translated_text: The pride of poets surely melted away through the <s>Vāsavadattā</s>,

children.text: śakty eva Pāṇḍu-putrāṇāṃ gatayā Karṇa-gocaram // 1.11 //
children.translated_text: just as [the pride] of the <s>Pāṇḍu</s> princes [melted] through the power [of <s>Karṇa</s>] that came within <s>Karṇa</s>'s range. ||1.11||

children.text: pada-bandhôjjvalo hārī kṛta-varṇa-krama-sthitiḥ /
children.translated_text: Brilliant in the binding of words, captivating, maintaining the proper sequence of description—

children.text: bhaṭṭāra-Hariścandrasya gadya-bandho nṛpâyate // 1.12 //
children.translated_text: the prose composition of the illustrious <s>Hariścandra</s> is truly regal. ||1.12||

body.text: a-vināśinam a-grāmyam akarot Sātavāhanaḥ /

children.text: viśuddha-jātibhiḥ kośaṃ ratnair iva subhāṣitaiḥ // 1.13 //
children.translated_text: with well-composed sayings of pure diction, as if with gems. ||1.13||

body.translated_text: <s>Sātavāhana</s> made an imperishable, unvulgar treasury

children.text: kīrtiḥ Pravarasenasya prayātā kumudôjjvalā /
children.translated_text: The fame of <s>Pravarasena</s>, bright as white lotuses, has traveled

children.text: sāgarasya paraṃ pāraṃ kapi-senâiva setunā // 1.14 //
children.translated_text: to the farthest shore of the ocean, like the monkey-army by means of the bridge. ||1.14||

children.text: sūtra-dhāra-kṛtârambhair nāṭakair bahu-bhūmikaiḥ /
children.translated_text: Through his many-staged dramas, commenced by the <s>sūtradhāra</s> (stage-manager),

children.text: sa-patākair yaśo lebhe Bhāso deva-kulair iva // 1.15 //
children.translated_text: furnished with sub-plots, <s>Bhāsa</s> won fame, as if [they were] temple towers. ||1.15||

children.text: nirgatāsu na vā kasya Kālidāsasya sūktiṣu /
children.translated_text: When the well-turned verses of <s>Kālidāsa</s> issue forth, in whom

children.text: prītir madhura-sāndrāsu mañjarīṣv iva jāyate // 1.16 //
children.translated_text: does delight not arise, as in sweet, dense clusters of blossoms? ||1.16||

body.text: samuddīpita-kandarpā kṛta-Gaurī-prasādhanā /

children.text: Hara-līlêva no kasya vismayāya Bṛhat-kathā // 1.17 //
children.translated_text: like the sport of <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>)—for whom is the <s>Bṛhatkathā</s> not a source of wonder? ||1.17||

body.translated_text: Kindling love, adorning <s>Gaurī</s>,

children.text: Āḍhyarāja-kṛtôtsāhair hṛdaya-sthaiḥ smṛtair api /
children.translated_text: Merely by being remembered, dwelling in the heart, the inspirations created by King <s>Āḍhya</s>

children.text: jihvântaḥ kṛṣyamāṇêva na kavitve pravartate // 1.18 //
children.translated_text: pull the tongue inward, as it were, and [one's tongue] does not venture into poetry. ||1.18||

children.text: tathâpi nṛ-pater bhaktyā bhīto nirvahaṇâkulaḥ /
children.translated_text: Nevertheless, out of devotion to the king, though fearful and anxious about the completion,

children.text: karomy ākhyāyikâmbho-dhau jihvā-plavana-cāpalam // 1.19 //
children.translated_text: I venture the fickleness of my tongue swimming in the ocean of the <s>ākhyāyikā</s>. ||1.19||

children.text: sukha-prabodha-lalitā suvarṇa-ghaṭanôjjvalaiḥ /
children.translated_text: Graceful in its easy awakening [of meaning], brilliant with ornaments of golden words,

children.text: śabdair ākhyāyikā bhāti śayyêva pratipādakaiḥ // 1.20 //
children.translated_text: an <s>ākhyāyikā</s> shines like a couch, with its supporting [elements]. ||1.20||

body.text: jayati jvalat-pratāpa-jvalana-prākāra-kṛta-jagad-rakṣaḥ /

children.text: sakala-praṇayi-manoratha-siddhi-śrī-parvato Harṣaḥ // 1.21 //
children.translated_text: a <s>Śrīparvata</s> (Mountain of Fortune) for the fulfillment of all his beloved ones' wishes! ||1.21||

body.translated_text: Victorious is <s>Harṣa</s>, who has made the rampart of blazing valor his world-protection,

body.text: evam anuśrūyate: purā kila bhagavān sva-lokam adhitiṣṭhan paramêṣṭhī vikāsini-padma-viṣṭhare samupaviṣṭaḥ sunāsīr a-pramukhair gīrvāṇaiḥ parivṛto brahmôdyāḥ kathāḥ kurvann anyāś ca nir-avadyā vidyā-goṣṭhīr bhāvayan kadācid āsāṃ-cakre. tathâsīnaṃ ca taṃ tribhuvana-pratīkṣyaṃ Manu-Dakṣa-Cākṣuṣa-prabhṛtayaḥ Prajāpatayaḥ sarve ca sapta-rṣi-puraḥ-sarā maha-rṣayaḥ siṣevire. kecid ṛcaḥ stuti-caturāḥ samudacārayan. kecid apaciti-bhāñji yajūṃṣy apaṭhan. kecit praśaṃsā-sāmāni sāmāni jaguḥ. apare vivṛta-

children.text: -kratu-kriyā-tantrān mantrān vyācacakṣire. vidyā-visaṃvāda-kṛtāś ca tatra teṣām anyonyasya vivādāḥ prādur abhavan.
children.translated_text: techniques of sacrificial ritual. And there, disputes arose among them over disagreements about knowledge.

body.translated_text: Thus it is heard: Once upon a time, the Blessed <s>Parameṣṭhin</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>), presiding over his own world, seated upon the blossoming lotus-throne, surrounded by the gods led by <s>Sunāsīra</s> (<s>Indra</s>) and others, was conducting sacred discourses and cultivating other blameless assemblies of learning. And as he sat thus, the one looked upon by the three worlds, <s>Prajāpatis</s> such as <s>Manu</s>, <s>Dakṣa</s>, <s>Cākṣuṣa</s>, and others, and all the great sages led by the Seven Seers, attended upon him. Some, skilled in praise, recited <s>Ṛc</s> hymns. Some read <s>Yajus</s> formulas in token of veneration. Some sang <s>Sāma</s> chants of laudation. Others expounded <s>mantras</s> that revealed the

body.text: athâtiroṣaṇaḥ prakṛtyā mahā-tapā munir Atres tanayas tārā-pater bhratā nāmnā Durvāsā dvitīyenÔpamanyu-nāmnā muninā saha kalahāyamānaḥ sāma-gāyan krodhândho visvaram akarot. sarveṣu ca teṣu śāpa-bhaya-pratipanna-mauneṣu muniṣv anyâlāpa-līlayā câvadhīrayati Kamala-saṃbhave Bhagavatī kumārī kiñcid unmukta-bāla-bhāve bhūṣita-nava-yauvane vayasi vartamānā, gṛhīta-cāmara-pracalad-bhuja-latā Pitāmaham upavījayantī, nirbhartsana-tāḍana-jāta-rāgābhyām iva sva-bhāvâruṇābhyāṃ pāda-pallavābhyāṃ samudbhāsamānā, śiṣya-dvayenêva pada-krama-mukhareṇa nūpura-yugalena vācālita-caraṇa-yugalā, dharma-nagara-toraṇa-stambha-vibhramaṃ bibhrāṇā jaṅghā-dvitayam, sa-līlam utka-kala-haṃsa-kula-kalâlāpa-pralāpini mekhalâdāmni vinyasta-vāma-hasta-kisalayā, vidvan-mānasa-nivāsa-lagnena guṇa-kalāpenêvâṃsâvalambinā brahmā-sūtreṇa pavitrī-kṛta-kāyā, bhāsvan-madhya-nāyakam an-ekam uktânuyātam apavarga-mārgam iva

children.text: hāram udvahantī, vadana-praviṣṭa-sarva-vidyā-laktaka-rasenêva pāṭalena sphuratā daśana-cchadena virājamānā, saṃkrānta-kamalâsana-kṛṣṇâjina-pratimāṃ madhura-gītā-karṇanâvatīrṇa-śaśi-hariṇām iva kapola-sthalīṃ dadhānā, tiryak-sâvajñam unnamitâika-bhrū-latā, śrotram ekaṃ visvara-śravaṇa-kaluṣitaṃ prakṣālayantîvâpāṅga-nirgatena locanâśru-jala-pravāheṇêtara-śravaṇena ca vikasita-sita-Sindhuvāra-mañjarī-juṣā hasatêva prakaṭita-vidyā-madā, śruti-praṇayibhiḥ praṇavair iva karṇâvataṃsa-kusuma-madhu-kara-kulair upāsyamānā, sūkṣma-vimalena prajñā-pratānenêvâṃśukenâcchādita-śarīrā, vāṅmayam iva nirmalaṃ dikṣu
children.translated_text: like the path to liberation—many-stranded, following after what has been spoken, with a shining central gem—radiant with a coral-red lower lip that gleamed as if the essence of lac from all the arts that had entered her mouth, bearing upon her cheek-surface the likeness of the black antelope-skin seat of the Lotus-born, [or rather] a moon-hare that had descended upon hearing her sweet singing, with one eyebrow-creeper raised obliquely in disdain, as if washing one ear that had been soiled by hearing the discordant singing with a stream of tear-water flowing from the corner of her eye, while with the other ear, adorned with a cluster of blooming white <s>Sindhuvāra</s> blossoms, she seemed to laugh, her intoxication with learning manifest, attended upon by clusters of bees on the flowers at her ear-ornament like <s>praṇava</s> (<s>Oṃ</s>) syllables dear to the <s>Vedas</s>, her body covered by a fine, spotless upper garment as if by the veil of <s>prajñā</s> (wisdom), scattering in the directions a moonlight of

children.text: daśana-jyotsnā-lokaṃ
children.translated_text: tooth-radiance,

children.text: vikirantī devī Sarasvatī śrutvā jahāsa.
children.translated_text: like the world of speech made visible—the goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s>, upon hearing [the discordant singing], laughed.

body.translated_text: Then the exceedingly irascible great ascetic, the sage <s>Durvāsas</s> by name, son of <s>Atri</s>, brother of the lord of stars [<s>Soma</s>], quarreling with a second sage named <s>Upamanyu</s>, blinded by anger, sang the <s>Sāma</s> chant discordantly. And while all those sages had fallen into silence from fear of his curse, and while the Lotus-born (<s>Brahmā</s>) was disregarding [the commotion] with an air of other-worldly conversation, the blessed goddess <s>Sarasvatī</s>, a maiden at the stage of youth when childhood has barely been shed and fresh adolescence adorned, with vine-like arms moving as she held a <s>cāmara</s> (flywhisk) and fanned the Grandfather, resplendent with the soles of her feet, red by nature as if reddened by the blows and rebukes [she administered], with both her feet made vocal by a pair of anklets jingling with the rhythm of her steps like a pair of pupils [reciting], bearing in her two calves the semblance of the pillars of the gateway-arch of the city of <s>Dharma</s>, with the tender shoot of her left hand placed upon the girdle-string whose tinkling murmured like a flock of eager geese in sport, her body purified by the sacred thread hanging from her shoulder like a strand of virtues clinging to the abode of the minds of the learned, bearing a necklace

body.text: dṛṣṭvā ca tāṃ tathā hasantīṃ sa muniḥ: "āḥ pāpa-kāriṇi, dur-gṛhīta-vidyā-lavâvalepa-dur-vidagdhe, mām upahasasi" ity uktvā śiraḥ-kampa-śīryamāṇa-bandha-viśarāror unmiṣat-piṅgalimno jaṭā-kalāpasya rociṣā siñcann iva roṣa-dahana-draveṇa daśa diśaḥ kṛta-kāla-saṃnidhānām ivândha-kārita-lalāṭa-paṭṭâṣṭâpadām antakântaḥ pura-maṇḍana-patra-bhaṅga-makarikāṃ bhru-kuṭim

children.text: ābadhnan, atilohitena cakṣuṣâmarṣa-devatāyai sva-rudhirôpahāram iva prayacchan, nirdaya-daṣṭa-daśana-cchada-bhaya-palāyamānām iva vācaṃ rundhan dantâṃśu-cchalena, aṃsâvasraṃsinaḥ śāpa-śāsana-paṭṭasyêva grathnan granthim anyathā kṛṣṇâjinasya, sveda-kaṇa-pratibimbitaiḥ śāpa-śaṅkā-śaraṇâgatair iva surâsura-munibhiḥ pratipanna-sarvâvayavaḥ, kopa-kampa-taralitâṅgulinā kareṇa prasādana-lagnām akṣara-mālām ivâkṣa-mālām ākṣipya kāmaṇḍalavena vāriṇā samupaspṛśya śāpa-jalaṃ jagrāha.
children.translated_text: —like the ornamental <s>makarikā</s> (fish-design) decorating the inner apartment of the palace of <s>Antaka</s> (Death)—as if offering his own blood as an oblation to the deity of fury with his exceedingly red eye, as if stopping his speech that seemed to flee in terror from his mercilessly bitten lips under the pretext of the gleam of his teeth, tying the knot of his black antelope-skin differently as if tying the knot of the decree of his curse that hung from his shoulder, with gods, demons, and sages reflected in his drops of sweat as if they had taken refuge in every limb of his body from fear of the curse, snatching with his hand—its fingers trembling with the agitation of rage—the rosary that clung to him as if begging for mercy, and touching the water of his <s>kamaṇḍalu</s> (water-vessel), he took the curse-water in hand.

body.translated_text: And seeing her laugh thus, the sage [said]: 'Ah, wicked one, ill-bred in the arrogance born of a mere smattering of improperly grasped learning, you mock me!'—and so saying, bathing the ten directions, as it were, with the molten fire of rage through the glow of his mass of matted hair, tawny and loosened by the shaking of his head, darkening the tablet of his forehead as if bringing the presence of Death [near], he knit his brow

body.text: atrântare svayambhuvo 'bhyāśe samupaviṣṭā devī mūrtimatī pīyūṣa-phena-paṭala-pāṇḍaraṃ kalpa-druma-dukūla-valkalaṃ vasānā, bisa-tantumayenâṃśukenôn-nata-stana-madhya-baddha-gātrikā-granthiḥ, tapo-bala-nirjita-tri-bhuvana-jaya-patākābhir iva tisṛbhir bhasma-puṇḍraka-rājibhir virājita-lalāṭâjirā, skandhâva-lambinā sudhā-phena-dhavalena tapaḥ-prabhāva-kuṇḍalī-kṛtena Gaṅgā-srotasêva yoga-paṭṭakena viracita-vaikakṣyakā, savyena brahmôtpatti-puṇḍarīka-mukulam iva sphaṭika-kamaṇḍaluṃ kareṇa kalayantī, dakṣiṇam akṣa-mālā-kṛta-parikṣepaṃ kambu-nirmitôrmikā-danturitaṃ tarjana-taraṅgita-tarjanīkam utkṣipantī

children.text: karam, "āḥ pāpa, krodhôpahata, durātman, a-jña, an-ātma-jña, brahma-bandho, muni-śeṭa, apasada, nirākṛta, katham ātma-skhalita-vilakṣaḥ surâsura-muni-manuja-vṛnda-vandanīyāṃ tri-bhuvana-mātaraṃ bhagavatīṃ Sarasvatīṃ śaptum abhilaṣasi" ity abhidadhānā, roṣa-vimukta-vetrâsanair oṅ-kāra-mukharita-mukhair utkṣepa-dolāyamāna-jaṭā-bhāra-bharita-digbhiḥ parikara-bandha-bhramita-kṛṣṇâjinâṭopa-cchāyā-śyāmāyamāna-divasair amarṣa-niḥśvāsa-dolā-preṅkholita-brahmalokaiḥ soma-rasam iva sveda-visara-vyājena sravadbhir agnihotra-pavitra-bhasma-smera-lalāṭaiḥ kuśa-tantu-cāmara-cīra-cīvaribhir āṣāḍhibhiḥ praharaṇī-kṛta-kamaṇḍalu-maṇḍalair mūrtaiś caturbhir vedaiḥ saha bṛsīm apahāya Sāvitrī samuttasthau.
children.translated_text: [she said:] 'Ah, sinner, overcome by anger, wicked-souled, ignorant, self-ignorant, Brahmin in name only, worst of sages, base-born, rejected one—how, embarrassed by your own stumbling, do you presume to curse the blessed <s>Sarasvatī</s>, the mother of the three worlds, worthy of the worship of all hosts of gods, demons, sages, and men?'—and so declaring, together with cane-armed [sages] with voices resonating with <s>Oṃkāra</s>, their masses of matted locks swaying with agitation and filling the directions, the daylight darkened by the shadow of the billowing black antelope-skin whirled by their girdle-bindings, the world of <s>Brahmā</s> rocked by the swinging of their sighs of indignation, their foreheads gleaming with the holy ash of the <s>agnihotra</s> fire as if oozing <s>soma</s>-juice under the pretext of drops of perspiration, with their garments of <s>kuśa</s>-grass fibers and bark-cloth strips, making weapons of their circles of <s>kamaṇḍalus</s>—<s>Sāvitrī</s>, together with the four <s>Vedas</s> in embodied form, rose from her cushion.

body.translated_text: At that moment, <s>Sāvitrī</s> (<s>Gāyatrī</s>), who was seated nearby to the Self-born (<s>Brahmā</s>), the goddess in embodied form, wearing a garment of bark-cloth from the Wish-fulfilling tree, white as a mass of ambrosia-foam, with the knot of her bodice tied at the center of her prominent breasts with a cord woven of lotus-fibers, her forehead-courtyard adorned with three lines of ash-marks as if with victory-banners of the conquest of the three worlds won by the power of austerity, wearing as a cross-belt a yoga-sash white as ambrosia-foam, coiled by the power of austerity like a stream of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> hanging from her shoulder, holding in her left hand a crystal <s>kamaṇḍalu</s> (water-vessel) like a lotus-bud of sacred origin, raising her right hand—encircled by a rosary, adorned with conch-shell rings, with the index finger waving in reproof—

body.text: Tato "marṣaya bhagavan, a-bhūmir eṣā śāpasya" ity anunāthyamāno 'pi vibudhaiḥ, "upādhyāya, skhalitam ekaṃ kṣamasva" iti baddhâñjali-puṭaiḥ prasādyamāno 'pi sva-śiṣyaiḥ, "putra, mā kṛthās tapasaḥ pratyūham" iti nivāryamāṇo 'py Atriṇā, roṣâveśa-vivaśo Durvāsāḥ "dur-vinīte, vyapanayāmi te vidyā-janitām unnatim imām. adhastād gaccha martya-lokam" ity uktvā tac-chāpôdakaṃ visasarja.
body.translated_text: Then <s>Durvāsas</s>, though beseeched by the gods: 'Forgive, Blessed One, this is no occasion for a curse,' though propitiated by his own students with folded palms: 'Teacher, pardon one error,' though restrained by <s>Atri</s> [himself]: 'Son, do not create an obstacle to your austerities'—overpowered by the seizure of rage, said: 'Ill-mannered one, I shall destroy this haughtiness born of your learning. Go down to the mortal world!'—and released the curse-water.

body.text: pratiśāpa-dānôdyatāṃ Sāvitrīm "sakhi, saṃhara roṣam. a-saṃskṛta-matayo 'pi jātyâiva dvi-janmāno mānanīyāḥ" ity abhidadhānā Sarasvaty eva nyavārayat.
body.translated_text: <s>Sarasvatī</s> herself restrained <s>Sāvitrī</s>, who was ready to deliver a counter-curse, saying: 'Friend, withdraw your anger. Even those of uncultivated minds, if twice-born by birth, are worthy of respect.'

body.text: atha tāṃ tathā śaptāṃ Sarasvatīṃ dṛṣṭvā pitāmaho Bhagavān kamalôtpatti-lagna-mṛṇāla-sūtrām iva dhavala-yajñôpavītinīṃ tanum udvahan, udgacchad-acchâṅgulīya-marakata-mayūkha-latā-kalāpena tri-bhuvanôpaplava-praśama-kuśâpīḍa-dhāriṇêva dakṣiṇena kareṇa nivārya śāpa-kalakalam, ati-vimala-dīrghair bhāvi-kṛta-yugârambha-sūtra-pātam iva dikṣu pātayan daśana-kiraṇaiḥ, Sarasvatī-prasthāna-maṅgala-paṭahenêva pūrayann āśāḥ, svareṇa sudhīram uvāca: "brahman, na khalu sādhu-sevito 'yaṃ panthāḥ yenâsi pravṛttaḥ. nihanty eṣa parastāt. uddāma-prasṛtêndriyâśva-samutthāpitaṃ hi rajaḥ kaluṣayati dṛṣṭim an-akṣa-jitām. kiyad dūraṃ vā cakṣur īkṣate. viśuddhayā hi dhiyā paśyanti kṛta-buddhayaḥ sarvān arthān a-sataḥ sato vā. nisarga-virodhinī cêyaṃ payaḥ-pāvakayor iva dharma-krodhayor ekatra vṛttiḥ. ālokam apahāya kathaṃ tamasi nimajjasi ? kṣamā hi mūlaṃ sarva-tapasām. para-doṣa-darśana-dakṣā dṛṣṭir iva kupitā buddhir na te ātma-rāga-doṣaṃ paśyati. kva mahā-tapo-bhāra-vaivadhikatā, kva puro-bhāgitvam ? ati-roṣaṇaś cakṣuṣmān andha eva janaḥ. na hi kopa-kaluṣitā vimṛśati matiḥ kartavyam a-kartavyaṃ vā. kupitasya prathamam andha-kārī bhavati vidyā, tato bhrukuṭiḥ. ādāv indriyāṇi rāgaḥ samāskandati, caramaṃ cakṣuḥ.

children.text: ārambhe tapo galati, paścāt sveda-salilam. pūrvam a-yaśaḥ sphurati, anantaram adharaḥ. kathaṃ loka-vināśāya te viṣa-pādapasyêva jaṭā-valkalāni jātāni. an-ucitā khalv asya muni-veṣasya hāra-yaṣṭir iva vṛtta-muktā citta-vṛttiḥ. śailūṣa iva vṛthā vahasi kṛtrimam upaśama-śūnyena cetasā tāpasâkalpam. alpam api na te paśyāmi kuśala-jātam. anenâti-laghimnâdyâpy upary eva plavase jñānôdanvataḥ. na khalv an-eḍa-mūkāḥ eḍā jaḍā vā sarva ete maharṣayaḥ. roṣa-doṣa-niṣadye sva-hṛdaye nigrāhye kim artham asi nigṛhītavān an-āgasaṃ Sarasvatīm. etāni tāny ātma-pramāda-skhalita-vailakṣyāṇi, yair yāpyatāṃ yāty a-vidagdho janaḥ" ity uktvā punar āha: "vatse Sarasvati, viṣādaṃ mā gāḥ. eṣā tvām anuyāsyati Sāvitrī. vinodayiṣyati câsmad-viraha-duḥkhitām. ātma-ja-mukha-kamalâvalokanâvadhiś ca te śāpo 'yaṃ bhaviṣyati" iti. etāvad abhidhāya visarjita-surâsura-muni-manuja-maṇḍalaḥ sa-saṃbhramôpagata-Nārada-skandha-vinyasta-hastaḥ samucitâhnika-karaṇāyôdatiṣṭhat. Sarasvaty api śaptā kiñ-cid adho-mukhī dhavala-kṛṣṇa-śārāṃ kṛṣṇâjina-lekhām iva dṛṣṭim urasi pātayantī surabhi-niḥśvāsa-parimala-lagnair mūrtaiḥ śāpâkṣarair iva ṣaṭ-caraṇa-cakrair ākṛṣyamāṇā śāpa-śoka-śithilita-hastā 'dho-mukhī-bhūtenôpadiśyamāna-martya-lokâvataraṇa-mārgêva nakha-mayūkha-jālakena
children.translated_text: "At the beginning, austerity melts away; afterwards, perspiration. First, infamy manifests; next, the lip trembles. How is it that matted locks and bark-garments have grown upon you, as upon a poison-tree, for the destruction of the world! Indeed, the activity of your mind, having abandoned proper conduct, is as ill-suited to this sage's garb as a pearl necklace that has lost its string. Like an actor, you vainly bear the artificial ascetic's costume with a mind devoid of tranquility. I see not even a trace of merit born in you. With this excessive lightness, even today you merely float on the surface of the ocean of knowledge. Surely all these great seers are not deaf-mutes, or sheep, or fools. When your own heart, the seat of the fault of anger, should be restrained, why have you restrained the faultless <s>Sarasvatī</s>? These are those embarrassments born of stumbling through one's own negligence, by which the unsophisticated are shown to be worthless." Having said this, he spoke again: "Dear child <s>Sarasvatī</s>, do not despair. This <s>Sāvitrī</s> will accompany you. She will console you when you are grieved by separation from us. And this curse of yours shall last only until you behold the lotus-face of your son." Having said this much and dismissed the assemblies of gods, demons, sages, and humans, placing his hand on the shoulder of <s>Nārada</s> who had hastily approached, he rose to perform his customary daily rites. And <s>Sarasvatī</s> too, having been cursed, with her face somewhat downcast, casting upon her breast a gaze white-and-dark like a streak of black antelope-skin, being drawn along by swarms of bees clinging to the fragrance of her sweet sighs—as if by the embodied syllables of the curse—with her hands loosened by the grief of the curse, as though the downward-turned network of rays from her nails pointed out the path of descent to the mortal world,

children.text: nūpura-vyāhārâhūtair bhavana-kalahaṃsa-kulair brahma-loka-nivāsi-hṛdayair ivânugamyamānā samaṃ Sāvitryā gṛham agāt.
children.translated_text: followed by flocks of household geese summoned by the jingling of her anklets, like the hearts of <s>Brahmaloka</s>'s residents following her, she went home together with <s>Sāvitrī</s>.

body.translated_text: Then the Blessed Grandfather (<s>Brahmā</s>), seeing <s>Sarasvatī</s> thus cursed, wearing a body white with a sacred thread like a lotus-fiber strand clinging to the mud of lotus-birth, restraining the tumult of the curse with his right hand whose rising clear emerald ring-stone sent forth creeper-like rays as if holding a sprinkler of <s>kuśa</s> grass for quelling the catastrophe of the three worlds, casting in the directions the beams of his teeth—long and exceedingly pure—as if laying the foundation-threads of a new age to come, filling the horizons with his voice as if with the auspicious kettledrum for <s>Sarasvatī</s>'s departure, spoke slowly: 'O Brahmin, this is surely not a path well-trodden by the good upon which you have set out. It destroys hereafter. For the dust raised by the unbridled horses of the senses clouds a vision that has not conquered the senses. And how far does the eye see? For those of cultivated intellect perceive all things, whether real or unreal, with purified understanding. And this conjunction of <s>dharma</s> and anger is inherently contradictory, like that of water and fire. Abandoning light, why do you plunge into darkness? For forbearance is the root of all austerities. Your intellect, when angered, like a vision skilled at seeing others' faults, does not see the defect of self-attachment. Where is the burden-bearing of great austerity, and where is this rushing ahead [in anger]? An exceedingly angry man, even though having eyes, is truly blind. For an intellect clouded by rage does not deliberate on what should or should not be done. First, knowledge darkens the angry one, then comes the frown. Passion first assails the senses; last of all, the eye.

body.text: atrântare Sarasvaty-avataraṇa-vārtām iva kathayituṃ madhyamaṃ lokam avatatārâṃśu-mālī. krameṇa ca mandāyamāne mukulita-bisinī-visara-vyasana-viṣaṇṇa-sarasi vāsare, madhu-mada-mudita-kāminī-kopa-kuṭila-kaṭâkṣa-kṣipyamāṇa iva kṣepīyaḥ kṣiti-dhara-śikharam avatarati taruṇatara-kapi-lapana-lohite lokâika-cakṣuṣi bhagavati, prasnuta-mukha-māheyī-yūtha-kṣarat-kṣīra-dhārā-dhavaliteṣv āsanna-candrôdayôddāma-kṣīrôda-laharī-kṣāliteṣv iva divyâśramôpaśalyeṣu, a-parâhṇa-pracāra-calite cāmariṇi cāmīkara-taṭa-tāḍana-raṇita-radane radati sura-sravantī-rodhāṃsi svairam Airāvate, prasṛtâneka-Vidyādharâbhisārikā-sahasra-caraṇâlaktaka-rasânulipta iva prakaṭayati ca tārā-pathe pāṭalatām, tārā-patha-prasthita-siddha-datta-dina-karâstam-ayârghyâvarjite rañjita-kakubhi, kusumbha-bhāsi sravati Pināki-praṇati-mudita-Saṃdhyā-sveda-salila iva rakta-candana-drave, vandāru-muni-vṛndāraka-vṛnda-badhyamāna-saṃdhyâñjali-vane, brahmôtpatti-kamala-sevâgata-sakala-kamalâkara iva rājati brahma-loke, samuccārita-tṛtīya-savana-brahmaṇi brahmaṇi, jvalita-vaitāna-jvalana-jvālā-jaṭālâjireṣv ārabdha-dharma-sādhana-śibira-nīrājaneṣv iva sapta-rṣi-mandireṣu, agha-marṣaṇa-muṣita-kilbiṣa-viṣa-gadô-

children.text: -llāgha-laghuṣu yatiṣu saṃdhyôpāsanâsīna-tapasvi-paṅkti-pūta-puline plavamāna-nalina-yoni-yāna-haṃsa-hāsa-danturitôrmiṇi Mandākinī-jale, jala-devatâtapatre patra-ratha-kula-kalatrântaḥpura-saudhe nija-madhu-madhurâmodini kṛta-madhupa-mudi mumudiṣamāṇe kumuda-vane, divasâvasāna-tāmyat-tāma-rasa-madhura-madhu-sa-pīti-prīte suṣupsati mṛdu-mṛṇāla-kāṇḍa-kaṇḍūyana-kuṇḍalita-kandhare dhuta-pakṣa-rāji-vījita-rājīva-sarasi rāja-haṃsa-yūthe, taṭa-latā-kusuma-dhūli-dhūsarita-sariti siddha-pura-puraṃdhri-dhammilla-mallikā-gandha-grāhiṇi sāyaṃtane tanīyasi niśā-niḥśvāsa-nibhe nabhasvati, saṃkocôdañcad-ucca-kesara-koṭi-saṃkaṭa-kuśe-śaya-kośa-koṭara-kuṭī-śāyini ṣaṭ-caraṇa-cakre, nṛtyôddhūta-Dhūrjaṭi-jaṭâṭavī-kuṭaja-kuḍmala-nikara-nibhe nabhas-talaṃ stabakayati tārā-gaṇe, saṃdhyânubandha-tāmre pariṇamat-tāla-phala-tvak-tviṣi kāla-megha-medure, medinīṃ mīlayati nava-vayasi tamasi taruṇatara-timira-paṭala-pāṭana-paṭīyasi samunmiṣati yāminī-kāminī-karṇa-pūra-campaka-kalikā-kadambake pradīpa-prakare, pratanu-tuhina-kiraṇa-kiraṇa-lāvaṇyâloka-pāṇḍu-ny-āśyāna-nīla-nīra-mukta-Kālindī-kūla-bāla-pulināyamāne śāta-kratave kraśa-
children.translated_text: among ascetics made light with elation; on sandbars purified by rows of ascetics seated for twilight worship, in the waters of the <s>Mandākinī</s> whose waves were dappled by the laughter of swimming swans—the vehicles of the Lotus-Born; in the palace-like mansions of the inner chambers of families of leaf-charioted bird-clans, sheltered by water-deities' parasols; as the night-lotus garden, fragrant with its own sweet honey, having delighted the bees, wished to rejoice; as flocks of royal geese, satisfied from sipping the sweet honey of lotuses languishing at day's end, wished to sleep, with necks coiled from scratching on soft lotus-stalks, fanning the lotus-pond with their waving wing-rows; with rivers grayed by the pollen of bank-creeper blossoms; in the evening breeze, faint as the sigh of night, bearing the scent of jasmine from the hair-braids of wives of <s>Siddha</s> cities; as swarms of bees slept in the cavities of lotus-bud cottages cramped by the tips of tall stamens rising from contraction; as the host of stars clustered across the vault of heaven, resembling a heap of <s>kuṭaja</s> buds from the forest of <s>Dhūrjaṭi</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) matted locks shaken by his dance; as the darkness thickened with dark clouds, coppery in the aftermath of twilight, with the hue of ripening palm-fruit rind; as the youthful darkness caused the earth to close its eyes; as multitudes of lamps bloomed, like clusters of <s>campaka</s>-bud ear-ornaments of Night the beloved, most skillfully tearing open the curtains of ever-fresher darkness; as <s>Śatakratu</s>'s (Indra's) heaven resembled the young sandbanks on the <s>Kālindī</s>'s banks, freed from dark waters, pale with the beauty of the light of the thin moon's slender rays, thin-

children.text: -yati timiram āśā-mukhe, kha-muci mecakita-vikacita-kuvalaya-sarasi śaśa-dhara-kara-nikara-kaca-grahâvile vilīyamāne māninī-manasîva śarvarī-śabarī-cikura-caye cāṣa-pakṣa-tviṣi tamasi, udite bhagavaty Udaya-giri-śikhara-kaṭaka-kuhara-hari-khara-nakhara-nivaha-heti-nihata-nija-hariṇa-galita-rudhira-nicaya-nicitam iva lohitaṃ vapur Udaya-rāga-dharam adharam iva vibhāvarī-vadhvā dhārayati śveta-bhānau, a-cala-cyuta-candra-kānta-jala-dhārā-dhauta iva dhvaste dhvānte, go-loka-galita-dugdha-visara-vāhini dantamaya-makara-mukha-mahā-praṇāla ivâpūrayituṃ pravṛtte payodhim indu-maṇḍale, spaṣṭe pradoṣa-samaye Sāvitrī śūnya-hṛdayām iva kim api dhyāyantīṃ sâsrāṃ Sarasvatīm avādīt: "sakhi, tri-bhuvanôpadeśa-dāna-dakṣāyās tava puro jihvā jihreti me jalpantī. jānāsy eva yādṛśyo visaṃsthulā guṇavaty api jane dur-janavan-nirdākṣiṇyāḥ kṣaṇa-bhaṅginyo dur-atikramaṇīyā na ramaṇīyā daivasya vāmā vṛttayaḥ. niṣkāraṇā ca nikāra-kaṇikâpi kaluṣayati manasvino 'pi mānasam a-sadṛśa-janād āpatantī. an-avarata-nayana-jala-sicyamānaś ca tarur iva vipallavo 'pi sahasradhā prarohati. ati-sukumāraṃ ca janaṃ saṃtāpa-paramâṇavo mālatī-kusumam iva mlānim ānayanti. mahatāṃ côpari nipatann aṇur api sṛṇir iva kariṇāṃ kleśaḥ kadarthanāyâlam. sahaja-sneha-pāśa-granthi-bandhanāś ca
children.translated_text: ning the darkness at the horizon's mouth; as the darkness, with the hue of a blue-jay's wing, like the tresses of Night the wild woman, dissolved in the sky, a lake darkened by blooming blue lotuses, made turbid by the grasp of the moon's mass of rays upon its hair, dissolving like the mind of an offended lady; as the blessed moon rose, bearing a ruddy body—reddened as if heaped with the blood flowing from its own deer struck by the weapon-like mass of sharp claws of a lion in the cavern-belt at the peak of <s>Udaya</s> mountain, bearing the flush of rising—wearing it like the lower lip of Night the bride as the white-rayed one displayed it; with the darkness dispelled, as if washed by streams of water from moonstones fallen from the mountains; as the disc of the moon, like a great ivory <s>makara</s>-mouthed waterspout, began to fill the ocean, carrying floods of milk flowing from the cow-world; when the time of early evening had clearly arrived—<s>Sāvitrī</s> spoke to <s>Sarasvatī</s>, who sat weeping and brooding on something as if empty-hearted: "Friend, before you who are skilled in giving instruction to the three worlds, my tongue is ashamed to speak. You know well how perverse are fate's dealings—without courtesy even toward the virtuous, like the wicked; breaking at every moment; impossible to overcome; not pleasing. Even a trifle of injury, causeless, falling from an unworthy person, sullies the mind of even the high-minded. And grief, like a tree watered by unceasingly flowing tears, sprouts a thousandfold. The atoms of anguish bring wilting to the excessively delicate, as to a jasmine flower. And even a small affliction falling upon the great suffices to torment, like a small goad for elephants. And bound by the knotted bonds of innate affection,

children.text: bāndhava-bhūtā dus-tyajā janma-bhūmayaḥ. dārayati dāruṇaḥ krakaca-pāta iva hṛdayaṃ saṃstuta-jana-virahaḥ, sā nârhasy evaṃ bhavitum. a-bhūmiḥ khalv asi duḥkha-kṣveḍâṅkura-prasavānām. api ca purā-kṛte karmaṇi balavati śubhe 'śubhe vā phala-kṛti tiṣṭhaty adhiṣṭhātari praṣṭhe pṛṣṭhataś ca ko 'vasaro viduṣi śucām. idaṃ ca te tri-bhuvana-maṅgalâika-kamalam a-maṅgala-bhūtāḥ katham iva mukham apavitrayanty aśru-bindavaḥ. tad alam. adhunā kathaya katamaṃ bhuvo bhāgam alaṅ-kartum icchasi. kasminn avatitīrṣati te puṇya-bhāji pradeśe hṛdayam. kāni vā tīrthāny anugrahītum abhilaṣasi. keṣu vā dhanyeṣu tapo-vana-dhāmasu tapasyantī sthātum icchasi. sajjo 'yam upacaraṇa-caturaḥ saha-pāṃśu-krīḍā-paricaya-peśalaḥ preyān sakhī-janaḥ kṣiti-talâvataraṇāya. an-anya-śaraṇā câdyâiva prabhṛti pratipadyasva manasā vācā kriyayā ca sarva-vidyā-vidhātāraṃ dātāraṃ ca śvaḥ-śreyasasya caraṇa-rajaḥ-pavitrita-tridaśâsuraṃ sudhā-sūti-kalikā-kalpita-karṇâvataṃsaṃ deva-devaṃ tri-bhuvana-guruṃ try-ambakam. alpīyasâiva kālena sa te śāpa-śoka-viratiṃ vitariṣyati" iti.
children.translated_text: one's native lands, having become kinsmen, are hard to abandon. Separation from beloved people rends the heart cruelly, like the fall of a saw. You should not be thus. You are no ground for the sprouting of poisonous shoots of sorrow. Moreover, when past <s>karma</s>, whether auspicious or inauspicious, stands powerful, bearing its fruit, driving from behind as the presiding force—what occasion is there for sorrow in one who is wise? And how can drops of tears, being inauspicious, defile this face of yours, the sole auspicious lotus of the three worlds? Enough of this. Now tell me—which part of the earth do you wish to adorn? In which meritorious region does your heart desire to descend? Which holy places do you wish to grace? In which blessed abodes of ascetic groves do you wish to dwell, performing austerities? Ready is this dear company of friends, skilled in service, graceful from the intimacy of playing together in childhood, for the descent to the earth's surface. And without other refuge, from this very day forth, devote yourself—in thought, word, and deed—to the bestower of all knowledge and giver of future welfare, him whose foot-dust sanctifies gods and demons, who wears the crescent-moon-bud as his ear-ornament—the god of gods, the teacher of the three worlds, the three-eyed <s>Tryambaka</s>. In but a short time, he will grant you the cessation of the grief of the curse."

body.translated_text: Meanwhile, as if to announce the news of <s>Sarasvatī</s>'s descent, the Garlanded-with-Rays descended to the middle world. And as the day gradually waned, with lakes saddened by the misfortune of their lotus-fiber clusters closing up; as the blessed lord, the sole eye of the world, red as the muzzle of a young monkey, descended most swiftly to the mountain-peak, as if hurled by the sidelong glances crooked with the anger of women delighted by the intoxication of spring; as the precincts of the divine hermitages were whitened by streams of milk flowing from the mouths of herds of she-buffaloes whose udders were dripping, as if washed by the waves of the unbounded Milk-Ocean at the approaching moonrise; as <s>Airāvata</s>, whose teeth resounded from striking the golden banks, freely gnawed the banks of the celestial river, while the yak-tailed attendants moved about in their afternoon stroll; and as the sky-path displayed a pinkness, as if smeared with the lac-dye from the feet of thousands of <s>Vidyādhara</s> women going forth to assignations; with the quarters reddened as if by the offering-water for the sunset presented by <s>Siddhas</s> journeying along the star-path; as liquid red sandalwood flowed, glowing like safflower, like the perspiration of <s>Saṃdhyā</s> (Twilight) delighted by the prostration of <s>Pinākin</s> (<s>Śiva</s>); in a forest of joined palms offered in evening worship by throngs of reverential sages; as <s>Brahmaloka</s> shone as though all the lotus-ponds had come to attend upon the lotus from which <s>Brahmā</s> originated; as the Brahmins chanted the prayers of the third <s>savana</s> (pressing); in the abodes of the Seven Sages, whose courtyards were matted with the flames of blazing sacrificial fires, as if performing the lustration of the encampment for the practice of <s>dharma</s>; with the eradication of the poison-mace of sin by the <s>aghamarṣaṇa</s> (sin-destroying) hymn—

body.text: evam-uktā mukta-muktā-phala-dhavala-locana-jala-lavā Sarasvatī pratyavādīt: "priya-sakhi, tvayā saha vicarantyā na me kāṃ-cid api pīḍām utpādayiṣyati brahma-loka-virahaḥ śāpa-śoko vā. kevalaṃ kamalâsana-sevā-sukham ārdrayati me hṛdayam. api ca tvam eva vetsi me bhuvi dharma-dhāmāni samādhi-sādhanāni yoga-yogyāni ca sthānāni sthātum" ity evam abhidhāya virarāma. raṇa-raṇakôpanīta-prajāgarā câ-nimīlita-locanâiva tāṃ niśām anayat
body.translated_text: Thus addressed, <s>Sarasvatī</s>, releasing drops of tears white as pearls from her eyes, replied: "Dear friend, so long as I wander with you, neither separation from <s>Brahmaloka</s> nor the grief of the curse will cause me any pain. Only the happiness of serving the Lotus-Seated One softens my heart with longing. Moreover, you yourself know the abodes of <s>dharma</s> on earth, the means of <s>samādhi</s>, and the places fit for <s>yoga</s> where I should dwell." Having said this, she fell silent. And, kept awake by the tinkling of her anklet-bells, she passed that night as if with unblinking eyes.

body.text: anyedyur udite bhagavati tri-bhuvana-śekhare khaṇa-khaṇāyamāna-skhalat-khalīna-kṣata-nija-turaga-mukha-kṣiptena kṣata-jenêva pāṭalita-vapuṣy udayâcala-cūḍā-maṇau jarat-kṛkavāku-cūḍâruṇâruṇa-puraḥsare virocane nâti-dūra-vartī vivicya pitāmaha-vimāna-haṃsa-kula-pālaḥ paryaṭann a-para-vaktram uccair agāyat:
body.translated_text: The next day, when the blessed ornament of the three worlds rose—the crest-jewel of the Eastern Mountain, its body made pink, as if reddened by blood cast from the mouth of its own horse wounded by the stumbling and jangling of its slipping bit, preceded by the ruddy redness of an old cock's crest—a guardian of the flock of swans at <s>Pitāmaha</s>'s (<s>Brahmā</s>'s) aerial palace, standing not far away, wandering about and selecting, sang aloud facing in no other direction:

body.text:
"taralayasi dṛśaṃ kim utsukām a-kaluṣa-mānasa-vāsa-lālite /
  avatara kala-haṃsi vāpikāṃ punar api yāsyasi paṅkajâlayam" //
body.translated_text:
"Why do you agitate your eager gaze, O gentle goose nurtured in the abode of a pure mind? /
Descend to the pond—you shall return again to the lotus-abode."

body.text: tac chrutvā Sarasvatī punar acintayat: "aham ivânena paryanuyuktā. bhavatu. mānayāmi muner vacanam" ity uktvôtthāya kṛta-mahī-talâvataraṇa-saṃkalpā parityajya viyoga-viklavaṃ sva-parijanaṃ jñāti-vargam a-vigaṇayyâvagaṇā triḥ pradakṣiṇī-kṛtya catur-mukhaṃ katham apy anunaya-nivartitânuyāyi-vrati-vrātā brahma-lokataḥ Sāvitrī-dvitīyā nirjagāma.
body.translated_text: Hearing that, <s>Sarasvatī</s> thought again: "It is as if I have been addressed by this one. So be it—I shall honor the sage's words." Having said this and risen, having resolved to descend to the earth's surface, abandoning her retinue of kinfolk distraught with separation, without regard, disregarding them, having circumambulated the Four-Faced One (<s>Brahmā</s>) three times, somehow having turned back by persuasion the crowds of devotees who wished to follow, she departed from <s>Brahmaloka</s> with <s>Sāvitrī</s> as her companion.

children.translated_text: with a tumultuous sound; like a jasmine garland on the head of the Slayer of <s>Andhaka</s> (<s>Śiva</s>); with its banks blocked by <s>Vālakhilya</s> sages clinging to them; with bark-garments washed by <s>Arundhatī</s> whitening its surface; with stars more glittering and shimmering, crossing its high leaping waves; with sandbars bristling from the sesame-water offerings poured by ascetics; with its far banks whitened by ancestral offerings dropped by <s>Pitāmaha</s>, purified by ablution; with fasts for eclipses indicated by the <s>kuśa</s>-grass beds of the Seven Sages sleeping on its margins; mottled with heaps of worship-flowers released by <s>Śacīpati</s> (Indra), purified by ritual sipping; garlanded with <s>mandāra</s> flowers fallen as used offerings from <s>Śiva</s>'s city; with its rocks contemptuous cleaving the caverns of Mount <s>Mandara</s>; its body churned by the pitcher-like breasts of the women of hosts of heavenly leaders; its current made resonant by tumbling over clusters of crocodiles and rocks; its banks sparkling with clusters of nectar-droplets from the moon flowing through the <s>suṣumnā</s>; its sands grayed by smoke from the fire-rituals of the learned; with <s>Vidyādharas</s> scattered in fright of treading on sand-<s>liṅgas</s> fashioned by <s>Siddhas</s>—like a sloughed skin of a celestial serpent; like a playful forehead-ornament of heaven the dandy; like a marketplace for the merchandise of merit; like a bolt placed upon the door of the city of Hell; like a cloth turban-band of King <s>Sumeru</s>; like a silk banner of <s>Kailāsa</s> the elephant; like the path of liberation; like the rim of the <s>Kṛtayuga</s>—the <s>Mandākinī</s>, chief queen of the king of the seven oceans—following her, <s>Sarasvatī</s> descended to the mortal world. And while still standing in the vault of the sky, she beheld—like a necklace of <s>Varuṇa</s>; like an immortal waterfall of the Moon-Mountain; like the exudation of moonstones of the <s>Vindhya</s>; like a stream of camphor-tree sap of the <s>Daṇḍaka</s> forest; like a spring of the essence of beauty of the directions; like a crystal slab-bed of the glory of the sky—the great river named <s>Hiraṇyavāha</s>, offspring of the blessed <s>Pitāmaha</s>, full of clear, cool, sweet water, which people call <s>Śoṇa</s>—

children.text: -yanti. dṛṣṭvā ca taṃ rāmaṇīyaka-hṛta-hṛdayā tasyaiva tīre vāsam aracayat. uvāca ca Sāvitrīm: "sakhi, madhura-mayūra-virutayaḥ kusuma-pāṃśu-paṭala-sikatila-taru-talāḥ parimala-matta-madhupa-veṇī-vīṇā-raṇita-ramaṇīyā ramayanti māṃ mandī-kṛta-Mandākinī-dyuter asya mahā-nadasyôpakaṇṭha-bhūmayaḥ. pakṣapāti ca hṛdayam atrâiva sthātuṃ me" iti. abhinandita-vacanā ca tathêti tayā tasya paścime tīre samavātarat. ekasmiṃś ca śucau śilā-tala-sanāthe taṭa-latā-maṇḍape gṛha-buddhiṃ babandha. viśrāntā ca nâti-cirād utthāya Sāvitryā sārdham uccitârcana-kusumā sasnau. pulina-pṛṣṭha-pratiṣṭhita-Śiva-liṅgā ca bhaktyā paramayā para-brahma-puraḥ-sarāṃ samyaṅ-mudrā-bandha-vihita-parikarāṃ dhruvā-gīti-garbhām avani-pavana-vana-gagana-dahana-tapana-tuhina-kiraṇa-yajamāna-mayīr mūrtir aṣṭāv api dhyāyantī suciram aṣṭa-puṣpikām adāt. a-yatnôpanatena phala-mūlenâmṛta-rasamam apy ati-śiśayiṣamāṇena ca svādimnā śiśireṇa śoṇa-vāriṇā śarīra-sthitim akarot. ati-vāhita-divasā ca tasmiṃl latā-maṇḍapa-śilā-tale kalpita-pallava-śayanā suṣvāpa. anyedyur apy anenâiva krameṇa naktaṃ-dinam aty-avāhayat.
children.translated_text: And seeing this, her heart captivated by its charm, she made her camp on that very bank. She said to <s>Sāvitrī</s>: 'Friend, the banks of this great river delight me—where the sweet cries of peacocks resound, where the bases of trees are sandy with heaps of pollen from flowers, where the melodious hum of fragrance-intoxicated bees sounds like the strumming of the <s>vīṇā</s> in braids of bees, and whose splendor puts the <s>Mandākinī</s> to shame. My heart inclines to remain here.' Her words were welcomed, and with <s>Sāvitrī</s>'s agreement she descended to the western bank. In a certain clean spot sheltered by a rock-slab, she made a bower of creepers along the bank her dwelling. After resting, she arose before long, and having gathered flowers for worship together with <s>Sāvitrī</s>, she bathed. Having placed a <s>Śiva-liṅga</s> on the surface of the sandbank, with supreme devotion, preceded by meditation on the Supreme <s>Brahman</s>, with all proper ritual gestures duly arranged, containing a <s>dhruvā-gīti</s> (fixed song), meditating for a long time on the eight forms—earth, wind, forest, sky, fire, sun, moon, and the sacrificer—she offered the eight-flower worship. She sustained her body with roots and fruits that came to hand effortlessly, and with cool, reddish water whose taste surpassed even nectar and whose sweetness exceeded all desire. Having passed the day, she slept on that rock-slab of the bower of creepers, making a bed of tender leaves. The next day too, she passed night and day in the very same manner.

body.translated_text: Then, gradually, following the <s>Mandākinī</s>—flowing constantly like a <s>dharma</s>-cow with white udders streaming downward,

children.translated_text: rushing straight toward her. Gradually, as its details became visible with its approach, in that great dust—gray as the belly of a <s>śaphara</s> fish—as if a host of <s>makara</s>s (sea-monsters) floating in water, she saw a troop of horses attended by about a thousand foot-soldiers running ahead—their forehead-locks knotted with clusters of long, curling hair-tendrils, their cheek-walls lit up with the gleam of white tooth-sticks, wearing brownish tunics mottled with the dark smear of black <s>aguru</s>-paste, with turbans made of their upper garments tied around their heads, bright golden bangles set firmly on their left forearms, swords secured with a tight knot of doubled silk-ribbon bands, their bodies hardened by ceaseless exercise, leaping into the air again and again like a herd of wind-swift deer, jumping over even and uneven ditches and thickets, carrying daggers at their sides, swords in hand, grasping various forest flowers, fruits, roots, and leaves gathered in service, and ceaselessly raising a clamor: 'Move, move! Go, go! Get out of the way! Clear the path ahead!'—most of them young men.

body.translated_text: As days passed in this way, and time went on, when the sun had risen about one watch above the horizon, she heard in the northern direction a deep, resounding thunder of horse-neighing that filled the cavities of the forest with echoes. Curious, she came out of the bower of creepers and looking out, she beheld a mass of dust, pale as the inner petals of a blooming <s>ketakī</s> flower, not very far away,

body.text: madhye ca tasya sârdha-candreṇa muktā-phala-jāla-mālinā vividha-ratna-khaṇḍa-khacitena śaṅkha-kṣīra-phena-pāṇḍureṇa kṣīrôdenêva svayaṃ Lakṣmīṃ dātum āgatena gagana-gatenâtapatreṇa kṛta-cchāyam, acchâcchenâbharaṇa-dyutīnāṃ nivahena diśām iva darśanânurāga-lagnena cakravālenânugamyamānam, ā-nitamba-vilambinyā mālatī-śekhara-srajā sakala-bhuvana-vijayârjitayā rūpa-patākayêva virājamānam, utsarpibhiḥ śikhaṇḍa-khaṇḍikā-padma-rāga-maṇer aruṇair aṃśu-jālair a-dṛśyamāna-vana-devatā-vidhṛtair bāla-pallavair iva pramṛjyamāna-mārga-reṇu-paruṣa-vapuṣam, bakula-kuḍmala-maṇḍalī-muṇḍa-mālā-maṇḍana-manohareṇa kuṭila-kuntala-stabaka-mālinā maulinā mīlitâtapaṃ

children.translated_text: his forehead-plate, naturally embraced by innate beauty as if fashioned with a second crescent from <s>Paśupati</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) matted-hair-crown, with its tawny luster from a paste of <s>manaḥśilā</s> (realgar) seeming to paint the sky itself; with the breadth of his eye—whose bold glance, supported by the onset of fresh youth, had reduced the three worlds to a blade of grass—spreading as if producing an autumn that covered the ten directions with thousands of lakes of blooming <s>kumuda</s>, <s>kuvalaya</s>, and <s>kamala</s> lotuses; handsome with his long nose-bridge, like a stream of beauty-water flowing from the moonstone-slab of his forehead-bank along the boundary-embankment of his elongated eye-rivers; with his mouth, fragrant with the most exquisite <s>sahakāra</s>-mango, camphor, <s>kakkola</s>, clove, and <s>pārijātaka</s> perfume, loud with the buzzing of bees intoxicated by that scent, as if bringing down spring complete with <s>Nandana</s> garden itself; with his innocent smiles, drawn out by playful jesting with intimate friends, whose teeth-moonlight bathed the directions, as if creating a wandering moon-glow in the sky again and again; perceived as if wearing a fresh green <s>kunda</s>-blossom ear-ornament with flowers, by the radiance rising from a swinging three-pronged ear-ornament set with an emerald between twin pearls thick as <s>kadamba</s> buds; his face shining with painted leaf-designs inscribed with fragrant musk-paste; his pair of arms bearing a pair of staffs, as it were, of <s>Makaraketu</s>'s (<s>Kāma</s>'s) banner, their peaks surmounted by unrestrained <s>makara</s>-shaped [arm-ornaments]; bearing a body like Mount <s>Mandara</s>, its center marked by a white sacred thread, as if bound by the wrathful stream of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> during the churning of the ocean; with a broad chest like a wide sandbank with a pair of beautiful, high, round <s>cakravāka</s>-breasts, dusted with camphor powder as if with sand, massed by the breadth of his stout arms, as if spreading the circle of directions before him; And seated while the two were seated, staying not very long, [<s>Sarasvatī</s>], addressing that second, older man, spoke: 'Sir, for a woman whose wealth is innate modesty, to speak first is an impropriety—especially for a maiden of good family, timid as a forest deer. Yet this eagerness of the ear, curious to hear news, urges the faculty of hearing that seeks fulfillment through sight. And at first sight, a good person offers affection as a welcoming gift, as it were. Even a timid person is made eloquent by the honey of regard offered by a superior with humility. Just as a bowstring on a bow that is bent without effort, so trust raises intimacy to the highest pitch in a good man who is naturally modest. And even the minds of the profoundly wise are struck with wonder by the Creator's extraordinary marvels when seen in the world for the first time. For the beauty of this great soul surpasses the three worlds. And this excessive goodness of His Highness, which is subordinate to nobility, prompts this conversation—not the flightiness that arises naturally in young women. So tell me: what region, bereft of good fortune and empty with the pangs of separation fully displayed, has been made desolate by your departure? And where are you bound? And who is this other youth, seemingly self-born—whose proud roar, as it were, has stolen <s>Hara</s>'s (Śiva's) roar—as if not born of another? And of what father, rich in accumulated austerities, is this nectar-raining <s>Kaustubha</s> gem, as it were, gladdening the heart of <s>Hari</s>? And who is his mother, worthy of the three worlds' homage, like the dawn-twilight of a great radiance? And what blessed syllables form his name?'

children.translated_text: the beautiful <s>Siddha</s> women moving about, slowly rose to the surface of the sky like a swan of the <s>Mandākinī</s> (heavenly <s>Gaṅgā</s>)—she, having performed her evening obeisances at the very beginning of the night, collapsed with relaxed limbs and lay on her bed of sprouts. <s>Sāvitrī</s> too, having performed the evening ritual observances as prescribed, at the proper time of sleep, took to her sprout-bed. Having become drowsy, she slept.

body.translated_text: Then, after he had crossed the <s>Śoṇa</s> [river] and in a short time <s>Dadhīca</s> had reached his father's hermitage, even after he was gone, she stood for a long time gazing in that very direction. And with difficulty, as it were, she withdrew her gaze. Then, having remained for just a moment, remembering that beauty of his form, her heart wondered again and again. Her eyes longed once more for the sight of him. As if against her will, her gaze was drawn by some [force] toward that very direction. Her mind, though unimpelled, went along with him. And from somewhere there arose in her heart an affection, like a fresh sprout on a young forest creeper. From then on, she passed the day as if languid, as if empty, as if drowsy. And when the sun set with its disc tilted westward—its glow copper-red like clusters of <s>lāṅgalikā</s> flowers, the lover of lotus-ponds, its rays at the crown red-blazing like a harsh headache—in the <s>Sāvitra</s> radiance consisting of the triple <s>Veda</s>; and when the mass of darkness, dark as young <s>tamāla</s> trees, pervading the sky, darkened the firmament; and when the moon, following the sound of the ankle-bells of

body.text: itarā tu muhur-muhur-aṅga-valanair vilulita-kisalaya-śayana-talā nimīlita-nayanâpi nâlabhata nidrām. acintayac ca: "martya-lokaḥ khalu sarva-lokānām upari, yasminn evaṃ-vidhāni bhavanti tri-bhuvana-bhūṣaṇāni sakala-guṇa-grāma-gurūṇi ratnāni. tathā hi: tasya mukha-lāvaṇya-pravāhasya niṣyanda-bindur induḥ. tasya ca cakṣuṣo vikṣepāḥ kumuda-kuvalaya-kamalâkarāḥ. tasya câdhara-maṇer dīdhitayo vikasita-bandhūka-vana-rājayaḥ. tasya câṅgasya para-bhāgôpakaraṇam anaṅgaḥ. puṇya-bhāñji tāni cakṣūṃṣi cetāṃsi yauvanāni vā straiṇāni, yeṣām asāv aviṣayo darśanasya. kṣaṇaṃ nu darśayatā ca tam anya-janma-janitenêva me phalitam a-dharmeṇa. kā pratipattir idānīm?" iti cintayanty eva kathaṃ-katham apy upajāta-nidrā cirāt kṣaṇam aśeta. suptâpi ca tam eva dīrgha-locanaṃ dadarśa.

children.text: svapnâsādita-dvitīya-darśanā câkarṇâkṛṣṭa-kārmukeṇa manasi nirdayam atāḍyata makara-ketunā. pratibuddhāyā madana-śarâhatāyāś ca tasyā vārtām ivôpalabdhum aratir ājagāma. tathā hi: tataḥ-prabhṛti kusuma-dhūli-dhavalābhir vana-latābhir a-tāḍitāpi vedanām adhatta. manda-mandam āruta-vidhutaiḥ kusuma-rajobhir a-dūṣita-locanâpy aśru-jalaṃ mumoca. haṃsa-pakṣa-tālavṛnta-vāta-vrāta-vitataiḥ Śoṇa-śīkarair a-siktâpy ārdratām agāt. preṅkhat-kādamba-mithunābhir an-ūḍhâpy aghūrṇata vana-kamalinī-kallola-dolābhiḥ. vighaṭamāna-cakravāka-yugala-vimṛṣṭair a-spṛṣṭâpi śyāmatām āsasāda viraha-niḥśvāsa-dhūmaiḥ. puṣpa-dhūli-dhūsarair a-daṣṭâpi vyaceṣṭata madhukara-kulaiḥ.
children.translated_text: Having obtained a second sight [of him] in a dream, the god with the <s>makara</s> banner (<s>Kāma</s>, the god of love), with a bow drawn to his ear, struck her mercilessly in the heart. And when she awoke, struck by <s>Madana</s>'s (Love's) arrow, sleeplessness came to her as if to receive her news. For from then on: she felt pain even though not struck by the forest creepers white with flower-dust. She shed tears even though her eyes were not defiled by the pollen shaken by gentle breezes. She became wet even though not sprinkled by the spray of the <s>Śoṇa</s> [river] scattered by the fan-like breezes from wild-goose wings. She reeled even though not rocked by the wave-swings of the forest lotus-ponds with their swaying pairs of <s>kādamba</s> birds. She turned dark even though not touched by the smoke of the sighs of separation wiped clean by separating pairs of <s>cakravāka</s> birds. She writhed even though not stung by the swarms of bees grey with flower-dust.

body.translated_text: But the other one, tossing her limbs again and again, the surface of her sprout-bed disordered, though her eyes were closed, could not find sleep. And she thought: 'The mortal world is truly above all worlds, since in it there exist such jewels that are ornaments of the three worlds, weighty with the full company of every virtue. For indeed: the moon is but a dripping drop of the stream of his facial beauty. Lakes of night-lilies, blue lotuses, and day-lotuses are but the scattered glances of his eyes. The splendors of blooming <s>bandhūka</s> flower groves are but the radiations of the gem of his lower lip. <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love) is merely the instrument of the transcendence of his body. Blessed are those eyes, those hearts, those feminine youths for whose sight he is not beyond reach. And he who showed me [that sight] for a moment—it is as if a merit [earned] in another birth bore fruit through <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness). What course of action is there now?' Thinking thus, she somehow, with difficulty, eventually became drowsy and slept for a brief moment. And even in sleep, she saw that same long-eyed one.

children.translated_text: a merchant-woman named <s>Mālatī</s> will come presently, following right behind, to learn news of you both. For she is the breath of the prince.' Hearing that, <s>Sāvitrī</s> spoke again: 'The prince is indeed of very great power, that he thus forms an attachment even to persons seen for a moment, whose identity is unknown. For as he was departing, his heart was, by chance, somehow caught upon us like a garment on roadside creepers for a moment. For the graciousness of your master's son is not empty, owing to his noble birth. The world is truly lazy, in that it does not, for any price, purchase the hearts of the great, whose friendship is so easily won. This is some extraordinary excess of generosity among great souls, unattainable by ordinary people, by which they make the three worlds their beneficiaries.' <s>Vikukṣi</s>, having remained for what seemed a long time with various conversations, departed to his desired destination.

body.translated_text: Then, after a few nights had passed, <s>Vikukṣi</s> came back by the same road to that very place, his retinue held back as before, accompanied only by the parasol-bearer, and paid his respects. <s>Sarasvatī</s>, seeing him coming toward her from afar, rose with delight and agitation, craning her neck like a forest deer, gazing—and as if bathed the road-weary [traveler] with a glance that whitened all ten directions. When he had taken his seat, <s>Sāvitrī</s> asked him with affection: 'Noble one, is the prince well?' He said: 'Blessed lady, he is well. And he remembers you both. children.translated_text: are is no mere anyone—you are my sister, friend, beloved companion, and equal to my life. Command this body for whatever task it is fit, be it small or great. My heart is an open door, unbarred, for you. I am bound to you as a wrist-thread of affection. Reveal, O fair one, what you wish to say.'  She then said: 'O goddess, you yourself know the sweetness of sense-objects, the greediness of the group of senses, the madness of fresh youth, and the fickleness of the mind. The irresistibility of the God of Love is well-known. Therefore you should not reproach me. Neither foolishness, nor fickleness, nor mere talkativeness is the cause of [my] loquacity. There is nothing that an extraordinary devotion to one's master cannot accomplish. Now then, O goddess, from the very moment you were seen by [my] lord, from that very time, desire has become his guru, the moon the lord of his life, the breeze from <s>Malaya</s> the cause of his sighs, anxieties have taken up positions in his innermost limbs, anguish has become his dearest friend, sleeplessness his intimate companion, his longings are all-pervading, his sighs are the advance-guard of his body, death stands at his side, his agitation is his escort, his fantasies are counsels grown old in the guidance of the intellect. body.translated_text: In due course, when the midday hour had passed and <s>Sāvitrī</s> had gone down to the <s>Śoṇa</s> river to bathe, <s>Mālatī</s>, with her attendants sent away, approached <s>Sarasvatī</s> who lay on a couch of flowers, and as if with an ulterior purpose, addressed her: 'O goddess, we have something to submit in private. I wish for the favor of your attention for a moment.' body.translated_text: Then <s>Sarasvatī</s>, with eyes wide open with delight, replied: 'Ah, I cannot say much. Here I am, you of the smile-laden speech, standing by your words. Take these my life-breaths.' And <s>Mālatī</s>, saying 'O goddess, whatever you command is a supreme favor,' having bowed, overwhelmed with joy, crossed the <s>Śoṇa</s> on a swift horse. And she went to <s>Cyavana</s>'s hermitage to fetch <s>Dadhīca</s>. The other [<s>Sarasvatī</s>] also made <s>Sāvitrī</s> aware of what had transpired, out of affection for her friend. And bearing the heavy burden of eager longing, with a languishing heart, she somehow managed to pass the remainder of the day as if it were an eon. body.translated_text: Then, by the dispensation of fate, <s>Sarasvatī</s> conceived a child. And with ease she gave birth to a son endowed with all auspicious marks. And to him, the moment he was born, she granted a boon: 'All the <s>Vedas</s> with their esoteric teachings, all the <s>śāstras</s> (sciences), and all the arts shall manifest of their own accord through my power.' Then, as if taking <s>Dadhīca</s> with her in her heart to display him with wifely pride, together with <s>Sāvitrī</s>, by the command of the Grandfather (<s>Brahmā</s>), she ascended once more to the world of <s>Brahmā</s>. And when she had departed, <s>Dadhīca</s> too, stricken in his heart as if by the <s>hrādinī</s> thunderbolt, entrusting the wife of his kinsman—a Brahmin born of the <s>Bhārgava</s> lineage—a sage's daughter named <s>Akṣamālā</s>, with the raising of his son, went to the forest, afflicted by separation, to practice austerities. At the very time when <s>Sarasvatī</s> gave birth to her son, <s>Akṣamālā</s> too bore a son. And she gradually raised both children without distinction, with the same breast-milk and other [nourishment]. One of them was named <s>Sārasvata</s> ('Son of <s>Sarasvatī</s>'), and the other bore the name <s>Vatsa</s>. And between the two, as if they were born of the same womb, there was an enviable affection.

body.text: atha Sārasvato mātur mahimnā yauvanârambha evâvir-bhūtâśeṣa-vidyā-saṃbhāras tasmin sa-vayasi bhrātari preyasi prāṇa-same suhṛdi Vatse vāṅ-mayaṃ samastam eva saṃcārayām āsa. cakāra ca kṛta-dāra-parigrahasyâsya tasminn eva pradeśe prītyā Prītikūṭa-nāmānaṃ nivāsam. ātmanâpy āṣāḍhī, kṛṣṇâjinī, akṣa-valayī, valkalī, mekhalī, jaṭī ca bhūtvā tapasyato janayitur eva jagāmântikam.
body.translated_text: Then <s>Sārasvata</s>, by his mother's greatness, even at the onset of youth, possessed the entire store of all learning made manifest; and he transmitted the entirety of the verbal arts to that cherished age-mate, his dearest friend, equal to his own life—his brother <s>Vatsa</s>. And he lovingly established for <s>Vatsa</s>, who had taken a wife, a dwelling in that very region, named <s>Prītikūṭa</s> ('Hill of Affection'). And he himself, having become a staff-bearer, wearing a black antelope-skin, a rosary-wearer, clothed in bark, girdle-wearer, and matted-haired, went to be near his father who was practicing austerities.

body.translated_text: When the rites of investiture with the sacred thread and so forth had been completed, and when he had returned [from the teacher's house] at about fourteen years of age, his father too, having performed everything that was prescribed by <s>śruti</s> (revealed scriptures) and <s>smṛti</s> (remembered tradition), all the meritorious acts proper for a <s>Brāhmaṇa</s>, in due course passed away before the tenth day. When his father had died, overwhelmed by great grief, terrifying, his heart burning day and night, he somehow passed a few days in his own house. As grief gradually thinned, by the independence [of youth] which was the cause of unruliness, by the abundance of curiosity natural to boyhood, and by the onset of youth which is the adversary of steadfastness, he became restless, indulging in many improprieties proper to childhood. And he had companions, friends, and associates of the same age. body.translated_text: While he was staying there, one day, drawing closed the pair of flower-seasons, the great <s>Kāla</s> (Time) named Summer yawned forth, with the loud white laughter of jasmine in full bloom. And the hot season, newly risen, scorching across the entire earth, brought about the release of all flower-bonds. The tresses of women were seized by <s>Kusumāyudha</s> (the Flower-Armed God of Love), as if they were clusters of fly-whisks still moist from the coronation-anointing of the king of seasons. Eyes languid with drowsiness could not bear even the light of gems, let alone the fierce sunlight. Nights, with their moons, were reduced to thinness—like rivers in the warm season, rejoiced over by <s>cakravāka</s> pairs. Not only did people desire to drink water fragrant with the fresh, pungent scent of <s>pāṭalā</s> flowers—they wished to drink even the wind, from the heat of the sun.

body.translated_text: In such an exceedingly fierce summer season, one day, as he [<s>Bāṇa</s>] was at home in the afternoon after having eaten, his half-brother named <s>Candrasena</s> entered and said: 'Here indeed, [there waits] from His Majesty, the lord of the four oceans, at whose foot-nail-gems the crown-jewel-rows of the entire circle of kings are polished as on a whetstone-corner, the foremost of all universal sovereigns, the Supreme Sovereign Lord <s>Śrī Harṣadeva</s>—[sent] by his [associate] named <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, a long-distance traveler, most wise among your acquaintances—a messenger waits at the door.' He [<s>Bāṇa</s>] said: 'Good sir, without delay, bring him in.'

children.translated_text: Having ascertained the meaning of the letter, he dismissed his attendants and asked for the oral message. <s>Mekhalaka</s> [the messenger] then said: 'Thus says the master to the wise one: The honorable one surely knows that belonging to the same <s>gotra</s> (clan), or having equal learning, or being of the same caste, or being raised together, or dwelling in the same region, or habitual acquaintance, or mutual affection, or hearing [of one another], or rendering unseen service, or having similar character—these are the causes of affection. But for you, my heart feels some inexplicable partisan affection as if toward an intimate kinsman, even though you are unseen, even though you are far away—like the <s>kumuda</s> (night-lily) pond for the moon. For without you, this emperor was [previously] made to believe this and that by wicked people. But that is not so. There is no one among good people who does not have friends, neutrals, and enemies. And something unseemly was uttered by some intolerant person, owing to [your] youthful fickleness and the waywardness of your character. The rest of the world takes it at face value and says the same. For the minds of the undiscerning are indeed fickle, following one after another like streams of water. And what can the lord of the earth do when his resolve has been made firm by hearing from many mouths? But we, being seekers of truth, have seen you clearly though you are far away. And the emperor has been informed on your behalf: that generally, in early youth, everyone offends through the follies of childhood. And this has been accepted by the master. Therefore, you should come to the royal court without delay. One who has not seen the Supreme Lord, even though living among kinsmen—with uncut hair—is not well regarded by me. And you should not be one who is dejected by the unevenness of service, nor one who is timid about approaching the Supreme Lord. For even though:

body.translated_text: Then, being brought in, he saw the letter-carrier entering—his legs stiffened and heavy from exceedingly long travel, his violent parasol restrained by a muddy cloth-wrapper, his neck-knot fastened with a patched, tattered cloth swinging at his back, his head encircled by a garland of letters whose intervals were indented by very tight string-bindings creating line-divisions. He asked from a distance itself: 'Good man, is all well with that kinsman-without-cause to the entire world, the noble <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>?' He said 'All is well,' bowed, and sat down not too far away. Having rested, he said: 'Here indeed, a letter from the master has been sent to the honorable one,' and untying it,

body.translated_text: Nevertheless, other kings are different, and this one is altogether different. The master, who has eclipsed <s>Nṛga</s>, <s>Nala</s>, <s>Niṣadha</s>, <s>Nahuṣa</s>, <s>Ambarīṣa</s>, <s>Daśaratha</s>, <s>Dilīpa</s>, <s>Nābhāga</s>, <s>Bharata</s>, <s>Bhagīratha</s>, and <s>Yayāti</s>, is composed of nectar. His glances are not corrupted by the <s>kālakūṭa</s> poison of egotism; his words do not stammer with the throat-choking malady of the poison of arrogance; his postures have not forgotten their composure through the delirium of excessive pride; his emotions are not distressed by the fever-fury of unbridled haughtiness; his gaits are not broken-limbed by the great convulsion of self-conceit; his speech does not consist of harsh syllables spat out from lips twisted by intoxication. Furthermore: his jewel-estimation is directed at virtuous men, not at fragments of stone. His adorning-intention is directed at qualities white as pearls, not at burdens of ornaments. His confidence in means is directed at generous actions, not at elephant-gnats. His great delight is in fame that surpasses all, not in life that is [mere] withered grass. His eagerness to adorn is directed at hopes that he has taken by the hand,

And lying alone, he reflected: 'What shall I do? I have been misjudged by the king. And thus has <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, a kinsman without cause, sent word. But service is hard. Servitude is precarious. A great royal court is exceedingly deep. children.translated_text: Having had all the auspicious rites of departure performed by the blessed <s>Mahāśvetā</s> named <s>Mālatī</s>, blessed with benedictions by the elder kinswomen, congratulated by the aged female attendants, permitted to depart by the <s>gurus</s> whose feet he saluted, kissed on the head by the reverenced family elders, his eagerness to travel encouraged by auspicious birds, having had the auspicious constellation-rite performed according to the astrologer's opinion, at an auspicious moment gazing upon a full water-pot placed on a courtyard platform smeared with fresh green cow-dung, its neck encircled with garlands of white flowers, whitened with five-fingered flour-marks, with a fresh mango sprout placed at its mouth—having bowed to the family deities, accompanied by his own <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> with flowers and fruits in their hands, chanting invincibly—setting his right foot forward first, he departed from <s>Prītikūṭa</s>.

body.translated_text: Then on another day, having risen and bathed early in the morning, wearing a white silk garment, holding a rosary, having repeated the auspicious verses and <s>mantra</s> syllables for departure many times, having performed with supreme devotion a worship to the god of gods, <s>Virūpākṣa</s> (<s>Śiva</s>)—preceded by a bath in milk, abundant with fragrant flowers, incense, perfume, banners, offerings, unguents, and lamps—having made oblation to the blessed <s>Āśuśukṣaṇi</s> (the sacrificial fire), whose flickering crest-flame was sparked by the splitting of husks of fresh sesame seeds in the first offering, its right-hand flame increased by copious ghee oblations, having given such gifts as he could to Brahmins, having circumambulated the eastward-facing household cow, wearing white body-paste, white garlands, white garments, with an ear-ornament made of <s>girikarṇikā</s> flowers woven with leaf-sprouts of <s>rocana</s>-painted <s>dūrvā</s> grass-tips, with a <s>siddhārthaka</s> (white mustard seed) affixed to his topknot, by his father's younger sister—who was, like a mother, with a heart moist with affection—wearing white garments, as if

children.translated_text: Having rested with bathing and eating attended to, together with <s>Mekhalaka</s>, when only one watch of the day remained after the king had dined, observing the many camp-enclosures of renowned sovereigns, he went gradually [toward the royal gate]—darkened by lord-elephants that were like mountains assembled from every island for the purpose of bridging the ocean of conquest: some brought for the coronation-turban ceremony, some procured for mounting the war-drums, some freshly captured, some won through raids, some arrived from traders, some brought out of curiosity at first sight, some sent by elephant-avenue keepers, some presented by village headmen, some summoned for the sport of mock combat, some dispatched as diplomatic envoys, some being given away and some being seized, some being released and some being stationed at posts—resplendent with banner-cloths, loud drums, conch-shells, chowries, and body-paint, as if adorned for the day of the <s>Puṣya</s> consecration-bath; and undulating with horses—whose hooves ceaselessly struck like <s>mṛdaṅga</s> drums, as if making the royal fortune dance, as if mocking the deer-race with the foam-laughter spreading from the corners of their mouths, as if making its speed-enfeebled shanks limp, as if summoning <s>Uccaiḥśravas</s> by their joyous neighing caused by mutual jostling, as if leaping skyward in rivalry with the Sun-god's steeds, with their decorative chowrie-garlands fluttering like <s>Yakṣas</s> toward the vault of heaven; and appearing tawny elsewhere with camel herds—some sent, some being sent, some returned from dispatches—with faces adorned with strings of cowrie shells like rows of letters counting the many <s>yojanas</s> traveled, decorated as if with stars, with ear-ornaments fashioned from red chowrie-tufts cut from the twilight-glow, with ears adorned with red lotuses as if [wearing] ruddy rice-paddies, with their beautiful golden <s>ghurughuruka</s> necklace-garlands ceaselessly jingling like old <s>karañja</s> groves rattling with hundreds of dried seed-pods, with matted net-tangles of five-colored wool-threads of varied hues dangling beside their ears, tawny as monkey-cheeks;
