children.translated_text: outside, his shoulder laden with a yoga-bundle held in his left hand containing bundles of books tied with thick-fringed cords—a mendicant holding a cane seat in his other hand. The king received him who had arrived with appropriate respect. And as the mendicant sat down, he asked: 'Where is <s>Bhairavācārya</s>?' The mendicant, his mind delighted by the respectful words of the king, reported that he was staying in an empty temple in a forest on the bank of the <s>Sarasvatī</s> river near the city. And he further said: 'The venerable one honors the great lord with words of blessing.' Having said this, he drew from the yoga-bundle five silver lotuses sent by <s>Bhairavācārya</s>, studded with gems, thickly smeared with unguent, meant for the inner apartments, and presented them.

body.translated_text: Then one day, as the day kissed the setting mountain at its close, a doorkeeper approached the king who was in the inner apartments and announced: 'Your Majesty! A wandering ascetic waits at the door and says: I have come to Your Majesty at the word of <s>Bhairavācārya</s>.' The king, hearing this, said eagerly: 'Where is he? Bring him here at once, let him enter.' And the doorkeeper did so. Before long, the king saw entering a tall man, with arms reaching to his knees, thin from begging yet appearing stout due to his thick-boned limbs, with a large head, a forehead with deep folds of wrinkles arranged in tiers, hollow cheeks devoid of flesh, eyes round and tawny as drops of honey, a slightly curved nose, one ear-lobe hanging exceedingly long, rows of teeth grotesquely prominent like gourd seeds, a horse-like slack lower lip, a long face with a hanging chin, wearing a sash fashioned from an ochre yoga-band hanging from his shoulders, with an upper garment made of a red-ochre-colored rag—as if dyed with mineral pigment—tied in a knot at the center of his chest, like passion itself cut to pieces. With a staff secured at the base by a repeated wrapping of young-growth binding, tied with a bamboo-bark cord for cleaning earthen vessels, crowned by a loincloth's peak, with a begging-bowl encased in a date-palm leaf box, with a water-pot set upon a triangular stand of three wooden boards and three sticks, with sandals placed

body.text: nara-patis tu priya-jana-praṇaya-bhaṅga-kātaro dākṣiṇyam anurudhyamāno grahaṇa-lāghavaṃ ca laṅghayitum a-samartho dolāyamānena manasā sthitvā ciraṃ kathaṃ-katham apy ati-saujanya-nighnas tāni jagrāha. jagāda ca: "sarva-phala-prasava-hetuḥ Śiva-bhaktir iyaṃ no mano-ratha-dur-labhāni phalati phalāni. yenâivam asmāsu prīyate tatra-bhagavān bhuvana-gurur Bhairavācāryaḥ. śvo draṣṭāsmi bhagavantam" ity uktvā ca maskariṇaṃ vyasarjayat. anayā ca vārtayā parāṃ mudam avāpa.
body.translated_text: But the king, anxious about offending the affections of his dear ones, yet respecting propriety, and unable to transgress the ease of acceptance, stood for a long time with a wavering mind, and somehow, overcome by excessive courtesy, accepted them. And he said: 'This devotion to <s>Śiva</s> of ours, the cause of the fruition of all things, bears fruits that are difficult to obtain even in imagination. That the venerable <s>Bhairavācārya</s>, teacher of the world, should thus be pleased with us!' 'Tomorrow I shall see the venerable one,' he said, and dismissed the mendicant. And by this news he attained supreme joy.

body.text: aparedyuś ca prātar evôtthāya vājinam adhiruhya samucchrita-śvetâtapatraḥ samuddhūyamāna-dhavala-cāmara-yugalaḥ katipayair eva rāja-putraiḥ parivṛto Bhairavācāryaṃ savitāram iva śaśī draṣṭuṃ pratasthe. gatvā ca kiñ-cid antaraṃ tadīyam evâbhi-mukham āpatantam anyatamaṃ śiṣyam adrākṣrīt. aprākṣīc ca: "kva bhagavān āste?" iti. so 'kathayat: "asya jīrṇa-mātṛ-gṛhasyôtareṇa bilva-vāṭikām adhyāste" iti. gatvā ca taṃ pradeśam avatatāra turagāt. praviveśa ca bilva-vāṭikām.
body.translated_text: The next day, rising at dawn itself, mounting his horse, with a raised white parasol, with a pair of white fly-whisks being waved, accompanied by only a few princes, he set out to see <s>Bhairavācārya</s>, as the moon to see the sun. Having gone some distance, he saw one of his very own disciples coming towards him. And he asked: 'Where does the venerable one dwell?' He replied: 'He resides in a <s>bilva</s> grove to the north of this old temple of the Mother.' Going to that spot, he dismounted from his horse and entered the <s>bilva</s> grove.

body.translated_text: Then, in the midst of a great throng of mendicants, early in the morning, having bathed, having offered the eight-

body.text: Bhairavācāryas tu dūrād eva rājānaṃ dṛṣṭvā śaśinam iva jala-nidhiś cacāla. Prathamatarôtthita-śiṣya-lokaś côtthāya pratyujjagāma. Samarpita-śrī-phalôpāyanaś ca Jahnu-karṇa-samudgīryamāṇa-Gaṅgā-pravāha-hrāda-gambhīrayā girā svasti-śabdam akarot.
body.translated_text: <s>Bhairavācārya</s>, seeing the king from afar, was stirred like the ocean at the sight of the moon. His disciples having risen first, he too rose and came forward to meet him. And when the king presented him with an offering of a <s>śrī-phala</s> (sacred fruit), he pronounced the word of blessing in a voice deep as the roar of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> stream pouring forth from <s>Jahnu</s>'s ear.

body.text: nara-patir api prīti-vistāryamāṇa-dhavalimnā cakṣuṣā pratyarpayann iva bahutarāṇi puṇḍarīka-vanāni lalāṭa-paṭṭa-paryastena côd-aṃśunā śikhā-maṇinā Mahêśvara-prasādam iva tṛtīya-nayanôdgamena prakāśayann āvarjita-karṇa-pallava-palāyamāna-madhu-karaḥ Śiva-sevā-samunmūlitâśeṣa-pāpa-lava-mucyamāna iva dūrād avanataḥ praṇāmam abhinavaṃ cakāra. ācāryo 'pi: "āgaccha. atrôpaviśa" iti śārdūla-carmâtmīyam adarśayat. upadarśita-praśrayas tu rājā matta-haṃsa-kala-gadgada-svara-subhagāṃ madhu-rasamayīṃ mahā-nadīm iva pravartayan vācaṃ vyājahāra: "bhagavan! nârhasi mām anya-nṛpa-skhalitaiḥ khalī-kartum. a-śeṣa-rāja-kopêkṣitāyā hata-lakṣmyāḥ khalv ayaṃ śīlâparādho draviṇa-daurātmyaṃ vā yad evam ācarati mayi guruḥ. a-bhūmir ayam upacārāṇām. alam ati-yantraṇayā. dūra-sthito 'pi mano-ratha-śiṣyo 'yaṃ jano bhavatām. mānanīyaṃ ca guruvan nôllaṅghanam arhati guror āsanam. āsatāṃ ca bhavanta evâtra" iti vyāhṛtyā parijanôpanīte vāsasi niṣasāda. Bhairavācāryo 'pi prītyân-atikramaṇīyaṃ nṛpa-vacanam anuvartamānaḥ pūrvavat tad eva vyāghrâjinam abhajata.
body.translated_text: The king too, as if returning many groves of white lotuses with his gaze whose whiteness expanded with delight, revealing the grace of <s>Maheśvara</s> as if by the emergence of a third eye through the radiant crest-jewel cast upon the panel of his forehead, with bees fleeing from his inclined ear-tendrils, bowing low from afar — as if being released from every particle of sin uprooted by devotion to <s>Śiva</s> — made a fresh salutation. The <s>Ācārya</s> too [said]: 'Come. Sit here' — and showed [him] his own tiger-skin [seat]. But the king, having displayed his humility, releasing speech beautiful as [the cry of] an intoxicated goose, sweet in its stammering tone, flowing like a great river made of honey, said: 'Blessed one! You should not make me a butt [of jest] by the stumbling of other kings. It is indeed the fault of character — or the wickedness of wealth — of that ill-fated Fortune, who is regarded with anger by all kings, that the <s>Guru</s> thus conducts himself toward me. This is not the ground for [such] courtesies. Enough of this excessive constraint! Even while standing far away, this person is a disciple in aspiration to your reverences. And the seat of the <s>Guru</s>, O venerable one, is to be honored, not transgressed. Let your reverences alone sit here.' Having said this, he sat upon a garment brought by an attendant. And the <s>Bhairavācārya</s>, following the king's words — which were not to be transgressed on account of his affection — resumed the same tiger-skin as before.

body.text: āsīne ca sa-rājake parijane śiṣya-jane ca samucitam ardhyâ-

children.text: -dikaṃ cakre. krameṇa ca nṛpa-mādhurya-hṛtântaḥ-karaṇaḥ śaśi-kara-nikara-vimalā daśa-nadī-dhitīḥ sphurantīḥ Śiva-bhaktīr iva sākṣād draśayann uvāca: "tāta! ati-namratâiva te kathayati guṇānāṃ gauravam. sakala-saṃpat-pātram asi. vibhavânurūpās tu pratipattayaḥ. janmanaḥ prabhaty a-datta-dṛṣṭir evâsmi svāpateyeṣu. yataḥ sakala-doṣa-kalāpânalêndhanair dhanair a-vikrītaṃ kva-cic charīrakam asti. bhaikṣa-rakṣitāḥ santi prāṇāḥ. dur-gṛhītāni kati-cid vidyante vidyâkṣarāṇi. bhagavac Chiva-bhaṭṭāraka-pāda-sevayā samupārjitāḥ kiyatyo 'pi saṃnihitāḥ puṇya-kaṇikāḥ. svī-kriyatāṃ yad atrôpayogârham. pratanu-guṇa-grāhyāṇi kusumānîva hi bhavanti satāṃ manāṃsi. api ca, vidvat-saṃmatāḥ śrūyamāṇā api sādhavaḥ śabdā iva sudhīre 'pi hi manasi yaśāṃsi kurvanti. vivaraṃ viśataḥ kutūhalasya phena-dhavalaiḥ srotobhir ivâpahriyamāṇo guṇa-gaṇair ānīto 'smi kalyāṇinā" iti.
children.translated_text: And gradually, his inner heart won over by the king's sweetness, as if directly displaying the devotions to <s>Śiva</s> — flashing like ten rivers of moonbeam-pure radiance — he said: 'Dear child! Your very great humility itself declares the weightiness of your virtues. You are the vessel of all prosperity. But [your] recognitions [of others' worth] are proportionate to [your] magnificence. From birth onward I have never cast a glance upon my own possessions. For somewhere there exists a body not sold for wealth — which is fuel for the fire of the entire aggregate of faults. My life has been sustained by alms. A few letters of learning have been [barely] grasped. At the lotus-feet of the blessed Lord <s>Śiva-bhaṭṭāraka</s>...'

body.translated_text: And when the king, his retinue, and the disciples had taken their seats, he performed the appropriate [rites] beginning with the <s>arghya</s> (offering of respect).

body.text: rājā tu taṃ pratyavādīt: "bhagavan! Anurakteṣv api śarīrâdiṣu sādhūnāṃ svāmina eva praṇayinaḥ. yuṣmad-darśanād upārjitam eva câ-parimitaṃ kuśala-jātam. anenâivâgamanena spṛhaṇīyaṃ padam āropito 'smi guruṇā" iti vividhābhiś ca kathābhiś ciraṃ sthitvā gṛham agāt.
body.translated_text: The king replied to him: 'Blessed one! Even for holy men who are attached to [their] body and the like, the masters alone are [their true] intimates. And from the sight of your reverences, an unlimited accumulation of merit has been earned. By this very arrival, I have been elevated by the <s>Guru</s> to an enviable station.' And having remained for a long time in various conversations, he went home.

body.text: anyasmin divase Bhairavācāryo 'pi rājānaṃ draṣṭuṃ yayau. tasmai ca rājā sântaḥ-puraṃ sa-parijanaṃ sa-koṣam ātmānaṃ niveditavān. sa ca vihasyôvāca: "tāta! kva vibhavāḥ, kva ca vayaṃ vana-vardhitāḥ?

children.text: dhanôṣmaṇā mlāyaty alaṃ latêva manasvitā. Khadyotānām ivâsmākam iyam a-parôpatāpinī rājate tejasvitā. bhavādṛśā eva bhājanaṃ bhūteḥ" iti sthitvā ca kaṃ-cit kālaṃ jagāma.
children.translated_text: Nobility withers from the heat of wealth, as a creeper withers. Like that of fireflies, this splendor of ours shines without causing heat to others. Persons like yourself alone are the [proper] vessels of prosperity.' And having remained for some time, he departed.

body.translated_text: On another day, the <s>Bhairavācārya</s> too went to see the king. And the king offered him his entire self — with the inner palace, with the retinue, with the treasury. And he, laughing, said: 'Dear child! What [connection is there between] riches and us, who have been reared in the forest?

body.text: parivrāṭ tenâiva krameṇa pañca pañca rājatāni puṇḍarīkāṇy upāyanī-cakāra. ekadā tu śveta-karpaṭâvṛtaṃ kim apy ādāya prāviśat. upaviśya ca pūrvavat sthitvā muhūrtam abravīt: "mahā-bhāga! bhavantam āha bhagavān yathâsmac-chiṣyaḥ Pātālasvāmi-nāmā brāhmaṇaḥ. tena brahma-rākṣasa-hastād apahṛto mahâsir Aṭṭahāsa-nāmā. so 'yaṃ bhavad-bhuja-yogyo gṛhyatām" ity abhidhāyâpahṛta-karpaṭâvacchādanāt parivārād ācakarṣa śarad-gagana-talam iva piṇḍatāṃ nītam, kālindī-pravāham iva stambhita-jalam, nandaka-jigīṣayā kṛṣṇa-kopitaṃ kāliyam iva kṛpāṇatāṃ gatam, loka-vināśāya prakāśita-dhārā-sāraṃ pralaya-kāla-megha-khaṇḍam iva nabhas-talāt patitam, dṛśyamāna-vikaṭa-danta-maṇḍalaṃ hāsam iva hiṃsāyāḥ, hari-bāhu-daṇḍam iva kṛta-dṛḍha-muṣṭi-graham, sakala-bhuvana-jīvitâpaharaṇa-kṣameṇa kāla-kūṭenêva nirmitam, kṛtânta-kopânala-taptenêvâyasā ghaṭitam, ati-tīkṣṇatayā pavana-sparśenâpi ruṣêva kvaṇantam maṇi-sabhā-kuṭṭima-patat-pratibimba-cchadmanâtmānam api dvidhêva pāṭayantam, ari-śiraś-cheda-lagnaiḥ kacair iva kiraṇaiḥ karālita-dhāram, muhur-muhus taḍid-unmeṣa-taralaiḥ prabhā-cakra-cchuritair jarjaritâtapam, khaṇḍaśaś chindantam iva divasam, kaṭâkṣam iva kāla-rātreḥ, karṇôtpalam iva kālasya, oṃ-kāram iva krauryasya alaṃ-kāram ahaṃ-kārasya, kula-mitraṃ kopasya, dehaṃ darpasya,

children.text: su-sahāyaṃ sāhasasya, apatyaṃ mṛtyoḥ, āgamana-mārgaṃ lakṣmyāḥ, nirgamana-mārgaṃ kīrteḥ, kṛpāṇam.
children.translated_text: a fine companion of daring, the offspring of Death, the approach-path of Fortune, the exit-path of Fame — [such was] the sword.

body.translated_text: The wandering ascetic, in that same manner, gradually offered as gifts five [and then another] five silver lotuses. But one day, carrying something covered in a white cloth, he entered. And having sat down and remained a moment as before, he said: 'O greatly fortunate one! The blessed one addresses you thus: A <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> named <s>Pātālasvāmī</s>, a disciple of ours, seized from the hand of a <s>Brahma-rākṣasa</s> (Brahmin-demon) a great sword named <s>Aṭṭahāsa</s> (Loud-Laughter). It is worthy of your arm — accept it!' Having said this, he drew from the attendant whose cloth-covering had been removed [a sword] — as if the autumn sky had been condensed into a mass, as if the current of the <s>Kālindī</s> (Yamunā) river had been arrested in its flow, as if eager to rival the [divine sword] <s>Nandaka</s>...

body.text: avani-patis tu taṃ gṛhītvā kareṇâyudha-prītyā pratimā-nibhenâliṅgann iva su-ciraṃ dadarśa. saṃdideśa ca: "vaktavyo bhagavān para-dravya-grahaṇâvajñā-dur-vidagdham api hi me mano yuṣmad-viṣaye na śaknoti vacana-vyatikrama-vyabhicāram ācaritum" iti. parivrāṭ tu gṛhīte tasmin parituṣṭaḥ "svasti bhavate. sādhayāmaḥ" ity uktvā nirayāsīt. nṛpaś ca prakṛtyā vīra-rasânurāgī tena kṛpāṇenâmanyata kara-tala-vartinīṃ medinīm.
body.translated_text: The king, having received it, gazed upon it for a long time — clasping [it] with his hand out of love for the weapon, as if embracing a statue. And he sent a message: 'Tell the blessed one: although my mind is ill-trained in the arrogance of [refusing] other people's possessions, in the domain of your reverences it is unable to commit the offense of transgressing [your] words.' The wandering ascetic, gratified when it was accepted, said 'Well-being to you! We shall accomplish [our purpose]' and departed. And the king, who was by nature devoted to the <s>vīra rasa</s> (heroic sentiment), considered the earth to be in the palm of his hand by virtue of that sword.

body.text: atha vrajatsu divaseṣv ekadā Bhairavācāryo rājānam upahvare sôpagraham avādīt: "tāta! svârthâlasāḥ parôpakāra-dakṣāś ca prakṛtayo bhavanti bhavyānām. bhavâdṛśāṃ cârthi-darśanaṃ mahôtsavaḥ praṇayanam ārādhanam artha-grahaṇam upakāraḥ. bhūmir asi sarva-loka-mano-rathānām. yenābhidhīyase. śrūyatām. bhagavato mahā-kāla-hṛdaya-nāmno mahā-mantrasya kṛṣṇa-srag-ambarânulepanenâkalpena kalpa-kathitena mahā-śmaśāne japa-koṭyā kṛta-pūrva-sevo 'smi. tasya ca vetāla-sādhanâvasānā siddhiḥ. a-sahāyaiś ca sā dur-avāpā. tvaṃ câlam asmai karmaṇe. tvayi ca gṛhīta-bhare bhaviṣyanty a-pare sahāyās trayaḥ ekaḥ sa evâsmākaṃ Ṭīṭibha-nāmā bāla-mitraṃ maskarī yo bhavantam upatiṣṭhate. dvitīyaḥ sa Pātālasvāmī. a-paro mac-chiṣya eva Karṇatāla-nāmā drāviḍaḥ. yadi sādhu manyase tato nīyatām ayaṃ diṅ-nāga-hasta-dīrgho gṛhītÂṭṭahāso niśām ekām eka-diṅ-mukhârgalatāṃ bāhuḥ." iti kṛta-vacasi ca tasminn andhakāra-praviṣṭa iva dṛṣṭa-prakāśaḥ prāptôpakārâvakāśaḥ pramuditenântar-ātmanā narêndraḥ samabhāṣata: "bhagavan! param anugṛhīto 'smy anena śiṣya-jana-sāmānyena nideśena kṛta-parigraham ivâtmānam evâimi" iti. nananda ca tena

children.text: narêndra-vyāhṛtena Bhairavācāryaḥ. cakāra ca saṃketam: "asyām evâgāminyām asita-pakṣa-catur-daśī-kṣapāyām iyatyāṃ velāyām amuṣmin mahā-śmaśāna-samīpa-bhāji śūnyâyatane śastra-dvitīyenâyuṣmatā draṣṭavyā vayam" iti.
children.translated_text: The <s>Bhairavācārya</s> [was gratified] by the king's words. And he made an appointment: 'On this very coming fourteenth night of the dark fortnight, at such-and-such an hour, in a certain deserted temple near the great cremation ground, Your Highness should see me, accompanied only by a sword.'

body.translated_text: Now, as days passed, one day the <s>Bhairavācārya</s> addressed the king privately with a request: 'Dear child! The dispositions of the noble are [naturally] sluggish in self-interest and skilled in benefiting others. For persons like you, the sight of a supplicant is a great festival; affection is worship; receiving a gift is a favor. You are the ground of all the world's desires — therefore I address you. Listen! I have previously accomplished the worship of the great <s>mantra</s> called <s>Mahākāla-hṛdaya</s> (Heart of Great Time), with dark garlands, garments, and ointment as the prescribed attire, in a great cremation-ground, through ten million repetitions of <s>japa</s>. And its <s>siddhi</s> (supernatural attainment) culminates in the mastery of a <s>vetāla</s> (animated corpse). But that [ritual] is not to be accomplished alone...'

body.text: athâtikrānteṣv ahaḥsu prāptāyāṃ ca tasyām eva kṛṣṇa-catur-daśyāṃ śaivena vidhinā dīkṣitaḥ kṣitipo niyamavān abhūt. kṛtâdhivāsaṃ ca saṃpādita-gandha-dhūpa-mālyâdi-pūjaṃ khaḍgam Aṭṭahāsam akarot. tataḥ pariṇate divase kenâpi karma-sādhanāya kṛta-rudhira-bali-vidhānāsv iva lohitâyamānāsu dikṣu, rudhira-bali-lampaṭāsu ca vetāla-jihvāsv iva lambamānāsu ca ravi-dīdhitiṣu, narêndrânurāgeṇa gṛhītâp-ara-diśi svayam iva dik-pālatāṃ cikīrṣati savitari, yātudhānīṣv iva vardhamānāsu taru-cchāyāsu, pātāla-tala-vāsiṣu vighnāya dānaveṣv ivôttiṣṭhatsu tamo-maṇḍaleṣu, nabhasi puñjī-bhavati, raudraṃ karma didṛkṣamāṇā iva nakṣatra-gaṇe vigāḍhāyāṃ śarvaryām, supta-jane niḥ-śabdas timite niśīthe, rājā sântaḥ-puraṃ parijanaṃ vañcayitvā vāma-kara-sphurat-sarur dakṣiṇa-kareṇôtkhātaṃ khaḍgam Aṭṭahāsam ādāya visarpatā ca khaḍga-prabhā-paṭalena nīlâṃśuka-paṭenêva darśana-bhayād avaguṇṭhita-nikhila-gātra-yaṣṭir an-ādiṣṭayâpy anugamyamāno rāja-lakṣmyā pṛṣṭhataḥ parimala-lagna-madhu-kara-veṇi-vyājena keśeṣv iva karma-siddhim ākarṣann ekākī nagarān niragāt. agāc ca tam uddeśam.
body.translated_text: Then, when [several] days had passed and that very dark fourteenth [night] had arrived, the king, initiated according to the <s>Śaiva</s> rite, took up his observances. And he consecrated the sword <s>Aṭṭahāsa</s> by the preparatory ritual, having performed worship with fragrance, incense, garlands, and the like. Then, when the day had declined — the directions reddening as if by someone performing a blood-offering ritual for the accomplishment of a [sorcerous] rite, the rays of the sun hanging down like the tongues of <s>vetālas</s> greedy for blood-offerings, the sun itself seeming to desire guardianship of a direction as if having grasped the western quarter out of devotion to the king, the shadows of trees growing like she-demons (<s>yātudhānīs</s>), [and the scene appearing as if the entrance to] the netherworld...

body.text: atha pratyupajagmus te trayo 'pi Drauṇi-Kṛpa-Kṛtavarmāṇa iva sauptike saṃnaddhāḥ snātāḥ sragviṇo gṛhīta-vikaṭa-veṣāḥ, kusuma-śekhara-saṃcāribhiḥ kriyamāṇa-mantra-śikhā-bandhā iva guñjadbhiḥ ṣaṭ-caraṇair uṣṇīṣa-paṭṭakāṃl lalāṭa-madhya-ghaṭita-vikaṭa-svastikā-granthīn-mahā-mudrā-bandhān iva dhārayanto mūrdhabhiḥ eka-śravaṇa-vivara-vitata-vimala-danta-patra-prabhā-loka-lepa-dhavalita-ka-

children.text: -polair mukhair āpibanta iva niśā-carâpacaya-cikīrṣayā śārvaram andhakāram, itara-karṇâvalambināṃ ratna-kuṇḍalānām acchâcchayā rucā go-rocanayêva mantra-parijaptayā samālabdhâṅgāḥ, sva-pratibimba-garbhān karma-siddhaye datta-puruṣôpahārān ivôllāsayanto niśitān nistriṃśān, nistriṃśâṃśu-saṃtāna-sīmantita-timirām ātmīyâtmīya-dig-vibhāga-saṃrakṣaṇāya tridhêva tri-yāmāṃ pāṭayantaḥ sârdha-candraiḥ kala-dhauta-budbudâvali-tarala-tārā-gaṇair niśāyā iva paruṣâsi-dhārā-nikṛttaiḥ khaṇḍair gṛhītaiś carma-phalakair a-kāṇḍa-śarvarīm a-parāṃ ghaṭayantaḥ, kāñcana-śṛṅkhalā-kalāpa-niyamita-nibiḍa-niṣpravāṇayaḥ, baddhâsi-dhenavaḥ, Ṭīṭibha-Karṇatāla-Pātālasvāmino niveditavantaś-câtmānam.
children.translated_text: with their cheeks whitened by the luminous coating of the radiance of spotless ivory earrings spread over one ear-cavity — [they seemed with] their faces to be drinking the nocturnal darkness out of desire to diminish the night-roamers; their limbs anointed as if with mantra-consecrated cow-bile, by the clear, amber radiance of the jeweled earrings hanging from the other ear; brandishing sharp swords — which carried their own reflections within [them] as if men offered as sacrifice for the accomplishment of the rite; with the darkness parted by the streams of sword-rays as if splitting the night in three — each for the protection of his own directional quarter; [holding] shields grasped [in the other hand] — with half-moon [marks], with bubbling rows of gilded stars trembling [upon them] — as if [they were] pieces of the night cruelly severed by harsh sword-edges.

body.translated_text: Then those three [companions] returned — armed like <s>Drauṇi</s> (<s>Aśvatthāman</s>), <s>Kṛpa</s>, and <s>Kṛtavarman</s> [were] at the night-raid — bathed, garlanded, having assumed fierce attire; wearing on their heads — with bees buzzing among their flower-garlands as if performing the tying of the mantra-topknot — turban-bands with fierce <s>svastika</s>-knots tied at the center of the forehead, [looking] like the great <s>mudrā</s>-seals;

body.text: avani-patis tu: "ko 'tra kaḥ?" iti trīn apṛcchat. ācacakṣire ca svaṃ svaṃ nāma trayo 'pi te. Tair eva cânugamyamāno jagāma tāṃ bali-dīpâloka-jarjarita-guggulu-dhūpa-dhūma-gṛhyamāṇa-dig-vibhāgatayā vikṣipyamāṇa-rakṣā-sarṣapârdha-dagdhândhakāra-palāyamāna-niśām iva samupakalpita-sarvôpakaraṇāṃ niḥ-śabdāṃ ca gambhīrāṃ ca bhīṣaṇāṃ ca sādhana-bhūmim.
body.translated_text: The king asked: 'Who is there?' — to [each of] the three. And all three announced their respective names. Accompanied by them, he went to that ground of [ritual] accomplishment — where the night seemed to be fleeing from the half-burnt darkness, with protective mustard-seeds being scattered, the directions being perceived through the smoke of guggulu incense burning in the light of offering-lamps — [a place] with all implements arranged, silent, deep, and terrifying.

body.text: tasyāṃ ca kumuda-dhūli-dhavalena bhasmanā likhitasya mahato maṇḍalasya madhye sthitaṃ dīptatara-tejaḥ-prasaram, pṛthu-pariveṣa-parikṣiptam iva śarat-savitāram, mathyamāna-kṣīrôdâvarta-vartinam iva mandaram, rakta-candanânulepino rakta-srag-ambarâbharaṇasyôttāna-śayasya śavasyôrasy upaviśya jāta-jāta-vedasi mukha-kuhare prārabdhâgni-kāryam, kṛṣṇôṣṇīṣam,

children.text: kṛṣṇâṅga-rāgam, kṛṣṇa-pratisaram, kṛṣṇa-vāsasam, kṛṣṇa-tilâhuti-nibhena vidyā-dharatva-tṛṣṇayā mānuṣa-nirmāṇa-kāraṇa-kāluṣya-paramâṇūn iva kṣayam upanayantam, āhuti-dāna-paryastābhiḥ preta-mukha-sparśa-dūṣitaṃ prakṣālayantam ivâśuśukṣaṇiṃ kara-nakha-dīdhitibhiḥ, dhūmâlohitena cakṣuṣā kṣatajâhutim iva huta-bhuji pātayantam, īṣad-vivṛtâdhara-puṭa-prakaṭita-sita-daśana-śikhareṇa dṛśyamāna-mūrta-mantrâkṣara-paṅktinêva mukhena kim api japantam, homa-śrama-sveda-salila-pratibimbitābhir āsanna-dīpikābhir dahantam iva karma-siddhaye sarvâvayavān, aṃsâvalambinā bahu-guṇena vidyā-rājenêva brahma-sūtraṇa parigṛhītaṃ Bhairavācāryam apaśyat. upasṛtya câkaron namas-kāram. abhinanditaś ca tena sva-vyāpāram anvatiṣṭhat.
children.translated_text: wearing black body-paint, a black wrist-cord, and black garments, as if through oblations resembling black sesame offerings, out of his thirst for <s>Vidyādhara</s>-hood, he was reducing to extinction the very atoms of impurity that caused his human form; as if with the radiance of his fingernails, thrown about from making oblations, he was cleansing the fire-altar defiled by contact with the mouths of ghosts; with eyes reddened by smoke, as if pouring an oblation of blood into the sacred fire; muttering something with his mouth, its slightly parted lower lip revealing the peaks of white teeth as if displaying visible rows of embodied <s>mantra</s>-syllables; as if burning all his limbs for the success of the rite with nearby lamps reflected in the perspiration from the exertion of the <s>homa</s> (fire-oblation); he saw <s>Bhairavācārya</s>, enveloped by a many-stranded sacred thread hanging from his shoulder, as if by the king of <s>vidyās</s> (sacred knowledge) himself. Approaching, he made obeisance, and welcomed by him, he carried on with his own appointed task.

body.translated_text: And in the center of a great <s>maṇḍala</s> (ritual diagram) drawn with ash white as night-lily dust, seated upon the chest of a corpse lying face-up, anointed with red sandalwood, wearing red garlands, garments, and ornaments — [sat the Ācārya], his radiance blazing all the more brightly, like the autumn sun encircled by a broad halo, like <s>Mandara</s> [mountain] revolving in the whirlpool of the churned milk-ocean — having begun the fire-rite in the cave of [the corpse's] mouth where the fire had [just been] kindled, wearing a black turban,

body.text: atrântare Pātālasvāmī śātakratavīm āśām aṅgī-cakāra, Karṇatālaḥ kauberīṃ parivrāṭ prācetasīm. rājā tu traiśaṅkavena jyotiṣâṅkitāṃ kakubham alaṃ-kṛtavān.
body.translated_text: Meanwhile, <s>Pātālasvāmī</s> took charge of the northeastern direction, <s>Karṇatāla</s> the northern, the ascetic the western, and the king adorned the direction marked by the constellation of <s>Triśaṅku</s>.

body.translated_text: Then, from hearing this unprecedented insult, with limbs that, though unwounded by weapons, under the pretense of perspiration of indignation seemed to vomit forth the sword-edge-water drunk in many battles, making himself feel lighter for battle as if unburdened of the mass of arrowhead-shafts from a hundred discharged arrows through what resembled horripilation, even <s>Aṭṭahāsa</s> (his sword) reflecting the host of stars seeming to laugh with contempt as it clearly displayed a row of white teeth, declaring his fortitude, blocking the ten directions with the circle of rays from his fingernails whirling as he tied his girdle, as if with a binding circle of <s>Nāga</s>-subduing <s>mantras</s> out of fear that the serpent might escape, the lord of men spoke with disdain: "Hey, crow-bellied crow! Are you not ashamed to demand tribute while I, the royal swan, stand here? But what use are these harsh words? Valor resides in the arm, not in speech. Take up your weapon. This is beneath you—my arm is not trained to strike those who have not taken up weapons." The <s>Nāga</s>, however, with even greater disdain said: "Come, what need of weapons? With my very arms I shall break your pride," and slapped his arms. The king too, ashamed to defeat an unarmed foe with a weapon in battle, cast aside <s>Aṭṭahāsa</s> the sword with its leather shield and bound it to his half-thigh, girding himself for wrestling. And the two fought, sprinkled with drops of blood from arms split by merciless blows, filling the world with sound, as it were, with arm-clubs falling like stone pillars. Before long the king threw the serpent to the ground, seized him by the hair, and drew out <s>Aṭṭahāsa</s> to cut off his head. But he saw among the garlands of his cross-belt the sacred thread. Withdrawing his weapon, he spoke: "Wretch! This is the seed that sustains your wickedness, for it is because of it that you boldly commit outrages." Saying this, he released him. And she spoke again: "By this excellence of courage and your extraordinary devotion to Lord <s>Śiva Bhaṭṭāraka</s>, you shall become on earth the founder of a great royal dynasty, like a third luminary beside the sun and moon—uninterrupted, growing in greatness day by day, consisting chiefly of men who are pure, noble, venerable, truthful, generous, valiant, and mighty. At the end of these words, she vanished.

Śrīkaṇṭho 'pi: "rājan! parākrama-krītaḥ kartavyeṣu niyogenânugrāhyo grāhita-vinayo 'yaṃ janaḥ" ity abhidhāya rājânumoditas tad eva bhūyo bhū-vivaraṃ viveśa.

children.text: nara-patis tu kṣīṇa-bhūyiṣṭhāyāṃ kṣapāyāṃ, pravātum ārabdhe prabudhyamāna-kamalinī-niḥśvāsa-surabhau, vana-devatā-kucâṃśukâpaharaṇa-parihāsa-svedinîva sâvaśyāya-śīkare parimalâkṛṣṭa-madhukṛti kumuda-nidrā-vāhini niśā-pariṇati-jaḍe tuṣāra-leśini vanânile, viraha-vidhura-cakra-vāka-cakra-niḥśvasita-saṃtāpitāyām ivâ-para-jalanidhim avatarantyāṃ tri-yāmāyāṃ, sākṣād-āgata-Lakṣmī-vilokana-kutūhalinīṣv iva samunmīlantīṣu nalinīṣu, unnidra-pakṣiṇi kṣarati kusuma-visaram iva tuhina-kaṇa-nikaraṃ mṛdu-pavana-lāsita-late kānane, kamala-lakṣmī-prabodha-maṅgala-śaṅkheṣv iva rasatsv antar-baddha-dhvanan-madhukareṣu mukulāyamāneṣu, kumudeṣu, ujjihāna-ravi-ratha-vāji-visṛṣṭaiḥ protha-paṭu-pavanaiḥ protsāyamāṇāsv iva vāruṇyāṃ kakubhi puñjī-bhavantīṣu śyāmā-latā-kalikāsu tārakāsu, mandara-śikharâśrayiṇi mandânila-lulita-kalpa-latā-vana-kusuma-dhūli-vicchurita iva dhūsarī-bhavati sapta-rṣi-maṇḍale, sura-vāraṇâṅkuśa iva cyute galati tārāmaye mṛge trīn api Ṭīṭibhâdīn gṛhītvā nāga-yuddha-vyatikara-malīmasāni śucini vana-vāpī-payasi prakṣālyâṅgāni nagaraṃ viveśa. anyasminn ahani teṣām ātma-śarīrân-antaraṃ snāna-bhojanāc chādanâdinā prītim akarot.
children.translated_text: Now the king, when the night was mostly spent — when the breeze began to blow, fragrant with the exhalations of awakening lotus-groves; when the forest wind was cool with dew-drops as though sweating from the embarrassment of stealing the bodice-cloths of forest-deities, perfume-attracting bees [hovering near]; when it bore the drowsiness of night-lotuses and carried specks of frost; when the three-watch night was descending into the western ocean, as if heated by the sighing of love-sick <s>cakravāka</s>-bird circles; when the lotus-groves were opening as if with curiosity to behold <s>Lakṣmī</s> (the goddess of fortune) arriving in person; when the forest was swaying its creeper-tips in the gentle wind, scattering what seemed a rain of flowers but was a shower of dew-drops, while the birds awoke — taking all three, <s>Ṭīṭibha</s> and the others, and having washed their limbs soiled from the encounter of the <s>nāga</s>-battle in the pure water of a forest pool, he entered the city. On another day, he showed his affection for them — which was inseparable from his own body — through bathing, feeding, clothing, and so forth.

body.translated_text: Thus addressed by the king, the one desiring to depart, having firmly embraced <s>Ṭīṭibha</s> and the others, gazing at the lord of the earth with tear-filled eyes streaming drops of dew like a grove of blue lotuses, again said to the king: 'Father! I say "I am going" — that is not fitting for affection. "You are my very life-breath" — that is merely a repetition. "Take this body" — that is making a distinction, hence out of place. "We have been purchased sesame by sesame" — that is not proportionate to the service rendered. "You are a kinsman" — that is as if making distance. "My heart is lodged in you" — that is not perceptible. "This accomplishment of mine imitates separation from you" — that is unbelievable. "Your service to us is causeless" — that is a paraphrase. "We should be remembered" — that is a command. In every respect, this person, cruel for his own ends, should be placed in mind among conversations with the ungrateful and tales of the wicked.' Having spoken thus, he flew up into the sky — his garland broken by the velocity, the shower of scattered pearls from its snapping striking the hosts of stars above. And parting the clusters of planets, he went to a dwelling befitting a <s>siddha</s> (accomplished being). <s>Śrīkaṇṭha</s> too, saying: 'O king! This person, purchased by valor, should be favored through employment in duties, and has been taught discipline' — thus speaking and receiving the king's approval, entered once more that same opening in the earth.

body.translated_text: And after the passing of some days, the <s>parivrāj</s> (wandering ascetic), though restrained by the king, departed for the forest. <s>Pātālasvāmin</s> and <s>Karṇatāla</s>, however, devoted to him through their love of valor, continued to serve that very [king]. body.text: atha tasmāt Puṣpabhūter dvija-vara-svêcchā-gṛhīta-koṣo nābhi-padma iva puṇḍarīkêkṣaṇāt, Lakṣmī-puraḥ-saro ratna-saṃcaya iva ratnâkarāt, guru-budha-kavi-kalābhṛt-tejasvi-bhū-nandana-prāyo graha-gaṇa ivôdaya-sthānāt mahā-bhāra-vāhana-yogyaḥ sāgara iva sagara-prabhāvāt, dur-jaya-bala-sa-nātho hari-vaṃśa iva śūrān nirjagāma rāja-vaṃśaḥ. Yasmād a-vinaṣṭa-dharma-dhavalāḥ prajā-sargā iva kṛta-mukhāt, pratāpâkrānta-bhuvanāḥ kiraṇā iva tejo-nidheḥ, vigraha-vyāpti-diṅ-mukhā giraya iva bhūbhṛt-pravarāt, dharaṇi-dhāraṇa-

children.text: -kṣamā dig-gajā iva brahma-karāt, udadhīn pātum udyatā jala-dharā iva ghanâgamāt, icchā-phala-dāyinaḥ kalpa-tarava iva nandanāt, sarva-bhūtâśrayā viśva-rūpa-prakārā iva śrīdharād ajāyanta rājānaḥ.
children.translated_text: ready to drink up the oceans, like rain-clouds from the monsoon-season; granting the desired fruit, like wish-fulfilling trees from <s>Nandana</s> (Indra's paradise); the refuge of all beings, like the varied forms of the universal form from <s>Śrīdhara</s> (Viṣṇu) — kings were born.

body.translated_text: Now, from that <s>Puṣpabhūti</s> — a royal lineage emerged: [like] a lotus from a navel-lotus of the lotus-eyed one, whose treasury was seized at will by the best of <s>brāhmaṇas</s>; like a collection of jewels, the forerunner of <s>Lakṣmī</s>, from the jewel-ocean; mostly composed of the brilliance of teachers, sages, poets, digit-bearers, luminaries, and earth-sons — like the host of planets from their place of rising; fit for bearing a great burden like the ocean from the power of <s>Sagara</s>; invincible in strength, like the dynasty of <s>Hari</s> (Viṣṇu) from which heroes emerged. From which [lineage] — kings were born: their subjects untainted in their white <s>dharma</s>, like the created orders from <s>Brahmā</s>'s mouth; their valor pervading the world, like rays from a treasury of brilliance; their physical forms extending in all directions of war, like mountains from the greatest of mountain-kings; capable of bearing the earth, like the directional elephants from the hand of <s>Brahmā</s>;

body.text: teṣu câivam utpadyamāneṣu krameṇôdapādi Hūṇa-hariṇa-kesarī sindhu-rāja-jvaro gūrjara-prajā-garo gāndhārâdipa-gandha-dvipa-kūṭa-pākalo lāṭa-pāṭava-pāṭaccaro mālava-lakṣmī-latā-paraśuḥ pratāpa-śīla iti prathitâ-para-nāmā Prabhākaravardhano nāma rājâdhirājaḥ. yo rājyâṅga-saṅgīny abhiṣicyamāna eva malānîva mumoca dhanāni. yaḥ parakīyenâpi kātara-vallabhena raṇa-mukhe tṛṇenêva dhṛtenâlajjata jīvitena. yaḥ kara-dhṛta-dhautâsi-pratibimbitenâtmanâpy adūyata samitiṣu sahāyena ripūṇāṃ puraḥ pradhaneṣu dhanuṣâpi namatā yo mānī mānasenâkhidyata. yaś cântar-gatâ-parimita-ripu-śastra-śalya-śaṅku-kīlatām iva niś-calām uvāha rāja-lakṣmīm. yaś ca sarvāsu dikṣu samī-kṛta-taṭâvaṭa-viṭapâṭavī-taru-tṛṇa-gulma-valmīka-giri-gahanair daṇḍa-yātrā-pathaiḥ pṛthubhir bhṛtyôpayogāya vyabhajatêva vasudhāṃ bahudhā. yaṃ câlabdha-yuddha-dohadam ātmīyo 'pi sakala-ripu-samutsārakaḥ parakīya iva tatāpa pratāpaḥ. yasya ca vahnimayo hṛdayeṣu,

children.text: jalamayo locana-puṭeṣu, mārutamayo niḥśvasiteṣu, kṣamāmayo 'ṅgeṣu, ākāśamayaḥ śūnyatāyāṃ, pañca-mahā-bhūtamayo mūrta ivâdṛśyata nihata-pratisāmantântaḥ-pureṣu pratāpaḥ. yasya câsanneṣu bhṛtya-ratneṣu pratibimbatêva tulya-rūpā samalakṣyata lakṣmīḥ. tathā ca yasya pratāpâgninā bhūtiḥ, śauryôṣmaṇā siddhiḥ, asi-dhārā-jalena vaṃśa-vṛddhiḥ, śastra-vraṇa-mukhaiḥ puruṣa-kārôktiḥ, dhanur-guṇa-kiṇena kara-gṛhītir abhavat. yaś ca vairam upāyanaṃ vigraham anugrahaṃ samarâgamaṃ mahôtsavaṃ śatruṃ nidhi-darśanam ari-bāhulyam abhyudayam āhavâhvānaṃ vara-pradānam avaskanda-pātaṃ diṣṭa-vṛddhiṃ śastra-prahāra-patanaṃ vasu-dhārā-rasam amanyata. yasmiṃś ca rājani nir-antarair yūpa-nikarair aṅkuritam iva kṛta-yugena, diṅ-mukha-visarpibhir adhvara-dhūmaiḥ palāyitam iva kalinā, sa-sudhaiḥ surâlayair avatīrṇām iva svargeṇa, surâlaya-śikharôddhūyamānair dhavala-dhvajaiḥ pallavitam iva dharmeṇa, bahir-uparacita-vikaṭa-sabhā-satra-prapā-prāg-vaṃśa-maṇḍapaiḥ prasūtam iva grāmaiḥ, kāñcanamaya-sarvôpakaraṇair vibhavair viśīrṇam iva meruṇā, dvija-dīyamānair artha-kalaśaiḥ phalitam iva bhāgya-saṃpadā.
children.translated_text: watery in their eye-sockets, windy in their sighs, earthy in their bodies, and space-like in their emptiness — as if embodied in the five great elements, visible in the inner chambers of slain neighboring feudatories. And his fortune, reflected as if in a mirror in his nearby servant-gems, was perceived as an equal likeness. And further: from his valor-fire came prosperity; from his courage-heat came success; from the stream of his sword-blade came the growth of his dynasty; from the mouths of his weapon-wounds came the declaration of his manliness; and from the callus of his bowstring came the grasping of [yet more] enterprises. And he considered enmity as tribute, war as a favor, the approach of battle as a great festival, the enemy as the sight of a treasure, a multitude of foes as prosperity, a battle-challenge as the granting of a boon, the fall of an assault as an increase of fortune, and the blow of a weapon as the delight of a shower of wealth. And in the reign of that king — [the land seemed] sprouted with unbroken rows of sacrificial posts as if by the Golden Age; [seemed to have] the <s>Kali</s> age fled by the sacrificial smoke spreading in all directions; [seemed to have] heaven descended in the whitewashed temples; <s>dharma</s> blossoming in the white flags fluttering on temple spires; the villages giving birth [to prosperity] by the assembly halls, hospices, water-stations, and pavilions constructed outside; [as if] <s>Meru</s> was crumbling in the all-golden implements and wealth; the fortune of destiny bearing fruit in the pots of wealth being given to <s>brāhmaṇas</s>.

body.translated_text: And among those thus arising in succession, there arose one who was a lion to the deer that were the <s>Hūṇas</s>, a fever to the <s>Sindhu</s> king, a poison to the <s>Gurjara</s> subjects, a blow to the skull of the elephant that was the <s>Gāndhāra</s> chief, a stormer of the cleverness of the <s>Lāṭa</s> people, an axe to the creeper of <s>Mālava</s>'s fortune — known by his other name '<s>Pratāpaśīla</s>' (of valorous conduct) — the king of kings named <s>Prabhākaravardhana</s>. He who, even while being consecrated to kingship, shed wealth as if they were impurities. He who was ashamed of a life maintained even by an enemy's cowardly follower holding [it] in battle like a blade of grass. He who was pained even by his own reflection in his drawn, polished sword as a companion in battles before enemies — he who was proud, and was vexed even by his bow bending before him in combats like a flatterer in his mind. And he bore the royal fortune — immovable as if studded with the nails and bolts of innumerable enemy weapons' barbs lodged within. And he, with his broad punitive expedition paths in all directions leveling the banks, hollows, treetops, thickets, trees, grass, bushes, anthills, mountains, and dense forests — seemed to divide the earth into many parts for his servants' use. And his own valor — though personal — uprooting all enemies completely, burned him like an external [force], [because he was] unsatisfied in his desire for battle. And his valor appeared — fiery in the hearts [of enemies],

the glory of the lineage of graces, the purificatory rite of womanhood, the success of the command of the <s>Makara</s>-bannered one (Kāma, god of love), the awakening of beauty's consciousness, the increase of fortune for love, the fulfilment of desire for loveliness, the divine gift for charm, the birth of lineage for passion, the boon-attainment for good fortune, the birthplace of attractiveness, the completion of creation for beauty, the prospect of youth, rain from a cloudless sky for elegance, the wiping away of ill-repute for prosperity, the nourishment of fame for character, the contentment of the heart for <s>dharma</s>, as if the creation by <s>Prajāpati</s> of the ultimate atom of the form of the fortune of benevolence; body.translated_text: And that king was by nature a devotee of the Sun. Every day at sunrise, having bathed, wearing white silk garments, his head covered with a white cloth, facing east, kneeling on the ground, on a spot anointed with saffron paste, he offered <s>arghya</s> (water-offering) with a cluster of red lotuses placed in a pure ruby vessel — as if with his own heart, devoted to the Sun. And the well-conducted one chanted his <s>japya</s> (recitation) — at dawn, midday, and day's end — for the sake of progeny, reciting with a concentrated mind the <s>mantra</s> called <s>Āditya-hṛdaya</s> (Heart of the Sun).

body.text: Bhakta-janânurodha-vidheyāni tu bhavanti devatānāṃ manāṃsi. yataḥ sa rājā kadā-cid grīṣma-samaye yad-ṛcchayā sita-kara-kara-sita-sudhā-dhavalasya harmyasya pṛṣṭhe suṣvāpa. vāma-pārśve câsya dvitīya-śayane devī Yaśomatī śiśye. pariṇata-prāyāyāṃ tu śyāmāyām, āsanna-prabhāta-velā-vilupyamāna-lāvaṇye lilambiṣamāṇe sīdat-tejasi tārakêśvare, karâgra-spṛṣṭa-kumudinī-pramoda-janmani śaśa-dhara-sveda iva galaty ati-śītale 'vaśyāya-payasi, madhu-mada-matta-prasupta-sīmantinī-niḥśvāsâhateṣu saṃkrānta-madeṣv iva ghūrṇamāneṣv antaḥ-pura-pradīpeṣu, rājani ca vimala-nakha-pratibimbitābhiḥ saṃvāhyamāna-caraṇa iva tārakābhiḥ visrabdha-prasāritair dig-aṅganānām ivârpitair aṅgair madhu-su-gandhibhiḥ sva-hasta-kamala-tālavṛnta-vātair iva śvasitair mukha-śriyā vījyamāne vimala-kapola-sthala-sthitena sita-kusuma-śekhareṇêva rati-keli-kaca-graha-lambitena pratimā-śaśi-bimbena virājite svapati devī Yaśomatī sahasâiva "ārya-putra! paritrāyasva paritrāyasva" iti bhāṣamāṇā bhūṣaṇa-raveṇa vyāharantîva parijanam utkampamānāṅga-yaṣṭir udatiṣṭhat.
body.translated_text: But the minds of deities are obedient to the devotion of their worshippers. For once, in the summer season, that king by chance fell asleep on the terrace of a palace white as moonbeams with its whitewash. And on his left side, on a second bed, Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s> lay. When the night was mostly advanced and the darkness was growing pale, when the charm of the moon-lord was being gradually stolen by the approaching dawn-hour, when his splendor was sinking and fading, when the exceedingly cold dew-water was falling — like the perspiration of the moon from the joy of touching the night-lily beds with his fingertips; when the inner-chamber lamps were flickering — as if intoxicated, having absorbed the madness from the sighs of women drunk with mead and sleeping in the perfumed night; and when the king — as if being fanned by the star-reflections on his polished nails, as if being massaged on the feet by the freely extended limbs of the female quarters of the sky, fragrant as honey, as if being fanned by the breezes of his own hand-lotus-leaf fans, his face radiant with the reflected image of the moon resting on the surface of his bright clear cheek like a white flower-crest, or like one caught in the hair during love-sport — while the king was sleeping, Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s> suddenly rose, saying 'Noble husband! Save me, save me!' — her body trembling, her ornaments jangling as if announcing [the event] to the attendants.

children.translated_text: Then, by that cry "Save me!"—never before heard in all the earth, let alone from the mouth of the queen—the king, as though his ears were scorched, abandoned sleep in a single instant. Drawing the bright-edged, unsheathed sword from the head of the bed with his right hand trembling with anger, as if parting the night with the blade like a hair-parting, tossing aside the upper garment with the tips of his left hand as if flinging away the intervening curtain of space, resplendent with a golden bracelet that had slipped from his wrist with the force of the throw and wandered through the directions as if his heart were searching for the cause of fear, shaking the palace with the tread of his left foot hastily set down, gleaming with a broken necklace that had fallen before him into the path of the sword's edge like a fragment of moonlight, reddening the horizons with his two eyes made exceedingly crimson by sleep and anger as though stained with the betel-juice clinging from <s>Lakṣmī</s>'s kiss, as if turning the night back again with a triple-crested frown that made all things blind with darkness—crying "My queen! Fear not, fear not!"—he sprang up with fury. And casting his gaze in all directions, when he saw nothing at all, he asked her the cause of her fear.

body.translated_text: Then, when the night-watch women had rushed in like household deities, and the attendants sleeping nearby had been awakened, and the heart-shaking terror had subsided, she spoke: "Noble husband! In a dream I saw two princes, radiant with splendor, filling the quarters as if with the heat of the young sun, making the living world appear as if lit by lightning—wearing crowns, earrings, armlets, and armor, bearing weapons, bathed in blood bright as <s>indragopaka</s> insects—being worshipped by the entire world with palms joined above upturned heads, and accompanied by a single maiden following them as if a moon-figure emerging from a <s>suṣumṇā</s> ray—they descended to the surface of the earth. And those two, as I wept, began to enter my womb by splitting it open with a weapon. I awoke, noble husband, crying out, my heart trembling."

body.translated_text: The king, hearing that, spoke to her with a heart filled with delight: "My queen! You grieve at a time for joy. The blessings of the elders are fulfilled. Our desires are accomplished. You are favored by the family deities. The blessed sun is gracious to you. Before long, the gaining of three exceedingly virtuous children will bring you joy." And descending, he performed the customary rituals as prescribed. <s>Yaśomatī</s> too was comforted by that speech of her husband.

body.translated_text: Then, after some portion of time had passed, in Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s>, Lord <s>Rājyavardhana</s> first took form in the womb. And while he was still in the womb, his mother turned pale as if from his fame. As if wearied by the weight of his virtues, she was unable to bear her own body. As if sated with the nectar-flow of his radiance, she became averse to food. Gradually, as the burden of the growing womb made her languid, though forbidden by the elders, she was somehow brought for worship by her friends with the support of their hands. Resting, she appeared like a <s>śālabhañjikā</s> (bracket-figure) against nearby pillars and walls. She could not lift her feet, which were enclosed as if by bees hiding in desire for lotuses. And she wandered slowly, as if being led along by the palace swans clinging to the rays of her toenails in their greed for lotus fibers. She stretched out her lotus-hand to grasp even her own reflections falling on jeweled walls, how much more toward her friends. As she moved slowly, the reflection sunk into the spotless jeweled floor seemed to grasp her foot-shoots, as if the earth were beginning its prior service to her. During the day, as she lay reclining, she appeared in the smooth hollow of her cheek like a <s>Lakṣmī</s> waiting for the time of delivery—resembling a doll made of folded betel-leaf on a cushion. At night, when she went to the palace terrace, the disc of the moon that had settled upon her breast-circles, whose garment had slipped from the churning of her womb, appeared like a white parasol held over her womb by some unseen hand. When she slept in her chamber, even the fan-bearers painted on the murals seemed to wave their fans. In her dreams, she was anointed by the four elephants of the quarters with water held in cups of lotus leaves in their trunks. When she awoke, even the <s>śālabhañjikā</s> attendants of the moonlit hall uttered the cry of "Victory" again and again. When summoning attendants, bodiless voices issued forth saying "Command us!" Even in play, she could not tolerate disobedience. Moreover, she had a desire to bathe in the combined waters of all four great oceans. Her heart longed to wander on the shores, in the vine-bowers, and on the sandy banks by the sea. Even in urgent matters, her brow-creeper moved with a playful arch. Though polished gem-mirrors were at hand, she had a passion for looking at her face in the surface of an unsheathed sword-blade. With <s>vīṇā</s>s set aside, the sounds of bowstrings, contrary to womanly nature, gave her pleasure. Her eyes delighted in caged lions. Even while bowing to elders, her head, as if arrested, somehow bent only with difficulty. And her friends, with eyes wide open in delight, as if whitening the palace with the thought of the approaching festival of delivery, constantly making offerings of <s>kumuda</s>, <s>kamala</s>, and <s>kuvalaya</s> lotus petals in every direction like an unceasing protective oblation, did not leave her side for even a moment. And great physicians, seated in appropriate places, carrying various medicines, gave the earth steadiness like mountains. Auspicious gems, like the hearts of the oceans come together with <s>Lakṣmī</s>, were tied at the knots of her necklace-cord.

body.translated_text: Then, after some further time had passed, in the month when <s>kandalī</s> plants bloom, when <s>kadamba</s> trees are in bud, when fresh shoots of grass grow thick, when lotuses are arrested, when the hearts of <s>cātaka</s> birds expand, when the sky is mute like a <s>mānasa</s> lake—in that rainy month, like <s>Viṣṇu</s> the discus-bearer in <s>Devakī</s>, joy arose simultaneously in the heart and the womb of <s>Yaśomatī</s>. Slowly, her body, slender as a staff, turned pale once more as if embraced by the merit of all the people. Her chest, with its beautiful nipples darkening with the onset of pregnancy, appeared to bear on its surface two sealed vessels of milk, as if sealed for the <s>cakravartin</s> (universal sovereign) to drink. Her gaze, long, smooth, and white as a river of milk, as if placed in reverence for nourishing with breast-milk, assumed a sweetness. Endowed with all auspicious

children.text: tataś ca prāpte jyeṣṭhāmūlīye māsi bahulāsu bahula-pakṣa-dvādasyāṃ vyatīte pradoṣa-samaye samārurukṣati kṣapā-yauvane sahasâivântaḥ-pure samudapādi kolāhalaḥ strī-janasya. nirgatya ca saṃbhramaṃ Yaśovatyāḥ svayam eva hṛdaya-nir-viśeṣā dhātryāḥ sutā Supātrêti nāmnā rājñaḥ pādayor nipatya "deva. diṣṭyā vardhase dvitīya-suta-janmanā" iti vyāharantī pūrṇa-pātraṃ jahāra.
children.translated_text: Then, when the month of <s>Jyeṣṭhā</s> arrived in its <s>mūla nakṣatra</s>, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, at the time of early evening when the youth of the night was about to ascend, suddenly there arose a commotion of women in the inner palace. And rushing out in haste, <s>Supātrā</s> by name—the daughter of <s>Yaśovatī</s>'s own nurse, inseparable from her heart—fell at the king's feet and, exclaiming "Your Majesty! By good fortune, you are blessed with the birth of a second son!"—carried away the full ceremonial vessel.

body.text: asminn eva ca kāle rājñaḥ parama-saṃmataḥ śataśaḥ saṃvāditâtîndriyâdeśaḥ, darśita-prabhāvaḥ saṃkalitī, jyotiṣi sarvāsāṃ graha-saṃhitānāṃ pāradṛśvā, sakala-gaṇaka-madhye mahito hitaś ca tri-kāla-jñāna-bhāg-bhojakas Tārako nāma gaṇakaḥ samupasṛtya vijñāpitavān: "deva! śrūyate māṃdhātā kilâivaṃ-vidhe vyatīpātâdi-sarva-doṣâbhiṣaṅga-rahite 'hani sarveṣûcca-sthāna-sthiteṣv evaṃ graheṣv īdṛśi lagne bheje janma. arvāk tato 'sminn antarāle punar evaṃ-vidhe yoge cakra-varti-janane nâjani jagati kaś-cid a-paraḥ. saptānāṃ cakra-vartinām agraṇīś cakra-varti-cihnānāṃ mahā-ratnānāṃ ca bhājanaṃ saptānāṃ sāgarāṇāṃ pālayitā sapta-tantūnāṃ sarveṣāṃ pravartayitā sapta-sapti-samaḥ suto 'yaṃ devasya jātaḥ" iti.
body.translated_text: At that very time, the king's most trusted astrologer, <s>Tāraka</s> by name—whose supernatural predictions had been verified hundreds of times, whose powers had been demonstrated, who was a master of mental calculation, who in astrology saw through all the planetary treatises, honored and valued among all the mathematicians, possessed of knowledge of the three times—approached and informed him: "Your Majesty! It is heard that <s>Māṃdhātā</s> was born on just such a day, free from all defects such as <s>vyatīpāta</s>, with all the planets situated in exalted positions, at just such an <s>lagna</s> (ascendant). Since then, in the intervening period, no other being has been born in the world at such a conjunction for the birth of a <s>cakravartin</s> (universal sovereign). This son of Your Majesty is born as the foremost of the seven <s>cakravartins</s>, worthy of the seven great jewels that are the marks of a <s>cakravartin</s>, protector of the seven oceans, promoter of all the seven sacred threads, equal to the seven-horsed sun."

children.translated_text: Though unbeaten, the consecration drum resounded with the deep sound of a churning ocean. Though unstruck, the auspicious instruments sounded. The echo of the instruments wandered through the horizons like a drum proclaiming fearlessness to all the worlds. The delighted horses, shaking their manes, neighed with their splendid mouths proudly grasping mouthfuls of fresh green <s>dūrvā</s> grass shoots. The elephants trumpeted melodiously as if dancing, playfully lifting the tips of their trunks. And soon a divine breeze blew, fragrant with a sweet heavenly scent, like the sigh of <s>Lakṣmī</s> releasing the discus-weapon. In the temples of the sacrificers, the <s>vaitāna</s> (sacrificial) fires blazed without fuel, their clockwise-turning crests of flame announcing the arrival of good fortune. From the surface of the earth, great treasures arose—vessels and coffers bound with chains of gold. In the directions, the <s>dikpālas</s> (guardians of the quarters) also seemed to raise a joyous clamor at the increase of destiny, resembling the echo of the beaten auspicious drums. At that very instant, the <s>dvijas</s> (twice-born), clad in white garments, Brahmin-faced, like <s>Prajāpatis</s> of the <s>Kṛtayuga</s>, assembled for the increase of the people. Like <s>Dharma</s> incarnate, the royal chaplain stood before them with fruits and sanctified water in his hands. The arriving elders of the clan appeared like the ancient customs themselves. Groups of released prisoners rushed about in confusion—their faces matted with trailing nets of beards, their bodies dark with thick crusts of grime—like kinsmen of the perishing <s>Kali</s> age. The plundered market-streets appeared like the abandoned camp-rows of <s>Adharma</s> departing at that time. Old nurses, surrounded by crowds of gleeful dwarfs and deaf-mutes looking upward, swarming with many children like newly manifested mother-goddesses, danced. And there commenced a great festival of the prince's birth—all royal protocol abandoned, the authority of the doorkeepers overturned, the staff of the rod-bearers removed, entry into the inner palace without restriction, master and servant made equal, no distinction between young and old, no difference between the well-mannered and the uncouth, the division between the intoxicated and sober impossible to discern, the conversation of noblewomen and courtesans indistinguishable, the entire populace of the camp dancing.

body.translated_text: At that very moment, even though not blown by anyone, the conches sounded with a high, sweet tone of their own accord.

body.translated_text: Gradually the festive joy expanded—in one place, the love of kings made manifest by the dancing of ancient, well-bred noble youths unaccustomed to dancing; in another, the king's favorite being dragged away by drunken lowly servant-girls beckoned by smiling kings; in another, the king bursting into uncontrollable laughter at the sight of aged feudatory lords dancing with intoxicated camp-procuresses clasping their necks; in another, the stratagems of a minister's secret love-affair being hinted at in songs sung by wicked little servants directed by a king's glance and gesture; in another, the crowd's laughter arising from an old mendicant being embraced by a bold, intoxicated <s>kuṭahārikā</s> woman; in another, a battle of unspeakable words begun between rogues and servants competing fiercely with one another; in another, an inner-palace guard who knew nothing of dance being forcibly dragged to dance by the king's women, acting the part of a slave-girl—the festival was like a mountain with its heaps of flowers, like a pleasure-house with its fountains of wine, like <s>Nandana</s> garden with its <s>pārijāta</s> scents, like a frost with its camphor-dust, like a great laughter with its drum-rolls, like the churning of <s>amṛta</s> with its great uproars, like a whirlpool with its <s>rāsaka</s> dance-circles, like a horripilation with the rays of ornamental gems, like a headband with

body.text: Skandhâvalambamāna-kesara-mālāḥ kāmboja-vājina ivâskandantaḥ, tarala-tārakā hariṇā ivôḍḍīyamānāḥ, sa-gara-sutā iva khanitrair nir-dayaiś caraṇâbhighātair dārayanto bhuvam, an-eka-sahasra-saṃkhyāś cikrīḍur yuvānaḥ. katham api tālâvacara-cāraṇa-caraṇa-kṣobhaṃ cakṣame kṣamā. kṣiti-pāla-kumārakāṇāṃ ca khelatām anyonyâsphālair ābharaṇeṣu muktā-phalāni pheluḥ. sindūra-reṇunā punar utpanna-hiraṇya-garbha-garbha-śoṇita-śoṇâśam iva brahmâṇḍa-kapālam abhavat. paṭa-vāsa-pāṃsu-paṭalena prakaṭita-Mandākinī-saikata-sahasram iva śuśubhe nabhas-talam. vipra-kīryamāṇa-piṣṭātaka-parāga-piñjaritâtapā bhuvana-kṣobha-viśīrṇa-pitā-maha-kamala-kiñjalka-rajo-rāji-rañjita iva rejur divasāḥ. Saṃghaṭṭa-vighaṭita-hāra-patita-muktā-phala-paṭaleṣu caskhāla lokaḥ.
body.translated_text: With manes of garlands hanging from their shoulders, charging like <s>Kamboja</s> horses, with restless, darting eyes, bounding like deer, like the sons of <s>Sagara</s> tearing open the earth with merciless digging tools and the blows of their feet—youths numbered in many thousands sported. The earth somehow endured the trampling of the feet of the dancers and acrobats. And as the young princes played, pearls burst from their ornaments with the mutual collisions. With <s>sindūra</s> dust, the vault of the sky became as if tinged red with the blood from the womb of the golden <s>Hiraṇyagarbha</s>, like the shell of the cosmic egg. With clouds of scented <s>paṭavāsa</s> powder, the surface of the sky shone as if displaying thousands of <s>Mandākinī</s> sandbars. The days glowed, their sunlight yellowed by scattered <s>piṣṭātaka</s> pollen, as though tinted by rows of filament-dust from <s>Brahmā</s>'s grandfather-lotus shaken by the trembling of the world. The people slipped on the carpets of pearls fallen from necklaces broken in the crush.

body.translated_text: And from all sides, as the women danced, the earth appeared reddened with the lac-dye dripping from their feet, as if made of passion itself. With the swelling bosoms rising everywhere, the great festival seemed made of auspicious water-vessels. With the tossing of vine-like arms, the living world shone as if made of lotus-fiber bracelets. With the flashing of coquettish smiles, time itself seemed made of lightning. With the rays from restless eyes, the days seemed made of black antelope-hide. With the <s>śirīṣa</s> flower-cluster ear-ornaments bobbing everywhere, the sunlight seemed made of parrot-feathers, casting a green shade. body.translated_text: At this very time, the brother of Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s> presented to the two princes his son as an attendant—about eight years of age, with waving curly side-locks fluttering, as if a reborn <s>Makaradhvaja</s> (Kāmadeva) with the smoke-streak of <s>Khaṇḍaparaśu</s>'s (Śiva's) wrathful fire still clinging to his head; showing with one half of his body darkened by the luster of a sapphire earring and the other whitened by the radiance of a three-pointed pearl, as if displaying a combined incarnation of <s>Hari</s> and <s>Hara</s>; with a flower-metal bracelet set upon his stout forearm, like <s>Paraśurāma</s> who had entered childhood, marked with the traces of the axe and noose worn thin by the destruction of the <s>Kṣatriyas</s>; with a budding curved coral-sprout strung on his neck-thread, like <s>Hiraṇyakaśipu</s> with a fragment of <s>Narasiṃha</s>'s claw broken by the hardness of his chest, reborn in another life; even in childhood a firm seed of the tree of valor—named <s>Bhaṇḍi</s>.

children.translated_text: with an exceedingly broad chest, as if offering unlimited room for his master's esteem; with the quiet, graceful motions of his hanging pair of arms, as if swimming across the vast ocean of youth; with a stout forearm marked by the line of bowstring-calluses—like the tendril of the flame of innate prowess bursting forth through the cluster of ruby-rays from the bracelet on his left hand; bearing the luster of his earring-gem like a tawny <s>rauravī</s> (deerskin), hanging from his high shoulder-ridge, held as if by a vow of weapon-bearing; carrying a face like the moon—with the reflection of the foliate scroll-pattern of his armlet's raised rim reflected in his cheeks, as if with <s>Rohiṇī</s> dwelling within his heart; with a downcast gaze of steady, unflickering eyes, as if teaching modesty to the lotus-groves that lifted their faces at the attainment of <s>Lakṣmī</s>; bearing on his head an <s>āmrātaka</s> (hog-plum) sprig as a hair-ornament, like devotion to his master; displaying a humility as if imparted by the merciless fear of breaking his bracelets, bestowed by every bow upon which it was placed; shining even in boyhood with conquered senses, like subdued enemies; following the path of good birth like a beloved friend, like a ground of trust; though radiant with splendor, yet adorned by pleasing temperament, like the sun resplendent with the moon dwelling within; challenging even mountains by his bodily hardness; as if purchasing the people heart and soul with his beauty, selling joy for the price of a mere glance—<s>Kumāragupta</s>; behind him the younger one, by his extreme tallness and fairness appearing like a moving mountain of realgar; as if kissed on the head by his departing fame, heavy and ungaudy, resembling the chaplet of a <s>mālatī</s> blossom; as if declaring through his meeting eyebrows the first sign of the long-awaited union of the mutually opposed qualities of modesty and youth; "yathâjñāpayati devaḥ" iti medinī-dolāyamāna-maulibhyām utthāya Rājyavardhana-Harṣau praṇematuḥ. tau ca pitaram. tataś cârabhya kṣaṇam api nimeṣoômeṣāv iva cakṣur-gocarād an-apayāntāv ucchvāsa-niḥśvāsāv iva naktaṃ-divam abhimukha-sthitau bhujāv iva satata-pārśva-vartinau kumārayos tau babhūvatuḥ.
body.translated_text: Having entered, the two from afar touched the ground with their four limbs and their heads and made obeisance. They took the appropriate seats indicated by the affectionate gaze of the king. After a moment, the king commanded them: 'From this day forward, you two must attend upon the princes.' 'As Your Majesty commands,' they said, and rising with heads that made the earth sway, <s>Rājyavardhana</s> and <s>Harṣa</s> bowed to them. And they bowed to the princes in return. From then on, never departing from their sight even for an instant—like the opening and closing of eyelids, like inhalation and exhalation night and day, like two arms always at their sides—those two became inseparable companions of the princes.

Dūta-saṃpreṣaṇâdibhiś ca tāṃ yayācire rājānaḥ.
body.translated_text: Now <s>Rājyaśrī</s> also, growing daily in familiarity with all the arts among her accomplished friends skilled in dance, song, and the rest, gradually grew up. In but a limited number of days she attained youth. The eyes of all kings fell upon her alone, like arrows upon a target. And kings sought her hand by sending envoys and the like.

children.translated_text: ...intolerable to me is this state of affairs, that children born of one's own body, cherished in one's lap, whom one cannot abandon, are unexpectedly taken away by those who arrive uninvited and sing their praises. These are indeed the branding-marks of worldly existence. This is the all-overpowering burning power of the fire of grief: that even when the state of being offspring is the same, good people are tormented when a daughter is born. For this reason, at the very time of birth, good people offer water to daughters with their tears. From this fear, sages who have not taken wives, who have abandoned dwelling in houses, resort to empty forests. For who among sentient beings could endure separation from children? The more the messengers of suitors arrive, the more does this pitiable anxiety, as if ashamed, enter my heart deeply. But what can be done? Still, householders must follow the ways of the world. And generally, even when other virtuous qualities exist in a suitor, the wise give weight above all to noble lineage. Standing at the head of all kings, worshipped by the entire world like the footprint of <s>Maheśvara</s> (the Great Lord), is the <s>Maukhari</s> dynasty. And there, the eldest son of its ornament <s>Avantivarman</s>, named <s>Grahavarmā</s>—who has come to earth like the lord of the planets, not inferior to his father in virtues—seeks her hand. If your mind also approves, then I wish to give her to him." When the lord had spoken thus, the queen, her heart overwhelmed with tenderness for her daughter, her eyes filled with tears, replied: "Noble husband! Mothers of daughters are indeed no different from wet-nurses, useful only for rearing. But in the matter of giving them away, their fathers are the authority. Only this: the love for a daughter, made special by tenderness, far exceeds the love for a son. How she may not suffer distress throughout her life—that, noble husband, only you know." The king then, his decision firm regarding the giving of his daughter, summoned his two sons also and made them aware of the matter. And on an auspicious day, into the hand of the chief envoy who had already been sent by <s>Grahavarmā</s> to request the maiden, he poured the water of the gift of his daughter in the presence of all the royal families.

body.translated_text: Having heard that, he dismissed the attendants and spoke to the chief queen standing beside him: 'Queen! Our daughter <s>Rājyaśrī</s> has become a young woman. children.translated_text: When he [the envoy], having accomplished his purpose, departed rejoicing, and as the wedding days drew near—all people adorned with lavishly distributed betel, scented powders, and flowers; caravans of artisans arriving summoned from every region; supplies being brought in by villagers gathered by the king's men from entire villages; numerous gifts from kings being presented by royal doorkeepers; the king's favorites busy with the gathering and hosting of invited groups of kinsmen; auspicious drums sounding with the sharp corner-strokes produced by the cupped palms of leatherworkers fierce with the intoxication of <s>madhu</s> (honey-wine); implements such as pestles, mortars, and stone-slabs being adorned with five-fingered flour-marks; images of the goddess <s>Indrāṇī</s> being installed in the halls being filled with continuous streams of bards appearing from every direction; the lines for the wedding-platform being laid by <s>sūtra-dhāras</s> (master builders) honored with white flowers, unguents, and garments; the pinnacles of palace-walls, streets, and ramparts being whitened by whitewashers who had climbed ladders with hands of plaster-and-camphor mixture; people's foot-tips being reddened by the flood of water from the washing of crushed <s>kusumbha</s> (safflower) materials; the courtyards rippling with horses and elephants being inspected as suitable for the dowry;
