children.translated_text: unwidowed women—with foreheads resplendent with lines of vermilion dust, singing wedding songs containing the names of the bride's and groom's clans that were sweet to the ears, with fingers smeared with many-colored pastes painting neck-cord designs, skilled at drawing decorative creeper-patterns, whitening water-pots, adorning rows of cool white-painted walls, dyeing unopened cotton-boll sprouts and wedding-bracelet wool-thread bindings, preparing <s>aṅga-rāgas</s> (body-unguents) compounded of <s>balāśana</s> (white sesame), ghee, thickened <s>kuṅkuma</s> (saffron) paste, and facial cosmetics that enhanced beauty, stringing garlands of cloves interspersed with <s>kakkola</s> (a spice) and <s>jātīphala</s> (nutmeg), their intervals studded with sparkling thick crystal-camphor fragments—surrounded on all sides by the wives of feudatory chiefs; and with cloths of many kinds—dyed and being dyed, reddened by veteran washerwomen skilled at producing manifold decorative designs, honored by the protocol-wise old women of the inner palace, with attendants pulling at both cloth-edges and swaying them, being dried in the shade, and when dry fashioned with leaf-spray designs at their further edges by skillful folding, some begun with saffron-paste starch-stiffening, some with upper garments being folded by maid-servants lifting their arms—fine <s>kṣauma</s> (linen), <s>bādara</s> (jute), <s>dukūla</s> (silk), spider-web-thread fabrics, <s>aṃśuka</s> (muslin), <s>netra</s> (fine cloth)—soft as the tender pith of young plantain, stealable by a breath, perceivable only by touch, resembling shed snake-skins—garments flashing on all sides like a thousand rainbows covered the scene; and with bedsteads canopied by shining <s>nicolaka</s> (bed-curtains) concealing flocks of swans, and bodices being studded with star-pearls, and countless thousands of silk-cloth strips being cut for various uses, and tent-pavilions resplendent with canopies of newly-dyed soft silk, and pavilion-halls with all their floors continuously covered by layers of <s>stavaraka</s> (floor-spreads), and pillars being wrapped with brightly patterned cloth—the royal palace was brilliant, delightful, excitement-producing, and auspicious.

body.text: devī tu Yaśomatī vivāhôtsava-paryākula-hṛdayā hṛdayena bhartari, kutūhalena jāmātari, snehena duhitari, upacāreṇa nimantrita-strīṣu, ādeśena parijane, śarīreṇa saṃcaraṇe, cakṣuṣā kṛtâkṛta-pratyavekṣaṇeṣu,

children.text: ānandena mahôtsave, ekâpi bahudhā vibhaktêvâbhavat. Bhū-patir apy upary upari visarjitôṣṭra-vāmī-janita-jāmātṛ-joṣaḥ saty apyâjñā-saṃpādana-dakṣe mukhêkṣaṇa-pare parijane samaṃ putrābhyāṃ duhitṛ-sneha-viklavaḥ sarvaṃ svayam akarot.
children.translated_text: with her joy in the great festival—though one, she seemed to be divided into many. The king too, his delight in his son-in-law increasing ever more through the camels being repeatedly dispatched [with gifts], though his attendants were competent at carrying out orders and devoted to watching his face, together with his two sons, overwhelmed by love for his daughter, did everything himself.

body.translated_text: Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s>, her heart agitated with the excitement of the wedding festival, was with her heart upon her husband, with her curiosity upon her son-in-law, with her affection upon her daughter, with her hospitality upon the invited women, with her commands upon the attendants, with her body in constant motion, with her eyes upon the inspection of what was done and what remained to be done,

body.text: evaṃ ca tasminn a-vidhavāmaya iva bhavati rāja-kule, maṅgalamaya iva jāyamāne jīva-loke, cāraṇamayeṣv iva lakṣyamāṇeṣu diṅ-mukheṣu, paṭaha-ravamaya iva kṛte 'ntarikṣe, bhūṣaṇamaya iva bhramati parijane, bāndhavamaya iva dṛśyamāne sarge, nirvṛtimaya ivôpalakṣyamāṇe kāle, lakṣmīmaya iva vijṛmbhamāṇe mahôtsave, nidhāna iva sukhasya, phala iva janmanaḥ, pariṇāma iva puṇyasya, yauvana iva vibhūteḥ, yauva-rājya iva prīteḥ, siddhi-kāla iva mano-rathasya vartamāne, gaṇyamāna iva janâṅgulībhiḥ, ālokyamāna iva mārga-dhvajaiḥ, pratyudgamyamāna iva maṅgalya-vādya-pratiśabdakaiḥ, āhūyamāna iva mauhūrtikaiḥ, ākṛṣyamāṇa iva mano-rathaiḥ, pariṣvajyamāna iva vadhū-sakhī-hṛdayair ājagāma vivāha-divasaḥ. prātar eva pratīhāraiḥ samutsārita-nikhilâ-nibaddha-lokaṃ viviktam akriyata rāja-kulam.
body.translated_text: And thus, when the royal household was as if composed entirely of unwidowed women, when the world of the living seemed made entirely of auspiciousness, when the directions appeared filled entirely with bards, when the sky seemed made entirely of drum-sounds, when the attendants appeared adorned entirely with ornaments, when all creation seemed composed entirely of kinsmen, when time appeared to consist entirely of joy, when the great festival seemed to overflow entirely with prosperity—as if it were the treasure of happiness, the fruit of birth, the culmination of merit, the prime of fortune, the crown-princedom of delight, the moment of fulfillment of all desires—being counted as it were on the fingers of the people, being observed as it were by the banners along the road, being greeted as it were by the echoing sounds of auspicious music, being summoned as it were by the astrologers, being drawn as it were by the longings of the heart, being embraced as it were by the hearts of the bride's friends—the wedding day arrived. Early that morning, the ushers cleared out all the people who had been admitted, and the royal palace was made private.

body.text: atha mahā-pratīhāraḥ praviśya nṛpa-samīpam "deva! jāmātur antikāt tāmbūla-dāyakaḥ Pārijātaka-nāmā saṃprāptaḥ" ity abhidhāya sv-ākāraṃ yuvānam adarśayat. rājā tu taṃ dūrād eva jāmātṛ-bahu-mānād darśitâdaraḥ "bālaka! kac-cit kuśalī Grahavarmā?" iti papraccha. asau tu samākarṇita-narâdhipa-dhvanir dhāvamānaḥ kati-cit padāny upasṛtya prasārya ca bāhū sevā-caturaś ciraṃ vasuṃ-dharāyāṃ nidhāya mūrdhānam utthāya "deva! kuśalī yathâjñāpayasy arcayati ca devaṃ namas-kāreṇa" iti vyajñāpayat. āgata-jāmātṛ-nivedanâgataṃ ca taṃ jñātvā kṛta-sat-kāraṃ rājā "yāminyāḥ prathame yāme vivāha-kālâtyaya-kṛto yathā na bhavati doṣaḥ" iti saṃdiśya pratīpaṃ prāhiṇot.
body.translated_text: Then the chief usher, entering the king's presence, said: "Your Majesty! From your son-in-law's party, a betel-bearer named <s>Pārijātaka</s> has arrived," and presented a handsome young man. The king, from afar itself showing respect out of regard for his son-in-law, asked: "Young man! Is <s>Grahavarmā</s> well?" And he, upon hearing the king's voice, ran forward a few steps, stretched out his arms, and with the skill of a practiced courtier, long prostrated his head upon the ground; then rising, announced: "Your Majesty! He is well, as Your Majesty commands, and he honors Your Majesty with his obeisance." And the king, understanding that he had come to announce the son-in-law's arrival, honored him and, instructing him "so that no fault arises from delay past the appointed wedding-hour of the first watch of the night," sent him back.

children.text: atha sakala-kamala-vana-lakṣmīṃ vadhū-mukha iva saṃcārya samavasite vāsare, vivāha-divasa-śriyaḥ pāda-pallava iva rajyamāne savitari, vadhū-varânurāga-laghū-kṛta-prema-lajjiteṣv iva vighaṭamāneṣu cakra-vāka-mithuneṣu, saubhāgya-dhvaja iva raktâṃśuka-su-kumāra-vapuṣi nabhasi sphurati saṃdhyā-rāge, kapota-kaṇṭha-karbure vara-yātrâgamana-rajasîva kaluṣayati diṅ-mukhāni timire, lagna-saṃpādana-sajja ivôjjihāne jyotir-gaṇe vivāha-maṅgala-kalaśa ivôdaya-śikhariṇā samutkṣipyamāṇe vardhamāna-dhavala-cchāye tārâdhipa-maṇḍale, vadhū-vadana-lāvaṇya-jyotsnā-paripīta-tamasi pradoṣe, vṛthôditam upahasatsv iva rajani-karam uttānita-mukhesu kumuda-vaneṣv ājagāma muhur muhur ullāsita-sphāra-sphuritâruṇa-cāmarair mano-rathair ivôtthita-rāgâgra-pallavaiḥ puro-dhāvamānaiḥ pādātair utkarṇa-kaṭaka-haya-pratiheṣita-dīyamāna-sv-āgatair iva vājināṃ vṛndair āpūrita-dig-vibhāgaḥ, cala-karṇa-cāmarāṇāṃ cāmīkaramaya sarvôpakaraṇānāṃ varṇaka-lambināṃ balināṃ ghaṇṭā-ṭāṅkāriṇāṃ kariṇāṃ ghaṭābhiḥ, ghaṭayann iva punar indûdaya-vilīnam andhakāram, nakṣatra-mālā-maṇḍita-mukhīṃ kariṇīṃ niśā-kara iva pauraṃdarīṃ diśam ārūḍhaḥ, prakaṭita-vividha-vihaga-virutais tālâvacara-cāraṇaiḥ puraḥ-sarair bālo vasanta ivôpavanaiḥ kriyamāga-kolāhalo gandha-tailâvaseka-sugandhinā dīpikā-cakra-vālâlokena kuṅkuma-paṭa-vāsa-dhūli-paṭalenêva piñjarī-kurvan sakalaṃ lokam, utphulla-mallikā-muṇḍa-mālā-madhyâdhyāsita-kusuma-śekhareṇa śirasā hasann iva sa-pariveṣa-kṣapā-karaṃ kaumudī-pradoṣam, ātma-rūpa-nirjita-makara-ketu-karâpahṛtena kārmukeṇêva kausumena dāmnā viracita-vaikakṣaka-vilāsaḥ, kusuma-saurabha-garva-bhrānta-bhramara-kula-kalakala-pralāpa-su-bhagaḥ pārijāta iva jātaḥ śriyā saha punar avatārito medinīm, nava-vadhū-vadanâvalokana-kutūhalenêva kṛṣyamāṇa-hṛdayaḥ patann iva mukhena pratyāsanna-lagno Grahavarmā tvaritam ājagāma.
children.translated_text: Then, when the day had ended—as if having transferred the beauty of all lotus-groves to the bride's face—as the sun was reddening like the foot-sprout of the wedding-day's splendor, as the <s>cakravāka</s> pairs were separating as if embarrassed that their love had been made light by the mutual passion of bride and groom, as the twilight-glow flashed across the sky like a banner of good fortune—delicate-bodied in its red garments—as the darkness, mottled as a pigeon's throat, muddied the faces of the directions like the dust of the approaching groom's procession, as the host of stars arose as if ready to accomplish the auspicious moment, as the moon's orb—with its growing white shadow—was raised up by the eastern peak like a wedding auspicious-vessel, as in the early evening the darkness was being drunk up by the moonlight of the bride's face's beauty, as the groves of night-lilies seemed to mock the moon for rising needlessly—filling the directions with his retinue, preceded by foot-soldiers running ahead like longings with their sprout-tips of passion eagerly rising and their broadly fluttering red chowries, with troops of horses greeted as if by the neighing of the pricked-eared camp-horses, with ranks of elephants—golden in all their trappings, draped with color-streamers, powerful, with bells clanging—as if recongealing the darkness that had dissolved at moonrise, mounted upon a she-elephant adorned with a garland of star-constellations like the moon upon the eastern quarter, preceded by heralds whose various bird-calls revealed [their art] like a young Spring-god with his pleasure-groves, creating an uproar along the road, making the entire world golden with the <s>kuṅkuma</s> (saffron) scented-powder dust-veil spread by the light of the lamp-circle and the anointing of fragrant oil, as if laughing at the moonlit evening with the crown of flower-crests set amid garlands of full-blown jasmine on his head, with a garland of flowers serving as a sash lending the grace of a bow-ornament like a flowery bow of <s>Kāma</s> (the God of Love)—a bow not conquered but surpassed by his own beauty—handsome with the humming murmur of swarms of bees bewildered by the fragrance of blossoms, as if born again as a <s>Pārijāta</s> tree descended to earth along with <s>Śrī</s> (<s>Lakṣmī</s>), his heart drawn as if by curiosity to behold the face of his new bride, falling forward as if face-first with the auspicious moment nearly at hand—<s>Grahavarmā</s> arrived swiftly.

children.text: rājā tu tam upa-dvāram āgataṃ caraṇābhyām eva rāja-cakrânugamyamānaḥ sa-sutaḥ pratyujjagāma. avatīrṇaṃ ca taṃ kṛta-namas-kāraṃ manmatham iva mādhavaḥ prasārita-bhujo gāḍham āliliṅga. yathā-kramaṃ pariṣvakta-Rājyavardhana-Harṣaṃ ca haste gṛhītvâbhyantaraṃ ninye. sva-nirviśeṣâsana-dānâdinā câinam upacāreṇôpacacāra.
children.translated_text: The king, however, accompanied by the circle of kings, went forth on foot with his sons to meet him who had arrived at the outer gate. And when he had dismounted and made his salutation, the king embraced him tightly with arms extended, as <s>Mādhava</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>) would embrace <s>Manmatha</s> (the God of Love). Having embraced <s>Rājyavardhana</s> and <s>Harṣa</s> in due order, he took him by the hand and led him within. And he honored him with courtesies such as offering a seat equal to his own.

body.text: na cirāc ca Gambhīra-nāmā nṛpateḥ praṇayī vidvān dvi-janamā Grahavarmāṇam uvāca: "tāta! tvāṃ prāpya cirāt khalu Rājyaśriyā ghaṭitau tejomayau sakala-jagad-gīyamāna-budha-karṇânanda-kāri-guṇa-gaṇau soma-sūrya-vaṃśāv iva Puṣpabhūti-Mukara-vaṃśau. prathamam eva kaustubha-maṇir iva guṇaiḥ sthito 'si hṛdaye devasya. idānīṃ tu śaśîva sirasā paramêśvareṇâsi voḍhavyo jātaḥ" iti.
body.translated_text: Before long, a learned Brahmin named <s>Gambhīra</s>, a favorite of the king, said to <s>Grahavarmā</s>: 'Dear son! By obtaining you, the <s>Puṣpabhūti</s> and <s>Mukara</s> dynasties—both radiant, their multitudes of virtues sung by the wise throughout the entire world and giving joy to ears—have at last been united through <s>Rājyaśrī</s>, like the lunar and solar dynasties. From the very first, like the <s>Kaustubha</s> gem, you have been established by your virtues in the heart of the king. But now, like the moon, you are to be borne upon the head by the Supreme Lord.'

body.text: evaṃ vadaty eva tasmin nṛpam upasṛtya mauhūrtikāḥ "deva! samāsīdati lagna-velā. vrajatu jāmātā kautuka-gṛham" ity ūcuḥ. atha narêndreṇa "uttiṣṭha, gaccha" iti gadito Grahavarmā praviśyântaḥ-puraṃ jāmātṛ-darśana-kutūhalinīnāṃ strīṇāṃ patitāni locana-sahasrāṇi vikaca-nīla-kuvalaya-vanānîva laṅghayann āsasāda kautuka-gṛha-dvāram. nivārita-parijanaś ca praviveśa.
body.translated_text: Even as he was saying this, the astrologers approached the king and said: 'Your Majesty! The auspicious moment approaches. Let the bridegroom proceed to the wedding-pavilion.' Then, told by the king 'Rise, go,' <s>Grahavarmā</s>, entering the inner palace, as if stepping over groves of blossoming blue <s>kuvalaya</s> lotuses—the thousands of glances falling from the women curious to see the bridegroom—reached the door of the wedding-pavilion. Having dismissed his retinue, he entered.

body.text: atha tatra katipayâpta-priya-sakhī-sva-jana-pramadā-prāya-parivārām, aruṇâṃśukâvaguṇṭhita-mukhīṃ prabāta-saṃdhyām iva sva-prabhayā niṣ-prabhān pradīpakān kurvāṇām, ati-saukumārya-śaṅkitenêva yauvanena nâti-nirbharam upagūḍhām, sādhvasa-nirudhyamāna-hṛdaya-deśa-duḥkha-muktair nibhṛtâyataiḥ śvasitair apayāntaṃ kumāra-bhāvam ivânuśocantīm, aty-utkampinīṃ patanabhiyêva trapayā niṣpandaṃ dhāryamāṇām, hastaṃ tāmarasa-pratipakṣam āsanna-grahaṇaṃ śaśinam iva rohiṇīṃ bhaya-vepamāna-mānasām avalokayantīm,

children.text: candana-dhavala-tanu-latām, jyotsnā-dāna-saṃcita-lāvaṇyāt kumudinī-garbhād iva prasūtām, kusumâmoda-nirhāriṇīṃ vasanta-hṛdyād iva nirgatām, niḥśvāsa-parimalâkṛṣṭa-madhu-kara-kulāṃ malaya-mārutād ivôtpannām, kṛta-kaṃdarpânusaraṇāṃ ratim iva punar-jātām, prabhā-lāvaṇya-mada-saurabha-mādhuryaiḥ kaustubha-śaśi-madirā-pārijātâmṛta-prabhavaiḥ sarva-ratna-guṇair a-parām iva surâsura-ruṣā ratnâkareṇa kalpitāṃ śriyam, snigdhena bālikâlokena sita-sindhuvāra-kusuma-mañjarībhir iva muktā-dīdhitibhiḥ kalpita-karṇâvataṃsām, karṇâbharaṇa-marakata-prabhā-harita-śādvalena kapola-sthalī-talena vinodayantīm iva hāriṇīṃ locana-cchāyām, adho-mukhaṃ vara-kautukâlokanâkulaṃ muhur-muhuḥ kṛta-mukhônnamana-prayatnaṃ sakhī-janaṃ hṛdayaṃ ca nirbhartsayantīṃ vadhūm apaśyat.
children.translated_text: her slender body pale as sandalwood, as if born from the womb of night-lilies that had stored up beauty through the gift of moonlight, as if emerged from the heart of spring that is delightful with the fragrance of flowers, her swarms of bees drawn by the perfume of her sighs as if born from the <s>Malaya</s> breeze, as if <s>Rati</s> (Love's consort) reborn having followed <s>Kandarpa</s> (the God of Love), fashioned as if by the gem-ocean in its vexation with gods and demons—an incomparable <s>Śrī</s> (<s>Lakṣmī</s>) endowed with all the virtues of gems through radiance, beauty, intoxication, fragrance, and sweetness derived from the <s>Kaustubha</s>, moon, wine, <s>pārijātaka</s>, and nectar; with ear-ornaments fashioned as it were from pearl-rays resembling clusters of white <s>sindhuvāra</s> blossoms through her tender girlish gaze; delighting as it were a doe-like shadow of her eyes with the surface of her cheek-region green-meadowed by the emerald radiance of her ear-ornaments; face downward, agitated by the eager curiosity to see the bridegroom, again and again making efforts to raise her face, reproaching both her friends and her heart—he beheld the bride.

body.translated_text: Then there, surrounded by an entourage consisting mostly of a few trusted dear friends, kinswomen, and young women; her face veiled with a red garment like the dawn twilight; making the lamps dim by her own radiance; embraced not too tightly by her youth as if from fear of excessive delicacy; mourning as it were the departing state of maidenhood with deep, long sighs released from the pain of the heart-region suppressed by bashfulness; trembling exceedingly, held motionless by modesty as if from fear of falling; her mind trembling with fear as she gazed at the hand—rival of the lotus—about to grasp her, like <s>Rohiṇī</s> looking at the approaching moon,

body.text: praviśantam eva taṃ hṛdaya-cauraṃ vadhvā samarpitaṃ jagrāha kaṃdarpaḥ. parihāsa-smera-mukhībiś ca nārībhiḥ kautuka-gṛhe yad yat kāryate jāmātā tat tat sarvam ati-peśalaṃ cakāra. kṛta-pariṇayânurūpa-veśa-parigrahāṃ gṛhītvā kare vadhūṃ nirjagāma. jagāma ca nava-sudhā-dhavalāṃ nimantritâgatais tuṣāra-śailôpatyakām iva try-ambakâmbikā-vivāhâhūtair bhūbhṛdbhiḥ parivṛtām, seka-su-kumāra-yavâṅkura-danturaiḥ pañcâsyaiḥ kalaśaiḥ komala-varṇikā-vicitrair a-mitra-mukhaiś ca maṅgalya-phala-hastābhir añjali-kārikābhir udbhāsita-paryantām, upādhyāyôpadhīyamānîndhana-dhūmāyamānâgni-saṃdhukṣaṇâkṣaṇikôpadraṣṭṛ-dvijām, upakṛśānu-nihitân-upahata-harita-kuśām saṃnihita-dṛṣad-ajinâjya-sruk-samit-pūlī-nivahām, nūtana-śūrpârpita-śyāmala-śamī-palāśa-miśra-lāja-hāsinīṃ vedīm. āruroha ca tāṃ divam iva sa-jyotsnaḥ śaśī. samutsasarpa ca vellitâruṇa-śikhā-pallavasya

children.text: śikhinaḥ kusumâyudha iva rati-dvitīyo raktâśokasya samīpam. hute ca huta-bhuji pradakṣiṇâvarta-pravṛttābhir vadhū-vadana-vilokana-kutūhalinībhir iva jvālābhir eva saha pradakṣiṇaṃ babhrāma. pātyamāne ca lājâñjalau nakha-mayūkha-dhavalita-tanur a-dṛṣṭa-pūrva-vadhū-vara-rūpa-vismaya-smera ivâdṛsyata vibhāvasuḥ.
children.translated_text: he approached the red <s>aśoka</s> tree. And when the oblation had been offered to the fire, he circumambulated it together with the flames—which turned rightward as if in eagerness to see the bride's face. And when the handful of parched rice was being poured, <s>Vibhāvasu</s> (Fire), his body whitened by the luster of her nails, appeared to smile in wonder at the unprecedented beauty of bride and groom.

body.translated_text: The very moment he entered, <s>Kandarpa</s> (Love) seized the heart offered by the bride to that thief of hearts. And amid women with faces smiling with jest, whatever the bridegroom was made to do in the wedding-pavilion, all that he performed with supreme grace. Having taken by the hand the bride dressed in attire befitting the completed wedding, he came out. And he went to the wedding altar—white as fresh plaster, like a <s>Tuṣāra</s> (Himalayan) mountain-slope frequented by mountains invited as guests to the wedding of <s>Tryambaka</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) and <s>Ambikā</s> (<s>Pārvatī</s>), its perimeter adorned with five-faced vases bristling with tender sprout-tips of delicate irrigation-softened barley and with women bearing auspicious fruits making oblations with joined hands, with a Brahmin priest feeding fresh fuel to the smoking, kindled sacred fire without a moment's delay, with freshly placed unbroken green <s>kuśa</s> grass near the fire, with heaps of grinding-stones, deerskins, ghee, sacrificial ladles, and bundles of sacrificial twigs placed nearby, smiling with <s>lāja</s> (parched rice) mixed with dark <s>śamī</s> and <s>palāśa</s> leaves placed on new winnowing fans. And he ascended it like the moon with its moonlight ascending to heaven. And with flickering red crest-flames of sprouts, like <s>Kusumāyudha</s> (the Flower-Weaponed Love-god) accompanied by <s>Rati</s>,

body.text: atrântare sv-accha-kapolôdara-saṃkrāntam anala-pratibimbam iva nirvāpayantī sthūla-muktā-phala-vimala-bāṣpa-bindu-saṃdoha-darśita-dur-dinā nirvadana-vikāraṃ ruroda vadhūḥ. udaśru-vilocanānāṃ ca bāndhava-vadhūnām udapādi mahān ākrandaḥ. parisamāpita-vaivāhika-kriyā-kalāpas tu jāmātā vadhvā samaṃ praṇanāma śvaśurau. praviveśa ca dvāra-pakṣa-likhita-rati-prīti-daivataṃ, praṇayibhir iva prathama-praviṣṭair ali-kulaiḥ kṛta-kolāhalam, ali-kula-pakṣa-pavana-preṅkholitaiḥ karṇôtpala-prahāra-bhaya-prakampitair iva maṅgala-pradīpaiḥ prakāśitam, eka-deśa-likhita-stabakita-raktâśoka-taru-tala-bhājâdhijya-cāpena tiryak-kūṇita-netra-tri-bhāgeṇa śaram ṛjū-kurvatā kāma-devenâdhiṣṭhitam, eka-pārśva-nyastena kāñcanâcāma-rukeṇêtara-pārśva-vartinyā ca dānta-śapharuka-dhāriṇyā kanaka-putrikayā sākṣāl Lakṣmyêvôddaṇḍa-puṇḍarīka-hastayā sa-nāthena sôpadhānena sv-āstīrṇena śayanena śobhamānam, śayana-śiro-bhāga-sthitena ca kṛta-kumuda-śobhena kusumâyudha-sāhāyakāyâgatena śaśinêva nidrā-kalaśena rājatena virājamānaṃ vāsa-gṛham.
body.translated_text: At this juncture, as if quenching the reflected image of fire that had migrated to the smooth hollow of her cheek, the bride wept without distortion of expression, showing an overcast day through a shower of tear-drops pure as large pearls. And a great wailing arose from the kinswomen whose eyes were filled with tears. The bridegroom, having completed the full sequence of wedding rites, together with the bride bowed before the parents-in-law. And he entered the bridal chamber—with <s>Rati</s> and <s>Prīti</s> painted as deities on the door-panels, made tumultuous by swarms of bees that had entered first as if from affection, illuminated by auspicious lamps trembling as if from fear of being struck by lotus ear-ornaments and set swaying by the wing-breeze of the bee-swarms; on one side painted with the God of Love seated beneath a blossoming red <s>aśoka</s> tree, his bow strung, one-third of his eye crosswise-narrowed, straightening an arrow, presiding over it; on one side adorned by a golden chowrie and on the other by a golden doll bearing a jeweled fan appearing as <s>Lakṣmī</s> herself with a raised white lotus in hand, making it appear attended; resplendent with a bed well-spread with cushions forming the lordly seat; and also resplendent with a silver sleeping-vessel standing at the head of the bed like the moon arrived to aid <s>Kusumāyudha</s> (Love), creating the beauty of a night-lily—the bridal chamber.

body.text: tatra ca hrītāyā nava-vadhūkāyāḥ parāṅ-mukha-prasuptāyā maṇi-bhitti-darpaṇeṣu mukha-pratibimbāni prathamâlāpâkarṇana-kautukâgata-gṛha-devatânanānîva maṇi-gavākṣakeṣu vīkṣamāṇaḥ kṣaṇadāṃ ninye. sthitvā ca śvaśura-kule śīlenâ-mṛtam iva śvaśrū-hṛdaye varṣann abhinavâbhinavôpacārair a-punar-uktāny ānandamayāni daśa dināni, dattvā ca rāja-dauvārikam iva rāja-kule raṇaraṇakaṃ yautaka-niveditānîva śambalāny ā-

children.text: -dāya hṛdayāni sarva-lokasya kathaṃ katham api visarjito nṛpeṇa vadhvā saha sva-deśam agamad iti.
children.translated_text: —somehow, with great difficulty, dismissed by the king, he went with the bride to his own country.

body.translated_text: There, gazing at the face-reflections of the shy new bride who had fallen asleep turned away—reflections appearing in the jeweled wall-mirrors as if the faces of household deities who had come in curiosity to hear the first conversation, appearing in the jeweled lattice-windows—he passed the night. And staying in the father-in-law's house, raining as it were nectar upon the mother-in-law's heart through his character, with ever-new and unrepeated courtesies, he spent ten joyous days. And having given a royal doorkeeper's gift as it were to the royal household, having presented wedding gifts, having received the hearts of all as if they were farewell provisions—

body.text: iti śrī-mahā-kavi-Bāṇa-bhaṭṭa-kṛtau Harṣacarite cakra-varti-janma-varṇanaṃ nāma caturtha ucchvāsaḥ.
body.translated_text: Thus ends the fourth <s>ucchvāsa</s> (chapter) named 'Description of the Birth of the Emperor' in the <s>Harṣacarita</s> composed by the great poet <s>Bāṇabhaṭṭa</s>.

children.text: pañcama ucchvāsaḥ
children.translated_text: Fifth <s>ucchvāsa</s> (chapter)

children.text: niyatir vidhāya puṃsāṃ prathamaṃ sukham upari dāruṇaṃ duḥkham /
children.translated_text: <s>Niyati</s> (Fate), having first bestowed happiness upon men, then heaping upon them terrible suffering,

children.text: kṛtvā lokaṃ taralā taḍid iva vajraṃ nipātayati // 5.1 //
children.translated_text: makes the world tremble and, like lightning, hurls the thunderbolt. // 5.1 //

children.translated_text: <s>Kāla</s> (Time), singular and revolving, brings down great men equally and in multitudes, with utter indifference,

children.translated_text: like an endless force toppling mountains. // 5.2 //

body.text: atha kadā-cid rājā Rājya-vardhanaṃ kavaca-haram āhūya Hūṇān hantuṃ hariṇān iva harir hariṇêśa-kiśoram a-parimita-balânuyātaṃ ciraṃ-tanair amātyair anuraktaiś ca mahā-sāmantaiḥ kṛtvā sâbhisaram uttarā-pathaṃ prāhiṇot.
body.translated_text: Then one day, the king, summoning <s>Rājyavardhana</s>—remover of the enemy's armor—sent him forth on the northern road to slay the <s>Hūṇas</s>, as a lion would send a young lion-cub to slay deer, attended by immeasurable forces, accompanied by long-serving ministers and devoted great feudatories.

body.text: prayāntaṃ ca taṃ devo Harṣaḥ kati-cit prayāṇakāni turaṅgamair anuvavrāja. praviṣṭe ca Kailāsa-prabhā-bhāsinīṃ kakubhaṃ bhrātari vartamāno nave vayasi vikrama-rasânurodhini kesari-śarabha-śārdūla-varāha-bahuleṣu tuṣāra-śailôpakaṇṭheṣûtkaṇṭhamāna-vana-devatā-kaṭâkṣâṃśu-śārita-śarīra-kāntiḥ krīḍan mṛgayāṃ mṛga-locanaḥ katipayāny ahāni bahir eva vyalambata. cakāra câkarṇântâkṛṣṭa-kārmuka-nirgata-bhāsura-bhalla-varṣī svalpīyobhir eva divasair niḥ-śvāpadāny araṇyāni.
body.translated_text: And Lord <s>Harṣa</s> followed his departing brother for several marches on horseback. And when his brother had entered the quarter gleaming with <s>Kailāsa</s>'s radiance, being in the bloom of youth that delights in the passion for valor, in the foothills of the snowy mountains abounding in lions, <s>śarabhas</s>, tigers, and boars, his body's luster sharpened by the side-glances of forest-goddesses eager with longing, the deer-eyed prince amused himself hunting and lingered outside for several days. And showering brilliant <s>bhalla</s> arrows released from his bow drawn to the ear's edge, within just a few days he cleared the forests of all wild beasts.

body.text: ekadā tu vāsateyyās turīye yāme pratyuṣasyêva svapne caṭula-jvālā-puñja-piñjarī-kṛta-sakala-kukubhā dur-nivāreṇa dava-huta-bhujā dahyamānaṃ kesariṇam adrākṣīt. tasminn eva ca dāva-dahane samutsṛjya śāvakān utplutya câtmānaṃ pātayantīṃ siṃhīm apaśyat. āsīc câsya cetasi: "loke hi lohebhyaḥ kaṭhinatarāḥ khalu sneha-mayā bandhana-pāśāḥ yad ākṛṣṭās tiryañco 'py evam ācāranti" iti. prabuddhasya câsya muhur-muhu-

children.text: -r dakṣiṇêtaram akṣi paspande. gātreṣu câkasmād eva vepathur vipaprathe. nir-nimittam evântar-bandhana-sthānāc cacālêva hṛdayam. a-kāraṇād eva câjāyata garīyasī duḥkhâsikā. kim idam iti ca samutpanna-vividha-vikalpa-vimathita-matir apagata-dhṛtiṣ cintā-vana-mita-vadanaḥ stimita-tārakeṇa cakṣuṣā samudbhidyamāna-sthalakamalinī-vanām iva cakāra cakorêkṣaṇaḥ kṣanaṃ kṣoṇīm. ahni ca tasmiñ śūnyenâiva ca cetasā cikrīḍa mṛgayām. ārohati ca harita-haye madhyam ahno bhavanam āgatyôbhayato manda-mandaṃ saṃvāhyamāna-tanu-tāla-vṛntaḥ kṣiti-tala-vitatām ati-śiśira-malayaja-rasa-lava-lulita-vapuṣam indu-dhavalôpadhāna-dhāriṇīṃ vetra-paṭṭikām adhiśayānaḥ sâśaṅka eva tasthau.
children.translated_text: —his left eye throbbed. And suddenly, trembling spread through his limbs. Without cause, his heart seemed to shift from its seat within the chest. And without reason, a most heavy foreboding arose. 'What is this?'—his mind churned by various arising doubts, his composure gone, his face measuring the distance of anxiety, with an eye whose pupil was fixed, the <s>cakora</s>-eyed prince gazed for a moment at the earth as if at a grove of lotuses sprouting from the ground. And on that day, with an empty mind, he went through the motions of hunting. And as the sun ascended to midday, having returned to his quarters, being gently fanned on both sides with slowly waving slender fan-palms, lying upon a cane mat spread on the ground—exceedingly cool with drops of fresh sandalwood-paste, bearing a moon-white pillow—he remained, filled with apprehension.

body.translated_text: One day, however, in the fourth watch of the night at the encampment, at the very break of dawn, in a dream he saw a lion being consumed by an uncontrollable forest fire, its flickering mass of flames making all the directions tawny. And in that very conflagration, he saw a lioness abandoning her cubs, leaping up, and hurling herself into the flames. And in his mind arose the thought: 'In this world, the bonds of affection, though made of love, are indeed harder than iron—since even animals, when drawn by such bonds, behave in this manner.' And when he had awoken, again and again—

body.text: atha dūrād eva lekha-garbhayā nīlī-rāga-mecaka-rucā cīra-cīrikayā racita-muṇḍa-mālakam, śramâtapābhyām āropyamāṇa-kāya-kālimānam, antar-gatena śoka-śikhinā 'ṅgāratām iva nīyamānam, ati-tvarā-gamana-drutatara-padôddhūyamāna-dhūli-rāji-vyājena rāja-vārtā-śravaṇa-kutūhalinyā medinyêvânugamyamānam, abhimukha-pavana-preṅkhat-pravitatôttarīya-paṭa-prānta-vījyamānôbhaya-pārśvam atitvarayā kṛta-pakṣam ivâśu parāpatantam, preryamāṇam iva pṛṣṭhataḥ svāmy-ādeśenâkṛṣyamāṇam iva purastād āyataiḥ śrama-śvāsa-mokṣaiḥ svidyal-lalāṭa-taṭa-ghaṭamāna-pratibimbakena kārya-kautukād apahriyamāṇa-lekham iva bhāsvatā saṃbhrama-bhraṣṭair ivêndriyaiḥ śūnyī-kṛta-śarīram, lekhârpita-prayojana-gauravād iva same 'pi vartmani śūnya-hṛdayatayā skhalantam, kāla-megha-śakalam iva patiṣyato dur-vārtā-vajrasya, dhūma-pallavam iva jvaliṣyataḥ śoka-jvalanasya, bījam iva phaliṣyato duṣ-kṛta-śāler a-nimitta-bhūta-dīrghâdhvagam Kuraṅgaka-nāmānam āyantam adrākṣīt.
body.translated_text: Then, from afar, he beheld arriving—with a shaven head wreathed as if with a garland of skulls by a dark indigo-hued pilgrim-cloth carrying a letter, his body's blackness intensified by exhaustion and sunburn as if being turned to charcoal by an internal fire of grief, as if being followed by the earth itself curious to hear the royal news on the pretext of the dust-trails shaken up by his hastening feet, being fanned on both sides by the outstretched edge of his fluttering upper-garment billowing in the oncoming wind as if given wings by haste and flying swiftly, as if being pushed from behind by his master's command and pulled from the front by the long exhalations of exhaustion, as if his letter were being stolen by the shining reflection produced on his perspiring forehead through the curiosity of the affair, as if his body were emptied by senses scattered in confusion, stumbling on even ground from the emptiness of heart due to the gravity of the letter's purpose—like a fragment of dark cloud portending the thunderbolt of ill tidings, like a wisp of smoke of the conflagration of grief about to blaze, like a seed of the harvest of misfortune about to bear fruit—a long-distance traveler without apparent cause, named <s>Kuraṅgaka</s>, coming toward him.

body.text: dṛṣṭvā ca pūrva-nimitta-paramparâvir-bhāvita-bhītir abhidyata hṛdayena. Kuraṅgakas tu kṛta-praṇāmaḥ samupasṛtya prathamam ānana-lagnaṃ viṣādam upaninye paścāl lekham. taṃ ca devo Harṣaḥ svayam evâdāyâvācayat. lekhârthenâiva ca samaṃ gṛhītvā hṛdayena saṃtāpam avagraha-rūpo 'bhyadhāt:

children.text: "Kuraṅgaka! kiṃ māndyaṃ tātasya?" iti. sa cakṣuṣā bāṣpa-jala-bindubhir mukhena ca khañjâkṣaraiḥ kṣaradbhir yugapad ācacakṣe: "deva! dāha-jvaro mahān" iti. tac câkarṇya sahasā sahasradhêvâsya hṛdayaṃ paphāla. kṛtâcamanaś ca janayitur āyuṣ-kāmo 'parimita-maṇi-kanaka-rajata-jātam ātma-paribarham aśeṣaṃ brāhmaṇasād akarot. abhukta evôccacāla. "dāpaya vājinaḥ paryāṇam" iti ca puraḥ-sthitaṃ śiraḥ-kṛpāṇaṃ bibhrāṇaṃ babhāṇa yuvānam. vepamāna-hṛdayaś ca sa-saṃbhrama-pradhāvita-parivardhakôpanītam āruhya turaṅgam ekāky eva prāvartata.
children.translated_text: '<s>Kuraṅgaka</s>! What is the affliction of my father?' And he, with tear-drops from his eyes and with faltering syllables from his mouth—both flowing simultaneously—reported: 'Your Majesty! A great burning fever.' Hearing that, suddenly his heart burst as if into a thousand pieces. And having performed the water-sipping rite, desiring long life for his father, he gave away to Brahmins all his personal possessions—an immeasurable quantity of gems, gold, and silver—in their entirety. And without having eaten, he rose. 'Have the horses saddled,' he said to a young man standing before him bearing a headsman's sword. And with trembling heart, mounting a horse brought by an attendant who had rushed forth in haste, all alone he set out.

body.translated_text: And seeing him, his fear aroused by the succession of prior omens, his heart seemed to split open. <s>Kuraṅgaka</s>, having bowed, approached and first conveyed the sorrow clinging to his face, and afterward the letter. And Lord <s>Harṣa</s>, taking it himself, read it. And together with the meaning of the letter, grasping grief along with his heart, he contained himself in the form of self-restraint and spoke:

body.text: a-kāṇḍa-prayāṇa-saṃjñā-śaṅkha-kṣubhitaṃ tu saṃbhramāt sajjī-bhūtam udbhūta-mukhara-khura-rava-bharita-sakala-bhuvana-vivaram āgatyâgatya sarvābhyo digbhyo dhāvamānam aśvo 'yam aḍhaukata. prasthitasya câsya pradakṣiṇêtaraṃ prayānto vināśam upasthitaṃ rāja-siṃhasya hariṇāḥ prakaṭayāṃ-babhūvuḥ. a-śiśira-raśmi-maṇḍalâbhimukhaś ca hṛdayam avadārayann iva dāva-śuṣke dāruṇi dāruṇaṃ rarāṇa vāyasaḥ. kajjala-maya iva bahu-divasam upacita-bahala-mala-paṭala-malinita-tanur abhimukham ājagāma śikhi-picchālâñchano nagnâṭakaḥ. dur-nimittair an-abhinandyamāna-gamanaś ca nitarām aśaṅkata. hṛdayena pitṛ-snehâhita-mradimnā ca tat tad upekṣamāṇas turaṅgama-skandha-baddha-lakṣyaṃ cakṣur a-vicalaṃ dadhāno duḥkham avasita-hasita-saṃkathas tūṣṇīṃ-bhūtena bhūpāla-lokenânugamyamāno bahu-yojana-saṃpiṇḍitam adhvānam ekenâivâhnā samalaṅghayat.
body.translated_text: Agitated by the conch-blast signaling the sudden departure, the army made ready in haste—this horse, with the loud clattering of hooves filling every cavity of the world, galloped back and forth running from all directions. And as he set forth, deer crossing to the left of his path made manifest the approaching destruction of the lion among kings. And facing the disc of the sun whose rays give no coolness, a crow cawed harshly on a wood dried by forest-fire, as if rending his heart. A naked ascetic, his body soiled by thick crusts of grime accumulated over many days, as if made of soot, marked with a peacock-feather crest, approached him face to face. And his journey being unwelcomed by these evil omens, he became greatly apprehensive. But with a heart softened by filial love, disregarding each of these signs, keeping his gaze fixed unwaveringly on the shoulder of his steed, his joyful conversation painfully brought to an end, accompanied by the silent company of kings, he crossed in a single day a road of many <s>yojanas</s> compressed into one.

body.translated_text: As the blessed sun sank low, as if grief-stricken upon learning the news of the king's decline, losing its luster—though entreated many times by the affectionate company of princes headed by <s>Bhaṇḍi</s>—he would not eat. And with the road ahead made clear by a chain of villagers seized by the herald going before him, he spent the night riding on.

children.translated_text: On another day, at noon, he reached the military camp—devoid of victory-cries, the sound of instruments having ceased, songs silenced, festivities suspended, bards no longer singing, market-wares no longer displayed—at various places being scratched as it were by the horn-tips of <s>Yama</s>'s buffalo in the form of curling columns of smoke from corner-oblations twisted by the force of the wind, being entangled as it were by the snare-nets of the god of death, with flocks of crows circling overhead announcing the approach of calamity like the iron bells adorning the buffalo of time harshly clanging above—in one place the <s>Ahirbudhnya</s> rite being propitiated by devoted kinsmen laid low in grief, in another the circle of mother-goddesses being appeased by noble youths burning lamps, in another <s>Drāviḍa</s> priests being entreated with offerings of severed heads to invoke the <s>Amardaka</s>, in another <s>Cāṇḍikā</s> being implored by <s>Āndhras</s> tearing open the ramparts of their arms, elsewhere <s>Mahākāla</s> being propitiated by new servants staggering and stupefied from the melting <s>guggulu</s> incense held on their heads, elsewhere a group of the king's intimates engaged in fire-offerings of their own flesh cut with sharpened blades, elsewhere the open sale of human flesh being conducted by well-known young princes—the camp seemed smeared with cremation-ground dust, seized by inauspiciousness, ravaged by demons, swallowed by the <s>Kali</s> age, covered by sheets of sin, plundered by the assaults of <s>Adharma</s>, overrun by the forces of impermanence, claimed by the sports of destiny—as if empty, as if asleep, as if robbed, as if ashamed, as if deceived, as if in a swoon.

And he heard the verse being sung by that very man:

children.translated_text: His heart breaking all the more at that, he gradually approached the royal gate where all entry had been forbidden. Dismounting from his horse, he saw coming out from within the young physician named <s>Suṣeṇa</s>, whose face lacked its usual color, as if his senses had been set loose. Making his salutation, he asked him: "<s>Suṣeṇa</s>! Is there any improvement in my father's condition or not?" He replied: "There is none at present; there might be if he were to see the prince." Slowly advancing, being bowed to by the gatekeepers, he entered the royal palace—where all possessions were being given away, where family deities were being worshipped, where the cooking of the <s>amṛta caru</s> (nectar oblation) had been commenced, where the <s>ṣaḍāhuti</s> (six-offering) fire-ritual was being performed, where trembling <s>dūrvā</s> grass shoots smeared with drops of curdled ghee were being offered, where the <s>Mahāmāyūrī</s> text was being recited, the pacification of the house was being conducted, the protective offering against evil spirits was being completed, where pious Brahmins had begun the chanting of the <s>Saṃhitā</s>, where the <s>Rudraikādaśī</s> was being recited, where the house of <s>Śiva</s> was resounding, where exceedingly pure <s>Śaiva</s> devotees were performing the ablution of <s>Virūpākṣa</s> with a thousand vessels of milk—and where in the courtyard kings sat, not too close, their minds aching from not having obtained an audience with their lord, receiving news through nearby attendants who rushed out from within, for whom bathing, eating, and sleeping had become mere routine, their attire dirty from having abandoned all care for themselves, motionless as if painted, spending night and day—and in the verandahs, with grief-stricken faces forming circles, whispering among themselves—one blaming the physicians' errors, another reciting the characteristics of an incurable disease, another reporting evil dreams, another elaborating ghost-stories, another revealing the predictions of astrologers, another singing of portents, yet another contemplating impermanence and denouncing the world of <s>saṃsāra</s> and condemning the workings of the <s>Kali</s> age, another reproaching fate and railing against <s>Dharma</s> and cursing the royal family deities, another lamenting the fortunes of the afflicted noble youths—thus attended by the outer retinue narrating the dire condition of the king, he entered the royal palace.

body.text: a-virala-bāṣpa-payaḥ-paripluta-locanena pitṛ-parijanena vīkṣyamāṇo vividhâuṣadhi-dravya-drava-gandha-garbham utkvathatāṃ kvāthānāṃ sarpiṣāṃ tailānāṃ ca prapacyamānānāṃ gandham ājighrann avāpa tṛtīyaṃ kakṣyântaram.
body.translated_text: Being gazed upon by his father's attendants, whose eyes were flooded with ceaseless tears, smelling the odors of various medicinal substances, ointments, and fragrances emanating from the boiling decoctions, ghees, and oils being cooked, he reached the third enclosure.

body.translated_text: Seeing him, his mind churned by the first onslaught of grief, he became as if fearful of his own destiny. He thought his father was already dwelling in the city of Death. For a moment he stood as if rejected by his own inner consciousness—shaken off by fortitude, made a field by agitation, emptied of joy, made subject by despair, bearing a heart as if made of fire, carrying senses that reeled as if corrupted by poison, surpassing even the netherworld in darkness, exceeding even the sky in emptiness—he could not find what to do. He touched fear with his heart and the earth with his head.

How much more so when it is personal! What shall I do?"

body.translated_text: Hearing this, with his syllables seized by a rush of tears, drawing a long sigh with great difficulty, he spoke: "My child! I know you love your father and have a very tender heart. In such circumstances, even the wisdom of the wise is bewildered. The affection for kinsmen is exceedingly hard to bear and overwhelms everything. Therefore you should not surrender yourself to grief. Though I burn with a raging, great burning fever, I burn even more from this anxiety about your welfare. Your thinness whittles me like a sharpened blade. My happiness, my kingdom, my dynasty, my life-breath, and my next world all rest in you. As for me, so for all subjects—the sufferings of one like you pain the entire surface of the earth. Those like you do not adorn the lineage of the meritless; you are the fruit of untainted <s>karma</s> accumulated over many lifetimes. Your auspicious marks proclaim sovereignty over all four oceans as if it were already in the palm of your hand. By your very birth I am fulfilled. I have no desire for continued life; it is only deference to the physicians that makes me take medicine. Moreover, my child, parents are but the means for the birth of those like you, who will arise through the merit of all subjects for the protection of the entire earth. Kings have kinsmen in their subjects, not in their blood relatives. So arise! Resume all your duties. And when you have eaten, I too shall myself take my prescribed diet." Thus addressed, the fire of grief blazed up exceedingly in his heart, as if about to consume it. Staying but a moment, by his father

body.translated_text: Escorted by a royal attendant, he went to his own quarters and took a few morsels of food—as if made of smoke since they caused tears to fall, as if made of fire since they generated burning in the heart, as if made of poison since they induced waves of fainting, as if made of great sin since they produced revulsion, as if made of alkali since they brought pain. Rinsing his mouth, he directed the chowrie-bearer: "Go find out how my father fares, and come back." Having gone and returned and told "Sire! The same condition," without even taking betel, with an anxious mind, as the sun was setting, he summoned all the physicians in private and asked with a despairing heart: "What should now be done in this condition?" They informed him: "Sire! Take courage. In just a few days you shall hear that your father has returned to his natural state and recovered."

Soothe the burning, <s>Indumatī</s>! Create delight with water-moist lotuses, <s>Madirāvatī</s>! Bring lotus-stalks, <s>Mālatī</s>! Wave the palm-leaf fan, <s>Āvantikā</s>! Hold my reeling head, <s>Bandhumatī</s>! Support my neck, <s>Dhāraṇikā</s>! Place a cool sprinkled hand on my chest, <s>Kuraṅgavatī</s>! Massage my arms, <s>Balāhikā</s>! Hearing such utterances of his father continuously, with a heart torn asunder, he passed the sorrowfully long night wide awake.

children.translated_text: turned pale. And he could not hold his heart, blinded by grief and as if being torn out. There was in his mind: "Granted, he himself no longer exists, but unlike others, the well-born man does not cause unpleasant, painful words to be heard. And as he has acted in this extremity—by entering the fire, he has made even brighter, like gold of noble nature refined by fire, the family honor of this son of a good house." And he thought again: "But perhaps this is indeed fitting for affection. Was not his master's father his father too? Was not the mother his mother, and we his brothers? Even for another master, lives maintained become causes for shame in this world when that master departs—how much more so for a father who was like nectar to his dependents, a sincere kinsman, never barren in his grace, of well-earned fame. Now it is fitting what he has done in burning himself. For does the glory of one more steadfast, who has stood the test of time, burn? He merely fell into the fire; but we are the ones who are burned. Blessed indeed is he, the foremost among the meritorious! But unfortunate is this very royal family, which has been separated from such a son of the house. Moreover, what great burden of duty remains even for these breaths of mine, what remaining task? What occupation is there, that even now these cruel life-breaths do not cease? What obstacle prevents the heart from splitting into a thousand pieces?" Tormented by grief, he did not go to the royal palace. He abandoned all duties. Falling on his bed, he wrapped himself head and all with his upper garment and lay there.

body.translated_text: At dawn, descending, even though a horse was brought near the palace gate by a groom, he came on foot to his own quarters. There, hastily, to summon his brother, he dispatched one after another swift-riding camel-keepers, fast over long distances. Having washed his face, he did not accept even the toilette offered by his attendants. Of the young princes standing before him in distress, he indistinctly heard the murmur "<s>Rasāyana</s>, <s>Rasāyana</s>." He asked them: "Good sirs! What about <s>Rasāyana</s>?" Asked, they all alike fell silent. Pressed again and again, tormented by grief, they somehow managed to say: "Sire! He has entered the fire." body.translated_text: For indeed, the earth first trembled—as if wishing to go along with her lord—with the entire ring of ancestral mountains swaying. In that interval, as if remembering the churning of <s>Dhānvantari</s>'s ocean, the oceans churned with waves clamorous from mutual collision. Comets rose on the horizons like the disheveled tresses of the directions, horrified at the impending absence of a protector—grotesquely twisted, spread out like peacock-feather crests. The world became grey with the smoke of the life-prolonging fire-oblations begun by the guardians of the quarters, its faces terrified by the comets. On the disc of the sun, whose luster had faded to the tawny hue of a heated iron vessel, someone, as if desiring the life of the king, offered a human sacrifice in the disguise of a terrifying headless <s>kabandha</s> body. The moon appeared with a blazing halo-ring around it, as if a rampart of fire had been constructed out of fear of <s>Svarbhānu</s> (Rāhu) gaping to swallow it. The devoted directions burned as if they had already entered the fire, adorned by the valor of the lord of the earth. The bride of the earth appeared reddened by showers of dripping blood-spray, as if she had donned a crimson-rayed garment to follow her lord in death. The gateways of the directions were shut by curtains of untimely dark clouds—like iron door-panels closed by the world-guardians frightened by the commotion of the king's destruction. The terrible thunderclaps of falling meteors swelled—heart-rending, roaring like sharp drums beaten at the departure of the lord of the dead. Rains of dust, tawny as camel hair, dimmed the radiance of the sun—as if raised from the hoof-hollows of <s>Yama</s>'s approaching buffalo. The rows of jackals howled, gazing upward with unmelodious cries, as if receiving the falling meteors, welcoming the flames of the funeral pyre. In the royal residence, the images of the family deities displayed their disturbance, their parted hair-braids smoking, their disheveled tresses seemingly manifesting grief. Near the throne, a swarm of bees buzzed about in confusion, bearing the agitation of its loosened

body.translated_text: On another day, from the royal palace, rushing toward him came <s>Velā</s> by name, a doorkeeper of <s>Yaśomatī</s>—her ornaments jangling and falling apart from the speed of her gait as if sounding a cry of victory for despair, with the palace geese craning their necks and seeming to ask from afar "What is this? What is this?" at the tinkling of her swaying anklet-ends from her hurried steps, and the house <s>sārasī</s> cranes, whose waist-chains echoed as their broad hips stumbled, seeming to point out the path to her blinded by tears—covering her face with the end of her garment stained red by a smear of blood from her forehead split against a door-panel unseen through her tears, as if covering her face with the hem of a red garment, crying out, dropping her cane-stick like a stream of molten gold from a bracelet melted by the heat of her grief, her upper garment fluttering in the wind from her mouth like a serpent-queen dragging her sloughed skin, her loosened mass of hair—darkest of dark, hanging from her bowed shoulders, tossed by the wind—like a bark garment of <s>tamāla</s> leaves befitting her sorrow, covering her breasts without any coiffure, shaking again and again the shoot of her hand whose palm was swollen, reddened and darkened from beating her breasts, as if scorched by repeatedly wiping away her exceedingly hot tears—as the waterfall of her eyes cascaded, seeming to bathe the people standing near in her reflected cheek-surface for their entry into the fire of grief—darkening the very day with the trembling, darting rays of her restless eye-stars as if burning it with her own sorrow—asking every person she met "Where is the prince? Where is the prince?"—she arrived. Greeted by the dejected eyes of the people, she approached, placed both hands on the floor, and with tears streaming down, as if sprinkling her drying grey lip with streams of the radiance of her teeth, looking downward, she informed him: "My lord! Save her, save her! While your father yet lives, the queen has resolved upon something!"

And there, of the royal queens preparing to die, he heard from afar: "Dear mango tree! Think of yourself, for your mother departs. Dear jasmine-cluster, my child! I go—bid me farewell. Without me, you are henceforth without protector, O sister, pomegranate-vine of the palace! Dear <s>raktāśoka</s>! Forgive me the blows of my feet and the offenses of breaking your ear-ornament sprigs. My little son, young <s>bakula</s> tree of the inner palace, spoiled by the indulgence of wine-gargling! I have seen you. Dear daughter, <s>priyangu</s> vine! Embrace me tightly, for I shall be hard to find. Noble <s>sahakāra</s> tree of the palace-gate! An offering of funeral water must be given—you are my offspring. Brother parrot in the cage! So that you do not forget me—why do you speak? I am going far from you. Dear <s>śārikā</s> bird! May we meet again in dreams. Mother! To whose care shall I entrust the peacock of the house that clings to the path? Mother! This pair of geese is to be cherished like a child—I, of little merit, have not been able to celebrate the wedding-festival of this <s>cakravāka</s> pair. O you who love your mother! Turn back. Dear house-deer! Bring near the <s>sauvidalla</s>-favorite <s>vallakī</s> lute, let me embrace it. <s>Candrasenā</s>! Let a last good look be taken of these people. <s>Bindumatī</s>! This is my final salutation to you. Maid! Release my feet. Noble <s>Kātyāyanikā</s>! Why do you weep? Fate has led me away. Dear old chamberlain! Why do you circumambulate me, an ill-fated woman? Foster-mother! Steady yourself—why do you fall at my feet? Sister! Take me to your neck for the last time—alas, my dear friend <s>Malayavatī</s> was not seen! <s>Kuraṅgavatī</s>! Here is my farewell <s>añjali</s>. <s>Sānumatī</s>! This is my final salutation. <s>Kuvalayavatī</s>! This is my last embrace. Friends! Forgive my quarrels of affection"—such and similar words he heard.

swelling sounds of the wailing household trying to restrain their distraught old kinsmen through gentle entreaties, her heart being carried away by the roaring of the caged lion that sounded like her husband's voice—adorned by her nurse and by her own devotion to her lord, supported by her fainting spell and by an aged woman who had long praised her, embraced by her friend and by her agony that had come together in calamity, surrounded by servants and by a grief that had seized every limb, attended by noble Brahmins and by their great sighs, followed by chamberlains and by sorrows exceedingly old—gazing tearfully even at the royal house-dogs, falling at the feet even of co-wives, bidding farewell even to painted figures, forming an <s>añjali</s> salutation even before the household birds, taking leave even of the animals, embracing even the trees of the palace—he saw his mother.

children.translated_text: Overwhelmed for her younger, beloved son as if seized by the heavy mountain-like force of anguish, sinking as into the netherworld of swoon-blind darkness, overcome by a flood of tears—as if by a store of affection long suppressed and now bursting forth in full—though she tried, she could not stop the rising of tears. With the unbearable intent of her grief made manifest by the trembling of her swelling breasts, her throat faltering as it was seized by sobs, her lower lip quivering with extraordinary agitation, her nostrils compressed by repeated throbbing, closing her eyes, flooding her spotless cheeks with a deluge of tears, covering with the hem of her thin garment—through which a clear stream of tears seeped, latticed by the rays of her fingernails—her slightly upturned moon-like face, her mind anguished, her breasts flowing with milk, remembering all of his infancy from the day of his birth when he lay in her lap, her heart gone to her kinsmen's house, she cried out again and again: 'Mother, Father! Do not behold this sinful one, setting out for the other world, so utterly grief-stricken!' calling to her parents; 'Alas, my child! You have not been seen by one whose fortune has expired!' crying out for her dearest, eldest son who was absent; 'She has become without a protector!' mourning her daughter living in her father-in-law's household; 'Merciless one! What wrong has this person done to you?' reproaching fate; 'There is no married woman as wretched in her share of sorrow as I!' blaming herself in manifold ways; 'I have been robbed by you, O cruel Death!' upbraiding Death at an untimely hour—she wept aloud with unrestrained throat for a very long time, like an ordinary woman.

body.translated_text: From a distance, his gaze filling with tears, he rushed forward: "Mother! Are you then abandoning me, this wretch of little merit? Be gracious! Turn back!" Even as he spoke these words, his crest being kissed, as it were affectionately, by the rays of her anklet-gems, he fell at her feet. But Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s>, while he lay thus with his sinful head bowed, his mind distraught—

Kailāsa-kalpe pravasati jīvêśvare jarat-tṛṇa-kaṇikā-laghīyasi jīvite lobha iti kva ghaṭate? api ca jīvantīm api māṃ nara-pati-maraṇâvadhīraṇa-mahā-pātakinīṃ na sprakṣyanti putra! putra-rājya-sukhāni. duḥkha-dagdhānāṃ ca bhūtir a-maṅgalā câ-praśastā ca nir-upayogā ca bhavati. vatsa! viśvastānāṃ yaśasā sthātum icchāmi loke na vapuṣā. tad aham eva tvāṃ tāvat tāta! prasādayāmi na punar manoratha-prātikūlyena kad-arthanīyâsmi." ity uktvā pādayor apatat.
children.translated_text: she stood, sighing deeply again and again, and said: 'My child! It is not that you are not dear, or without virtues, or deserving of abandonment. Along with my milk, you drank my very heart. And at this time, the veil of abundant lordly grace prevents my eyes from seeing you clearly. Moreover, my son! I am not the heartless <s>Lakṣmī</s> (Fortune), ever novel in her eagerness to gaze upon other men, a mere instrument of sovereignty, nor am I <s>Kṣamā</s> (Forbearance). I am a wife of noble family, whose sole wealth is her virtue, born in a family white with <s>dharma</s>. Have you forgotten that I am the wife of one fierce in a hundred battles, a man of supreme might, the consort of a lion as a lioness? One such as I—born of heroes, wife of a hero, mother of heroes—purchased by the price of valor, how could she act otherwise? By your father, of such a kind—comparable to <s>Bharata</s>, <s>Bhagīratha</s>, and <s>Nābhāga</s>, the foremost of kings—my hand was taken. His feet I served with my head, worshipped with the consecration-ablution from golden pitchers brought by the wives of countless feudatory lords bustling in attendance. The honor of the coronation as chief queen, difficult to attain even in desire, was won by my forehead. My breasts were suckled by sons such as you, bearing garments of Chinese silk fluttering in the breeze of fly-whisks waved by crowds of captive enemy queens. Upon the heads of my co-wives was placed my pair of feet, worshipped with the garland of crest-rubies of all the wives of the army-camp bowing in homage. Thus with all my limbs fulfilled, what more do I, whose merit is exhausted, desire? I wish to die as one still unwedded to widowhood. And I cannot, bereft of my noble husband, make meaningless lamentations like <s>Rati</s> when her lord was burnt. Like the dust of your father's feet, being first to announce his ascent to heaven, I shall be honored among the celestial women who love heroes. And what will the fire burn of me who am already burnt by the sight of freshly witnessed terrible grief? And for me, death at this moment is more courageous than life. Exceedingly gentle is this fire compared to the fire of grief for my husband, fueled by inexhaustible love. When my lord of life has departed to a realm resembling <s>Kailāsa</s>, how can there be attachment to a life lighter than a withered blade of grass? Moreover, even if I live, my son, the merits of sons, kingdom, and happiness will not touch me, a great sinner for having ignored a king's death. And the prosperity of those burnt by grief is inauspicious, unpromising, and useless. My child! I wish to remain in the world through fame trusted by the faithful, not through my body. So I myself first beseech you, my dear! Do not torment me by opposing my heart's desire.' Having said this, she fell at his feet.

body.translated_text: And when the surge of grief had subsided, she lovingly raised up her son. With her hand she wiped the gaze of her weeping son—his tears heaped upon the fringe of his lashes, streaming ever more abundantly as if melting. She herself too, wiping again and again her own eyes that kept filling up—their whiteness being absorbed by an intense, deep red hue, their rims simmering and overflowing with tears, their lashes flecked with fine white drops, ceaselessly streaming with a succession of the finest tear-drops—and drawing up to the tip of her ear the tendril of hair hanging limp with grief from her tear-dampened cheek, and pushing aside the disheveled mass of hair that had slipped across her forehead tangled with loose strands drooping down, and lifting with her hand her breast-cloth that had slipped somewhat, moist and filled with the flow of tears, and washing her lotus-face with the milk streaming from her breast—white as the outpouring from the beak of a royal swan of silver, bereft of the charm-key marked with delicate copper-red lines of the submerged cloth-hem shimmering with the lattice of nail-rays—and drying her hands on the clean fold of a cloth held by the attendants who were mute with sorrow, fixing her quiet pair of eyes upon her son's face, for a long time

children.text: sa tu sa-saṃbhramam apanīya caraṇa-yugalam avanamita-tanur ubhaya-kara-vidhṛta-vapuṣam avani-tala-gata-śirasam udanamayan mātaram. dur-nivāratāṃ ca śucaḥ samavadhārya kula-yoṣid-ucitāṃ ca tām eva śreyasīṃ manyamānaḥ kriyāṃ kṛta-niścayāṃ ca tāṃ jñātvā tūṣṇīm adho-mukho 'bhavat.
children.translated_text: But he, in agitation, drew away his pair of feet, and bending low, raised up his mother who held her body with both hands and whose head was on the ground. Understanding the irresistible nature of grief, and considering that very act to be the noblest one befitting a woman of good family, and knowing her resolve to be firm, he fell silent with downcast face.

children.translated_text: even when anxious with love, noble birth approves what befits the time and place. And Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s>, embracing him and smelling his head, went out on foot from the inner apartments, as if obstructed by the directions filled with the echoes of the citizens' cries, and proceeded to the bank of the <s>Sarasvatī</s>. There, having worshipped the glorious fire with glances timid by womanly nature, like clusters of red lotuses in bloom, like a lunar form she entered the fire, as the moon enters the sun. The other one too (<s>Harṣa</s>), overwhelmed by his mother's death, surrounded by his kinsmen, went to his father's side. He saw his father with barely remaining life-breath, his pupils rolling, like the king of stars wishing to set. And seized by an unbearable surge of grief, his composure was abandoned by love. Embracing his lotus-feet—caressed by the garlands of diadems of all proud kings—with tears pure and clear streaming ceaselessly, dissolving as if the luster of his eyes, melting as if the beauty of his face, flowing as if the nectar-essence of his countenance, like a great cloud embodied as eyes he rained tears and, with cries released unrestrained, wept for a very long time.

children.translated_text: useless for one whose sole pursuit is the accumulation of fame spotless as moonbeams. 'Make the feudatories your own'—this is purposeless for one who has made the world his own by the multitude of his virtues. 'Bear the burden of the kingdom'—this is an unfitting separation for one fit to bear the burden of the three worlds. 'Protect the subjects'—this is a mere restatement for one who has barred the mouths of the quarters with the bolts of his long arms. 'Guard the retainers'—this is a mere appendage for one comparable to the World-Guardians. 'Practice weapons constantly'—what can be commanded to one whose forearms are darkened by the calluses of the bowstring? 'Restrain every form of fickleness'—for one who has conquered his senses even in the freshest youth, my words seem to have no scope. 'Enemies must be utterly destroyed'—this is merely the concern of his inborn splendor itself.' Even as he was speaking thus, the lion among kings closed his eyes, never to open them again, and the scion of the Sun passed away.

body.translated_text: The king, his sight failing, his hearing clinging to the unceasing sound of weeping, recognizing him, said slowly, slowly: 'Son! You should not be thus. For men such as you are not devoid of great fortitude. Great fortitude is the first support of the world, and after that, the rule of a king. Where you stand, the foremost of the resolute, the refuge of all supreme excellence—where is there room for weakness?' 'You are the lamp of the family'—this is like diminishing one whose splendor equals the sun. 'You are a lion among men'—this is like an insult to one whose valor is enhanced by keen wisdom. 'This earth is yours'—this is like a redundancy for one whose sovereignty is proclaimed by his very marks. 'Seize Fortune'—this is contradictory for one already seized by Fortune herself. 'Rule over this world'—this is an inadequate charge for one fit to bear the burden of three worlds. 'Accept the treasury'—this is

body.translated_text: At that very moment, the Sun too was severed from his radiance as if from his life-force. And then, as if ashamed of the offense of his own son (<s>Yama</s>) in stealing the king's life, he turned downward. As if internally scorched by the fire of grief at the king's absence, he grew red. Slowly, slowly, as if following worldly custom for the purpose of asking unwelcome tidings, he descended from the sky. As if wishing to offer to the lord of men
