children.text: -kośeṣu kuśeśayeṣu sphuṭita-dig-vadhū-hṛdaya-rudhira-paṭala-plava iva galite raktâtape, krameṇa ca lokântaram upagatavaty anurāga-śeṣe jāte tejasām adhīśe, gagana-tala-vitanyamāna-bahala-rāga-pāṭalāyāṃ preta-patākāyām iva pravṛttāyāṃ saṃdhyāyāṃ, śava-śibikâlaṃkāra-kṛṣṇa-cāmara-mālāsv iva sphurantīṣu darśana-pratikūlāsu timira-lekhāsu, asitâguru-kāla-kāṣṭhāyāṃ kenâpi citāyām iva racitāyāṃ rajanyāṃ, dantâmala-patra-prasādhita-karṇikāsu kesara-mālā-kalpita-muṇḍa-mālikāsu, anumartum ivôdyatāsu prahasita-mukhīṣu kumuda-lakṣmīṣu, avatarat-tridaśa-vimāna-kiṅkiṇī-kvaṇita iva śrūyamāṇe, śākhi-śikhara-kulāya-līyamāna-śakuni-kula-kūjite, nāka-patha-prasthita-pārthiva-pratyudgata-puru-hūtâtapatra iva pūrvasyāṃ diśi dṛśyamāne candramasi, narêndraḥ svayaṃ samarpita-skandhair gṛhītvā śava-śibikāṃ Śibi-samaḥ sāmantaiḥ pauraiś ca purohita-puraḥsaraiḥ saritaṃ Sarasvatīṃ nītvā nara-pati-samucitāyāṃ citāyāṃ hutâśa-satkriyayā yaśaḥ-śeṣatām anīyata.
children.translated_text: as streaks of darkness appeared, repulsive to the sight, like garlands of black fly-whisks adorning a corpse-bier; as night was fashioned like a funeral pyre of dark aloe-wood and black timber; as the lotuses of the night displayed beauty with their ears adorned by toothbrush-leaf petals and their garlands of filaments arranged like rosaries of skulls, as if rising to follow in death with smiling faces; as the cooing of flocks of birds nestled in the nests atop tree-branches was heard, like the tinkling of bells on the descending chariots of the gods; as the moon appeared in the eastern quarter like the white parasol of the thousand-eyed <s>Indra</s> come forth to welcome the departed king on the heavenly path—the young king (<s>Harṣa</s>), shouldering the funeral bier himself, equal to <s>Śibi</s>, accompanied by the feudatories and citizens with the <s>purohita</s> (royal priest) at their head, carried it to the river <s>Sarasvatī</s>, and on a pyre befitting a king, through the sacred rite of fire, he was reduced to a residue of fame alone.

body.translated_text: And thus, as if storing up vast dispassion at the great sovereign's death, the sun's body grew calm; as the radiance-garlanded one entered the cavern of the mountain, as if the heat were being extinguished, dampened by the storm-clouds of tears gathered from the multitude of people; as the world grew red with the glow of the universally tear-reddened eyes of all people; as the day turned dark, as if scorched by the heat of the burning sighs of countless men; as the lotus-pools released their blooms, as if <s>Lakṣmī</s> (Fortune) had set forth to follow the departed king; as the earth grew dark with its shadow turning round, as if darkening from grief for its lord; as the <s>cakravāka</s> birds, mourning and uttering piteous cries, took refuge at the edges of the forests, like grieving householders who had abandoned their families; as the lotuses hid their seed-pods, as if afraid of the breaking of their parasols; as the red sunlight faded, like a flood of blood from the shattered hearts of the quarter-brides; and as gradually the lord of luminaries passed to the other world, with only a residue of his affection remaining, as twilight spread, reddened with the thick color of passion extending across the sky like a banner of the dead;

body.text: devo 'pi Harṣaḥ puñjī-bhūtena sakalenêva jīva-lokena lokena rāja-kula-saṃbaddhenâ-śeṣeṇa śoka-mūkena parivṛto 'ntar-vartinâpi śokânala-taptena sneha-draveṇa bahir iva sicyamāno nirvyavadhānāyāṃ dharaṇyām upaviṣṭa eva tāṃ niśīthinīṃ Bhīmarathī-bhīmām akhilāṃ sa-rājako jajāgāra. ajani câsya cetasi tāte dūrī-bhūte saṃpraty etāvān khalu jīva-lokaḥ, lokasya bhagnāḥ panthānaḥ, manorathānāṃ khilī-bhūtāni bhūti-sthānāni, sthagitāny ānandasya dvārāṇi, suptā satya-vāditā, luptā loka-yātrā, vilīnā bāhu-śālitā, pralīnā priyâlāpitā, proṣitāḥ puruṣa-kāra-vihāra-vikārāḥ, samāptā samara-śauṇḍatā, dhvastā para-guṇa-prītiḥ, viśrāntā viśvāsa-bhūmayaḥ, apadāny apadānāni, nir-upayogāni śāstrāṇi, nir-avalambanā vikramâika-rasatā, kathâvaśeṣā viśeṣa-jñatā, dadātu jano jalâñjalim aurjityāya, pratipadyatāṃ pravrajyāṃ prajā-pāla-

children.text: -tā badhnātu vaidhavya-veṇīṃ vara-manuṣyatā, samāśrayatu rāja-śrīr āśrama-padam, paridhattāṃ dhavale vāsasī vasumatī, vahatu valkale vilāsitā, tapasyatu tapo-vaneṣu tejasvitā, prāvṛṇotu cīvare vīratā, kva gamyatāṃ punas tasya kṛte kṛta-jñatayā, kva punaḥ prāpsyati tādṛśān mahā-puruṣa-nirmāṇa-paramâṇūn paramêṣṭhī, śūnyāḥ saṃvṛttā daśa diśo guṇānām, jagaj jātam andhakāraṃ dharmasya, niṣ-phalam adhunā janma śastrôpajīvinām. tātena vinā kutas tyās tādṛśyo divasam asama-samara-rasa-samārabdha-kalaha-kathā-kaṇṭakita-subhaṭa-kapola-bhittayo vīra-goṣṭhyaḥ. api nāma svapne 'pi dṛśyeta dīrgha-rakta-nayanaṃ punas tan-mukha-sarojam, janmântare 'pi punaḥ pariṣvajyeta tal-loha-stambhâbhyadhika-garima-garbhaṃ bhuja-yugalam. lokântare 'pi putrêty ālapataḥ punaḥ punaḥ śrūyeta sā sudhā-rasam udgirantī mathyamāna-kṣīra-sāgarôdgāra-gambhīrā bhāratîti. etāni cânyāni ca cintayata evâsya katham api sā kṣayam iyāya yāminī.
children.translated_text: humanity bind the widow's braid; let royal fortune take refuge in the hermitage; let the earth don white garments; let grace wear bark; let radiance perform austerities in the ascetic groves; let heroism don the mendicant's robe. Where can one go further in gratitude for his sake? Where again will the Creator find such atoms for the fashioning of great souls? The ten directions have become empty of virtues; the world has become darkness for <s>dharma</s>; henceforth the birth of those who live by weapons is fruitless. Without father, whence will come those assemblies of heroes—those daily gatherings whose tales of quarrels begun in the incomparable relish of battle made the cheek-walls of warriors bristle with goosebumps? If only that lotus-face with its long red eyes could be seen again even in a dream; if only that pair of arms, bearing within them a weight surpassing iron pillars, could be embraced again even in another birth; if only that voice—pouring forth nectar, deep as the churning of the milk-ocean—could be heard again and again even in another world, as he calls out 'My son!'" Thinking these and other such thoughts, that night somehow came to an end for him.

body.translated_text: Lord <s>Harṣa</s> too, surrounded by the entire populace, as if heaped into one mass, all connected with the royal household, mute with grief—though the grief-fire's heat was internal, it was as if he were being doused externally by the melting flow of affection—seated on the bare ground, together with his king [title], kept vigil through that entire night, terrible as the river <s>Bhīmarathī</s>. And there arose in his mind: 'Now that father has departed, so much indeed is the world of the living; the paths of the world are broken; the abodes of fortune for one's desires have become barren; the doors of joy are blocked; truthful speech has fallen asleep; the course of the world has been disrupted; the prowess of arms has dissolved; sweet discourse has perished; the sports and transformations of manly enterprise have departed; the intoxication of battle has ended; delight in the virtues of others has been destroyed; the grounds of trust have been exhausted; heroic deeds are now without foundation; scriptures are without purpose; the single passion for valor is without support; discernment survives only as a tale. Let the people offer a water-oblation to energy; let the guardianship of subjects adopt the life of renunciation; let the choicest of

body.text: tataḥ śucêva mukta-kaṇṭham āraṭatsu kṛkavāka-kuleṣu, gṛha-giri-taru- śikharebhyaḥ pātayatsv ātmānaṃ mandira-mayūreṣu, parityakta-nija-nivāseṣu ca vanāya prasthiteṣu patra-ratheṣu, sadyas-tanū-bhūte tāmyati tamasi, mandī-bhūtâtma-sneheṣv a-bhāvam abhilaṣatsu pradīpeṣu, sphurad-aruṇa-kiraṇa-valkala-prāvṛta-vapuṣi pravrajyām iva pratipanne nabhasi, prabhāta-samayena samuttīryamāṇāsu pārthivâsthi-śakala-kalāsv iva kalaviṅka-kaṃdharā-dhūsarāsu tārakāsu, bhū-bhṛd-dhātu-garbha-kumbha-dhāriṣu vividha-saraḥ-sarit-tīrthâbhimukheṣu prasthiteṣu vana-kari-kuleṣu, śāva-śuci-siktha-paṭala-pāṇḍure, piṇḍa ivâpara-payo-nidhi-pulina-parisare, pātyamāne śaśini, krameṇa ca nṛpa-citânala-dhūma-visara-dhūsarī-kṛta-tejasîva, nara-pati-śoka-pāvaka-dāha-kiraṇa-kalaṅka-kālī-kṛta-cetasîva, proṣita-samastântaḥpura-puraṃdhri-mukha-candra-vṛndôdvega-vidrāṇa-vapuṣîva, prathamâstam-ita-rohiṇī-raṇaraṇaka-vimanasîva, câstam-upagate rāja-nikare, rājatîva deve divam ārūḍhe savitari, parivṛtte rājya iva rajanī-prabandhe,

children.text: prabuddha-rāja-haṃsa-maṇḍala-prabodhyamānaḥ paṅkajâkara iva cacāla snānāya devo Harṣaḥ. tataś ca nūpura-rava-virāma-mūka-manda-mandira-haṃseṣu, śokâkula-katipaya-kañcuki-mātrâvaśeṣeṣu śuddhânteṣu, patita-yūthapa iva vana-gaja-yūthe, kakṣyântara-vartini pitṛ-parijane, viṣādiny upari-rudan-niṣādini ca stambha-niṣaṇṇe, niṣpanda-mande rāja-kuñjare, mandurā-pālakâkranda-kathite câjira-bhāji, rāja-vājini viśrānta-jaya-śabda-kalakale ca śūnye ca mahā-sthāna-maṇḍape dahyamāna-dṛṣṭir nirjagāma rāja-kulāt. agāc ca Sarasvatī-tīram. tasyāṃ snātvā pitre dadāv udakam. apasnātaś câ-niṣpīḍita-maulir eva paridhāyôdgamanīya-dukūla-vāsasī niḥśvāsa-paro nir-ātapatro nir-utsāraṇaḥ samupanīte 'pi saptau caraṇābhyām eva nāsâgrâsaktena rakta-tāmarasa-tāmreṇa cakṣuṣā hṛdayâvaśeṣasyâpi pitur dāha-śaṅkayā śokâgnim iva udgirann a-tāmbūlasyâpi sucira-prakṣālitasya kalpa-taru-kisalaya-komalasyêva sva-bhāva-pāṭalasyâdharasyâdhara-pallavasya prabhayā māṃsa-rudhira-kavalān iva hṛdayâbhighātād udvamann uṣṇa-niḥśvāsa-mokṣair bhavanam ājagāma.
children.translated_text: as if the collection of kings had set, as if the sun had ascended to heaven like the divine king, as if the succession of nights had turned like the kingdom—like a lotus-pond being awakened by the circle of awakened royal swans, Lord <s>Harṣa</s> stirred for his bath. Then, with the palace-swans silent and sluggish in the absence of the sound of anklet-bells, with the inner apartments reduced to only a few grief-stricken chamberlains, like a herd of forest elephants that has lost its leader, with the retinue of his father standing in the inner courtyard, with the royal elephant seated against a pillar—dispirited above, weeping with the <s>niṣāda</s> (mahout) below—sluggish and motionless, with the royal horse standing in the open courtyard whose story was told by the wailing of the stable-keeper, with the great assembly-hall empty, its tumult of cries of 'Victory!' silenced—with burning gaze he departed from the royal palace. He went to the bank of the <s>Sarasvatī</s> river. Having bathed in it, he offered water-oblations to his father. And after bathing, without even wringing out his topknot, donning the funerary silk garments, absorbed in sighing, without parasol, without attendants to clear the way, though a palanquin was brought he went on foot, with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose—his eyes red as a crimson lotus—as if belching forth the fire of grief from fear that even the remaining portion of his father in his heart might be consumed, with the radiance of his lower lip—naturally pink, tender as the sprout of a wish-fulfilling tree, even though long-washed and untouched by betel—he appeared as if vomiting morsels of flesh and blood from the blow to his heart, and releasing hot sighs, he came home.

body.translated_text: Then, as the cock-families cried out at full throat as if with grief, as the palace peacocks threw themselves down from the peaks of houses, hills, and trees, as the birds, abandoning their own dwellings, set out for the forest, as the darkness grew suddenly thin and faint, as the lamps—their self-love diminished—longed for extinction, as the sky donned the bark garment of flickering red dawn-rays as if taking to renunciation, as the stars at the time of dawn were setting—pale as fragments of a king's cremation-bones, grey as the throats of <s>kalaviṅka</s> birds—as the herds of forest elephants, bearing vessels from the mineral-caves of the mountains, set out toward the shores and banks of various lakes and rivers, as the moon—pale-white as a slab of fresh pure beeswax, like a lump on the sandy shore of the western ocean—was sinking, and gradually, as if its radiance had been made grey by the spreading mass of smoke from the king's funeral fire, as if its mind had been blackened by the stain of the rays of the burning fire of the king's grief, as if its body had been made to flee by the anxiety of the host of full-moon-faces of the ladies of the departed king's inner apartments, as if dispirited by the jingling of the first-set <s>Rohiṇī</s>,

body.text: rāja-vallabhās tu bhṛtyāḥ suhṛdaḥ sacivāś ca tasminn evâhani nirgatya priyaṃ putra-dāram utsṛjyôdbāṣpair bandhubhir vāryamāṇā api bahu-nṛpa-guṇa-gaṇa-hṛta-hṛdayāḥ ke-cid ātmānaṃ bhṛguṣu babandhuḥ, ke-cit tatrâiva tīrtheṣu tasthuḥ, ke-cid anaśanair āstīrṇa-tṛṇa-kuśā vyathamāna-mānasāḥ śucam asamām aśamayan, ke-cic chalabhā iva vaiśvānaraṃ śokâvega-vivaśā viviśuḥ, ke-cid dāruṇa-duḥkha-dahana-dahyamāna-hṛdayā gṛhīta-vācas tuṣāra-śikhariṇaṃ śaraṇam upāyayuḥ, ke-cid vindhyôpatyakāsu vana-kari-kula-kara-śīkarâsāra-sicyamāna-tanavaḥ pallava-śayana-śāyinaḥ saṃtāpam aśamayan, ke-cit saṃnihitān api viṣayān utsṛjya sevā-vimukhāḥ paricchinnaiḥ piṇḍakair aṭavī-bhuvaḥ śūnyā jagṛhuḥ, ke-cit pavanâśanā dharma-dhanā dhamad-dhamanayo munayo babhūvuḥ,

children.text: ke-cid gṛhīta-kāṣāyāḥ kāpilaṃ matam adhijagire giriṣu, ke-cid ācoṭita-cūḍā-maṇiṣu śiraḥsu śaraṇī-kṛta-Dhūrjaṭayo jaṭā jaghaṭire. apare pari-pāṭala-pralamba-cīvarâmbara-saṃvītāḥ svāmy-anurāgam ujjvalaṃ cakruḥ. anye tapo-vana-hariṇa-jihvâñcalôllihyamāna-mūrtayo jarāṃ yayuḥ. a-pare punaḥ pāṇi-pallava-pramṛṣṭair ātāmra-rāgair nayana-puṭaiḥ kamaṇḍalubhiś ca vāri vahanto gṛhīta-vratā muṇḍā viceruḥ.
children.translated_text: some, having taken the ochre robe, adopted the <s>Kāpila</s> (Sāṅkhya) doctrine in the mountains; some, on heads from which the crest-jewels had been struck off, having taken refuge in <s>Dhūrjaṭi</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), donned matted locks. Others, wrapped in garments of long flowing ochre-pink mendicant cloth, made their devotion to the master shine bright. Yet others grew old with their bodies being licked by the tongue-tips of the forest-deer of the hermitage. Still others, their eyes reddened and wiped with the sprouts of their hands, carrying water in water-vessels, having taken vows, wandered about with shaven heads.

body.translated_text: But the king's devoted servants, friends, and ministers, on that very day, having gone out, having abandoned their beloved wives and children, restrained even by weeping kinsmen—their hearts seized by the multitude of the king's virtues—some bound themselves to <s>bhṛgu</s> (cliff-edges), some stood at those very holy bathing places, some, with minds tormented, spread grass and <s>kuśa</s> and through fasting quenched their incomparable grief, some, overpowered by the force of grief, entered the fire like moths, some, their hearts being burned by the fire of terrible suffering, having lost their speech, took refuge in the snowy mountain, some, their bodies sprinkled by the spray from the trunks of forest elephant herds on the slopes of the <s>Vindhya</s>, lying on beds of leaves, quenched their anguish, some, abandoning even the territories that were at hand, turning away from service, took to the empty wilderness-lands subsisting on limited alms, some became sages—subsisting on wind, wealthy only in <s>dharma</s>, their veins throbbing [with ascetic fire],

body.text: devam api Harṣaṃ tad-avasthaṃ pitṛ-śoka-vihvalī-kṛtam, śriyaṃ śāpa iti, mahīṃ mahā-pātakam iti, rājyaṃ roga iti, bhogān bhuj-aṅgā iti, nilayaṃ niraya iti, bandhuṃ bandhanam iti, jīvitam a-yaśa iti, dehaṃ droha iti, kalyatāṃ kalaṅka iti, āyur a-puṇya-phalam iti, āhāraṃ viṣam iti, viṣam a-mṛtam iti, candanaṃ dahana iti, kāmaṃ krakaca iti, hṛdaya-sphoṭanam abhyudaya iti ca manyamānam, sarvāsu kriyāsu vimukham, pitṛ-pitāmaha-parigrahâgatāś ciraṃ-tanāḥ kula-putrāḥ, vaṃśa-kramâhita-gauravāś ca grāhya-giro guravaḥ, śruti-smṛtîtihāsa-viśāradāś ca jarad-dvi-jātayaḥ, śrutâbhijana-śīla-śālino mūrdhâbhiṣiktāś câmātyā rājāno, yathāvad-adhigatâtma-tattvāś ca saṃstutā maskariṇaḥ, sama-duḥkha-sukhāś ca munayaḥ, saṃsārâsāratva-kathana-kuśalā brahma-vādinaḥ, śokâpanayana-nipuṇāś ca paurāṇikāḥ paryavārayan.
body.translated_text: And Lord <s>Harṣa</s> himself, in that state—overwhelmed by grief for his father, regarding prosperity as a curse, the earth as a great sin, kingship as a disease, pleasures as serpents, home as hell, kinsmen as bondage, life as infamy, the body as treachery, well-being as a stain, lifespan as the fruit of demerit, food as poison, poison as nectar, sandalwood as fire, desire as a saw, and the bursting of the heart as good fortune—turning away from all activities, was surrounded by long-serving family sons who had come through the care of his father and grandfather; by venerable <s>gurus</s> whose authority was established through the succession of the dynasty, whose words were to be heeded; by aged twice-born men learned in the <s>Śrutis</s>, <s>Smṛtis</s>, and <s>Itihāsas</s>; by anointed ministers and kings distinguished in learning, noble birth, and character; by esteemed ascetics who had truly realized the nature of the self; by sages who shared equally in sorrow and joy; by expounders of <s>Brahman</s> skilled in describing the worthlessness of worldly existence; and by narrators of the <s>Purāṇas</s> expert in the dispelling of grief.

body.text: a-svatantrī-kṛtaś ca tair manasâpi nâlabhata śokânupravaṇam ācaritum. pracura-mitrânunīyamānaś ca sanābhibhiḥ kathaṃ katham apy āhārâdikāsu kriyāsv ābhimukhyam abhajata. bhrātṛ-gata-hṛdayaś câcintayat: "api nāma tātasya maraṇaṃ mahā-pralaya-sadṛśam idam upaśrutya āryo bāṣpa-jala-snāto na gṛhṇīyād valkale. nâśrayed vā rāja-rṣir āśrama-padam. na viśed vā puruṣa-siṃho giri-guhām. aśru-salila-nirbhara-bharita-nayana-nalina-yugalo vā paśyed a-nāthāṃ pṛthivīm. prathama-vyasana-viṣama-vihvalaḥ smared ātmānaṃ vā puruṣôttamaḥ. a-nityatayā janita-vairāgyo vā na

Has anyone ever had, or will anyone ever have, such a bodily stature—tall as a golden palm tree? And such a great face-lotus, blooming upward toward the day like the sun's beloved? Who else is so proud, so valiant, so generous?" Thinking these and other such thoughts, his heart eager for a meeting, watching for the arrival of his brother, he somehow endured.

body.translated_text: And made unfree by them, he could not even in his mind follow the inclination of grief. And being gradually consoled by his abundant friends and blood-relatives, he somehow turned his attention to eating and other activities. And with trembling heart, he asked a certain man who was entering with an especially hurried pace: "Friend! Tell me. Has my noble brother arrived?" He said softly: "Your Majesty! As you surmise—at the gate." And hearing this, his mind softened by the boundless tenderness stored in his love for his own brother, he somehow did not give up his life along with the flood of tears that welled up.

body.translated_text: Then, when the twice-born had eaten the first <s>preta-piṇḍa</s> (funerary rice-ball) offering, when the distressing days of impurity had passed, when the paraphernalia near the king—beds, seats, chowries, parasols, vessels, palm-leaf manuscripts, weapons, and the like—was being given to the Brahmins, burning the eyes [with grief], when the bones had been taken to the holy places together with the hearts of the people, when the funeral-pyre monument had been marked with its cairn—a <s>caitya</s> (memorial) plastered with lime, the arrow of grief planted within it—when the great war-elephant, the conqueror of many battles, had been released to the forest, and gradually, as the wailings grew faint, as the lamentations became sparse, as the tears subsided, as the sighs grew slack, as the syllables of "Alas! How cruel!" became indistinct, as the beds of mourning were being removed, as the ears became capable of hearing counsel, as the hearts became fit for the attention of persuasion, as the king's virtues became something to enumerate, as grief took on a regional character, as poetic elegies had been composed, and when the king had come to exist only in dreams as a vision, only in the heart as a dwelling, only in portraits as a form, only in poems as a name—Lord <s>Harṣa</s>, one day, having set aside his duties, saw himself being surrounded by a great crowd of people, led by the assembled mass of elderly kinsmen, approaching silently with heads bowed and faces mute,

children.translated_text: shadowless; like a quarter of the sky empty with the departure of its guardian elephant; like a mountain trembling, split by the blow of a mighty thunderbolt; as if purchased by emaciation, as if enslaved by compassion, as if made a servant by despondency, as if made a pupil by pitiableness, as if blinded by affliction, as if made mute by silence, as if crushed by torment, as if steamed by anguish, as if gathered up by anxiety, as if plundered by lamentation, as if seized by dispassion, as if rejected by reflection, as if scorned by wisdom, as if kept at a distance by its unconquerability—devoured by a grief that was beyond the awakening of the aged-wise, beyond the remedy of well-spoken words, beyond the reach of the instructions of elders, beyond the power of scriptural authority, beyond the path of the efforts of intellect, beyond the scope of the entreaties of friends, beyond the domain of sensory enjoyments, beyond the ground of accumulations of time's gradual course—he beheld his elder brother. And as if his body were being tossed upward by the entire bundle of sprouts of affection surging forth in his agitation, he rose involuntarily.

body.translated_text: And immediately, as if announced by the wailing that had entered first, released by the gate-keepers like a forerunner of the retinue—surrounded by attendants whose numbers had been stolen by the haste of the long rapid journey, with the parasol-bearer fallen behind, the garment-carrier trailing, the water-vessel bearer having stumbled, the spittoon-bearer having dropped away, the betel-server fainting, the sword-bearer limping, consisting mostly of only a few visible servants, their bodies dark and gaunt from many days without bathing, eating, or sleeping; as if being given refuge by the shelterless earth that had gradually arrived, having turned his body grey by the incessant road-dust; his body made motley by long white bandages binding the arrow-wounds from the battle of victory over the <s>Hūṇas</s>, as if by the sidelong glances of the approaching royal <s>Lakṣmī</s>; as if announcing the weight of sorrow through his extremely emaciated limbs—their flesh offered as it were in the grief-fire for the purpose of saving the life of the lord of the earth; bearing as it were embodied grief mounted upon his head, now bare of its crest-jewel, with disheveled and soiled locks, its diadem gone; marked by the surface of his forehead which seemed to weep with lines of sweat melted by the heat, longing to fall at his father's feet; ceaselessly sprinkling the earth with a copious stream of tear-water as if it had fainted from the death of its beloved lord; bearing cheeks as if hollowed out by the ceaseless falling stream of endless continuous tears, worn thin by grief; marked by the disc of his lower lip from which the betel-stain seemed to flow and melt through the passage of his exceedingly hot breath; bearing the region of his ear which was darkened by the sapphire-blue rays of the ear-ornament reduced to a mere stud, as if scorched by the great fire of grief born from the recently heard news of his father's death; marked by the face-moon darkened as it were by the grief-grown stubble, studded with garlands of dark-blue pupil-rays from downcast, fixed eyes whose expression, though not clearly manifest, was evident; body.translated_text: Then, seeing him from afar, Lord <s>Rājyavardhana</s>, wishing to release the flood of tears long suppressed, as if encompassing all sorrows with his pair of arm-staffs extended very far, grasping him by the neck, placing him now upon his fallen, emaciated chest with its garments slipped down, now upon his neck, now upon his shoulder, now in the hollow of his cheek—wept in such a manner that the hearts of all seemed to split open as if their bonds were being torn asunder. He released his voice in full-throated lamentation. Streams of tears flowed as if from veins in the eyes. The people, remembering the king, and even the king's favorite—echoing like a reverberation—wept unrestrainedly. And after a very long time, somehow, having discharged the water of his eyes like <s>Parjanya</s> (the rain-god) in autumn, he subsided of his own accord. And having sat down, with the water brought by an attendant, with the clusters of his trembling fingernail-rays creating as it were a line of foam upon the great water-flood, his vision still stolen by the faint opening of eyelids upon which clusters of tear-drops clinging to the lash-tips still gathered, he somehow washed his eyes. And with a cloth presented by the betel-server, he wiped his face—hot with exceedingly warm tears, burned as it were—as if with a fragment of moonlight-cloth. And having stood in silence for a long time, he rose and went to the bathing-place. And there, standing, pressing out the ornaments, his crown with its locks disheveled and scattered in alarm, with residual indignation still trembling—

Savidha-viraha-vyādhi-vidhura-vadhū-bādhyamānaṃ babandha bandhāv iva vibuddha-bandhūka-bhāsi bhāsvati sâsrāṃ dṛśaṃ cakra-vāka-cakra-vālam. saṃcarantyāḥ sa-madhu-kara-ravaṃ kairavâkaraṃ kalahaṃsa-ramaṇī-ramaṇīyaṃ māṇikya-kāñcī-kiṅkiṇī-jālam ivâcakāṇa śriyaḥ. prakaṭa-kalaṅkam udayamānaṃ viśaṅkaṭa-viṣāṇôtkīrṇa-paṅka-saṃkara-śaṅkara-barkura-śakvara-kakud-a-kūṭa-saṃkāśam akāśatâkāśe śaśâṅka-maṇḍalam.
body.translated_text: Lord <s>Harṣa</s> too, having bathed in the same manner, his form placed upon a cushion spread on the ground not far from him, sat nearby in silence. Gazing again and again at his elder brother whose mind was anguished, his own heart seemed to split into a thousand pieces. For the sight of one's own [kin] is the very youth of grief. And for the people, that day was more terrible even than the day of the king's death. In the entire city, no one cooked, no one bathed, no one ate. Everywhere, everyone wept. And only by this course did the day pass. And the sun—as if fashioned anew by <s>Tvaṣṭṛ</s>'s chisel, as if disgorging thick blood, its hue red as fresh flesh-cuttings—sank into the ocean of the farther shore, ruddy as <s>mañjiṣṭhā</s> (madder), the ruddy charioteer of the dawn. The swarm of bees made wretched by the closing <s>kamalinī</s> (lotus) buds swooned in the lotus-lake. As if stricken by the illness of separation from its companion, the flock of <s>cakravāka</s> (ruddy sheldrake) pairs bound a tearful gaze upon the radiant setting sun, glowing like awakened <s>bandhūka</s> flowers, as if upon fetters. The radiance of <s>Śrī</s> (Fortune), moving about, resounded with the humming of bees through the night-lily beds, lovely with <s>kalahaṃsa</s> (swan) maidens, like a tinkling girdle of ruby bells. The orb of the moon, with its stain plainly visible, rose in the sky—resembling the hump-peak of a terrifying bull of <s>Śaṃkara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) scratched by wide-set horns and smeared with mud.

children.translated_text: '—what is it that this heart of mine, forced into cruelty by the workings of fate, wishes to say to you? The perverseness that is easily found in boyhood, running counter to love, should not be resorted to. Like a servant, do not create an obstacle to what I desire. Listen—surely you know the ways of the world. When <s>Māṃdhātā</s>, protector of the three worlds, died, was not the kingdom carried on by <s>Purukutsa</s>? Or by <s>Raghu</s> when <s>Dilīpa</s> died, at whose arching eyebrow-creeper the eighteen island-continents were commanded? Or by <s>Rāma</s> when <s>Daśaratha</s> died, upon whose chariot in the midst of the great demon-battle the gods rode? Or by <s>Bharata</s> when <s>Duṣyanta</s> died, who had reduced the four oceans to puddles? Let those stand. By our own father's father—of well-known name, who in a lifespan grey with the spreading smoke of a hundred and more sacrifices performed by our father—when that grandfather had gone to the other world, was not the kingdom administered? And him whom grief overpowers, the learned call a coward. For women are the proper domain of sorrows. Yet what can I do? It is this nature of mine—whether it be cowardice or effeminacy—that I have become such a dwelling-place of the fire of grief for my father. For when the lord of the earth perished, my tears flowed out entirely like mountain-streams; when that great radiance set, the light of my wisdom was extinguished in a state of darkness for all ten directions; my heart blazed up; as if fearing self-immolation, discrimination does not approach me even in dreams; by the overwhelming anguish, all my fortitude has melted like lac; at every step, my mind swoons like a doe struck by a poisoned arrow; as if hating men, my memory wanders far away, avoiding me; like a mother, my steadfastness has departed together with my father; like debts lent at usurious interest, my sorrows increase day by day; my body rains down torrents of tears from the eyes, as if filled with clouds born from the accumulation of smoke from the fire of grief. All the five peoples depart to the five elements. The foolish world speaks falsely. Father, even having merely assumed the state of fire, does not burn me so. Rather, it is thus—seizing this heart that seems as if beyond the concerns of the next world, grief has risen up, irrepressible like the submarine fire against the ocean, like a thunderbolt against a mountain, like decay against the moon, like <s>Rāhu</s>

children.text: -yikam iva hṛdayam avaṣṭabhya vyutthitaḥ śoko dur-nivāro vāḍava iva vāri-rāśim, pavir iva parvatam, kṣaya iva kṣapâkaram, Rāhur iva ravim, dahati dārayati tanū-karoti kavalayati ca mām. kāmaṃ na śaknoti me hṛdayaṃ tādṛśasya Sumeru-kalpasya kalpa-mahā-puruṣasya vinipātam aśru-bindubhir eva kevalair ati-vāhayitum. rājye viṣa iva cakorasya me viraktaṃ cakṣuḥ. bahu-mṛta-paṭâvaguṇṭhanāṃ rañjita-raṅgāṃ janaṅgamānām iva vaṃśa-bāhyām an-āryāṃ śriyaṃ tyaktum abhilaṣati me manaḥ. kṣaṇam api dagdha-gṛhe śakunir iva na pārayāmi sthātum. so 'ham icchāmi manasi vāsasîva su-lagnaṃ sneha-malam idam a-malaiḥ śikhari-śikhara-prasravaṇaiḥ sv-accha-sroto-mbubhiḥ prakṣālayitum āśrama-pade. yatas tvam antarita-yauvana-sukhām an-abhimatām api jarām iva Puru-rājñayā guror gṛhāṇa me rājya-cintām. tyakta-sakala-bāla-krīḍena Hariṇêva dīyatām uro Lakṣmyai. parityaktaṃ mayā śastram." ity abhidhāya ca khaḍga-grāhiṇo hastād ādāya nijaṃ nistriṃśam utsasarja dharaṇyām.
children.translated_text: against the sun—it burns me, it splits me, it wastes me, it devours me. Truly, my heart cannot carry the downfall of such a one—equal to <s>Sumeru</s>, a great man of the cosmic age—merely by a few tear-drops alone. My eye has turned away from the kingdom as the <s>cakora</s> bird's from poison. My mind desires to renounce this glory—ignoble, outside the lineage, like the wealth of itinerant performers who cover themselves with the cloths of the many dead and paint the stage. I cannot bear to remain even for a moment, like a bird in a burning house. Therefore I wish to wash away this stain of attachment, clinging firmly to my mind as to a garment, with the pure, crystal-clear waters of mountain-peak streams at a hermitage. Therefore, by the command of your elder, accept from me the burden of the kingdom, as <s>Puru</s> accepted from the king's order the old age that was unwelcome, with the pleasures of youth set aside. Like <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>), who abandoned all the play of childhood, let the chest be given to <s>Lakṣmī</s> (royal fortune). I have renounced weapons.' And having said this, taking his own sword from the hand of the sword-bearer, he cast it upon the ground.

body.translated_text: And at this hour, approached by the chief feudatories whose words could not be gainsaid, he somehow ate without having wished to. And when morning came and all the kings had entered, he addressed Lord <s>Harṣadeva</s> who stood nearby: 'Son! You are the ground for the weighty charges of the elders. Even in childhood, father's mind was grasped by you as if by a banner of virtues. Since you are such an obedient—'

body.text: atha tac chrutvā niśita-śikhena śūlenêvâhataḥ pravidīrṇa-hṛdayo devo Harṣaḥ samacintayat: "kiṃ nu khalu mām antareṇâryaḥ kena-cid a-sahiṣṇunā kiñ-cid grāhitaḥ kupitaḥ syāt. utânayā diśā parīkṣitu-kāmo mām. uta tāta-śoka-janmā cetasaḥ samākṣepo 'yam asya. āho-svid ārya evâyaṃ na bhavati, kiṃ vāryeṇânyad evâbhihitam anyad evâśrāvi

Karmaṇām an-anukūla-samagra-graha-cakra-vāla-vilasitaṃ vā. athavā tāta-vināśa-niḥ-śaṅka-kali-kāla-krīḍitaṃ yenâyaṃ yaḥ kaś-cid iva yat-kiñ-cana-kāriṇaṃ mām a-Puṣpabhūti-vaṃśa-saṃbhūtam iva, a-tāta-tanayam iva, an-ātmânujam iva, a-bhaktam iva, a-dṛṣṭa-doṣam api śrotriyam iva surâpāne, sad-bhṛtyam iva svāmi-drohe saj-janam iva nīcôpasarpaṇe, su-kalatram iva vyabhicāre, ati-duṣkare karmaṇi samādiṣṭavān. tad etat tāvad anurūpaṃ yac chauryônmāda-madirônmatta-samasta-sāmanta-maṇḍala-samudra-mathana-mandare tādṛśi pitari mṛte tapo-vanaṃ vā gamyate valkalāni vā gṛhyante tapāṃsi vā sevyante. yā tu mayi rājâjñā sā dagdhe 'pi dāha-kāriṇī mayy avagraha-glapite dhanvanîvâṅgāra-vṛṣṭiḥ. tad a-sadṛśam idam āryasya. yady api ca vibhur an-abhimānaḥ. dvi-jātir an-eṣaṇaḥ, munir a-roṣaṇaḥ, kapir a-capalaḥ kavir a-matsaraḥ, vaṇig a-taskaraḥ priya-jānir a-kuhanaḥ, sādhur a-daridraḥ, draviṇavān a-khalaḥ, kīnāśo 'n-akṣi-gataḥ, mṛgayur a-hiṃsraḥ, pārāśarī brāhmaṇyaḥ, sevakaḥ sukhī, kitavaḥ kṛta-jñaḥ, parivrāḍ a-bubhukṣuḥ, nṛ-śaṃsaḥ priya-vāk, amātyaḥ satya-vādī, rāja-sūnur a-dur-vinītaś ca jagati dur-labhaḥ, tathâpi mamârya evâcāryaḥ. ko hi nāma tad-vidhe nipatite rāja-gandha-kuñjare janayitari cêdṛśe vi-phalī-kṛta-viśāla-śilā-stambhôru-bhuje bhū-bhuji bhrātari tyakta-rājye jyāyasi nava-vayasi tapo-vanaṃ gacchati sakala-loka-locana-jala-pātâ-pavitraṃ mṛd-golakaṃ vasudhâbhidhānaṃ dhana-mada-khela-nikhila-khala-mukha-vikāra-lakṣaṇâkhyāyamāna-nīcâcaraṇāṃ śrī-saṃjñikāṃ subhaṭa-kuṭumba-karma-kumbha-dāsīṃ caṇḍālo 'pi kāmayeta. katham iva saṃbhāvitam aty-antam an-ucitam idam āryeṇa. kim upalakṣitam an-avadātam idaṃ mayi. kiṃ vâsya cetasaś cyutaḥ Saumitrir vismṛtā vā Vṛkodara-prabhṛtayaḥ. an-ape-
children.translated_text: by my ears emptied of hearing by grief. And the noble one wished to say one thing, but another fell from his mouth. Or perhaps this is fate's device for the destruction of the entire dynasty. Or the beginning of the exhaustion of all my merit. Or the display of an entirely unfavorable conjunction of planets working against my <s>karma</s>. Or perhaps this is the sport of the <s>Kali</s> age, emboldened by my father's death, by which this person has commanded me—as though I were some nobody, as though I were a doer of trivial things, as though I were not born of the <s>Puṣpabhūti</s> lineage, as though I were not my father's son, as though I were not his own brother, as though I were not a devotee—to do an exceedingly difficult task: like a Vedic scholar commanded to drink liquor despite no fault being found, like a faithful servant to treachery against his master, like a gentleman to approach the lowly, like a virtuous wife to adultery. And so this much would be fitting—that when such a father has died, who was like Mount <s>Mandara</s> churning the ocean of the entire feudatory circle intoxicated with the wine of warlike frenzy—one should go to the forest of austerities, or take up bark garments, or practice penances. But this royal command laid upon me burns me even when already burnt, like a rain of embers upon a desert already scorched by drought. This is unworthy of the noble one. Although a lord without pride, a twice-born without greed, a sage without anger, a monkey without fickleness, a poet without envy, a merchant without thievery, a beloved wife without deceit, a good man without poverty, a wealthy man without wickedness, a farmer without disgrace, a hunter without cruelty, a <s>Pārāśarī</s> born of a Brahmin, a servant who is happy, a gambler who is grateful, a wandering ascetic without hunger, a cruel man with pleasant speech, a minister who speaks the truth, and a prince who is not ill-mannered—all these are rare in the world—yet my noble brother alone is my teacher. For who indeed, when such a father—a royal elephant in rut—has fallen, when such an earth-protecting lord with pillar-like thighs of vast stone-arms rendered fruitless lies [dead], when the elder brother has renounced the kingdom and in his youth goes to the forest of penance—who, even an outcast, would desire this clod of earth called the world, purified only by the tears shed from all the world's eyes, this royal fortune whose low behavior is proclaimed by the grimaces on the faces of all the wicked sporting in the intoxication of wealth—a pot-washing slave-girl for the household of warriors? How could the noble one conceive of this utterly improper thing? What impurity has he perceived in me? Or has <s>Saumitri</s> (Lakṣmaṇa) fallen from his mind, or have <s>Vṛkodara</s> (Bhīma) and the others been forgotten? Not

children.text: -kṣita-bhakta-janā svârthâika-niṣpādana-niṣṭhurā nâsīd iyam āryasyêdṛśī prabhaviṣṇutā. api cârye tapo-vanaṃ gate jijīviṣuḥ ko manasâpi mahīṃ dhyāyet. kuliśa-śikhara-khara-nakhara-pracaya-pracaṇḍa-capeṭâpāṭita-matta-mātaṅgôttamâṅga-mada-cchaṭâcchurita-cāru-kesara-bhāra-bhāsvara-mukhe kesariṇi vana-vihārāya vinirgate nivāsaṃ giri-guhāṃ kaḥ pāti pṛṣṭhataḥ. pratāpa-sahāyā hi sattvavantaḥ. kaś capalāṃ rāja-lakṣmīṃ praty anurodho 'yam āryasya yadîyam api na cīvarântarita-kucā kuśa-kusuma-samit-palāśa-pūlikāṃ vahantī tatrâiva tapo-vane vana-mṛgîva nīyate jarā-jālinī. kiṃ vā mamânena vṛthā bahudhā vikalpitena tūṣṇīm evâryam anugamiṣyāmi. guru-vacanâtikrama-kṛtaṃ ca kilbiṣam etat tapo-vane tapa evâpāsyati". Ity avadhārya manasā prathamataraṃ gatas tapo-vanam adho-mukhas tūṣṇīm avātiṣṭhat.
children.translated_text: regarding his devoted people, ruthless only in accomplishing his own purpose—such was not the noble one's power. Moreover, when the noble one has gone to the forest of austerities, who would even in his mind think of ruling the earth while wishing to live? When the lion has gone out for a forest excursion—his face resplendent with the mass of beautiful mane splattered with the rut-fluid of the finest bull elephants whose skulls have been split open by the fierce slaps of the clusters of his sharp nails hard as the tips of a thunderbolt—who guards his cave-dwelling from behind? For the valiant have their prowess as their ally. And what attachment does the noble one have to this fickle royal fortune, if even she, her breasts concealed beneath a bark garment, carrying bundles of <s>kuśa</s> grass, flowers, kindling wood, and <s>palāśa</s> leaves, is not led like a forest doe to that very forest of penance, caught in the net of old age? But why do I uselessly deliberate thus at such length? I shall simply follow the noble one in silence. And the sin of transgressing an elder's command—this penance itself in the forest of austerities will expiate." Having thus resolved in his mind, he who had earlier gone to the forest of austerities stood downcast and silent.

body.translated_text: Then, hearing that, Lord <s>Harṣa</s>, as if struck by a sharpened trident, his heart torn asunder, reflected: 'Has my noble brother perhaps been made angry by someone intolerant, in my absence, made to believe something? Or does he wish to test me in this direction? Or is this a derangement of mind born from the grief of our father? Or perhaps this is not my noble brother at all? Or has the noble one said one thing while something else was heard—

body.text: atrântare pūrvâdiṣṭenâiva rudatā vastra-karmântikena samupasthāpiteṣu valkaleṣu, nir-daya-kara-tala-tāḍana-bhiyêva kvâpi gate hṛdaye, raṭati rāja-straiṇe tāram a-brahmaṇyam ūrdhva-doṣṇi virudati, vipra-jane, pāda-praṇati-pare, phūt-kurvati paura-vṛnde, vidrāti vidruta-cetasi ciraṃtane parijane, parijanâvalambite, gate varṣīyasi, vepamāna-vapuṣi, paryākula-vāsasi, śoka-gadgada-vacasi, vigalita-nayana-payasi, nivāraṇôdyata-manasi, viśati bandhu-varge, nir-āśeṣu nakha-likhita-maṇi-kuṭṭimeṣv avāṅ-mukheṣu, niḥśvasatsu sāmanteṣu, sa-bāla-vṛddhāsu tapo-vanāya prasthitāsu sarvāsu prajāsu sahasâiva praviśya śoka-viklavaḥ prakṣarita-nayana-salilo rājya-śriyaḥ paricārakaḥ Saṃvādako nāma prajñātatamo vimuktâkrandaḥ sadasy ātmānam apātayat.
body.translated_text: Meanwhile, when bark garments had been brought by the weeping textile-worker as previously ordered, when his heart had fled somewhere as if in fear of a merciless slap, when the royal women wailed loudly, when the Brahmin community raised their arms and cried out "Alas, unrighteousness!" bowing at his feet, when the assembly of townspeople exclaimed "Fie!", when the aged, long-serving retainers scattered in distracted minds, when the elders departed supported by attendants—their bodies trembling, their garments disheveled, their words choked with grief, their eyes shedding tears, their minds bent upon restraining him—when the circle of kinsmen entered, when the feudatory lords, heads bowed, faces downward, sat hopeless, scratching the jeweled floor with their nails, sighing, when all the subjects, young and old together, set out for the forest of penance—suddenly, entering in a frenzy of grief, streaming tears from his eyes, a most trusted attendant of <s>Rājyaśrī</s> named <s>Saṃvādaka</s>, letting out a wail, threw himself down in the assembly.

children.translated_text: endurance?" He, somehow managing to speak, said: "Your Majesty! The deeds of base-souled men, like those of ghosts, are generally aimed at vulnerable points. For on that very day when the news spread that the king had passed away, on that very day Lord <s>Grahavarman</s> was made to leave the world of the living along with his merit by the wicked king of <s>Mālava</s>. And the princess <s>Rājyaśrī</s>, her feet kissed by a pair of iron fetters, has been bound like a thief's wife and cast into prison in <s>Kānyakubja</s>. And the rumor is that the evil-minded one, considering the army to be leaderless, intends to seize even this land and is about to march here." When this was reported, the lord's power blazed forth.

body.translated_text: Then, alarmed, Lord <s>Rājyavardhana</s> himself along with his brother questioned him: "Good man! Speak! Speak! children.translated_text: as if awakening his valor which had been put to sleep by the poison of grief, he addressed his younger brother: "Long-lived one! Here is this royal house, here are these kinsmen, here is this retinue, here is this land, and these are the subjects protected by the iron bar of the king's arms. I go this very day for the annihilation of the <s>Mālava</s> royal house. This alone is the wearing of bark garments, this alone is penance, and this alone is the means for the removal of grief—the chastisement of an utterly insolent enemy. This insult of the <s>Puṣpabhūti</s> dynasty by the <s>Mālavas</s> is like deer seizing the mane of a lion, frogs striking a cobra, calves capturing a tiger, water-snakes gripping the throat of <s>Garuḍa</s>, logs commanding fire to burn, darkness obscuring the sun. My anguish is concealed by a greater wrath. Let all the kings and elephants remain here together with you. Let this one man, <s>Bhaṇḍi</s> alone, follow me with a mere ten thousand horses." Having spoken thus, he immediately ordered the march-drum to be sounded.

body.translated_text: Then, hearing such an unignorable, unanticipated, sudden new calamity—from the unprecedented nature of the insult, from the natural intolerance of his character toward the insults of others, from the abundance of pride in fresh youth, from his birth in a field of heroes, and from love for his sister who was the very ground of compassion—that grief, though so deeply rooted, though exceedingly heavy, was destroyed in a single instant. And suddenly, like a lion entering a mountain cave, a fearsome surge of anger entered his deep heart. A terrible frown burst upon his forehead-plate, darkening like the river <s>Yamasvā</s>, its wave-like wrinkles of knitted brows made tremulous with the agitation of <s>Kāliya</s> fearing the approach of <s>Keśiniṣūdana</s> (Kṛṣṇa). His left hand-shoot, touching with its nail-ray waterfalls the crag-like peak of his arm—broad as the frontal globes of the elephants of the directions—performed as it were an anointment for the burden of battle, stroking it in pride. His other hand grasped the terrible sword, which surged up again, its belly filled with streaming sweat-water, as if seizing the hair of the wicked <s>Mālava</s> for his uprooting, trembling as if eager to grasp the tresses of the fortune of the evil. A tawny glow of rage appeared on his cheeks—as if the dust of <s>sindūra</s> shaken by <s>Rājalakṣmī</s> performing an auspicious ceremony, delighted at his grasping the weapon. And his right foot rose upward and mounted his left thigh-staff as if swelling with pride at the thought of trampling the crest-jewels of all approaching kings. His other lotus-foot scratched the jeweled floor, as if a streak of smoke spat out by the harsh grinding of his big toe, like a freed flame-tip intended to depopulate the earth of heroes. If it is because I am young—then all the more I should not be abandoned. If I am to be protected—the cage of your arms is the place of protection. If I am incapable—where have I been tested? If I am to be nurtured—separation diminishes. If I cannot bear hardship—then I am placed on the side of women. If 'let him enjoy comfort'—that great comfort of the road goes only with you, for the fire of separation is more unbearable. If 'let him protect the household'—your fortune dwells in your sword. If 'the rear is empty'—your valor still stands. If 'the kingdom is unattended'—it is well-bound by the noble one's virtues. If 'a great one needs no external ally'—he counts me as something apart, though I am but a small accessory. If 'I depart'—what excessive burden is the dust of your feet? If 'the journey of two is inopportune'—then favor me with the command to go. If 'it is mere weakness of brotherly affection'—that is a fitting fault. body.translated_text: Raising him up, the elder brother spoke again: "Dear one! Why, by insisting on taking up such a vast enterprise, is weight forcibly loaded upon an enemy that is exceedingly light? A lion's full preparation for a deer is excessively humiliating. How many don their armor to set fire to straw? Moreover, for you there remains the earth of eighteen continents—a lotus-pond of eight auspicious signs—as the domain of your valor. For the winds that carry mountain ranges do not gird themselves against a flimsy heap of cotton. Nor do the elephants of the directions, bold in their affection for the ramparts of <s>Sumeru</s>, exert themselves upon a tiny anthill. You shall wield, in the conquest of the horizons, a bow—great comet of the apocalyptic destruction of all earthly kings, its body adorned with vine-patterns of beautiful gold-leaf—like <s>Māṃdhātā</s>. But in this irresistible hunger for the destruction of the enemy that has risen in me, let this one morsel of anger be permitted to the solitary one. Let your lordship remain." Having spoken thus, on that very day he marched out against the enemy.

And most terrible portents, foretelling the destruction of no insignificant king, do not cease even for a moment. Every day <s>Rāhu</s> is seen assailing the disc of the sun as if with an unbroken body like a <s>kabandha</s> (headless torso). The Seven Sages emit belchings of smoke as if disgorging all the planets, turned grey as though swallowed by the time of the destruction of austerities. Day after day, terrible conflagrations of the directions are seen. The host of stars falls from the vault of the sky like a shower of ash-particles from the burning of the directions. The moon is lustreless, as if grieving at the falling of the stars. Night after night, the quarters with their trembling stars behold in the sky what seems a fierce planetary war, with blazing meteors here and there. The wind, indicating a change of kingdom, seems to make the earth move, carrying somewhere a thick veil of dust mixed with hissing gravel fragments. I do not see anything auspicious in the horoscope. In this our dynasty, who can oppose <s>Kṛtānta</s> (Death), who crushes even the tender like an elephant crushing a <s>karīra</s> (caper bush)? In every way, may all be well with my noble brother." Having reflected thus, somehow steadying his heart—which was inwardly broken, anguished with brotherly love, and seemed to be melting—he rose and performed the routine sequence of duties as they were being carried out.

body.translated_text: And while he was in the audience-hall, he suddenly saw entering—followed by a crowd of people with dejected faces filing in after him, his body wrapped in a soiled cloth like a red thread of the smoke of hot sighs of unbearable grief, his face bowed as if from the shame of still being alive, his gaze fastened on the tip of his nose-bridge, his face mute yet announcing his master's calamity through unceasing drops of tears with hair standing on end from far-reaching grief—a man named <s>Kuntala</s>, the chief equerry, <s>Rājyavardhana</s>'s most trusted intimate. And upon seeing him, suspicion arose; and at the moment of hearing the terrible unwelcome news, he was seized simultaneously in all his limbs as if by the world-guardians—in his eyes by water, in the moon of his face by sighing, in his heart by fire, in his lap by the earth. And from him he heard that his brother—who had effortlessly defeated the <s>Mālava</s> army, yet whose trust had been built up by the false courtesies of the lord of <s>Gauḍa</s>—had been slain while alone, unarmed, and unsuspecting, in that very one's own dwelling.

children.translated_text: And hearing this, the supremely radiant one, his surge of grief being kindled by the spreading fire of fierce anger, instantly blazed up. Then, shaking his head with indignation—his body seeming showered with sparks from the shattering fragments of his crest-jewel—as if belching the fire of rage, as if drinking up the lifespans of all radiant beings with his lower lip curled in fury and ceaselessly quivering, showing as it were the conflagration of the directions through the casting of his reddened gaze, stormy with showers of sweat-spray from the fire of rage being burned as it were by the unbearable heat of his innate valor, attended by his own limbs trembling as if frightened by this fury never before witnessed—like <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) having assumed the <s>Bhairava</s> form, like <s>Hari</s> (<s>Viṣṇu</s>) having manifested the <s>Narasiṃha</s> form, like a sun-stone mountain blazing at the sight of the spreading radiance of another, like the day of cosmic dissolution with its form made unbearable by twelve risen suns, like a great portent-wind causing all the mountains of the earth to tremble, like the <s>Vindhya</s> with the height of its body ever increasing, like a great serpent enraged by the oppression of a wicked serpent-king, like <s>Parīkṣit</s> prepared to burn all serpents, like <s>Vṛkodara</s> (<s>Bhīma</s>) thirsting for enemy blood, like the elephant of the gods charging at the rival elephant—as if the first coming of manliness, as if the madness of intoxication, as if the onset of arrogance, as if the youthful incarnation of splendor, as if the total mobilization of pride, as if the dawning age of the heat of youth, as if the royal consecration of the relish of battle, as if the festival-day of intolerance—he attained the utmost terribleness.

Even in merely uttering the name of this evildoer, my tongue seems to be stained with the filth of his sin. But what was it that my noble brother agreed to, by which that base one, entering like a shameless wood-worm, brought to destruction a sandalwood pillar that delighted the entire world? Surely this fool, greedy for the taste of honey, snatching at my noble brother's life as if it were honey, did not foresee the calamity of the swarm of arrows that would fall. By defiling his own house, the vilest of <s>Gauḍa</s> has accumulated nothing but exceedingly foul infamy—like the soot of a lamp placed in the meshes of a net. But even when the sun—the crest-jewel of the three worlds—has set, the moon has been appointed by the Creator for the suppression of darkness, the enemy of the righteous path, as the sole lion sporting in the pleasure-grove of the planetary host. And even when the goad—the enforcer of discipline—is broken, there still exists for the training of the wild elephant the sharp lion's claw, capable of splitting the firm forehead-slabs of all maddened elephants. Such villains, destroyers of precious gems of valor like wicked jesters—are they not deserving of execution by all? Where will the evil-minded one go now?" body.translated_text: And he said: "Setting aside that vilest of <s>Gauḍa</s> lords—who else would thus extinguish such a great soul, one who at that very moment had by genuine arm-valor conquered the entire array of kings, who had laid down his weapons? Like fire born of smoke [killing] one born from a water-pot [i.e., like an ignoble thing destroying a noble one]—by such a death, condemned by the entire world of heroes, has my noble brother been slain. And leaving aside that ignoble one—whose hearts in the lake of whose minds would the virtues of my noble brother's valor not stir to partisanship, like royal swans white as the foam-masses of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>, recalling the prowess of <s>Paraśurāma</s>? How could the rays [hands] of that exceedingly fierce one have extended, unheeding of affection, to take my noble brother's life—like the scorching summer sun drying up the waters of a lotus-pond?

children.translated_text: —with terrifying intervals of the cresting-breaking waves of the horns of <s>Yama</s>'s buffalo; and by common report alone the southern quarter is [his domain], but in truth the furrowed brow of a warrior is <s>Yama</s>'s dwelling-place. And it is a wonder that the manes of heroes in battle, with their lion-roars released, do not burst forth together with the multitude of goose-bumps born from the passion-excitement-thrill of audacity. Only two things are the vessel for the store of wealth gathered from the four oceans—the terrible submarine fire or the heart of a great man. For the radiant one, until all the oceans are attained, how can there be cessation of the innate fire? The lord of serpents, who bears with his body merely a lump of earth, carries in vain the burden of his widely spread great hoods. But the taste of the pleasure of unimpeded dominion and conquest over the earth—only the arms of heroes know it, their forearms blazing with the weight of the trunks of the guardian elephants of the quarters. Like the sun, with his foot-sprouts grasped by the upturned lotus-pools, a hero passes his days in ease, his splendor unbroken. But for the coward—deer-hearted like the moon, pale-backed—how can there be even two nights of steady fortune? The heroic sentiment, blossoming, showers immeasurable heaps of fame. The paths of manliness are cleared ahead by the advancing blaze of valor. The gates of pride are those that cause enemies to flee at the very sound. The directions of heroism are emptied, illuminated by the flash of weapons. Like the earth by a shower of enemy blood-spray, even royal fortune is enamored. Like the row of toenails by the rubbing on the whetstone-edges of the crest-gems of many kings' crowns, even sovereignty grows brilliant. Like the palms of the hands by ceaseless practice of weapons, even the faces of enemies grow dark. Like the body by hundreds of bandages bound on various wounds, even fame grows white. Falling upon the door-panels of enemy chests as upon armor, fierce sword-blows vomit forth even royal fortune like the flame-crest of fire. And he whose kinsman has been slain by the enemy—that spirited man, by striking the chests of the enemy's women, tells the grief of his heart. He breathes with the wind-blast of the fall of the harsh sword-creeper, he weeps with the torrential fall [of blood] of enemies whose breath has been stopped,

children.translated_text: he gives water through the eyes of enemy women—that one is the better, not the other. And the awakened do not bind their kinship-feeling to bodies that are momentary, like those seen in dreams and then lost. The body-consciousness of heroes rests in enduring fame. And like a jewel-lamp whose nature is to blaze ceaselessly with spreading radiance, the murky soot-stain of grief does not touch one who is exceedingly radiant. You are the foremost of the valiant, the first recipient among the wise, the chief of the capable, the vanguard of the noble-born, the leader of the radiant, the first among the impatient. And these chest-door-walls of fine warriors are always at your command—with the fire of anger constantly smoking nearby, easily quenched by the water of the sword's edge, embraced by the shade of their formidable arm-forests, cool resting-grounds for courage. Therefore, what [trouble] is one vile lord of the <s>Gauḍas</s>? Act in such a way that no one else ever behaves thus again. Set the chowries of all the earth's would-be conquerors—whose ambitions of conquest are false, who lust for the allegiance of the whole world—swinging with the sighs of their inner-palace women. Cut short with circles of vultures blinded by the scent of blood their obsessions with the shade of parasols. Remove with the sweat of hot blood the eye-disease of the amorous sidelong glances of the wanton harlot of ill-fortune. Calm with the piercing of sharp arrowheads the swellings of misdirected valor. Uproot with the great medicine of chains of heavy iron fetters the sluggish ailments of feet spoiled by the whim of desiring a footstool. Destroy with the caustic application of the syllables of sharp commands the itching in the ears for the sound of 'Victory.' Remove with the forehead-ointment of the sandalwood-paste of your toenail-rays the affliction of stiff-necked, unbowed, frozen heads. Extract with the pincers of the messages of hand-given tribute the thorns of the evil sport of arrogance feverish with the heat of wealth. Shatter with the lamp-blazes of the radiance of jeweled footstools the darkness of the frown-knots of the bluster of dried-up warriors. Conquer with the health gained by the lightness of foot-trampling that casts down head-gravity the great fever of false pride. Soften with the warmth of cupped palms joined in constant obeisance of service the calluses of the bowstring-marks. And do not forsake that path—coveted by the three worlds—

children.translated_text: Setting aside the grief fit for a coward, seize the royal fortune that comes by hereditary succession, as a lion seizes a doe. Your Majesty! With the king gone to divine state, and with <s>Rājyavardhana</s>'s life devoured by the wicked <s>Gauḍa</s> serpent, in this great cosmic dissolution, for the upholding of the earth—

children.text: -dhāraṇāyâdhunā tvaṃ śeṣaḥ. samāśvāsaya a-śaraṇāḥ prajāḥ. kṣmā-patīnāṃ śiraḥsu śarat-savitêva lalāṭaṃ-tapān prayaccha pāda-nyāsān. a-hitānām abhinava-sevā-dīkṣā-duḥkha-saṃtapta-śvāsa-dhūma-maṇḍalair nakhaṃ-pacaiḥ pracalita-cūḍā-maṇi-cakra-vāla-bālâtapaiś câyāhi kalmāṣa-pādatām. api ca hate pitary ekākī tapasvī mṛgaiḥ saha saṃvardhitaḥ sahaja-brāhmaṇya-mārdava-su-kumāra-manāḥ kṛta-niścayaś caṇḍa-cāpa-vanâṭani-ṭāṅkāra-nāda-nirmadī-kṛta-dig-gajaṃ guñjaj-jyā-jāla-janita-jagaj-jvaraṃ samagram udyatam eka-viṃśati-kṛtvaḥ kṛta-vaṃśam utkhātavān rājanyakaṃ Paraśurāmaḥ, kiṃ punar naisargika-kāya-kārkaśya-kuliśāyamāna-mānaso mānināṃ mūrdhanyo devaḥ. tad adyâiva kṛta-pratijño gṛhāṇa Gauḍâdhipâdhama-jīvita-dhvastaye jīvita-saṃkalanâkula-kālâkāṇḍa-daṇḍa-yātrā-cihna-dhvajaṃ dhanuḥ. na hy ayam a-rāti-rakta-candana-carcā-śiśirôpacāram antareṇa sāmyati paribhavânala-pacyamāna-dehasya devasya duḥkha-dāha-jvara su-dāruṇaḥ. nikāra-saṃtāpa-śānty-upāya-parikṣaye hi hiḍimbā-cumbanâsvāditam iva ripu-rudhirâ-mṛtam a-mandarôpāyam apāyi pavanâtma-jena. Jāmadagnyena ca śāmyan manyu-śikhi-śikhā-saṃjvara-sukhāyamāna-sparśa-śītaleṣu kṣatriya-kṣataja-hradeṣv asnāyi." ity uktvā vyaraṃsīt.
children.translated_text: —you alone now remain, like <s>Śeṣa</s>. Console the unprotected subjects. Like the autumn sun upon the foreheads of kings, bestow the imprint of your feet upon their heads as forehead-scorching marks. Attain the state of mottled feet through those who burn with the anguish of the pain of newly undertaken service, with the smoke of their sighs, and through the young dawn-glows of the circles of their dislodged crest-jewels. Moreover, when his father was slain, alone, an ascetic, raised among deer, with a mind naturally tender from his innate Brahminical softness, having made his resolve, <s>Paraśurāma</s>—with the sound of his fierce bow twanging in the threshing-floor of the forest driving mad the guardian elephants of the quarters, with the trembling net of his bowstring generating a world-fever—uprooted the entire marshaled warrior-class twenty-one times and extinguished the lineage. How much more so the lord, whose mind is naturally hard as diamond from his innate bodily toughness, the crown of the proud? Therefore, this very day, having made your vow, take up the bow—the banner signifying the untimely march of the staff of <s>Kāla</s> (Death), agitating the thread-of-life of the vile lord of the <s>Gauḍas</s>, for the destruction of his life. For this terrible burning-fever of grief in the lord—whose body is being consumed by the fire of humiliation—will not be soothed without the cooling remedy of anointing with the blood-sandalwood-paste of the enemy. For indeed, when the means of pacifying the burning anguish of insult were exhausted, <s>Pavana-ātmaja</s> (the son of the Wind, <s>Bhīma</s>) drank the nectar of enemy blood—tasted first through the kiss of <s>Hiḍimbā</s>—without the need for a <s>Mandara</s>-like remedy. And by <s>Jāmadagnya</s> (<s>Paraśurāma</s>), to cool the fever of the conflagration of his wrath, bathing was done in lakes of warrior-blood cool and soothing to the touch.' Having spoken thus, he fell silent.

body.translated_text: "Your Majesty! Base men, upon whom disgraced Fortune has taken refuge somewhere, do not realize that they are being mocked—just as crows, made filthier by a cuckoo that has become soiled, [fail to notice]. For the defects of Fortune—blindness and the like—are the symptoms of the disease of jaundice. Those of dull wit, their sun obscured by the shade of the parasol, forget any other radiant being. Or what can the wretched one do—he whose back is always turned in cowardice, who has never even seen the faces of angered warriors, blazing with the fire of wrath, their cheeks bristling with goosebumps from the swelling of unsurpassed supreme valor? That wretched one does not know that proud men, when wronged, like black-magic rites, instantly bring about the complete annihilation of an entire clan. Radiant men, even when struck in water, blaze forth. This deed—skilled at causing a fall into the lowest irrecoverable hell—befits only that one who is excluded from every assembly of heroes. For when the bow—the chief treasure of battle—is held by the proud, and when the sword—a pleasure-garden of lotuses for the sport of <s>Kamalā</s>'s (<s>Lakṣmī</s>'s) love-swans—is at hand, the means of the wretched, even such as the churning of the ocean, are nothing for the attainment of <s>Śrī</s> (Fortune)—how much less methods like these! And those whom the Creator has appointed to protect the earth—since the mountains themselves, as if unable, disgorge iron for the sake of striking with arm-bars hard as the thunderbolt—how could such arm-mighty men, kinsmen of spotless fame, contemplate even in thought an unworthy deed? For before the hands of great warriors, blazing with a radiance that overpowers all planetary bodies, the hands of the sun are lame in seizing the directions. The great

body.text: devas tu Harṣas taṃ pratyavādīt: "karaṇīyam evêdam abhihitaṃ mānyena. itarathā hi me gṛhīta-bhuvi bhogi-nāthe 'pi dāyāda-dṛṣṭir īrṣyālor bhujasya. upari gacchatîcchati nigrahāya graha-gaṇe 'pi bhrū-latā calitum. a-namatsu śaileṣv api kaca-graham abhilaṣati dātuṃ karaḥ. tejo-dur-vidagdhān arka-karān api cāmarāṇi grāhayitum īhate hṛdayam. rāja-śabda-ruṣā mṛga-rājānām api śirāṃśi vāñchati pādaḥ pāda-pīṭhī-kartum. svacchanda-loka-pāla-svêcchā-gṛhītānām ākṣepâdeśāya diśām api sphuraty adharaḥ. kiṃ punar īdṛśe dur-jāte jāte jātâmarṣa-nirbhare ca manasi nâsty evâvakāśaḥ śoka-kriyā-karaṇasya? api ca hṛdaya-viṣama-śalye

children.text: musalye jīvati jālme jagad-vigahite Gauḍâdhipâdhama-caṇḍāle jihremi śuṣkâdhara-puṭaḥ poṭêva pratikāra-śūnyaṃ śucā śūt-kartum. a-kṛta-ripu-balâbalâ-vilola-locanôdaka-dur-dinasya me kutaḥ kara-yugalasya jalâñjali-dānam. a-dṛṣṭa-Gauḍâdhama-citā-dhūma-maṇḍalasya vā cakṣuṣaḥ sv-alpam apy aśru-salilam. śrūyatāṃ me pratijñā: "śapāmy āryasyâiva pāda-pāṃsu-sparśena, yadi parigaṇitair eva vāsaraiḥ sakala-cāpa-cāpala-dur-lalita-nara-pati-caraṇa-raṇaraṇāyamāna-nigaḍāṃ nir-Gauḍāṃ gāṃ na karomi tatas tanūnapāti pīta-sarpiṣi pataṅga iva pātakī pātayāmy ātmānam"" ity uktvā ca mahā-saṃdhi-vigrahâdhikṛtam Avantikam antika-stham ādideśa: "likhyatām. ā ravi-ratha-cakra-cīt-kāra-cakita-cāraṇa-mithuna-muktasānôr udayâcalāt, ā Trikūṭa-kaṭaka-kuṭṭāka-ṭaṅka-likhita-Kākutstha-Laṅkā-luṇṭhana-vyatikarāt Suvelāt, ā vāruṇī-mada-skhalita-Varuṇa-vara-nārī-nūpura-rava-mukhara-kuhara-kukṣer asta-gireḥ, ā guhyaka-gehinī-parimala-sugandhi-gandha-pāṣāṇa-vāsita-guhā-gṛhāc ca Gandhamādanāt, sarveṣāṃ rājñāṃ sajjī-kriyantāṃ karāḥ kara-dānāya śastra-grahaṇāya vā, gṛhyantāṃ diśaś cāmarāṇi vā, namantu śirāṃsi dhanūṃṣi vā, karṇa-pūrī-kriyantām ājñā maurvyo vā, śekharī-bhavantu pāda-rajāṃsi śirastrāṇi vā, ghaṭantām añjalayaḥ kari-ghaṭā-bandhā vā, mucyantāṃ bhūmaya iṣavo vā, samālambyantāṃ vetra-yaṣṭayaḥ kunta-yaṣṭayo vā, su-dṛṣṭaḥ kriyatām ātmā mac-caraṇa-nakheṣu kṛpāṇa-darpaṇeṣu vā. parāgato 'ham. paṅgor iva me kuto nivṛttis tāvad yāvan na kṛtaḥ sarva-dvīpântara-saṃcārī sakala-nara-pati-mukuṭa-maṇi-śilâlokamayaḥ pāda-lepaḥ." iti kṛta-niścayaś ca muktâsthāno visarjita-rāja-lokaḥ snānârambhâkāṅkṣī sabhām atyākṣīt. utthāya ca svasthavan niḥ-śeṣam āhnikam akārṣīt. agalac ca darpa-prasara iva śruta-pratijñasya śāmyad-ūṣmā divasas tri-bhuvanasya.
children.translated_text: this pestle, this wretch, this world-despised vilest of the vile—the <s>caṇḍāla</s> lord of the <s>Gauḍas</s>—lives, I am ashamed, with my lips dry like a eunuch, to weep in grief devoid of retaliation. How can there be the offering of water-oblations from the pair of hands of one like me, for whom the overcast day of tears from eyes unsteady with the failure to defeat the enemy's forces has not occurred? Or even a small amount of tear-water from eyes that have not seen the circle of smoke from the funeral pyre of the vile <s>Gauḍa</s>? Hear my oath: 'I swear by the very dust of the noble one's feet—if within a counted number of days I do not make the earth free of <s>Gauḍas</s>, with the feet of all kings—giddy in the wanton mischief of their bows' fickleness—clanking in fetters, then may I, a sinner, hurl myself into the fire like a moth into ghee-fed flames.' And having spoken thus, he commanded <s>Avantika</s>, the chief minister of war and peace, who stood nearby: 'Let it be written: From the eastern mountain—from whose peak the screech of the sun-chariot's wheel startles pairs of <s>Cāraṇa</s> celestials into releasing their hold—to <s>Suvela</s>, with the <s>Trikūṭa</s> ridge scarred by the chiseled inscriptions of <s>Kākutstha</s> (<s>Rāma</s>)'s plundering of <s>Laṅkā</s>; from the western mountain, in whose cave-belly the tinkling of the anklets of <s>Varuṇa</s>'s noble wives stumbling in the intoxication of <s>Vāruṇī</s> wine resounds; and from <s>Gandhamādana</s>, whose cave-dwellings are perfumed by the fragrant touchstones scented with the perfume of <s>Guhyaka</s> (Yakṣa) wives—let all kings prepare their hands either for the offering of tribute or for the grasping of weapons! Let them seize the directions or the chowries! Let their heads bow or their bows! Let their ears receive commands or bowstrings! Let their crests bear the dust of my feet or helmets! Let their palms join in homage or bind elephant-battle formations! Let them release lands or arrows! Let them grasp reed-staffs [of submission] or spear-shafts! Let them see themselves well in my toenails or in sword-mirrors! I am on the march. Like a lame man, I will know no turning back until the sole-ointment is made—composed entirely of the light of the crest-gems of all kings' crowns—traversing every island-continent.' And having made his resolve, he left his seat, dismissed the assembly of kings, and, eager to begin his ablutions, departed from the court. And rising, he performed the entire daily routine as if in good spirits. And the day passed for the three worlds as if its heat were subsiding, like the spreading of his pride, having heard his oath.

body.translated_text: Lord <s>Harṣa</s>, however, replied to him: 'What has been said by the venerable one is indeed what must be done. For otherwise, my arm, jealous even of the lord of serpents who has taken hold of the earth, would cast a covetous glance at his heritage. My brow-creeper desires to move for the subjugation even of the host of planets that ascend above. My hand longs to seize by the hair even mountains that do not bow. My heart seeks to make even the rays of the sun, foolish in their splendor, wave as chowries. My foot, in its anger at the word 'king,' desires to make even the heads of the kings of beasts into footstools. My lip quivers to issue commands for the rebuke even of the directions, whose guardians freely follow their own will. How much more so when such a wretch has been born and my mind is full of uncontainable rage—there is simply no room for the performance of mourning rites? Moreover, while this heart-embedded thorn,

body.text: tataś ca nijâdhikārâpahāra-bhīta iva bhagavaty api kvâpi gate gata-

children.text: -tejasy a-hima-bhāsi, tāmarasa-vaneṣv api nigūḍha-śilī-mukhâlāpeṣu trāsād iva saṃkucatsu, vihaga-gaṇeṣv api samupasaṃhṛta-nija-pakṣa-vikṣepa-niś-caleṣu bhiyêvâ-prakaṭī-bhavatsu, bhuvana-vyāpinīṃ saṃdhyāṃ pratijñām iva mānayati nata-śirasi ghaṭitâñjali-vane jane sakale, sva-pada-cyuti-cakita-dik-pāla-dīyamānâbhraṃliha-loha-prākāra-valaya-kalitāsv iva bahala-timira-mālā-tiro-dhīyamānāsu dikṣu pradoṣâsthāne nâti-ciraṃ tasthau. naman-nṛpa-loka-lolâṃśuka-pavana-kampita-śikhair dīpikā-cakra-vālair api praṇamyamāna iva prāhiṇôllokaṃ pratiṣiddha-parijana-praveśaś ca śayana-gṛhaṃ prāviśat. uttānaś ca mumocâṅgāni śayana-tale. dīpa-dvitīyaṃ ca tam abhisara iva labdhâvasaras tarasā bhrātṛ-śoko jagrāha. jīvantam iva hṛdaye nimīlita-locano dadarśâgrajam. upary upari bhrātṛ-jīvitânveṣiṇa iva prasasruḥ śvāsāḥ. dhavalâṃśuka-paṭântenêva câśru-jala-plavena mukham ācchādya niḥ-śabdam ati-ciraṃ ruroda. cakāra cetasi: kathaṃ nāmâkṛtes tādṛsyā yuktaḥ pariṇāmo 'yam īdṛśaḥ. pṛthu-śilā-saṃghāta-karkaśa-kāya-bandhāt tātād a-calād iva loha-dhātuḥ kaṭhinatara āsīd āryaḥ. kathaṃ câsya me hata-hṛdayasyârya-virahe sakṛd api yuktaṃ samucchvasitum. iyaṃ sā prītir bhaktir anuvṛttir vā. bāliśo 'pi kaḥ saṃbhāvayed ārya-maraṇe maj-jīvitam. tat tādṛśam aikyam eka-pada eva kvâpi gatam. a-yatnenâiva hata-vidhinā pṛthak-kṛto 'smi. dagdha-roṣântarita-śucā su-ciraṃ ruditam api na mukta-kaṇṭhaṃ gata-ghṛṇena mayā. sarvathā lūtā-tantu-cchaṭā-cchidurās tucchāḥ prītayaḥ prāṇinām. loka-yātrā-mātra-nibandhanā bāndhavatā yatrâham api nāma para ivârye svarga-sthe svastha ivâse. kiṃ ca daiva-hatakena phalam āsāditam īdṛśi paraspara-prīti-bandha-nirvṛta-hṛdaye sukha-bhāji bhrātṛ-mithune vighaṭite. tathā ca candramayā iva jagad-āhlādino lokântarī-bhūtasya lagna-citâgnaya ivâryasya ta eva dahanti guṇāḥ. ity etāni cânyāni ca hṛdayena paryadevata. prabhātāyāṃ ca śarvaryāṃ pratīhāram ādi-deśâ-śeṣa-gaja-sādhanâdhikṛtaṃ Skandaguptaṃ draṣṭum icchāmîti.
children.translated_text: while the sun's rays were not yet cool; as even the lotus-groves contracted as if in fear, their arrow-tip-like conversations hidden; as even flocks of birds, having folded their wings, became motionless as if hiding in terror; as all the people, with bowed heads and joined palms, honored the twilight pervading the world like a sacred vow; as the directions were concealed behind dense garlands of darkness, as if encircled by sky-touching iron rampart-rings offered by the direction-guardians alarmed at the loss of their stations—he did not remain long at the evening hall. As if bowed to even by the rows of lamps whose flames flickered in the wind stirred by the garments of the swaying assembly of bowing kings, he dismissed the court. Forbidding the entry of attendants, he entered the bedchamber. And lying on his back, he released his limbs upon the bed. And as if finding an opportunity, the grief for his brother swiftly seized him who was alone with only a lamp for company, like a secret lover arriving. With closed eyes he saw his elder brother alive as it were in his heart. Sighs issued forth again and again, as if searching for his brother's life. Covering his face with the flood of tears as with the hem of a white cloth, he wept soundlessly for a very long time. He reflected in his mind: 'How can such an outcome befit such a person? My brother was harder than iron-ore from father, who was unshakable as a mountain with a body-frame rough as masses of broad rock. And how is it right for me, broken-hearted, to draw even a single breath in separation from my brother? Is this what love, devotion, and loyalty amount to? What fool would believe in my life when my brother is dead? That such oneness has vanished in a single step! I have been separated effortlessly by accursed fate. Though grief masked by smoldering anger has made me weep long, I have not wept with unrestrained throat, shameless as I am. In every way, the affections of living beings are worthless, fragile as strands of a spider's web. Kinship is merely a tie of worldly convention, where even I now sit composed, as if a stranger, while my brother dwells in heaven. What fruit has been obtained by one accursed by fate, now that this pair of brothers, whose hearts delighted in mutual bonds of love, sharing in happiness, has been torn apart? And just as the moon delights the world, so the very virtues of my brother, now passed to the other world, burn me like funeral fires that cling to the pyre.' These and other such thoughts he mourned in his heart. And when the night had passed, he commanded the doorkeeper: 'I wish to see <s>Skandagupta</s>, the superintendent of the entire elephant establishment.'

children.translated_text: royal-lineage-long nose-ridge; drinking in the extent of the directions with the reach of his pair of eyes, exceedingly affectionate, sweet, white, and vast, as if with a flood of consumed milk; with a forehead more massively broad than the slope of <s>Meru</s>; with a naturally curling, comely lock of soft dark-hued baby-hair—as if grown from the constant shade of an uninterrupted parasol-shadow—seeming to shear the sun's rays robbed of their light; though his bow-work had been abandoned since the enemy's party was destroyed, the deep sound of his weighty virtues was heard to the ends of all quarters; though all rutting elephants were under his control, untouched by intoxication himself; though powerful, full of affection; though earthly, full of virtues; standing above the generous as above elephants; bearing a servitude enviable as sovereignty, yet not degraded; a kinsman without cause to the refined, an unpaid servant to the devoted, an unbought slave to the learned—<s>Skandagupta</s> entered the royal court. children.translated_text: how much less so masses of splendor such as you. Only, through the account of the divine <s>Rājyavardhana</s>'s fate, Your Majesty has already seen something of the villainy of wicked men. Such indeed are the ways of the world—in every village, every city, every region, every continent, every direction, the dress, appearance, diet, speech, and customs of peoples differ. Therefore let this trusting of everyone—born of a naturally guileless heart accustomed to the customs of one's own land—be abandoned. Your Majesty daily hears many reports of the consequences of the fault of carelessness. Just as <s>Nāgasena</s>, born of the <s>Nāga</s> dynasty, whose secret mantras were overheard by a mynah bird, met his destruction in <s>Padmāvatī</s>. And the fortune of <s>Śrutavarman</s>, whose secrets were heard by a parrot, was shattered in <s>Śrāvastī</s>. And <s>Suvarṇacūḍa</s>, whose counsel was betrayed while he was sleeping, met his death in <s>Mṛttikāvatī</s>. And the beautiful golden fly-whisk bearer of the <s>Yavana</s> king, who read the letters of secret correspondence through their reflection on his crest-jewel, went to her death. And the army of <s>Vidūratha</s>, with drawn swords, crushed <s>Bṛhadratha</s> of <s>Mathurā</s>, covetous of much, while he was digging up treasure on a dark night. And soldiers of <s>Mahāsena</s>, emerging from the limbs of a decoy elephant, slew <s>Vatsapati</s>, who was in the habit of strolling in elephant-forests. And <s>Mitradeva</s>, taking a seat among the actors, cut off the head of <s>Sumitra</s>, son of <s>Agnimitra</s>, who was excessively fond of dance, with a sword-creeper as if it were a lotus-stalk. And enemy men, disguised as music students, having hidden sharpened blades in the hollow interior of gourd-lutes, cut off the head of <s>Śarabha</s>, lord of <s>Aśmaka</s>, who was fond of stringed instruments. And one who was weak in wisdom—
