children.translated_text: And <s>Candragupta</s>, disguised in the attire of a woman, destroyed the <s>Śaka</s> lord. And the calamities wrought by women upon the heedless have certainly come within the hearing of Your Majesty. For instance, <s>Suprabhā</s>, for the sake of her son's kingdom, killed <s>Mahāsena</s>, king of <s>Kāśī</s>, with parched grains smeared with honey-sweetened poison. And <s>Ratnavatī</s>, feigning passion born of love's pride, killed <s>Parantapa</s>, the <s>Jārūthya</s> lord of <s>Ayodhyā</s>, with a mirror ending in a razor's edge. And <s>Devakī</s>, enamored of her brother-in-law, killed <s>Devasena</s> the <s>Sauhmya</s> with an ear-lotus whose pollen was kissed with poison-powder. And the beloved <s>Uṣā</s>, jealous of her co-wives, killed <s>Rantideva</s> of <s>Vairantya</s> with a jeweled anklet showering the bitter dust of a poisonous compound. And <s>Bindumatī</s> killed <s>Vidūratha</s> of the <s>Vṛṣṇi</s> clan with a weapon concealed in her braid. And <s>Haṃsavatī</s> killed <s>Vīrasena</s> of <s>Sauvīra</s> with a girdle-gem smeared with poisoned wine. And <s>Pauravī</s>, her face anointed with an invisible antidote, killed <s>Somaka</s>, lord of the <s>Pauravas</s>, by making him gargle with poisoned liquor." Having spoken thus, he ceased, and went out to carry out his master's command.

body.translated_text: And as he sat down, not too near, the divine <s>Harṣa</s> then spoke to him: 'You have heard in full the details of this calamity of my brother and of what we intend to do. Therefore let the elephant forces that have gone out to pasture be quickly brought in. The fire of anguish at my brother's humiliation cannot tolerate even the slightest delay in our departure.' Thus addressed, he bowed and submitted: 'Let the master consider the command as already fulfilled. However, devotion to the lord has a small matter to submit. Let Your Majesty hear it. For Your Majesty has undertaken everything befitting one born in the <s>Puṣpabhūti</s> lineage—befitting your noble birth, your innate splendor, your pair of arms long as the trunks of directional elephants, and your extraordinary brotherly love. Even wretched worms called <s>kākodara</s> (black-bellied) do not endure insult—

children.translated_text: —the <s>śālabhañjikā</s> (bracket-figures) in the assembly hall wept, their breasts struck by the blows of their trembling palms. Warriors saw themselves as headless <s>kabandhas</s> in the depths of mirrors, their heads appearing to wander as if in fear of imminent hair-seizure. On the crest-jewels of the royal queens, footprints appeared bearing the marks of discus, conch, and lotus. The maidservants' fly-whisks suddenly fled from the shoots of their hands. Even in lovers' quarrels, the soldiers long showed their backs, turning away from the proud ladies. On the cheeks of cow-elephants, the drinking-parties of honey-bees were dispersed. The horses, as if faint from smelling the scent of <s>Yama</s>'s buffalo, would not touch even fresh green barley, not even the provender of straw-fed elephants. The languid palace peacocks would not dance, though coaxed by the rhythmic clapping of girls with jingling bracelets. Night after night, with eyes fixed upward as if gazing upon the hosts of dusty deer, the packs of dogs howled shrilly and causelessly at the gateway. The <s>Koṭavī</s> (the owl-goddess) roamed the gardens by day, wagging her forefinger as if counting the life-spans of the doomed. On the jeweled floors, lines of green grass sprouted in winding patterns like braids of deer-hooves. In the wine-goblets, the reflections of the face-lotuses of the warrior-women appeared without collyrium or <s>gorocanā</s> adornment, as if their braids were already tied for mourning. The earth trembled as if startled at the imminent seizure of its own self. Showers of blood fell upon the bodies of the brave, crimson as the glow of blooming <s>bandhūka</s> flowers, appearing like the streaks of red sandalwood paste of the adornment for execution. Falling in throngs, the blazing torches did not cease—consuming the hosts of stars with the shower of dense, flashing sparks and embers—as if performing the circumambulation-fire for the perishable fortune. A harsh whirlwind rampaged from house to house, snatching away fly-whisks, parasols, and fans like a first gatekeeper carrying them off.

body.translated_text: Lord <s>Harṣa</s> too established all the protocols of the kingdom. Then, when Lord <s>Harṣa</s>, having thus taken his vow, was about to announce his departure for the conquest of the directions, at the funerals of the feudatory lords whose lives had ended, many forms of portents spread. For close at hand, restless herds of black antelope appeared here and there, like the glances of Death's messengers. Swarms of bees hummed with a buzzing that resembled the clanking of <s>Lakṣmī</s>'s anklets as she departed. The inauspicious jackals howled dismally even during the day for a long time, emitting streams of fire from their long-opened, distorted mouths, inauspicious in their inauspicious purpose. Forest pigeons fell, their wing-feathers tawny as the cheeks of young monkeys, as if gorged on corpse-flesh. The garden trees simultaneously put forth untimely blossoms as if bidding farewell. Restless—

body.translated_text: Thus ends the sixth <s>ucchvāsa</s> (chapter), titled "The Description of the King's Vow," in the <s>Harṣacarita</s> composed by the illustrious <s>Bāṇabhaṭṭa</s>.

body.translated_text: Then, after some days had passed, on a day carefully calculated hundreds of times by the circle of astrologers, a day declared most auspicious and suitable for the victory-march in all four directions, the auspicious moment for the military expedition having been fixed—bathing with golden vessels washed by time, like autumnal clouds skilled in releasing water—performing with supreme devotion the worship of the blessed <s>Nīlalohita</s> (Śiva), offering into the fire whose crests of flame spiraled clockwise, giving to Brahmins by the thousands gem-studded, silver, and gold <s>tilapātras</s> (sesame-vessels) and cows by the tens of millions with their hooves, horns, and horn-tips adorned with gold-leaf ornaments—seating himself upon the auspicious throne spread with a tiger-skin, anointing his body from head to toe with sandalwood white as his own fame (having first anointed his weapons), wearing a pair of <s>dukūla</s> garments marked with the emblem of a royal <s>haṃsa</s> pair, fashioning upon his head a white flower-garland like the crescent moon that was the insignia of the supreme lord, placing upon his ear a fresh <s>dūrvā</s> grass shoot yellowed with <s>gorocanā</s> whose emerald rays seemed like an ear-ornament, tying upon his wrist the auspicious departure-thread along with the royal signet-ring, his head sprinkled with showers of sanctified water scattered by the hands of the gratified and worshipped royal chaplain—sending costly vehicles to the kings and ornaments glazed with the luster of abundant gems, distributing gifts of favor that liberated the communities of distressed paupers and noble youths,

body.text: nâti-dūre ca nagarād upa-Sarasvati nirmite mahati tṛṇamaye, samuttambhita-tuṅga-toraṇe, vedī-vinihita-pallava-lalāma-hema-kalaśe, baddha-vana-mālā-dāmni, dhavala-dhvaja-mālini, bhramac-chukla-vāsasi, paṭhad-dvi-janmani mandire prasthānam akarot. tatra-sthasya câsya grāmâkṣapaṭalikaḥ sakala-karaṇi-parikaraḥ "karotu devo divasa-grahaṇam adyâivâ-vandhya-śāsanaḥ śāsanānām" ity abhidhāya vṛṣâṅkām abhinava-ghaṭitāṃ hāṭakamayīṃ mudrāṃ samupaninye. jagrāha ca tāṃ rājā. samupasthāpite ca prathamata eva mṛt-piṇḍe paribhraśya kara-kamalād adho-mukhī mahī-tale papāta mudrā. mandâśyāna-paṅka-paṭale mṛdu-mṛdi Sarasvatī-tīre parisphuṭaṃ vyarājanta rājayo varṇānām. a-maṅgalâśaṅkini ca viṣīdati parijane nara-patir akaron manasy etat: "a-tattva-darśinyo hi bhavanty a-vidagdhānāṃ dhiyaḥ. tathā hi: eka-śāsana-mudrâṅkā bhūr bhavato bhaviṣyatîti niveditam api nimittenânyathā gṛhṇanti grāmyāḥ." ity abhinandya manasā mahā-nimittaṃ tat sīra-sahasra-saṃmita-sīmnāṃ grāmāṇāṃ śatam adād dvijebhyaḥ. nināya ca tatra taṃ divasam. pratipannāyāṃ śarvaryāṃ saṃmānita-sarva-rāja-lokaḥ suṣvāpa.
body.translated_text: Not far from the city, at a great pavilion of thatch erected by the <s>Sarasvatī</s> river, with lofty gateways raised high, with golden vessels adorned with leaf-ornaments placed upon the altars, with garlands of forest-vines tied about, with rows of white banners, with fluttering white garments, with Brahmins reciting—he performed the departure ceremony. And while he was stationed there, the village-records officer, accompanied by his entire staff, saying "Let Your Majesty make the territorial grant this very day, so that the edicts are not in vain," presented to him a freshly fashioned golden seal bearing the bull-emblem. The king took it. But when a lump of clay was first brought forward, the seal slipped from his lotus-hand and fell face-down upon the ground. On the soft, slightly moist mud on the bank of the <s>Sarasvatī</s>, the royal letters of the script shone forth clearly. While the retinue was sinking into gloom suspecting an evil omen, the king resolved in his mind: "The judgments of the unsophisticated are indeed blind to the truth. For: 'The earth shall bear the impression of your single seal of authority'—this is what the omen actually declares, but the vulgar interpret it otherwise." Thus approving the great omen in his heart, he gave to Brahmins a hundred villages each measuring a thousand ploughlands. He spent the day there. When night fell, having honored all the kings, he slept.

body.text: atha galati tṛtīye yāme supta-samasta-sattva-niḥ-śabde dik-kuñjara-jṛmbhamāṇa-gambhīra-dhvanir atāḍhyata prayāṇa-paṭahaḥ. agrataḥ sthitvā ca muhūrtam iva punaḥ prayāṇa-krośa-saṃkhyāpakāḥ spaṣṭam aṣṭāv adīyanta prahārāḥ paṭahe paṭīyāṃsaḥ.
body.translated_text: Then, as the third watch waned, when all creatures were asleep and silence reigned, the march-drum was struck—deep-sounding as the yawning of the elephants of the quarters. Standing before [the army] for what seemed but a moment, eight loud, expert blows were then clearly given on the drum, signaling the number of <s>krośas</s> of the day's march.

body.translated_text: When the king had set forth, like the trumpeting of the elephants of the quarters frightened by the dense tumult, there spread in every direction, louder and louder, the echo of instruments on the shores of the horizons. From elephants enraged at the directional elephants, streams of ichor flowing in three currents, darkened by swarms of bees, flowed like thousands of braids of the <s>Yamunā</s>. Birds suspected it was sunset time, the sun's disc reddening from heaps of vermillion powder. The sounds of war-drums were drowned by the sounds of elephant ear-flaps enriched by the clamor of bees. The massed chowries, being waved, seemed to sip up the whole world, animate and inanimate. The sky was continuously sprinkled with balls of foam, white as <s>sindhuvāra</s> garlands, cast by the breath of horses. Forests of parasols with tall golden poles, pale as clusters of <s>tagara</s> flowers massed together, seemed to drink in the daylight, the eight directions having been lost in their mutual collision. The day shone dimly with the faint sunlight of rows of crown-jewels, real daylight being shut out by the night of dust. The directions, made to ring by the clanging of silver and golden ornamental vessel-sets, rendered all resonance deaf. Elephants sprinkled the circle of directions with warm drops of ichor, as if to extinguish the fire of enemy prowess. The lightning-like flickering of crest-jewels'

body.text: āsanna-vartināṃ ca "tatra-bhavatā māṃdhātrā pravartitāḥ panthāno dig-vijayāya a-pratihata-ratha-raṃhasā raghuṇā laghunâiva kālenâkāri kakubhāṃ prasādanam. śarâsana-dvitīyaḥ karadī-cakāra cakraṃ kramâgata-bhuja-balâbhijana-dhana-madâvaliptānāṃ bhūbhujāṃ pāṇḍuḥ. pāṇḍavaḥ Savyasācī Cīna-viṣayam atikramya rāja-sūya-saṃpade krudhyad-gandharva-dhanuṣ-koṭi-ṭāṅkāra-kūjita-kuñjaṃ Hemakūṭa-parvataṃ parājaiṣṭa. saṃkalpântarito vijayas tarasvinām. sa-hima-himavad-vyavahito 'py uvāha bāhu-bala-vyatikara-kātaraḥ karaṃ Kauravêśvarasya kiṅkara ivâkṛtī drumaḥ. nâti-jigīṣavaḥ khalu pūrve yenâlpa eva bhū-bhāge bhūyāṃso Bhagadatta-Dantavakra-Krātha-Karṇa-Kaurava-Śiśupāla-Sālva-Jarāsaṃdha-Sindhurāja-prabhṛtayo 'bhavan bhū-patayaḥ. saṃtuṣṭo rājā

children.text: Yudhiṣṭhiro yo hy asahata samīpa eva Dhanañjaya-jaya-janita-jagat-kampaḥ kiṃ-puruṣāṇāṃ rājyam. alasaś Caṇḍakośo yo na prāvikṣat kṣmāṃ jitvā strī-rājyam. hrasīya evântaraṃ tuṣāra-giri-gandha-mādanayoḥ utsāhinaḥ. kiṣkuḥ Turuṣka-viṣayaḥ. prādeśaḥ Pārasīka-deśaḥ. śaśa-padaṃ Śaka-sthānam. a-dṛśyamāna-pratiprahāre Pariyātre yātrâiva śithilā. śaurya-śulkaḥ su-labho dakṣiṇā-pathaḥ. dakṣiṇârṇava-kallolânila-calita-candana-latā-saurabha-sundarī-kṛta-darī-mandirād Dardurād adrer nedīyasi malayo malaya-lagna eva ca mahêndraḥ." ity evaṃ-prāyān udyoga-dyotakānām ālāpān pārthiva-kumārāṇāṃ bāhu-śālināṃ śṛṇvann evâsasādâvāsam. mandira-dvāri côbhayataḥ sa-bahu-mānaṃ bhrū-latābhyāṃ visarjita-rāja-lokaḥ praviśya câvatatāra bāhyâsthāna-maṇḍapa-sthāpitam āsanam ācakrāma. apāsta-samāyogaś ca kṣaṇam āsiṣṭa.
children.translated_text: <s>Yudhiṣṭhira</s>, who endured nearby the kingdom of the <s>Kiṃpuruṣas</s> (mythical beings), though the earth trembled with the conquests of <s>Dhanañjaya</s> (<s>Arjuna</s>). Lazy was <s>Caṇḍakośa</s>, who did not enter the kingdom of women after conquering the earth. Very short indeed is the distance between the snowy mountain and <s>Gandhamādana</s> for the energetic. The <s>Turuṣka</s> (Turkish) territory is but a cubit. The <s>Pārasīka</s> (Persian) land is but a span. The <s>Śaka</s> (Scythian) domain is but a hare's footprint. Against the <s>Pāriyātra</s> (western mountains), where no counter-blow is seen, the campaign itself grows slack. The southern road is easily won, its bride-price being valor alone. From Mount <s>Dardura</s>—whose cavern-chambers are made lovely by the fragrance of sandalwood creepers swaying in the breeze of the southern ocean waves—<s>Malaya</s> is very near, and <s>Mahendra</s> is virtually clinging to <s>Malaya</s>.' Hearing such talk from the arm-mighty princes, radiating eagerness for enterprise, he reached his quarters. At the entrance of his palace, dismissing the royal entourage on both sides with a respectful movement of his eyebrow-creepers, he entered, dismounted, and proceeded to the seat placed in the outer audience-pavilion. And having dismissed his attendants, he sat for a moment.

body.translated_text: And as he went, he heard such talk as this from the nearby arm-mighty princes, radiating eagerness for enterprise: 'The paths for the conquest of the directions were first set by that lord <s>Māṃdhātā</s>. By <s>Raghu</s>, whose chariot-speed was unchecked, in a short time the pacification of the quarters was accomplished. Bearing his bow as his companion, <s>Pāṇḍu</s> made tributary the entire circle of kings—swollen with the intoxication of hereditary arm-strength, noble lineage, and wealth. The <s>Pāṇḍava</s> <s>Savyasācī</s> (<s>Arjuna</s>), crossing beyond the land of <s>Cīna</s> (China), for the purpose of the <s>Rājasūya</s> sacrifice, conquered Mount <s>Hemakūṭa</s>, whose groves resounded with the twanging of the tips of hostile <s>Gandharva</s> bows. For the courageous, victory is separated only by resolve. Even the <s>Druma</s> tree—separated by the snowy <s>Himālaya</s>, yet trembling with fear at the onset of arm-power—bore tribute to the lord of the <s>Kauravas</s> like a servant. Not very ambitious indeed were the ancients, since in a small territory alone there were many kings such as <s>Bhagadatta</s>, <s>Dantavakra</s>, <s>Krātha</s>, <s>Karṇa</s>, the <s>Kauravas</s>, <s>Śiśupāla</s>, <s>Śālva</s>, <s>Jarāsandha</s>, the king of <s>Sindhu</s>, and others. "ehy ehi" iti sa-bahu-mānam āhūtaś ca pradhāvito 'pasṛtaḥ pāda-pīṭha-luṭhita-lalāṭa-lekho nyasta-hastaḥ pṛṣṭhe pārthivenôpasṛtya bhūyo namaś cakre. snigdha-narêndra-dṛṣṭyā nirdiṣṭam a-viprakṛṣṭaṃ sa pradeśam adhyāste. tato rājā tiraścīṃ tanum īṣad iva dadhānaś cāmara-grāhiṇīm antarāla-vartinīṃ samutsārya saṃmukhīnas taṃ sa-praśrayaṃ papraccha: "Haṃsavega! śrīmān kac-cit kuśalī kumāraḥ?"

children.text: iti. sa tam anvavādīt: "adya kuśalī yenâivaṃ sneha-snapitayā sauhārda-dravârdrayā sa-gauravaṃ girā pṛcchati devaḥ" iti.
children.translated_text: He replied: 'Today he is well, since Your Majesty inquires with words bathed in such affection, moist with the flowing tenderness of friendship, and full of gravity.'

body.translated_text: Then there, an usher, placing his hand-sprout upon the surface of the earth, reported: 'Your Majesty! An intimate ambassador named <s>Haṃsavega</s>, sent by the prince who is lord of <s>Prāg-jyotiṣa</s> (Assam), waits at the gateway.' The king said eagerly and with respect: 'Bring him in at once.' Then the usher, from skill and deference to the king, went out in person. And immediately <s>Haṃsavega</s> entered the royal palace, modestly, his very form happily conveying handsome beauty that delighted the eyes, his gravity of virtues being surpassed [only by his grace], accompanied by a great retinue of men bearing abundant gifts. From afar itself, with his body touching the ground in the five-limbed prostration, he made his obeisance. Called with respect, 'Come, come!', he rushed forward, drew near, his forehead-line pressed against the footstool, his hand placed on the king's back, and bowed again. Directed by the king's affectionate gaze to a not-too-distant spot, he sat down. Then the king, slightly turning his body sideways, having the chowrie-bearer standing between them step aside, and facing him directly, asked respectfully: '<s>Haṃsavega</s>! Is the illustrious prince well?'

body.text: sthitvā ca muhūrtam iva punaḥ sa caturam uvāca: "catur-ambhodhi-bhoga-bhūti-bhājana-bhūtasya devasya sad-bhāva-garbham apahāya hṛdayam ekam anyad anurūpaṃ prābhṛtam eva dur-labhaṃ loke tathâpy asmat-svāminā saṃdeśam a-śūnyatāṃ nayatā pūrvajôpārjitaṃ Vāruṇâtapatram Ābhogâkhyam anurūpa-sthāna-nyāsena kṛtârthī-kṛtam etat. asya ca kutūhala-kṛnti bahūny āścaryāṇi dṛsyante. tathā hi: prati-divasaṃ praviśati śaitya-hetoś chāyāyāḥ kiraṇa-sahasrād ekâikaḥ somasya raśmir asmin. yasmin praviṣṭe pradhyānân-antaraṃ svādavôdanta-vīṇôpadeśâcāryāś cyotanti candra-bhāsām ambhasāṃ maṇi-śalākābhyo yāvad-iccham acchā dhārāḥ. pracetā iva yaś caturṇām arṇavānām adhipatir bhūto bhāvī vā tam idam anugṛhṇāti cchāyayā nêtaram. idaṃ ca na saptârcir dahati, na pṛṣad-aśvo harati, nôdakam ārdrayati, na rajāṃsi malinayanti, na jarā jarjarayatîti. etat tāvad anugṛhṇātu dṛśā devaḥ saṃdeśam api visrabdhaṃ śroṣyati." ity evam abhidhāya vivṛtyâtmīyaṃ puruṣam abhyadhāt: "uttiṣṭha! darśaya devasya" iti.
body.translated_text: And having paused as if for a moment, he spoke again with cleverness: 'For Your Majesty, who is the vessel of the enjoyment and fortune of the four oceans, except a heart containing genuine goodwill, no other fitting gift is easy to find in the world. Nevertheless, our master, in order to make this message not empty-handed, has this ancestral <s>Vāruṇa</s> (divine) parasol named <s>Ābhoga</s> presented through placement in an appropriate station, thereby fulfilling its purpose. And many wonders are seen in it, arousing curiosity. For instance: every day, for the sake of coolness, one by one, a single ray of the moon out of a thousand enters it; and upon its entry, without interruption, as if of their own accord, crystal-clear streams of waters—bright as moonbeams—drip as much as one desires from gem-rods, like teachers instructing sweet <s>vīṇā</s>-playing through sweet-toothed discourse. Like <s>Pracetas</s> (<s>Varuṇa</s>), who has been or will be lord of the four oceans, it graces only him with its shade—no other. Moreover, the seven-flamed fire does not burn it, the spotted-horsed wind does not carry it away, water does not wet it, dust does not soil it, old age does not cause it to decay.' Having said this, he added: 'Let Your Majesty first grace this with his gaze; he shall then hear the message at ease.' And having spoken thus, he turned to his own man and said: 'Rise! Show it to His Majesty.'

body.text: citrīyamāṇa-cetāś ca sa-rājako rājā daṇḍânusārâdhirohiṇyā dṛṣṭyā sâdaram aikṣiṣṭa tat tilakam iva tri-bhuvanasya, śaiśavam iva śveta-dvīpasya, aṃśâvatāramiva śarad-indoḥ, hṛdayam iva dharmasya, niveśam iva śaśi-lokasya, danta-maḍalaka-dyuti-dhavalaṃ mukham iva cakra-vartitvasya, mauktika-jāla-parikara-sitaṃ sīmanta-cakram iva divaḥ, bahala-jyotsnā-śuklôdaram aindavam iva pariveṣa-valayaṃ śauklyâpahasita-śaṅkha-śrīkaṃ śravaṇa-maṇḍalam iva niś-calatāṃ gatam Airāvatasya, śveta-Gaṅgâvarta-pāṇḍuraṃ padam iva tri-bhuvana-vandanīyaṃ tri-vikramasya, pracetasaś cūḍā-maṇi-marīci-śikhābhir iva śliṣṭhābhir mānasa-bisa-tantumayībhiś cāmarikâvalībhir viracita-pariveṣam, upari cakra-varti-lakṣmī-nūpura-svana-śravaṇa-dohada-niś-calenêva lakṣmaṇā vitata-patreṇa haṃsena sa-nāthī-kṛta-śikharam, sparśavatā ca prabhāva-stambhitena mandākinī-mṛṇālena mukulita-phaṇena vāsukinêva nītena daṇḍatāṃ dyotamānam, dhavalimnā kṣālayad iva nakṣatra-patham, prabhā-pravāha-prathimnā prāvṛṇvad iva divasam, samucchrāyeṇâdhaḥ-kurvad iva divam, upari-sthitam iva sarva-maṅgalānām, śveta-maṇḍapam iva śriyaḥ, stabakam iva brahma-stambasya, nābhi-maṇḍalam iva jyotsnāyāḥ, viśada-hāsam iva kīrteḥ, phena-rāśim iva khaḍga-dhārā-jalānām, yaśaḥ-paṭalam iva śaurya-śālitāyāḥ, trailaukyâdbhutaṃ mahac chatram.
body.translated_text: And the king, his mind filled with wonder, together with the assembled kings, looked with reverence at that great parasol with a gaze that ascended along the staff—that <s>tilaka</s>-mark of the three worlds, that infancy of the White Continent, that partial incarnation of the autumn moon, that heart of <s>Dharma</s>, that abode of the lunar realm, whose face—white with the lustre of ivory ornaments—was like the face of universal sovereignty, whose pearl-net-encircled hair-parting circle was like the parting-circle of heaven, whose halo—white-bellied with dense moonlight—was like a lunar ring, whose earring-disc—whose whiteness mocked the beauty of conch—was like the disc of <s>Airāvata</s>'s ear become motionless, whose footprint—white as the eddy of the white <s>Gaṅgā</s>—was like the footprint of <s>Trivikrama</s> worshipped by the three worlds, surrounded by a halo fashioned by rows of yak-tail fly-whisks made of <s>Mānasa</s> lotus-fibers clinging like the crest-gem rays of <s>Varuṇa</s>, its peak crowned by a marked swan with spread wings—motionless as if fixed by the longing to hear the sound of <s>Cakravartin Lakṣmī</s>'s anklets above—gleaming with its staff made rigid, like <s>Vāsuki</s> with folded hood, paralyzed by power, turned into a staff from a <s>Mandākinī</s> lotus stalk endowed with substance—washing the path of the stars with its whiteness, covering the day with the breadth of its radiance-stream, humbling the sky with its height, standing above all auspicious things—the white pavilion of <s>Śrī</s>, the flower-cluster of the pillar of <s>Brahman</s>, the navel-disc of moonlight, the bright laughter of Fame, the foam-heap of sword-stream waters, the sheet of glory of heroic majesty—the great parasol, a wonder of the three worlds.

Haṃsavegaṃ ca prīyamāṇo babhāṣe: "bhadra! sakala-ratna-dhāmnaḥ paramêśvara-śiro-dhāraṇârhasyâsya mahâtapatrasya mahârṇavād iva kumuda-bāndhavasya kumārāl lābho na vismayāya. bāla-vidyāḥ khalu mahatām upakṛtayaḥ" iti. apanīte ca tasmāt pradeśāt prābhṛta-saṃbhāre kṣaṇam iva sthitvā "Haṃsavega! viśramyatām" iti pratīhāra-bhavanaṃ visarjayāṃ-babhūva. svayam apy utthāya snātvā maṅgalâkāṅkṣī prāṅ-mukhaḥ prāviśad ābhogasya chāyām.
body.translated_text: The king, his heart delighted at the sight of the parasol, accepted it in his mind as an auspicious omen at the very start of his march. And he spoke affectionately to <s>Haṃsavega</s>: "Good sir! That this great parasol—a treasury of all gems, worthy to be borne upon the head of the supreme lord—has been obtained from a prince, as if the moon's friend were obtained from the great ocean, is no cause for wonder. The childhood services of the great are indeed their truest benefactions." And when the tribute had been removed from that place, after standing for a moment, he dismissed him saying "<s>Haṃsavega</s>! Go rest" to the gatekeepers' quarters. He himself, rising and bathing, desiring auspiciousness, entered the shade of <s>Ābhoga</s>'s [parasol], facing east.

body.translated_text: And as he entered its shade, the moon-disc seemed to be reduced to the state of a crest-jewel by the chill born of the shadow; the camphor particles seemed to dissolve upon his forehead-terrace as if moonstone-gems were dripping water; necklaces seemed to be bound upon his throat, with frost formed by falling dewdrops; a continuous rain of <s>haricandana</s> paste seemed to fall upon his chest; his heart seemed to become exceedingly cool as if made of <s>kumuda</s> lotuses; as if a hidden block of ice were melting, it spread across his limbs. Filled with wonder, he resolved in his mind: "What other reward could match this imperishable gift, except its counterpart?" And at mealtime he sent to <s>Haṃsavega</s>: the remaining sandalwood paste wrapped in a clean white cloth along with a polished coconut, and the garments that had touched his body, and an ear-ornament called <s>Taraṅgaka</s> that reddened the daylight with the glow of exceedingly precious rubies, and a waist-cord called <s>Pariveśa</s> studded with clusters of bright pearls shaped like autumn stars, and abundant food. And thus in this manner the day gradually passed.

children.translated_text: gift. With all lotus-groves closing their petals, the earth with its continents stood before the king as if with palms joined in a salutation of service. The twilight-glow seized the world, its friend the folded-palm salutation of all living beings bound together, as if made of the passion of kings. The eastern direction turned dark as if apprehensive of the <s>Gauḍas</s>' offense. The earth assumed a blackness, with its accumulated masses of darkness extinguished, as if the fire-flames of other kings' valor were all quenched. The horizons shed an abundant cluster of stars, lovely as <s>tavara</s> blossoms, like the flowers of the king's evening worship. The path of the <s>Milky Way</s> shone in the sky, grey with dust, as if the path was made by the rut-scent of the camp's state elephant driving across the sky. The moon rose to the vault of the sky, abandoning the surface of the earth as if forsaking the eulogy that had been smelled by the angry tiger-king. The moon's rays pierced the ten directions, breaking hearts of proud ladies like the news of the departure-march. The lords of the armies were agitated, their brave spirits trembling, as if terrified by the new king's conquest-march. Darkness, its continuous mass of all hopes released, entered the caves and crevices of mountains, like anxiety entering the hearts of kings. The sleep of the <s>kumuda</s> lotus-groves perished, like the sleep in the eyes of the feudatory lords.

Śaṃtanor Bhāgīrathyāṃ Bhīṣma iva kumāraḥ samabhavat. ayam asya ca śaiśavād ārabhya saṃkalpaḥ stheyān sthāṇu-pādâravinda-dvayād ṛte nâham anyaṃ namas-kuryām iti īdṛśaś câyaṃ mano-rathas śeṣâvayavānām api sāhāyaka-saṃpādana-mano-ratho nir-avakāśaḥ kim uta bāhya-janasya. catuḥ-sāgara-grāma-grahaṇa-ghasmarasya pṛthivy-eka-deśa-dānôpanyāsenâpi kā tuṣṭiḥ. children.translated_text: In the lineage of that great-souled one, after many great earth-lords equal to <s>Meru</s> had passed—<s>Bhagadatta</s>, <s>Puṣpadatta</s>, <s>Vajradatta</s>, and others—the great-grandson of <s>Mahārāja Bhūtivarman</s>, grandson of <s>Candramukhavarman</s>, son of His Majesty <s>Sthitivarman</s> of <s>Kailāsa</s>-firm stability, was born a <s>mahārājādhirāja</s> named <s>Susthiravarman</s>, a mass of splendor whom people called <s>Mṛgāṅka</s> (the Moon). He was born together with his pride, as if it were an elder brother. Even as a boy, he made all the <s>dvijas</s> accept gifts out of affection, and all his enemies accept them out of enmity. In him, the supreme sweetness of royal fortune born in the house of salt was exceedingly rare. And he took the conches of the army-generals but not their gems; he took the stability of the earth but not its tribute; he took the gravity of mountains but not their harshness. Of that lord of auspicious name, from Queen <s>Śyāmādevī</s>, a son was born—<s>Bhāskaradyuti</s>, also known as <s>Bhāskaravarman</s>—a prince like <s>Bhīṣma</s> born to <s>Śantanu</s> from <s>Bhāgīrathī</s>. And from childhood this has been his resolve, firmer than the two lotus-feet of <s>Sthāṇu</s> (Śiva): 'I shall bow to no other.' And this desire, rare in the three worlds, can be fulfilled by one of three things: either by the conquest of the entire world, or by death, or by a friendship with a peerless hero in the world, a god-like friend, whose blazing valor causes the conflagration of the directions. And the friendship of kings mostly depends upon practical purpose. And what purpose could there be whose presentation would induce Your Majesty into friendship? For Your Majesty, who gathers glories, regards wealth as merely an external thing. And for one who relies solely upon his own arms, even the desire for the assistance of his other limbs finds no scope—how much less that of an outsider? For one who devours the village of the four oceans, what satisfaction is there even in the offer of a single portion of the earth? Even the lure of bestowing beautiful princesses avails nothing for one whose gaze is spoiled by seeing the lotus-face of <s>Lakṣmī</s>. Thus, since all possible means of approach are unfeasible in this matter, merely entreaty alone is what he clings to—let Your Majesty hear. The lord of <s>Prāgjyotiṣa</s> desires an imperishable alliance with Your Majesty—like <s>Ekapiṅga</s> (Kubera) with the enemy of <s>Anaṅga</s> (Śiva), like <s>Daśaratha</s> with the Splitter of Mountains (Indra), like <s>Dhanañjaya</s> (Arjuna) with the Lotus-eyed One (Kṛṣṇa), like <s>Vakarttana</s> (Karṇa) with <s>Duryodhana</s>, like the Malaya breeze with spring. And if Your Majesty's friendship reaches the heart of an ascetic and understands that friends perform service in alternation—then why delay? Let the command be given. Let the lord of <s>Kāmarūpa</s> experience, like Mount <s>Mandara</s> upon <s>Viṣṇu</s>, Your Majesty's tight embraces, with fragments of armlet-gems and bracelet-jewels clinking from the clash of their massive armlet-tips—

children.text: -kalāni gāḍhôpagūḍhāni devasya kāma-rūpâdhipatiḥ. asminn ātṛpter an-avarata-vimala-lāvaṇya-saubhāgya-sudhā-nirjhariṇi mukha-śaśini cirāc cakṣuṣī lālayatu prāg-jyotiṣêśvara-śrīḥ. nâbhinandati ced devaḥ praṇayam ājñāpayatu kiṃ kathanīyaṃ mayā svāmina" iti.
children.translated_text: Let the glory of the lord of <s>Prāgjyotiṣa</s> feast its eyes at length upon this face-moon of Your Majesty, from which ceaselessly flows the nectar-stream of spotless beauty and charm, never satiating. If Your Majesty does not accept this friendship, then command what I should tell my master," he concluded.

body.translated_text: At this hour, the king, seated beneath the spread canopy, having dismissed his retinue saying "Go for now," commanded <s>Haṃsavega</s>: "Tell me the message." Bowing, he began to narrate: "Your Majesty! In ancient times, by the blessed Earth, pregnant from her union with the Great Boar (<s>Mahāvarāha</s>), a son named <s>Naraka</s> was born in the netherworld. Of this hero, even in childhood the crest-jewels of the world-guardians bowed at his feet in homage; and even the sun, though the enjoyer of the three worlds, mighty-armed, though merely glanced at with an angry sidelong look by the <s>cakravākī</s> of his palace-lotus-pond, did not set without his command, his chariot turned back in fear. And he seized from <s>Varuṇa</s> this parasol, which was the external form of his heart.

body.text: virata-vacasi tasmin bhū-pālaḥ pūrvôpalabdhair eva gurubhir guṇair āropita-bahu-mānaḥ kumāre su-dūram Ābhogâtapatra-vyatikareṇa tu parāṃ koṭim āropite premṇi lajjamāna iva sâdaraṃ jagāda: "Haṃsavega! katham iva tādṛśi mahâtmani mahâbhijane puṇya-rāśau guṇīnāṃ prāgrahare paro-kṣa-suhṛdi snihyati mad-vidhasyânyathā svapne 'pi pravarteta manaḥ. sakala-jagad-uttāpana-paṭavo 'pi śiśirāyante tri-buvana-nayanânanda-kare kamalâkare karās tigma-tejasaḥ. su-bahu-guṇa-krītāś ca ke vayaṃ sakhyasya. saj-jana-mādhuryāṇām a-bhṛta-dāsyo daśa diśaḥ. ekântâvadātôttāna-svabhāva-saṃbhṛta-sādṛśyasya kumudasya kṛte kenâbhihitaḥ śiśira-raśmiḥ. śreyāṃś ca saṃkalpaḥ kumārasya. svayaṃ bāhu-śālī mayi ca samālambita-śarâsane suhṛdi Harād ṛte kam anyaṃ namasyati. saṃvardhitā me prītir amunā saṃkalpena. avalepini paśāv api kesariṇi bahu-māno hṛdayasya kiṃ punaḥ suhṛdi. tat tathā yatethāḥ yathā na ciram iyam asmān kleśayati kumāra-darśanôtkaṇṭhā" iti.
body.translated_text: When he had ceased speaking, the king—in whom great respect had already been established by the weighty virtues previously observed in the prince, and whose affection had now been raised to the highest pitch by the encounter with the parasol of <s>Ābhoga</s>—spoke as if with bashfulness, respectfully: '<s>Haṃsavega</s>! When such a great soul, of great lineage, a treasury of merit, the chief patron of the virtuous, an unseen friend, shows affection—how could the mind of one such as me turn otherwise, even in a dream? Even the rays of the fierce-rayed sun, though skilled at scorching the entire world, become cool in the lotus-bed that delights the eyes of the three worlds. And we—who are we, purchased for friendship by so very many virtues? The ten directions are unpaid servants of the sweetness of good men. Who told the cool-rayed moon about the night-lily, which had accumulated a resemblance through its exclusively pure, white, open nature? And the resolve of the prince is most excellent. He himself is mighty of arm, and having taken up the bow as a friend of mine—whom other than <s>Hara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) does he bow to? My delight has been increased by this resolve. Even toward a lion, an arrogant beast, the heart feels great respect—how much more so toward a friend? Therefore, exert yourself so that this longing for a meeting with the prince does not torment us for long.'

body.text: Haṃsavegas tu vijñāpayāṃ-babhūva: "deva! kim a-param idānīṃ kleśayaty abhijātam abhihitaṃ devena. sevā-bhīravo hi santaḥ, tatrâpi viśeṣeṇâyam ahaṃkāra-dhano Vaiṣṇavo vaṃśaḥ. āstāṃ tāvad asmat-svāmi-vaṃśaḥ. paśyatu devaḥ puruṣasya hi sevāṃ prati dur-jananyêvâti-vṛddhayā dur-gatyā vâbhimukhī-kriyamāṇasya, kuṭumbinyêvâ-saṃtuṣṭayā tṛṣṇayā vā preryamāṇasya, dur-apatyair iva yauvana-janitair-nānâbhilāṣibhir a-sat-saṃkalpair vâkulī-kriyamāṇasya, jarat-kumārīm iva para-mārgaṇa-yogyām ati-mahatīṃ vā avasthāṃ paśyataḥ, sva-gṛhe dur-bandhubhir iva duḥ-sthitaiḥ samagrair grahair vā grāhyamāṇasyâbhiyogaṃ, purātanair ati-dus-tyajair bhṛtyair iva malinaiḥ karmabhir vânuvartyamānasya, sakala-śarīra-saṃtāpa-karaṃ karīṣâgnim iva duṣ-kṛtinaḥ

children.text: kṛta-cittasya saṃpraveṣṭuṃ rāja-kulam upahata-sakalêndriya-śakter iva mithyâiva hṛdaya-gata-viṣaya-grāma-grahaṇâbhilāṣasya, prathamam eva toraṇa-tale vandana-mālā-kisalayasyêva śuṣyato dvāra-rakṣibhir niruddhasya, pīḍitasya praviśato dvāre hariṇasyêvâ-parair hanyamānasya, kari-karma-carma-puṭasyêva muhur-muhuḥ pratihāra-maṇḍala-kara-prahārair nirasyamānasya, nidhi-pādapa-prarohasyêva draviṇâbhilāṣād adho-mukhī-bhavataḥ, dūram a-mārgaṇasyâpy ati-viprakṛṣṭa-vivṛtta-visarjitasyôdvegaṃ vrajataḥ, a-kaṇṭakasyâpi caraṇa-tala-lagnasyâkṛṣya kṣepīyaḥ kṣipyamāṇasya, a-makara-ketor apy a-kālôpasarpaṇâ-prakupitêśvara-dṛṣṭi-dagdhasya, pralayam upagacchataḥ kaper iva kopa-nirbhartsitasyâpy abhinna-mukha-rāgasya, brahma-ghna iva prati-divasa-vandanôddhṛṣṭa-śiraḥ-kapālasya, sparśa-rahitasyâ-śubha-karmāṇi nirvahataḥ, tri-śaṅkor ivôbhaya-loka-bhraṣṭasya naktaṃ-dinam avāk-śirasas tiṣṭhataḥ, vājina iva kavala-vaśena sukha-vāhyam ātmānaṃ vidadhānasya, an-aśana-śāyina iva hṛdaya-sthāpita-jīva-nāśasya, śarīraṃ kṣapayataḥ śuna iva nija-dāra-parāṅ-mukhasya, jaghanya-karma-lagnam ātmānaṃ tāḍayataḥ, pretasyêvân-ucita-bhūmi-dīyamānânna-piṇḍasya, bali-bhuja iva jihvā-laulyôpayukta-puruṣa-varcaso vṛthā vihitâyuṣo jīvitaḥ, śmaśāna-pādapān iva piśācasya dagdha-bhūtyā paruṣī-kṛtān rāja-
children.translated_text: who has resolved to enter the royal court—his power of all the senses impaired, as if in vain desiring to seize the village of objects dwelling within the heart; withering at the very first threshold like a garland's sprout-tip beneath the festoon-arch, blocked by the door-keepers; tormented upon entering the gate, like a deer slain by others; repeatedly struck back by the slaps of the circle of ushers, like an elephant-worker's leather-folded bag; bowing face-down from greed for wealth like the sprout of a treasure-tree; going in agitation even though not a supplicant, having been turned back, dismissed, and sent far away; though not a thorn, being pulled out more swiftly, stuck at the sole of a foot, and flung away; though not the banner-bearer of <s>Kāma</s> (Love), being burned by the glance of the lord angered by his untimely approach; like a monkey meeting its end, scolded with furious reproach yet with unbroken color on his face; like a slayer of Brahmins, his skull-cap daily polished from the bowing of salutations; devoid of touch [with the sacred], performing inauspicious deeds; like <s>Triśaṅku</s>, fallen from both worlds, standing head-downward night and day; like a horse, making himself easily rideable by the control of the morsel; like one sleeping hungry, placing the destruction of life within the heart; wasting his body like a dog, turned away from his own wife; striking himself caught in base work; like a ghost, being given food-offerings at unfitting grounds; like a crow-offering, living with existence pointlessly spent, his human vigor consumed by the greed of the tongue; approaching the king's

children.text: -vallabhān upasarpataḥ viparīta-jihvā-janita-mādhuryair oṣṭha-mātra-prakaṭita-rāgai rāja-śukâlāpaiḥ śiśor iva mugdha-vilobhyamānasya, vetālasyêva narêndra-prabhāvâviṣṭasya na kiṃ-cin nâcarataḥ, citra-dhanuṣa ivâlīka-guṇâdhyāropaṇâika-kriyā-nitya-namrasya nirvāṇa-tejasaḥ, saṃmārjanī-samupārjita-rajaso 'vakara-kūṭasyêva nirmālya-vāhinaḥ, kapha-vikāriṇa iva dine dine kaṭukair udvejyamānasya, saugatasyêvârtha-śūnya-vijñapti-janita-vairāgyasya kāṣāyāṇy abhilaṣataḥ, niśāsv api mātṛ-bali-piṇḍasyêva dikṣu vikṣipyamāṇasya, a-śauca-gatasyêva kuśayana-janita-samadhikatara-duḥkha-vṛtteḥ, tulā-yantrasyêva paścāt-kṛta-gauravasya toyârtham api namataḥ, ati-kṛpaṇasya śirasā kevalenâ-saṃtuṣṭasya vacasâpi pādau spṛśataḥ, nir-daya-vetri-vetra-tāḍana-trastayêva trapayā tyaktasya, dainya-saṃkocita-hṛdaya-hṛtâvakāśayêvâhopuruṣikayā parivarjitasya, kutsita-karmâṅgī-karaṇa-kupitayêvônnatyā viyuktasya, dhana-śraddhayā kleśān upārjayataḥ. sva-vṛddhi-buddhyâvamānaṃ saṃvardhayato mūḍhasya, saty api vividha-kusumâdhivāsa-surabhiṇi vane tṛṣṇayâñjalim uparacayataḥ, kula-putrasyâpi kṛtâgasa iva bhīta-bhītasya samīpam upasarpataḥ, darśanīyasyâpy ālekhya-kusumasyêva niṣ-phala-janmanaḥ, viduṣo 'pi vaidheyasyêvâpaśabda-mukhasya, śaktimato 'pi śvitriṇa iva saṃko-
children.translated_text: favorites—made harsh like cremation-ground trees by the scorched fortune of the demon—being charmed like a child by the sweet nothings of royal parrots with sweetness generated by an inverted tongue, with passion displayed only on the lips; like a vampire, possessed by the power of a king, doing nothing that is not done; like a rainbow, whose splendor is extinguished, ever bowed in the sole activity of stringing false virtues; like a refuse-heap sweeping up dust, carrying away discarded offerings; like one suffering from phlegm-disorder, being daily irritated by bitter things; like a Buddhist monk, desiring the ochre robes out of the dispassion born from petitions empty of substance; being tossed about in every direction even at night, like an offering-ball for the mother-goddesses; like one in ritual impurity, with sleep on <s>kuśa</s> grass generating ever-greater suffering; like a balance-scale, bowing even for the sake of water, his weight put behind him; exceedingly wretched, not content with the head alone, touching the feet even with words; abandoned by shame as if frightened by the beating of the merciless usher's staff; deserted by pride as if its space were taken away by a heart contracted by wretchedness; separated from dignity as if angered by the acceptance of despicable tasks; earning afflictions through faith in wealth; a fool who cultivates insult through the notion of self-advancement; even when there exists a forest fragrant with various flower-perfumed breezes, through craving joining his palms [in supplication]; even a nobleman, approaching timidly as if guilty; even handsome, his birth fruitless like a painted flower; even learned, uttering wrong syllables like a servant; even powerful, with hands contracted together like a leper—

children.text: -cita-kara-yugalasya, sama-samutkarṣeṣu nir-agni-pacyamānasya, nīca-samī-karaṇeṣu nir-ucchvāsaṃ mriyamāṇasya, paribhavais tṛṇī-kṛtasya, duḥkhânilenâ-nirvṛter jvalataḥ, bhaktasyâpy a-bhaktasya, nir-ūṣmaṇaḥ saṃtāpayato bandhūn, vimānasyâpy a-gatikasya, cyuta-gauravasyâpy adhastād gacchataḥ, niḥ-sattvasyâpi mahā-māṃsa-vikrayaṃ kurvataḥ, nir-madasyâpy a-svatantra-vṛtteḥ, a-yogino 'pi dhyāna-vaśī-kṛtâtmanaḥ, śayyôtthāyaṃ praṇamato dagdha-muṇḍasya, gotra-vidūṣakasya naktaṃ-dinaṃ nṛtyato manasvi-janaṃ hāsayataḥ, kulâṅgārasya vaṃśaṃ dahataḥ, nṛ-paśos tṛṇe 'pi labde kandharām avanamayataḥ, jaṭhara-paripūraṇa-mātra-prayojana-janmano māṃsa-piṇḍasya garbha-rogasya mātuḥ, a-puṇyānāṃ karmaṇām ācaraṇād bhṛtakasya kiṃ prāyaś-cittam, kā pratipatti-kriyā, kva gatasya śāntiḥ, kīdṛśaṃ jīvitam, kaḥ puruṣâbhimānaḥ, kiṃ-nāmāno vilāsāḥ, kīdṛśī bhoga-śraddhā, prabala-paṅka iva sarvam adhastān nayati dāruṇo dāsa-śabdaḥ. dhik tad ucchvasitam upayātu nidhanaṃ dhanam, a-bhava-nirbhūter astu tasyā namo bhagavadbhyas tebhyaḥ sukhebhyas tasyâyam añjalir aiśvaryasya tiṣṭhatu dūra eva sā śrīḥ śivaṃ sa paricchadaḥ karotu yad artham uttamâṅgaṃ gāṃ gamiṣyaty a-śāpânugraha-kṣamas tapasvī mukha-priya-rataḥ klībo pūti-māṃsamayaḥ kṛmir a-gaṇyamāno narakaḥ, pāda-rajo-dhūsarôttamâṅgo jaṅgamaḥ pāda-pīṭhaḥ puṃs-kokilaḥ kāku-kvaṇiteṣu, śikhī sukha-kara-kekāsu,
children.translated_text: —being cooked without fire among equals of higher rank; dying breathlessly among those equalized with the low; reduced to straw by humiliations; burning without cessation by the wind of sorrow; devoted yet undevoted; without warmth yet causing anguish to kinsmen; having a vehicle yet without a path; having lost dignity yet still descending further; devoid of courage yet conducting a great trade in flesh; without intoxication yet with his conduct not in his own control; not a <s>yogī</s> yet with his self subjugated by meditation; bowing at rising and retiring like a tonsured monk; one who defames his clan, dancing night and day, making spirited men laugh; a coal of the family, burning his lineage; a man-beast who bows his neck even for a blade of grass obtained; born for the sole purpose of filling his belly, a lump of flesh, a disease of his mother's womb—for such a hireling who performs unmeritorious deeds, what is the expiation? What is the course of action? Where has he gone that he might find peace? What kind of life is this? What claim to manly pride? What are these so-called pleasures? What faith in enjoyment? Like powerful mud, that terrible word 'servant' drags everything downward. Fie on that breathing—let wealth meet its destruction, let there be obeisance to those blessed comforts that arise from non-existence, let this be the salutation of sovereignty, let that glory stay far away indeed, let that retinue bring auspiciousness—for the sake of which the wretched one, unable to curse or bless, an ascetic who delights in what pleases the mouth, a eunuch, a worm of putrid flesh, an unworthy hell, will go headfirst to the earth, his head grey with the dust of feet, a walking footstool, a male cuckoo in plaintive calls, a peacock in pleasing cries,

children.text: sthūla-kūrmaḥ kroḍa-kaṣaṇeṣu, śvā nīca-cāṭu-karaṇeṣu, kṛkalāsaḥ śiro-viḍambanāsu, jāhaka ātma-saṃkocaneṣu, veṇur mūrcchanāsu, veśyā-kāyaḥ karaṇa-bandha-kleśeṣu, palālaṃ sattva-śāliṣu, pratipādakaḥ pāda-saṃvāhanāsu, kandukaḥ kara-tala-tāḍaneṣu, vīṇā-daṇḍaḥ koṇâbighāteṣu, varākaḥ sevako 'pi martya-madhye rājilo 'pi vā, bhogī pulāko 'pi vā, kalamo varaṃ kṣaṇam api kṛtā mānavatā mānavatā na mato namatas trailokyâdhirājyôpabhogo 'pi manasvinaḥ. tad evam abhinanditâsmadīya-praṇayo devo 'pi divasaiḥ katipayair eva parāgataḥ prāg-jyotiṣêśvara iti karotu cetasi" ity uktvā tūṣṇīm abhūt. a-cirāc ca namas-kṛtya nirjagāma.

body.translated_text: <s>Haṃsavega</s>, however, submitted: 'Your Majesty! What further thing now afflicts the noble-born? What Your Majesty has said is already spoken. For good men are averse to servitude—and especially this <s>Vaiṣṇava</s> lineage, whose wealth is its pride. Let our master's dynasty be set aside for now. Let Your Majesty observe: for a man facing servitude—being directed toward it by misfortune as if by an evil mother through extreme old age, or being driven by insatiable desire as if by a discontented wife, or being agitated by wicked fantasies born of youth and various cravings as if by evil offspring, or seeing an exceedingly great state fit for another's pursuit as if an aging maiden, or being seized in his own home by all the planets in their adverse positions as if by wicked kinsmen in their discomfort, or being followed by ancient sins difficult to abandon as if by old servants who are soiled, causing burning anguish to the entire body like cow-dung fire, like a sinner

body.translated_text: The king too passed that night with his heart seized by eagerness to see the prince. For the self-offering of great men is a spell of enchantment that needs no root or <s>mantra</s>. And at dawn, having given abundant return-gifts dispatched under the charge of a chief return-envoy, he sent <s>Haṃsavega</s> back. And from that point onward, he himself advanced by unceasing marches toward the enemy. But one day, he heard from a letter-carrier that <s>Bhaṇḍi</s>—having brought with him all the <s>Mālava</s> king's possessions won by the arm-strength of <s>Rājyavardhana</s>—had arrived and encamped nearby. And hearing this, his grief for his brother being kindled anew, his heart became anxious to see him; he entered a darkness as it were of swooning; and having suspended all activities, he waited for a moment in his own palace—with the retinue hushed into silence by the ushers' restraint, with the company of kings in attendance—watching for his arrival.

body.translated_text: The king too, seeing him, rose and went forward with halting steps, raised him up, embraced him tightly by the neck, and wept piteously for a very long time. And when the force of his grief had subsided, he came back as before and sat upon his own seat. And when <s>Bhaṇḍi</s> had first washed his face, the king too washed his face. And when some small measure of time had elapsed, he asked about the circumstances of his brother's death. And <s>Bhaṇḍi</s> narrated the entire account as it had occurred. Then the king said to him: 'What has happened regarding <s>Rājyaśrī</s>?' He replied: 'Your Majesty! When Lord <s>Rājyavardhana</s> had attained the divine state, and when the one named <s>Gupta</s> had seized <s>Kuśasthala</s>, the princess <s>Rājyaśrī</s> escaped from her prison and entered the <s>Vindhya</s> forest with her retinue—so I have heard from common report. Many people have been sent as searchers for her, but they have not returned to this day.' Hearing this, the king said: 'What use are other trackers? Where she is, there I myself shall go, having set aside all other business. And let you too advance with the army toward the <s>Gauḍas</s>.' Having said this, he rose and went to the bathing-place. And having had his mourning-beard shaved by the chief usher's household barber after his bath, he dined together with <s>Bhaṇḍi</s>—to whom he showed his favor through the sending of personal garments, flowers, body-ointments, and ornaments—and spent the day with him.

children.translated_text: Then the next day, at dawn itself, <s>Bhaṇḍi</s> approached the king and reported: 'May Your Majesty behold the military equipment with its accoutrements won by the arm-strength of the illustrious <s>Rājyavardhana</s> from the king of <s>Mālava</s>.' Permitted by the king with the words 'Let it be so,' he proceeded to display [the spoils]. And these were: elephants numbering many thousands—their temple-plates muddy with matted swarms of bees buzzing with the fragrance of the incessantly dripping ichor-liquor, like mobile cheek-mountains, as if thunderclouds descended to earth bearing cupped handfuls of deep rumbling sound, releasing the scent of forests of blossoming <s>saptacchada</s> trees, as if autumn days heaped together; and horses swift as deer, charming with their circles of beautiful golden chowries; and special ornaments that turned the ten directions into multiple rainbows with the play of their rays showering streams of young sunlight; and startlingly brilliant necklaces of pearls—flooded to the horizons by their own radiance, with the wanton fragrance of the breasts of <s>Mālavī</s> women maddened by <s>Smara</s> (Love); and yak-tail fans, as if needles threaded with clusters of the moon-lord's rays, like his own [pieces of] fame; and a white parasol with a golden stalk—like the white lotus-dwelling of <s>Śrī</s> (Fortune); and courtesans—like <s>Apsarasas</s> descended through their passion for the daring relish of many battles; and royal regalia such as thrones, beds, and chairs; and the entire <s>Mālava</s> royal household with their feet immobilized by iron fetters; and all the numbered inventory documents; and treasury vessels pressed with ornamental seals. Having surveyed all this, the king directed his superintendents to take charge of it as appropriate. And on another day, setting out on horseback to search for his sister, he headed for the <s>Vindhya</s> forest and reached it in just a few marches.

with posts matted with bunches of fresh young mango-fruit clusters being kept moist by sprout-bundles moistened with water-spray; whose waters were drunk by the rows of resting mendicants' bags—the forest-entrance wayside stations seemed to dismiss the summer-heat with their coolness; children.text: -rān, bhārāṃś ca madhuno mākṣikasya mayūrâṅgajasyâ-kliṣṭa-madhûcchiṣṭa-cakra-mālānāṃ lambamāna-lāmajjaka-muñja-jūṭa-jaṭānām apa-tvacāṃ khadira-kāṣṭhānāṃ kuṣṭhasya kaṭhora-kesari-saṭâbhāra-babhruṇaś ca rodhrasya bhūyaso bhārakān, lokenâdāya vrajatā pravicita-vividha-vana-phala-pūrita-piṭaka-mastakābhiś câbhyarṇa-grāma-gatvarībhis tvaramāṇābhir vikraya-cintā-vyagrābhir grāmeyakābhir vyāpta-dig-antaram itas tataś ca yukta-śūra-śakura-śākvarāṇāṃ purāṇa-pāṃsûtkira-karīṣa-kūṭa-vāhinīnāṃ dhūrgata-dhūli-dhūsara-sairibha-sa-roṣa-svara-sāryamāṇānāṃ saṃkrīḍac-caṭula-cakra-cītkāriṇīnāṃ śakaṭa-śreṇīnāṃ saṃpātaiḥ, saṃpādyamāna-dur-balôrvī-virūkṣa-kṣetra-saṃskāram ārakṣa-kṣipta-dānta-vāhaka-daṇḍôḍḍīyamāna-hariṇa-helā-laṅghita-tuṅga-vaiṇava-vṛtibhiś ca nikhāta-gaura-karaṅka-śaṅku-śaṅkita-śaśaka-śakalita-tuṅga-śuṅgaiḥ, prayatna-prabhṛta-viśaṅkaṭa-viṭapair vācair aikṣavaiḥ, su-bahubhiḥ śyāmāyamānôpakaṇṭham ati-viprakṣṭântarair marakata-snigdha-snuhā-vāṭa-veṣṭitaiḥ, kārmuka-karmaṇya-vaṃśa-viṭapa-saṃkaṭaiḥ, kaṇṭakita-karañja-rāji-duṣ-praveśyaiḥ, urubūka-vacā-vaṅgaka-surasa-sūraṇa-śigru-granthi-parṇa-gavedhukā-garmud-gulma-gahana-
children.translated_text: carrying water in yellow pots, preceded by a pair of strong trudging bullocks yoked together—entering the forest for the purpose of gathering firewood; and with outcast hunters going about with their wild-beast killing apparatus—trap-bundles and nooses thickly piled up in the huts erected at the edge—carrying nets, snares, and circular basket-traps of animal-sinew cords; and with bird-catchers bearing cages holding captured <s>krakaraka</s> (partridge), <s>piñjala</s>, and other birds, with small snare-ropes hanging from hunting-bows slung over their shoulders; and with flocks of <s>capeṭaka</s> (Malabar starlings) wandering about, greedy for the creeper-liana ladies smeared with drops of dripping birdlime; and with young hunter-lads at play—walking about with puppy offspring of snare-dogs, enticing with flattery the packs of dogs trembling with eagerness at the partridges hidden among the grass-clumps—sporting at the bird-and-game hunt; [he saw people] carrying bundles of bark-cloth for dyeing—tawny-hued as the throats of mature <s>cakravāka</s> birds; and sackfuls of <s>dhātakī</s> blossoms of mineral-like hues, recently gathered; and abundant loads of <s>atasī</s> (flax) stalks with their bundle-roots, meant for stuffing; and loads of honey—of wild bees' honeycomb, of <s>mayūrāṅga</s> (a kind of bee)—with their chains of unbroken beeswax-comb, and dangling matted bunches of <s>lāmajjaka</s> (fragrant grass) and <s>muñja</s> reed; and heavy loads of peeled <s>khadira</s> (catechu) wood, of <s>kuṣṭha</s> (costus root), and especially of <s>rodhra</s> (a dyestuff tree) tawny as a fierce lion's mane; and with village-women from the nearby village—their basket-tops filled with various selected forest fruits, hastening eagerly, preoccupied with thoughts of selling—the directions were pervaded; and here and there, with the intersections of lines of carts—yoked with <s>śūra</s>, <s>śakura</s>, and <s>śākvara</s> bulls, carrying heaps of old manure, dust, and dung-cakes, driven with angry shouts amid the dust-grey buffalo made grey by wheel-raised dust, their playful restless wheels screeching—

children.text: -gṛha-vāṭikaiḥ, nikhātôcca-kāṣṭhâropita-kāṣṭhâluka-latā-pratāna-vihita-cchāyaiḥ, parimaṇḍala-badarī-maṇḍapaka-tala-nikhāta-khādira-kīla-baddha-vatsa-rūpaiḥ, katham api kukkuṭa-raṭitânumīyamāna-saṃniveśair aṅganā-śasti-stambha-tala-viracita-pakṣi-pūpikâvāpikair vikīrṇa-badara-pāṭala-paṭalaiḥ, veṇu-poṭa-dala-nala-kalita-śaramaya-vṛti-vihita-bhittibhiḥ, kiṃśuka-gorocanā-racita-maṇḍala-maṇḍapa-balvaja-baddhâṅgāra-rāśibhiḥ, śālmalī-phala-tūla-saṃcaya-bahulaiḥ, saṃnihita-nala-śāli-śālūka-khaṇḍa-kumuda-bīja-veṇu-taṇḍulaiḥ, saṃgṛhīta-tamāla-bījaiḥ, bhasma-malina-mlāna-kāśmarya-kūṭa-vyādhṛta-kaṭair āśyāna-rājādana-madana-phala-sphītair madhūkâsava-madya-prāyaiḥ, kusumbha-kumbha-gaṇḍa-kusūlair a-virahita-rāja-māṣa-trapuṣa-karkaṭikā-kūṣmāṇḍâlābu-bījaiḥ, poṣyamāṇa-vana-biḍāla-māludhāna-nakula-śāli-jāta-jātakâdibhir aṭavī-kuṭumbināṃ gṛhair upetaṃ vana-grāmakaṃ dadarśa. tatrâiva ca taṃ divasam aty-avāhayad iti.
children.translated_text: and the fields of feeble land being prepared by the guards whipping the tamed yoke-animals whose rods set the deer flying and contemptuously leaping over the tall bamboo fences; and with the sugarcane fields whose broad-branched stalks had been carefully planted, with huge shoots growing tall and thick, whose vicinities darkened with <s>śyāmāka</s>, widely spaced, enclosed by hedges of smooth <s>snuhā</s> (euphorbia) green as emerald; and narrow with bamboo thickets whose branches were suitable for bow-making; and hard to enter through rows of thorny <s>karañja</s>; and with kitchen-gardens thick with groves of <s>urubūka</s> (castor), <s>vacā</s> (calamus), <s>vaṅgaka</s> (brinjal), <s>surasa</s> (basil), <s>sūraṇa</s> (yam), <s>śigru</s> (drumstick), <s>granthiparṇa</s>, <s>gavedhukā</s> (wild millet), <s>garmut</s>, and other bush-plants; with shade provided by climbing creeper-trellises of <s>kāṣṭhāluka</s> (yam) vines raised on tall planted stakes; with calf-forms tied to <s>khadira</s>-wood pegs driven into the ground in the courtyards of circular <s>badarī</s> (jujube) arbors; the settlements somehow discernible from the crowing of cocks; with bird-cake-feeding basins arranged at the base of the courtyard pillars by the women; strewn with layers of pink <s>badara</s> (jujube) fruits; with walls made of reed-work fences fashioned from woven bamboo-splits, reeds, and <s>śara</s> (arrow-grass); with circles of floors of <s>kiṃśuka</s> (flame-of-the-forest) and <s>gorocanā</s> (cow-bile pigment) decorations, pavilions, and heaps of charcoal bound with <s>balvaja</s> (coarse grass); abundant with stores of silk-cotton fruit-floss; with rice, <s>śālūka</s> (lotus-root) pieces, <s>kumuda</s> (lily) seeds, and bamboo-rice stored nearby; with <s>tamāla</s> seeds gathered; with mats spread over heaps of ash-grey withered <s>kāśmarya</s> wood; with stores of overripe <s>rājādana</s> and <s>madana</s> fruits swelling; mostly stocked with <s>madhūka</s> (mahua) liquor; with pots of <s>kusumbha</s> (safflower) along with <s>kusūla</s> (grain-bin) jars; not lacking seeds of <s>rāja-māṣa</s> (king's bean), cucumber, melon, pumpkin, and gourd; with forest cats, <s>māludhāna</s> (mongoose-like animals), mongooses, and domestic <s>śāli</s> rice-bird chicks being raised—he beheld a forest village with such houses of the forest-dwelling families. And there he spent that day.

body.translated_text: Then, as he entered, from afar itself he saw forest tracts with their fearsome <s>vaṭa</s> (banyan) trees encircled by cattle-pens constructed from heaps of dry branches—the trees turned grey with smoke from the fires of forest-grain seed-storage chambers burning <s>ṣaṣṭika</s> rice-chaff; with tiger-traps set up by cowherd-boys enraged at the killing of their calves; with the axes of firewood-gatherers from other villages being forcibly seized by lawless forest-guards; with platforms for <s>Cāmuṇḍā</s> shrines constructed in clearings of dense trees—the forest outskirts being announced; and at the very edge, with feeble farmers cultivating mostly with hoes, busy with supporting their families, whose grain-field plots of abundant ripe paddy on the high ground were encroached upon by the authoritative speech [of officials]; and with <s>kāpila</s> (tawny) fields—narrow, hard as iron with their black soil, with thick sprouts growing at every spot from posts erected at various stations, difficult to approach due to the profuse <s>śyāmāka</s> growth, abounding in <s>alambusa</s> (reed) grass, with sparse plots not lacking <s>kokilākṣa</s> (thorny) shrubs; and with the land around the cultivated area—its ground beaten by the exceedingly busy coming and going of many [people]—indicated as infested by wild beasts through the high watchtowers erected nearby; and with the plowing being done with great difficulty,

body.text: iti śrī-mahā-kavi-Bāṇa-bhaṭṭa-kṛtau Harṣacarite chatra-labdhir nāma saptama ucchvāsa.
body.translated_text: Thus ends the seventh <s>ucchvāsa</s> (chapter) named 'The Obtaining of the Parasol' in the <s>Harṣacarita</s> composed by the illustrious great poet <s>Bāṇabhaṭṭa</s>.

children.text: aṣṭama ucchvāsaḥ.
children.translated_text: Eighth <s>Ucchvāsa</s> (Chapter).

children.text: sahasā saṃpādayatā mano-ratha-prārthitāni vastūni /
children.translated_text: By fate, which suddenly brings about the things longed for by one's desires,

children.text: daivenâpi kriyate bhavyānāṃ pūrva-sevêva // 8.1 //
children.translated_text: even for the blessed, a prior service as it were is performed. ||8.1||

children.text: vidvaj-jana-saṃparko naṣṭêṣṭa-jñāti-darśanâbhyudayaḥ /
children.translated_text: The company of the learned, the joyful sight of lost and beloved kinsmen,

children.text: kasya na sukhāya bhavane bhavati mahā-ratna-lābhaś ca // 8.2 //
children.translated_text: the acquisition of a great jewel in one's home—for whom are these not a source of happiness? ||8.2||

body.text: athâparedyur utthāya pārthivas tasmād grāmakān nirgatya viveśa Vindhyâṭavīm. āṭa ca tasyām itaś cêtaś ca su-bahūn divasān. ekadā tu bhū-pater bhramata evâṭavika-sāmantasya Śarabhaketoḥ sūnur Vyāghraketur nāma kuto 'pi kajjala-śyāmala-śyāma-latā-valayenâdhilalāṭam uccaiḥ kṛta-mauli-bandham, andha-kāriṇīm a-kāraṇa-bhuvā bhrukuṭi-bhaṅgena tri-śākhena tri-yāmām iva sāhasa-saha-cāriṇīṃ lalāṭa-sthalīṃ sadā samudvahantam, avataṃsitâika-śuka-pakṣaka-prabhā-haritāyamānena pinaddha-kācara-kāca-maṇi-karṇikena śravaṇena śobhamānam, kiṃ-cic cullasya pravirala-pakṣmaṇaś cakṣuṣaḥ sahajena rāga-rociṣā rasāyana-rasôpayuktaṃ tāra-kṣavaṃ kṣatajam iva kṣarantam, avanāṭa-nāsikam cipiṭâdharam, cikina-cibukam, a-hīna-hanûtkaṭa-kapola-kūṭâsthi-paryantam īṣad-avāgra-grīvā-bandham, skanna-skandhârdha-bhāgam, an-avarata-kaṭhina-kodaṇḍa-kuṇḍalī-karaṇa-karkaśa-vyāyāma-vistāritenâṃsalenôrasā hasantam iva taṭa-śilā-prathimānaṃ, Vindhya-girer ajagara-garī-

children.text: -yasā ca bhuja-yugalena laghayantaṃ, tuhina-śaila-śāla-drumāṇāṃ drāghimāṇam, varāha-bāla-valita-bandhanābhir nāga-damana-jūṭikā-vāṭikābhir jaṭilī-kṛta-pṛṣṭhe prakoṣṭhe pratiṣṭhāṃ gataṃ godanta-maṇi-citraṃ trāpuṣaṃ valayaṃ bibhrāṇam, atundilam api tuṇḍibham, ahīramaṇī-carma-nirmita-paṭṭikayoś citra-citraka-tvak-tārakita-parivārayā saṃkubjâjina-jālakitayā śṛṅgamaya-masṛṇa-muṣṭi-bhāga-bhāsvarayā pārada-rasa-leśa-lipta-samasta-mastikayā kṛpāṇyā karālita-viśaṃkaṭa-kaṭi-pradeśam, prathama-yauvanôllikhyamāna-madhya-bhāga-bhraṣṭa-māṃsa-bharitāv iva sthavīyasāv ūru-daṇḍau dadhatam, accha-bhalla-carmamayena bhallī-prāya-prabhūta-śarabhṛtā śabala-śārdūla-carma-paṭa-pīḍitenâli-kula-kāla-kambala-lola-lomnā pṛṣṭha-bhāga-bhājā bhastrâbharaṇena pallavitam iva kārśyam upadarśayantam, uttara-tri-bhāgôttaṃsita-cāṣa-piccha-cāru-śikhare khadira-jaṭā-nirmāṇe khara-prāṇe pracura-mayūra-pitta-patra-latā-citrita-tvaci tvaci sāra-guṇe guruṇi vāma-skandhâdhyāsita-dhanuṣi doṣi lambamānenâvāk-śirasā śita-śara-kṛttâika-nala-kavi-vara-praveśitêtara-jaṅgha-janita-svastika-bandhena bandhūka-lohita-rudhira-rāji-rañjita-ghrāṇa-vartmanā vapur-vitati-vyakta-vibhāvyamāna-komala-kroḍa-roma-śuklimnā śaśena śitâṭanī-śikhâgra-grathita-grīveṇa câpāvṛta-cañcûttāna-tāmra-tālunā tittiriṇā varṇaka-muṣṭim iva mṛgayāyāḥ darśayantam, viṣama-viṣa-dūṣita-vadanena ca vivarṇena kṛṣṇâhinêva mūla-gṛhītena vyagra-dakṣiṇa-karâgram, jaṅgamam iva giri-taṭa-tamāla-pādapam, yantrôllikhitam aśma-sāra-stambham iva bhramantama, añjana-śilā-cchedam iva calantam, ayaḥ-sāram iva girer Vindhyasya galantam, pākalaṃ kari-kulānām, kāla-pāśaṃ kuraṅga-yūthānām, dhūma-ketuṃ mṛga-rāja-cakrāṇām, mahānavamī-mahaṃ mahīṣa-maṇḍalānām, hṛdayam iva hiṃsāyāḥ, phalam iva pāpasya, kāraṇam iva kali-kālasya, kāmukam iva kāla-rātreḥ, śabara-yuvānam ādāyâjagāma. dūre ca sthāpayitvā vijñāpayāṃ-babhūva: "deva! sarvasyâsya Vindhyasya svāmī sarva-pallī-patīnāṃ
children.translated_text: —and making light, with his pair of fame-spreading arms, the length of the <s>śāla</s> trees of the Himalaya, wearing on his forearm—made shaggy by clusters of wristbands for elephant-taming twisted with boar-bristle bindings—a tin bracelet variegated with cow-tooth gems, pot-bellied though not fat, his broad waist-region made fearsome by a sword whose belt-straps were made of <s>ahīramaṇī</s> leather, studded with the skin of the spotted civet-cat, netted with a shrunken hide-mesh, gleaming with a smooth horn-grip, its entire pommel smeared with a film of mercury—bearing two massive thigh-staffs as if the middle part of his first youth were being carved away and the fallen flesh-mass had filled them—displaying his leanness as if it were blossoming, with a quiver-ornament on his back made of clear bear-skin, filled with an abundance of broadhead arrows, pressed with a dappled tiger-skin cloth, its hair waving like a dark blanket of bee-swarms—with a bow seated on his left shoulder, heavy, of good string, its skin painted with abundant peacock-bile leaf-vine patterns, made of <s>khadira</s>-wood root, powerful, its upper third-part crested with a beautiful peak of jay feathers—and hanging from the bowstring head-downward, a hare with its legs crossed in a <s>svastika</s> knot formed by one leg cut by a sharp arrow and the other thrust into it, its nasal channel stained with <s>bandhūka</s>-red lines of blood, the whiteness of its soft belly-fur clearly visible across its body's expanse—and a francolin partridge with its neck threaded through the tip of a sharp arrowhead, its beak open, the copper-red roof of its mouth exposed—displaying as it were a fistful of the colors of the hunt—and with the tip of his right hand engaged by a discolored black serpent seized at the root, its face marred by the venom of deadly poison—like a moving <s>tamāla</s> tree on a mountainside, like an iron pillar engraved by a machine seeming to revolve, like a walking fragment of collyrium-rock, like the iron essence of Mount <s>Vindhya</s> flowing down—the doom of elephant herds, the death-noose of deer herds, the comet of lion-prides, the <s>Mahānavamī</s> festival for buffalo-circles, the very heart of violence, the fruit of sin, the cause of the <s>Kali</s> age, the lover of the dark night of doom—he brought along a <s>Śabara</s> youth. Stationing him at a distance, he reported: "Your Majesty! The lord of all this <s>Vindhya</s> region, the chief of all the village chieftains,

children.text: prāgraharaḥ śabara-senā-patir Bhūkampo nāma. tasyâyaṃ Nirghāta-nāmā svasrīyaḥ sakalasyâsya Vindhya-kāntārâraṇyasya parṇānām apy abhijñaḥ kim uta pradeśānām. enaṃ pṛcchatu devo yogyo 'yam ājñāṃ kartum." iti kathite ca Nirgātas tu kṣiti-tala-nihita-mauliḥ praṇāmam akarot. upaninye ca tittiriṇā saha śaśôpāyanam. avani-patis tu saṃmānayan svayam eva tam aprākṣīt: "aṅga! abhijñā yūyam asya sarvasyôddeśasya? vihāra-śīlāś ca divaseṣv eteṣu bhavantaḥ? senā-pater vânyasya vā tad-anujīvinaḥ kasya-cid udāra-rūpa nārī na gatā bhaved darśana-gocaram?" iti.
children.translated_text: is a <s>Śabara</s> general named <s>Bhūkampa</s>. This man is his nephew, named <s>Nirghāta</s>, who knows every leaf of this entire <s>Vindhya</s> wilderness, let alone its localities. Let Your Majesty question him—he is fit to execute a command." When this was reported, <s>Nirghāta</s> placed his head upon the ground and made his salutation. He presented the hare and the francolin as offerings. The king, honoring him, personally asked: "Friend! Are you people familiar with this entire region? Have you been roaming about in these parts lately? Has any woman of noble appearance—belonging to the general or to any of his dependents—perchance come within your sight?"

body.translated_text: Then the next day, rising, the king departed from that hamlet and entered the <s>Vindhya</s> forest. And he wandered in it here and there for many days. One day, while the king was roaming, from somewhere appeared the son of the forest chieftain <s>Śarabhaketu</s>, a man named <s>Vyāghraketu</s>—bearing upon his forehead a high-tied turban-knot encircled by a dark creeper-band black as lampblack; his brow-area always bearing a three-forked frown—dark as night, companion of daring, as if a <s>bhṛkuṭī</s> born without cause; his ear adorned with a single parrot-feather tilted as an ornament, its green luster giving a greenish tinge, bound with a glass-bead and <s>kāca-maṇi</s> (crystal) earring; from his slightly squinting eye with sparse eyelashes, through its natural red glow, as if discharging drops of blood like the medicinal elixir of <s>kṣava</s> (pungent sneezing powder); with a depressed nose and flattened lower lip; a pointed chin; with the area around his full, prominent jawbones and cheek-ridges not deficient in handsomeness; a slightly forward-stooping neck-set; with the shoulder-region half-sloping; his chest—broadened by the rigorous exercise of the constant hard bending of the stiff bow into a circle—laughing as it were at the breadth of cliff-slabs, like the <s>Vindhya</s> mountain's python-

body.text: Nirghātas tu bhū-pālâlāpana-prasādenâtmānaṃ bahu-manyamānaḥ praṇanāma, darśitâdaraṃ ca vyajñāpayat: "deva! prāyeṇâtra hiraṇyo 'pi nâ-parigatāḥ saṃcaranti, senā-pateḥ kuta eva nāryaḥ? nâpy evaṃ-rūpā kā-cid a-balā. tathâpi devâdeśād idānīm anveṣaṇaṃ prati prati-dinam an-anya-kṛtyaiḥ kriyate yatnaḥ. itaś cârdha-gavyūti-mātra eva muni-mahite mahati mahī-dhara-mālā-mūla-ruhi mahī-ruhāṃ ṣaṇḍe 'pi piṇḍa-pātī prabhūtânte-vāsi-parivṛtaḥ pārāśarī Divākaramitra-nāmā giri-nadīm āśritya prativasati, sa yadi vinded vārtām" iti. tac chrutvā nara-patir acintayat: "śrūyate hi tatra-bhavataḥ su-gṛhīta-nāmnaḥ svargatasya Grahavarmaṇo bāla-mitraṃ maitrāyaṇīyas trayīṃ vihāya brāhmaṇâyano vidvān utpanna-samādhiḥ saugate mate yuvâiva kāṣāyāṇi gṛhītavān" iti. prāyaśaś ca janasya janayati suhṛd api dṛṣṭo bhṛśam āśvāsam. abhigamanīyāś ca guṇāḥ sarvasya. kasya na pratīkṣyo muni-bhāvaḥ. bhagavatī ca vaidheye 'pi dharma-gṛhiṇī garimāṇam āpādayati, pravrajyā kiṃ punaḥ sakala-jana-mano-muṣi viduṣi jane. yato naḥ kutūhali hṛdayam abhūt satatam asya darśanaṃ prati prāsaṅgikam evêdam āpatitam ati-kalyāṇaṃ paśyāmaḥ prayatna-prārthita-darśanaṃ janam iti. prakāśaṃ câbravīt: "aṅga! samupadiśa tam uddeśaṃ yatrâste sa piṇḍa-pātī" iti. evam uktvā ca tenâivôpadiśyamāna-vartmā prāvartata gantum.
body.translated_text: <s>Nirghāta</s>, valuing himself highly at the king's gracious address, bowed, and respectfully informed him: "Your Majesty! Even golden deer scarcely roam here undetected—how could the general's women? Nor is there any such woman of that description. Nevertheless, at Your Majesty's command, efforts are being made daily with undivided attention in the matter of the search. And just half a <s>gavyūti</s> from here, a <s>Pārāśarī</s> (Brahmin descended from Parāśara) named <s>Divākaramitra</s>, living on alms-food, surrounded by a large community of resident disciples, dwells by a mountain stream in a great grove of trees rooted at the base of a mountain ridge, honored by sages—if he might know something." Hearing that, the king reflected: "It is indeed heard that the young friend of the late <s>Grahavarman</s> of auspicious name—a <s>Maitrāyaṇīya</s> Brahmin by birth, learned, who had attained <s>samādhi</s>, abandoned the three <s>Vedas</s> and even in his youth took the saffron robes in the <s>Saugata</s> (Buddhist) doctrine." And generally, the sight of even a friend brings great solace to a person. And the virtues of everyone are to be approached. Whose saintly state is not worthy of respect? And even in regard to a <s>Vaidehī</s> marriage, the wife of <s>Dharma</s> brings weight—how much more so renunciation, especially in a learned person who captivates the minds of all people. Since our heart has been curious about seeing him constantly, this has come about as if of its own accord as a supremely auspicious occasion—let us see the person whose audience we had long wished for." And he said openly: "Friend! Point out the place where that alms-gatherer resides." Having spoken thus, guided by that very man, he set out to go.

body.translated_text: Then the king thought to himself: "The reverend one must surely be nearby." Dismounting at the mountain stream and performing ablutions, he stationed the cavalry in that very spot—where the forest depths were deafened by the simultaneous neighing of the horses released for rest—and assuming the modesty befitting a visit to an ascetic, with his heart and with his right hand holding <s>Mādhavagupta</s>'s shoulder, accompanied by only a few kings, he set out to proceed on foot.
