And filled with great reverence inspired by his exceedingly serene and profound bearing, he reverently bowed to him from afar with his head, his speech, and his mind.

body.translated_text: Then, amidst those trees, being announced from afar by adherents of various lands stationed at various places—some leaning against posts, some seated on rock-surfaces, some dwelling in vine-bowers, some hidden in forest-thickets, some sitting in the shade of branches, some residing at the roots of trees—<s>Ārhatas</s> (Jains) free from passion, <s>Maskarins</s> (naked ascetics), those in white garments, pale-clad Buddhist monks, <s>Bhāgavatas</s> (Vaiṣṇavas), <s>Varṇins</s> (Brahmin students), hair-pluckers (Jain ascetics), <s>Kāpilas</s> (Sāṃkhya adherents), <s>Jainas</s>, <s>Lokāyatikas</s> (materialists), <s>Kāṇādas</s> (Vaiśeṣika adherents), <s>Aupaniṣadas</s> (Vedānta followers), <s>Aiśvarakāraṇikas</s> (those holding God as cause), <s>Kārandhami</s> ascetics, teachers of <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>, <s>Paurāṇikas</s>, <s>Sāptatantavas</s> (Sāṃkhya-yoga followers), <s>Śaivas</s>,

body.text: Divākaramitras tu maitrīmayaḥ prakṛtyā viśeṣatas tenâ-pareṇâ-dṛṣṭa-pūrveṇâ-mānuṣa-lokôcitena sarvâbhibhāvinā mahânubhāvâbhoga-bhājā bhrājiṣṇunā bhū-pater a-prākṛtenâkāra-viśeṣeṇa tena câbhijātya-prakāśakena garīyasā praśrayeṇa câhlāditaś cakṣuṣi ca cetasi ca yugapad agrahīt. vīra-svabhāvo 'pi ca saṃpādita-sa-saṃbhramâbhyutthānaḥ saṃkalayya kiṃ-cid udgamanakena vilolaṃ vilambamānaṃ vāmâṃsāc cīvara-paṭântam utkṣipya cân-ekâbhaya-dāna-dīkṣā-dakṣiṇo dakṣiṇaṃ mahā-puruṣa-lakṣaṇa-lekhā-praśastaṃ snigdha-madhurayā vācā sa-gauravam ārogya-dānena rājānam anvagrahīt. abhyanandac ca sv-āgata-girā gurum ivâbhyāgataṃ bahu manyamānaḥ svenâsanenâddhvam atrêti nimantrayāṃ-cakāra. pārśva-sthitaṃ ca śiṣyam abravīt: "āyuṣman! upānaya kamaṇḍalunā pādôdakam" iti. rājā tv acintayat: "a-lohaḥ khalu saṃyamana-pāśaḥ śaujanyam abhijātānām. sthāne khalu tatra-bhavān guṇânurāgī Grahavarmā bahuśo varṇitavān asya guṇān" iti. prakāśaṃ câbabhāṣe: "bhagavan! bhavad-darśana-puṇyânugṛhītasya mama punar ukta ivâyam ārya-prayuktaḥ pratibhāty anugrahaḥ. cakṣuḥ-pramāṇa-prasāda-svī-kṛtasya ca para-karaṇam ivâsanâdi-dānôpacāra-ceṣṭitam. ati-bhūmir bhūmir evâsanaṃ bhavādṛśāṃ puraḥ saṃbhāṣaṇâ-mṛtâbhiṣeka-prakṣālita-sakala-vapuṣaś ca

children.text: me pradeśa-vṛttiḥ. pādyam apy apārthakam. āsatāṃ bhavanto yathā-sukham. āsīno 'ham" ity abhidhāya kṣitāv evôpāviśat.
children.translated_text: a mere spot of ground suffices. Even the foot-water is superfluous. Let the venerable ones be seated at their ease. I shall sit here'—and so saying, he sat down upon the bare ground.

body.translated_text: <s>Divākaramitra</s>, who was by nature full of loving-kindness, was especially delighted by that extraordinary, never-before-seen, befitting-more-than-the-human-world, all-surpassing, partaking of great majesty's splendor, resplendent, uncommon distinction of the king's bearing, and by that weighty modesty which revealed his noble birth; and he received him simultaneously in his eyes and in his heart. Though heroic by nature, having risen with respectful haste, gathering up with a slight lifting motion the edge of his <s>cīvara</s> (monastic robe) that was swaying and slipping from his left shoulder, and being skilled in the consecration of bestowing fearlessness many times over, with his right hand—adorned with the auspicious marks of a great being—in an affectionate and sweet voice, he blessed the king with respectful gravity by the gift of health. He welcomed him with words of greeting, and esteeming the visitor greatly as if a <s>guru</s> had come, he invited him to his own seat saying 'Please rest here from your journey.' And he said to a disciple standing nearby: '<s>Āyuṣman</s> (Long-lived one)! Bring water for washing the feet with the <s>kamaṇḍalu</s> (water-vessel).' The king, however, thought to himself: 'Truly, the bond of restraint for the noble-born is not made of iron—it is graciousness. Rightly indeed did the venerable <s>Grahavarman</s>, who was devoted to virtues, praise his qualities many times over.' And he spoke aloud: 'Venerable sir! For me, who have been blessed by the merit of beholding you, this favor bestowed by the noble one appears as though already spoken. And for one who has been received by the grace measured by your very gaze, the gestures of hospitality such as offering a seat seem like something done for another. The ground itself is more than sufficient a seat before ones such as you; and for me, whose entire body is being washed by the nectar-ablution of conversing in your presence,

body.text: "alaṃ-kāro hi paramârthataḥ prabhavatāṃ praśrayâtiśayaḥ, ratnâdikas tu śilâbhāraḥ" ity ākalayya punaḥ punar abhyarthyamāno 'pi yadā na pratyapadyata pārthivo vacanaṃ tadā svam evâsanaṃ punar api bheje bhadantaḥ. bhū-pati-mukha-nalina-nihita-nibhṛta-nayana-yugala-nigaḍa-niś-calī-kṛta-hṛdayaś ca sthitvā kāṃ-cit kāla-kalāṃ kali-kāla-kalmaṣa-kāluṣyam iva kṣālayann a-malābhir danta-mayūkha-mālābhir mūla-phalâbhyavahāra-saṃbhavam udvamann iva ca parimala-subhagaṃ vikaca-kusuma-paṭala-pāṇḍuraṃ latā-vanam avādīt: "adya-prabhṛti na kevalam ayam a-nindyo vandyo 'pi prakāśita-satsāraḥ saṃsāraḥ. kiṃ nāma nâlokyate jīvadbhir adbhutaṃ yena rūpam a-cintatôpanatam idaṃ dṛk-patham upagatam. evaṃ-vidhair anumīyante janmântarâvasthita-sukṛtāni hṛdayôtsavaiḥ. ihâpi janmani dattam evâsmākam amunā tapaḥ-kleśena phalam a-su-labha-darśanaṃ darśayatā devānāṃ-priyam. ā tṛpter āpītam a-mṛtam īkṣaṇābhyām. jātaṃ nir-utkaṇṭhaṃ mānasaṃ nivṛtti-sukhasya. mahadbhiḥ puṇyair vinā na viśrāmyanti saj-jane tvādṛsi dṛśaḥ. su-divasaḥ sa tvaṃ yasmiñ jāto 'si. sā su-jātā jananī yā sakala-jīva-loka-jīvita-janakam ajanayad āyuṣmantam. puṇyavanti puṇyāny api tāni yeṣām asi pariṇāmaḥ. su-kṛta-tapasas te paramâṇavo ye tava parigṛhīta-sarvâvayavāḥ. tat su-bhagaṃ saubhāgyam āśrito 'si yena. bhavyaḥ sa puruṣa-bhāvo bhavaty avasthito yaḥ. yat satyaṃ mumukṣor api me puṇya-bhājam ālokya punaḥ śraddhā jātā manuja-janmani. nêcchadbhir apy asmābhir dṛṣṭaḥ kusumâyudhaḥ. kṛtârtham adya cakṣur vana-devatānām. adya sa-phalaṃ janma pādapānāṃ yeṣām asi gato gocaram. a-mṛtamayasya bhavato vacasāṃ mādhuryaṃ kāryam eva. asya tv īdṛśe śaiśave vinayasyôpādhyāyaṃ dhyāyann api na saṃbhāvayāmi bhuvi. sarvathā śūnya asīd a-jāte dīrghâyuṣi guṇa-grāmaḥ. dhanyaḥ sa bhūbhṛd yasya vaṃśe maṇir iva muktāmayaḥ saṃbhūto 'si. evaṃ-vidhasya ca puṇyavataḥ kathaṃ-cit prāptasya kena priyaṃ samāca-

children.text: -rāma iti pāriplavaṃ ceto naḥ. sakala-vana-cara-sârtha-sādhāraṇasya kanda-mūla-phalasya giri-sarid-ambhaso vā ke vayam. a-parôpakaraṇī-kṛtas tu kāya-kalir ayam asmākam. sarvasvam avaśiṣṭam iṣṭâtithyāya. svâyattāś ca vidyante vidyā-bindavaḥ kati-cit. upayogaṃ tu na prītir vicārayati. yadi ca nôparuṇaddhi kaṃ-cit kārya-lavam a-rakṣaṇīyâkṣaraṃ vā kathanīyaṃ tat kathayatu bhavān sa śrotum abhilaṣati hṛdayaṃ sarvam idaṃ naḥ. kena kṛtyâti-bhāreṇa bhavyo bhūṣitavān bhūmim etām a-bhramaṇa-yogyām? kiyad-avadhir vā 'yaṃ śūnyâṭavī-paryaṭana-kleśaḥ kalyāṇa-rāśeḥ? kasmāc ca saṃtapta-rūpêva te tanur iyam a-saṃtāpârhā vibhāvyate?" iti.
children.translated_text: —is the anxious wavering of our minds. Who are we, possessors of roots, tubers, and fruits common to all the forest-dwellers, or of mountain-stream water? Yet this bodily frame of ours has not been made an instrument for serving others. All that remains is left over for the hospitality of cherished guests. And there are a few drops of learning at our own disposal. But affection does not deliberate about their use. If it does not obstruct some small piece of business, or if there is something to be told that contains syllables not to be guarded, then let the lord tell it—this heart of ours longs to hear everything. By what great burden of duty has the blessed one adorned this ground unfit for wandering? And what is the limit of this toil of roaming through the desolate wilderness for one who is a treasury of auspiciousness? And why does this body of yours, unworthy of suffering, appear as though scorched?'

body.translated_text: 'For truly, the supreme ornament of the powerful is the excess of their humility; jewels and the like are but a burden of stone'—reflecting thus, and though entreated again and again, when the king would not accept his words, the <s>Bhadanta</s> (Venerable Elder) resumed his own seat. And fixing his gaze steadily upon the lotus-face of the king, with his heart made motionless as if by the shackles of his pair of eyes placed gently upon it, he remained for a brief moment as if washing away the impurity of the sinful age of <s>Kali</s>, and with immaculate rays of his teeth—as if disgorging the fragrance born of his diet of roots and fruits—he spoke, addressing the bower of creepers, pale-white with masses of blossoming flowers and lovely with perfume: 'From this day forward, not only is this <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence), which has revealed its goodness, blameless—it is even worthy of veneration. What wonder indeed is not seen by the living, when this unthought-of, spontaneously arrived form has come within the range of sight? By such joyous festivals of the heart, one can infer the good deeds stored up in previous births. Even in this very birth, by showing us this beloved-of-the-gods—so rare to behold—he has already given us the fruit of that ascetic toil. The nectar has been drunk to satiety by the eyes. The mind has become free of longing for the happiness of cessation. Without great merits, the eyes do not find rest in a virtuous person such as you. Blessed is that day on which you were born. Blessed is that mother who gave birth to the long-lived one, the giver of life to all living beings in the entire world. Blessed indeed are those merits of which you are the fruition. Well-performed are the austerities of those atoms which have been taken up by all your limbs. Blessed is the good fortune to which you are devoted. Worthy is that manly nature which abides steadfastly in you. In truth, even for me—one who desires liberation—upon seeing one so full of merit, faith has been born anew in human birth. Even without our wishing it, we have beheld the flower-arrowed one (<s>Kāmadeva</s>). Today the eyes of the forest deities have attained their purpose. Today the birth of the trees is fruitful, those into whose range of perception you have come. That your speech should possess sweetness is only natural, since you are made of nectar. But as for this degree of modesty at such a young age, even pondering it I cannot conceive of its teacher on this earth. The entire host of virtues was surely empty before the long-lived one was born. Blessed is that king in whose dynasty you were born like a pearl-gem in a mountain. And for such a meritorious one who has somehow come to us, how we might do something pleasing—

body.text: rājā tu sâdarataram abravīt: "ārya! darśita-saṃbhrameṇânena madhura-sa-visaram a-mṛtam iva hṛdaya-dhṛti-karam an-avarataṃ varṣatā vacasâiva te sarvam anuṣṭhitam. dhanyo 'smi yad evam abhyarhitam an-upacaraṇīyam api mānyo manyate mām. asya ca mahā-vana-bhramaṇa-parikleśasya kāraṇam avadhārayatu matimān. mama hi vinaṣṭa-nikhilêṣṭa-bandhor jīvitânubandhasya nibandhanam ekâiva yavīyasī svasâvaśeṣā. sâpi bhartur viyogād vairi-paribhava-bhayād bhramantī katham api Vindhya-vanam idam, a-śubha-śabara-bala-bahulam, a-gaṇita-gaja-kula-kalilam, a-parimita-mṛga-pati-śarabha-bhayam, uru-mahiṣa-muṣita-pathika-gamanam, ati-niśita-śara-kuśa-paruṣam, avaṭa-śata-viṣamam aviśat. atas tām anveṣṭuṃ vayam aniśaṃ niśi niśi ca satatam imām aṭavīm aṭāmaḥ. na câinām āsādayāmaḥ. kathayatu ca gurur api yadi kadā-cit kutaś-cid vane carataḥ śruti-patham upagatā tad-vārtā" iti.
body.translated_text: The king then spoke with even greater respect: 'Noble sir! By this speech of yours, which like nectar continuously rains down what is sweet yet astringent, sustaining the composure of the heart while showing agitation, everything has already been accomplished. I am blessed that the venerable one thus honors me, unworthy though I am of such homage. And the cause of this great toil of wandering through the vast forest—let the wise one take note. For I, having lost all my beloved kinsmen, the sole remaining bond to my life is my one youngest sister who alone survives. She too, out of fear of humiliation by enemies following the loss of her husband, wandering somehow entered this <s>Vindhya</s> forest—swarming with hosts of inauspicious <s>Śabaras</s> (wild tribesmen), teeming with herds of elephants beyond count, terrifying with innumerable lions and <s>śarabhas</s> (eight-legged mythical beasts), its paths blocked by great buffalo, bristling with sharp <s>śara</s> and <s>kuśa</s> grass, and treacherous with hundreds of pits. Therefore, to search for her, we ceaselessly, night after night, wander through this wilderness. Yet we cannot find her. Let the <s>guru</s> (teacher) also tell us if perchance, while moving about in the forest, some news of her has reached his ears.'

body.text: atha tac chrutvā jātôdvega iva bhadantaḥ punar abhyadhāt: "dhīman! na khalu kaś-cid evaṃ-rūpo vṛttânto 'smān upāgatavān. a-bhājanaṃ hi vayam īdṛśānāṃ priyâkhyānôpāyanānāṃ bhavatām." ity evaṃ

children.text: bhāṣmāṇa iva tasminn a-kasmād āgtayâ-paraḥ śamini vayasi vartamānaḥ saṃbhrānta-rūpa iva purastād uparacitâñjalir jāta-karuṇaḥ prakṣarita-cakṣur bikṣur abhāṣata: "bhagavan bhadanta! mahat karuṇaṃ vartate. bālâiva ca balavad-vyasanâbhibhūtā bhūta-pūrvâpi kalyāṇa-rūpā strī śokâveśa-vivaśā vaiśvānaraṃ viśati. saṃbhāvayatu tām a-proṣita-prāṇāṃ bhagavān. abhyupapadyatāṃ samucitaiḥ samāśvāsanaiḥ. an-uparata-pūrvaṃ kṛmi-kīṭa-prāyam api duḥkhitaṃ dayā-rāśer āryasya gocara-gatam" iti.
children.translated_text: a <s>bhikṣu</s> (monk) arrived unexpectedly—one who was advanced in age yet beyond the stage of tranquility, appearing flustered, standing before him with palms joined in supplication, filled with compassion, his eyes streaming with tears—and spoke: 'Venerable <s>Bhadanta</s>! A great calamity is at hand. A young woman, overcome by a powerful disaster, once beautiful in appearance, distraught with the seizure of grief, is about to enter the fire (<s>Vaiśvānara</s>). Let the Venerable One consider her—she may yet have life in her. Let her be succored with appropriate consolations. For nothing that has ever come within the range of the noble one—a mass of compassion—has gone uncomforted, even if it be a mere worm or insect in distress.'

body.translated_text: Then, hearing that, the <s>Bhadanta</s> (Venerable Elder), as if agitated, spoke again: 'Wise one! No such account has reached us. For we are not fit vessels for such precious gifts as reports of glad tidings from ones such as you.' Even as he was speaking thus,

body.text: rājā tu jātânujâśaṅkaḥ sôdarya-snehāc cântar-druta iva duḥkhena dodūyamāna-hṛdayaḥ katham api gadgadikā-gṛhīta-kaṇṭho vikala-vāg-bāṣpāyamāṇa-dṛṣṭiḥ papraccha: "pārāśarin! kiyad-dūre sā yoṣid evaṃ-jātīyā jīved vā kālam etāvantam iti. pṛṣṭā vā tvayā bhadre! kâsi, kasyâsi, kuto 'si, kim-arthaṃ vanam idam abhyupagatâsi, viśasi ca kiṃ-nimittam analam? ity āditaś ca prabhṛti kārtsnyena kathyamānam icchāmi śrotuṃ katham āryasya gatā darśana-gocaram ākārato vā kīdṛśo" iti.
body.translated_text: The king, suspecting it was his younger sister, his heart melting inwardly from fraternal affection, his heart throbbing with anguish, his throat somehow seized by a choking sob, his speech faltering, his gaze brimming with tears, asked: 'Son of <s>Parāśara</s>! How far away is that woman? And might she of such description still be alive after all this time? And did you ask her—"Good lady! Who are you, whose are you, whence do you come, for what reason have you entered this forest, and why do you seek to enter the fire?" I wish to hear the account from the very beginning, told in full, of how she came within the range of the noble one's sight, and what she looks like.'

body.text: tathâbhihitas tu bhūbhujā bhikṣur ācacakṣe: "mahā-bhāga! śrūyatām: ahaṃ hi pratyuṣasy evâdya vanditvā bhagavantam anenâiva nadī-rodhasā sâikata-su-kumāreṇa yadṛcchayā vihṛtavān ati-dūram. ekasmiṃś ca vana-latā-gahane giri-nadī-samīpa-bhāji bhramarīṇām iva hima-hata-kamalâkara-kātarāṇāṃ rasitaṃ sāryamāṇānām ati-tāra-tāna-vartinīnāṃ vīṇā-tantrīṇām iva jhāṛkāram eka-tānaṃ nārīṇāṃ ruditam a-dhṛti.karam ati-karuṇam ākarṇitavān asmi. samupajāta-kṛpaś ca gato 'smi taṃ pradeśam. dṛṣṭavān asmi ca dṛṣat-khaṇḍa-khaṇḍitâṅguli-galal-lohitena ca pārṣṇi-praviṣṭa-śara-śalākā-śalya-śūla-saṃkocita-cakṣuṣā câdhvanīna-śrama-śvayathu-niś-cala-caraṇena ca sthāṇava-vraṇa-vyathita-gulpha-baddha-bhūrja-tvacā ca vāta-khuḍa-kheda-khañja-jaṅghā-jāta-jvareṇa ca pāṃsu-pāṇḍura-picchakena ca kharjūra-jūṭa-jaṭā-jarjarita-jānunā ca śatāva-

children.text: -rī-vidāritôruṇā ca vidārī-dārita-tanu-dukūla-pallavena côtkaṭa-vaṃśa-viṭapa-kaṇṭaka-koṭi-pāṭita-kañcuka-karpaṭena ca phala-lobhâvalambitânamra-badarī-latā-jālakair utkaṇṭakair ullikhita-su-kumāra-karôdareṇa ca kuraṅga-śṛṅgôtkhātaiḥ kanda-mūla-phalaiḥ kad-arthita-bāhunā tāmbūla-viraha-virasa-mukha-khaṇḍita-komalâmalakī-phalena kuśa-kusumâhati-lohitānāṃ śvayathumatām akṣṇāṃ lepī-kṛta-manaḥ-śilena ca kaṇṭakī-latā-lūnâlaka-leśena ca kena-cit kisalayôpapāditâtapatra-kṛtyena kena-cit kadalī-dala-vyajana-vāhinā kena-cit kamalinī-palāśa-puṭa-gṛhītâmbhasā kena-cit pātheyī-kṛta-mṛṇāla-pūlikena kena-cic Cīnâṃśuka-daśā-śikya-nihita-nālikera-kośa-kalaśī-kalita-sarala-tailena, katipayâvaśeṣa-śoka-vikala-kalā-mūka-kubja-vāmana-badhira-barbarā-viralenâ-balānāṃ cakra-vālena parivṛtām, āpat-kāle 'pi kulôdgatenêvâmucyamānāṃ prabhā-lepinā lāvaṇyena, pratibimbitair āsanna-vana-latā-kisalayaiḥ sa-rasair duḥkha-kṣatair ivântaḥ-paṭalī-kriyamāṇa-kāyām, kaṭhora-darbhâṅkura-kṣata-kṣāriṇā kṣatajenânusaraṇâlaktakenêva rakta-caraṇām, unnālenânyatara-nārī-dhṛtenâravindinī-dalena kṛta-cchāyam api vicchāyaṃ mukham udvahantīm, ākāśam api śūnaytayâtiśayānām, mṛnmayīm iva niś-cetanatayā marunmayīm iva niḥ-śvāsa-saṃpadā pāvakamayīm iva saṃtāpa-saṃtānena salilamayīm ivâśru-prasravaṇena viyanmayīm iva nir-avalambanatayā taḍinmayīm iva pāriplavatayā śabdamayīm iva paridevita-vāṇī-bāhulyena mukta-muktâṃśuka-ratna-kusuma-kanaka-patrâbharaṇāṃ kalpa-latām iva mahā-vane patitām, paramêśvarôttamâṅga-pāta-dur-lalitâṅgāṃ gaṅgām iva gāṃ gātam, vana-kusuma-dhūli-dhūsarita-pāda-
children.translated_text: lacerated by <s>śatāvarī</s> thorns, with her thin silk garment torn by <s>vidārī</s> creepers, with her bodice reduced to rags by the tips of thorns on the fierce bamboo branches, with the tender palms of her hands scratched by thorny snares of drooping <s>badarī</s> (jujube) creeper nets from which she had hung while grasping for fruit, her arms ill-used by roots, tubers, and fruits dug up by deer-antler points, her mouth made tasteless by the absence of betel and chewing unripe <s>āmalakī</s> (gooseberry) fruit, with <s>manaḥśilā</s> (realgar) paste applied to her swollen eyes reddened from being struck by <s>kuśa</s> grass flowers, with tresses of hair shorn by thorny creepers—attended by someone holding a parasol fashioned from a leaf-shoot, by someone carrying a fan of plantain leaf, by someone holding water in a cupped lotus-leaf vessel, by someone who had made provision for the journey with a bundle of lotus-stalks, by someone bearing a flask-gourd of <s>sarala</s> (pine) oil placed in a sling made of strips of Chinese silk; surrounded by a sparse retinue of the powerless—a few remaining mute, crippled, hunchbacked, dwarfed, deaf, and barbarian attendants enfeebled by grief—yet not abandoning even in calamity the luster of beauty that seemed born of her noble lineage; children.translated_text: like a tender creeper-shoot; like a dawn-moon wishing to depart to another world; displaying the beauty of her long, white eyes dampened by the release of her own tears, fading like a lotus-pond of the <s>Mandākinī</s> (heavenly Ganges); like a night-lotus closing its petals in the unbearable touch of sunrays, passing the day in grief; wan and pale in body like a dawn-lamp-flame whose wick has burnt out and belied its promise; like a wild she-elephant submerged in a great lake, guarded by attendant elephants pressing from the sides—she had entered the depths of the forest and of meditation; she stood at the foot of a tree and at death; she had fallen into the lap of her nurse and into great calamity; she was separated from her husband and from happiness; she was drained by wandering and of life-breath; she was distraught with her tangled tresses and with the means of death; she was discolored by the dust of the road and by bodily anguish; she was burnt by fierce sunlight and by widowhood; her face was held by her hand and by silence; she was held by her dear friends and by grief; likewise with fallen kinsmen and fallen graces; with released ear-ornaments and a released self; with abandoned ornaments and abandoned enterprises; with broken bangles and broken hopes; with maidservants and with shoots of <s>darbha</s> grass as needles clinging to her feet; with her eyes and her beloved fixed in her heart; with long sighs of grief and long tresses; with a body and merit wasted away; with elderly women and streams of tears falling at her feet; with an entourage and a life barely remaining—she was listless in opening her eyes, skillful in shedding tears; constant in anxieties, severed from hopes; thin in body, heavy in sighing; filled with grief, empty of fortitude; beset by weariness, void of heart; firm in her resolve, shaken from composure. Moreover, she was a dwelling of misfortunes, a repository of sorrows, a resting-place of instabilities, a support of the unsupported, an abode of despairs, a ground for calamities, a pursuit of ill-fortune, an agitation of agitations, a cause of pity, the very extreme of helplessness—such a woman. body.translated_text: Thus addressed by the king, the <s>bhikṣu</s> (monk) narrated: 'Great-souled one! Hear: At dawn today, having paid my respects to the Venerable One, I wandered of my own accord a very great distance along this very riverbank, soft with sand. And in a certain dense thicket of forest creepers near a mountain stream, I heard the weeping of women—most pitiable and unbearable—that was incessant and high-pitched like the humming of female bees distressed by a frost-stricken lotus pond, like the twanging sound of <s>vīṇā</s> strings drawn out in a single sustained, extremely high-pitched tone. Filled with compassion, I went to that spot. children.translated_text: I, impelled by an overwhelming compassion, wished to speak to her but reflected in my mind: 'How shall I address this great-souled lady? "My child"—too intimate. "Mother"—mere flattery. "Sister"—self-aggrandizement. "Your Majesty"—the language of servants. "Princess"—unclear. "Lay devotee"—wishful thinking. "Mistress"—implies accepting servitude. "Good woman"—suitable for other women. "Long-lived one"—unpleasant given her condition. "Auspicious one"—contradicted by her state. "Moon-faced one"—unsuited for a sage. "Young one"—lacking gravity. "Noble lady"—imputing old age. "Blessed one"—the opposite of the result. "Madam"—too commonplace.' Moreover: '"Who are you?"—ill-bred. "Why do you weep?"—makes her remember the cause of grief. "Do not weep"—does not befit without removing the cause of sorrow. "Take comfort"—on what grounds? "Welcome"—stale. "Are you comfortable?"—false.' Even as I was thus deliberating, from that group of women another woman rose—noble in appearance, distraught with grief—approached, and touching my pair of feet with tear-drops that burned like signals of her incomparable heart's anguish, lowering her head with a few streaks of grey, she addressed my heart with exceedingly piteous words: 'Venerable sir! The monastic life is generally compassionate to all beings. <s>Buddhists</s> are skilled in the vow of destroying suffering once undertaken. The teaching of the blessed <s>Śākyamuni</s> is the very home of compassion. The community of the <s>Jainas</s> is always ready to serve all people. <s>Dharma</s> of the sages is the means of attaining the next world. And no greater source of merit is celebrated in the world than the saving of life. Young women are by nature grounds of compassion—how much more so when overwhelmed by misfortune? And virtuous people are proven fields for the words of the afflicted. For this our mistress—without support due to her father's death, her husband's demise, her brother's exile, the ruin of her remaining circle of kinsmen, her exceedingly tender heart, and her childlessness; humiliated by base enemies; noble-spirited by nature; her delicacy tormented by the hardship of wandering through this great forest; her heart made helpless by many such afflictions piling one upon another, bestowed by her cursed fate—

children.text: -sanair viklavī-kṛta-hṛdayā, dāruṇaṃ duḥkham apārayantī soḍhuṃ nivārayantam an-ākrānta-pūrvaṃ svapne 'py avagaṇayya guru-janam anunayantīr a-khaṇḍita-praṇayā narmasv api samavadhīrya priya-sakhīr vijñāpayantam a-śaraṇam an-ātham aśru-vyākula-nayanam a-paribhūta-pūrvaṃ manasâpi paribhūya bhṛtya-vargam agniṃ praviśati. paritrāyatām. āryo 'pi tāvad a-sahya-śokâpanayanôpāyôpadeśa-nipuṇāṃ vyāpārayatu vāṇīm asyām" iti câti-kṛpaṇaṃ vyāharantīm aham utthāpyôdvignataraḥ śanair abhihitavān: "ārye! yathā kathayasi tathā. asmad-girām a-gocaro 'yam asyāḥ puṇyâśayāyāḥ śokaḥ. śakyate cen muhūrta-mātram api trātum upariṣṭān na vy-arthêyam abhyarthanā bhaviṣyati. mama hi gurur a-para iva bhagavān sugataḥ samīpa-gata eva /
children.translated_text: unable to bear her terrible grief, disregarding her elders who restrain her—never before defied even in her dreams—dismissing with unbroken affection her dear friends who entreat her even in jest—spurning with her mind even her servant-class who plead with her shelterless, without a protector, with eyes swimming in tears, never before treated with contempt—she is entering the fire. Save her! And let the noble one also direct his speech, skilled in teaching the means of removing unbearable grief, toward her.' And I, raising up this woman who spoke so piteously, rose in great agitation and slowly said: 'Noble lady! It is as you say. This grief of hers, a woman of holy disposition, is beyond the reach of my words. But if she can be kept alive even for a single moment longer, this entreaty will not have been in vain. For my teacher, to whom the blessed <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha) is like a second self, is close by.

Duḥkhândha-kāra-paṭala-bhiduraiś ca saugataiḥ su-bhāṣitaiḥ svakīyaiś ca darśita-nidarśanair nānā-gama-gurubhir girāṃ kauśalaiḥ kuśala-śīlām enāṃ prabodha-padavīm āropayiṣṭati" iti. tac ca śrutvā "tvaratām āryaḥ" ity abhidadhānā sā punar api pādayoḥ patitavatī. so 'ham upagatya tvaramāṇo vyatikaram imam a-dhṛti-karam a-śaraṇa-kṛpaṇaṃ bahu-yuvati-maraṇam ati-karuṇam atra-bhavate gurave niveditavān" iti.
body.translated_text: When I have told him this story, the supremely compassionate one will surely come. And with Buddhist sayings that pierce the veil of the darkness of grief, and with his own demonstrated examples, and with the discursive skills of teachers of various scriptures, he will lead her, who is naturally virtuous, to the path of awakening.' Hearing that, saying 'Let the noble one hasten!' she fell at my feet once again. And so I came in haste and reported this matter to the venerable teacher—this distressing incident that robs one of composure, this pitiable helplessness, this death of many women, this exceeding pathos.'

body.text: atha bhūbhṛd bhaikṣavaṃ samavadhārya tad-bhāṣitam aśru-miśritam a-śrute 'pi svasur nāmni nimnī-kṛta-manā manyunā sarvâkāra-saṃvādinyā daśayâiva dūrī-kṛta-saṃdeho dagdha iva sôdaryâvasthā-śravaṇena śravaṇayoḥ śramaṇâcāryam uvāca: "ārya! niyataṃ sâivêyam an-āryasyâsya janasyâti-kaṭhina-hṛdayasyâti-nṛśaṃsasya manda-bhāgyasya bhaginī bhāga-dheyair etām avasthāṃ nītā niṣ-kāraṇa-vairibhir varākī vidīryamāṇaṃ me hṛdayam evaṃ nivedayati" ity uktvā tam api śramaṇam abhyadhāt: "ārya! uttiṣṭha. darśaya kvâsau. yatasva prabhūta-prāṇa-paritrāṇa-puṇyôpārjanāya yāmaḥ, yadi kathaṃ-cij jīvantīṃ saṃbhāvayāmaḥ" iti bhāṣamāṇa evôttasthau.
body.translated_text: Then the king, hearing the words of the Buddhist monk—mixed with tears—even without hearing his sister's name, his mind sinking with grief, his doubt removed by the circumstances that matched in every detail, as if burnt by hearing of his sister's condition, said to the <s>śramaṇa</s> (Buddhist) teacher: 'Noble one! Surely this is she—my sister, the poor woman brought to this state by her fortune—the sister of this ignoble, exceedingly hard-hearted, exceedingly cruel, and wretched person. Her destiny-appointed fate informs my bursting heart thus.' Having said this, he urged the monk: 'Noble one! Rise. Show me where she is. Exert yourself for the merit of saving many lives. Let us go—perhaps we may somehow find her still alive!' Even as he spoke, he rose to his feet.

children.translated_text: assembly of feudatories following behind leading their horses, and with that son of the <s>Śākyas</s> (the Buddhist monk) pointing the way in front, he set forth on foot to that place, drinking the distance as it were with rapid steps. And gradually drawing near, from behind a screen of creeper-forest he heard the manifold cries of the great company of women who wished to die, suited to the occasion: 'O holy <s>Dharma</s>! Run quickly. Where are you, O family deity? O goddess Earth, do you not give courage to your grieving daughter? Where has the fortune of the <s>Puṣpabhūti</s> household gone? O lord of the <s>Mukhara</s> line, do you not awaken this bride—widowed, afflicted with manifold sorrows, without a protector? O Blessed One, when your devotees are in fever, O <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha), are you asleep? O royal <s>dharma</s>, falling upon the house of <s>Puṣpabhūti</s>, how have you become indifferent? Even in you, O <s>Vindhya</s>, friend in misfortune, this joining of palms is in vain. O Mother Great Forest, do you not hear this woman fallen into calamity, crying out? O Sun, be gracious, protect this faithful wife without refuge. O ungrateful wretch, O outcaste of character, laboriously protected yet not protecting this princess! What have the auspicious marks foretold? Alas, O Queen <s>Yaśomatī</s>, full of love for your daughter, you have been robbed by the thief of cursed fate! O King, when your daughter is burning, O you of fiery valor, do you not come down? Your love for your child has slackened! O great King <s>Rājyavardhana</s>, do you not rush to her? Your love for your sister has grown feeble! Alas, how cruel is the state of the departed! Away with you, O wicked fire, shameless one burning without mercy toward women! O brother Wind, I am your servant—quickly convey the news of the queen's burning to the divine <s>Harṣa</s>, the remover of the suffering of afflicted people! O utterly pitiless grief, you dog-cooker of sorrow, you are gratified! O grief-giving demon of separation, you are satisfied! In this desolate forest, to whom shall I cry, to whom shall I tell, to whom shall I go for refuge, in which direction shall I turn, what shall I do, I who am without fortune? <s>Gāndhārikā</s>, this noose of creepers has been seized! O demoness <s>Mocanikā</s>, release this struggle over the branch! <s>Kalahaṃsī</s>, you are killing—what more, even the head? <s>Maṅgalikā</s>, her throat is released—why do you still weep? <s>Sundarī</s>, the company of friends grows distant! <s>Śabarikā</s>, how will you remain upon this inauspicious funeral-bier? <s>Sutanu</s>, you too of slender body will fall when bodies fall! children.translated_text: '<s>Vatsikā</s>, how will you dwell in the undesired city of the dead? <s>Nāgarikā</s>, you have attained dignity through this devotion to your mistress. <s>Virājikā</s>, you have shone in this calamity of the princess through your resolve to spend your life. O water-vessel bearer who knows well the glory of leaping from a cliff, you are blessed. <s>Ketakī</s>, how could one find such a good mistress even in a dream? <s>Menakā</s>, may the god of fire, burning the body, grant servitude to the princess birth after birth. <s>Vijayā</s>, fan the flames. <s>Sānumatī</s>, bow! <s>Indīvarikā</s> wishes to go to heaven. <s>Kāmadāsī</s>, make room for the circumambulation of the fire. <s>Vicārikā</s>, arrange the fire. Scatter, <s>Kirātikā</s>, a heap of flowers. <s>Kurarikā</s>, build the pyre studded with the buds of <s>kurubaka</s> blossoms. O chowrie-bearer, take the chowrie. Once more, <s>Narmadā</s>, the unrestrained laughter fashioned in jest must be endured at the neck. Dear <s>Subhadrā</s>, may your journey to the next world be blessed. <s>Grāmeyikā</s>, you who love unrustic virtues, go to a good destiny. <s>Vasantikā</s>, make way. The parasol-bearer bids farewell—princess, bestow a glance. Your beloved <s>Vijayasenā</s> is giving up her life. Here is <s>Muktikā</s>, the drama-director, wailing aloud, right beside you. At your feet falls your esteemed betel-bearer, princess—<s>Patralatā</s>. <s>Kaliṅgasenā</s>, this is the last embrace. Press me firmly to your chest. The life-breaths depart, <s>Vasantasenā</s>. <s>Mañjulikā</s>, how many times will you wipe this eye smeared with a thousand tears of insufferable grief, and how long will you weep embracing me? Such is the lot of creation, <s>Yaśodhanā</s>. Do you still try to steady me, <s>Mādhavikā</s>? Where is this state fit for consolations? The time has passed, <s>Kālindī</s>, for the joined palms of entreaty of friends. Mad <s>Mattapālikā</s>, leave behind the entreaties of loving prostrations. Loosen, <s>Cakoravatī</s>, the grasping of my feet, O persistent one. <s>Kamalinī</s>, what use is this repeated reproaching of fate? The happiness of union with friends was not long enjoyed. Venerable chief attendant <s>Taraṅgasenā</s>, my salutation. Friend <s>Saudāminī</s>, I have seen you. Bring the flowers for the worship of the fire-god, <s>Kumudikā</s>. Give me, <s>Rohiṇī</s>, the support of your hand for ascending the pyre. Mother, nurse, be brave. Such indeed are the fruits of the deeds of those who have committed sins—

body.translated_text: Then, by the touch of his hand—which was pleasant, as if dripping a potion competent to revive through the insipid essence of the herbs bound at the wrist of a beloved brother, as if vomiting the inconceivable power of nectar from his signet-gems, as if emitting ambrosia through the moon-rays of his nails, as if binding upon her head a moonstone crest-jewel dripping cool spray released at moonrise, as if extinguishing her burning heart with a lotus-stalk-like finger exceedingly cool, as if drawing life back from somewhere—<s>Rājyaśrī</s> suddenly opened her eyes. And thus, clinging to the neck of her brother whose arrival had been unanticipated, whose sight had been unthought of, who had suddenly appeared as if seen in a dream, releasing a thick stream of tear-water from her two eyes as if from the mouths of two river-channels, cruelly overwhelmed by the mass of grief surging forth with its full weight of sisterly affection aroused at that very moment, crying out 'Alas father! Alas mother! Alas friends!'—and again and again in full voice wailing at the top of her lungs for a very long time—though being consoled by her brother who covered her mouth with his hand, saying 'Child, be steady'; though being entreated by the teacher saying 'Noble lady, heed the word of your elder brother, your <s>guru</s>'; though being implored by the assembly of kings saying 'Princess, do you not see the lord's condition? Enough of this excessive weeping'; though being informed by the attendants saying 'Mistress, look upon your brother'; though being restrained by the aged kinswomen saying 'Daughter, rest and then you may cry again'; though being soothed by her friends saying 'Dear friend, how long will you weep?

body.text: śanair ācāryas tu tathā Harṣa iti vijñāya vivardhitâdaraḥ su-tarāṃ muhūrtam ivâtivāhya nibhṛta-saṃjñā-jñāpitena śiṣyeṇôpanītaṃ nalinī-dalaiḥ svayam evâdāya namro mukha-prakṣālanāyôdakam upaninye. narêndro 'pi sâdaraṃ gṛhītvā prathamam an-avarata-rodanâtāmraṃ cira-pravṛttâśru-jala-jālaṃ rakta-paṅgajam iva svasuś cakṣur akṣālayat paścād ātmanaḥ. prakṣālita-mukha-śaśini ca mahī-pāle sarvato niḥ-śabdaḥ saṃbabhūva sakalo likhita iva lokaḥ. tato narêndro manda-mandam abravīt svasāram: "vatse! Vandasvâtra-bhavantaṃ bhadantam. eṣa te bhartur hṛdayaṃ dvitīyam asmākaṃ ca guruḥ" iti. rāja-vacanāt tu rāja-duhitari pati-paricaya-śravaṇôdghātena punar ānīta-netrâmbhasi namantyām ācāryaḥ prayatna-rakṣitâgamâgata-bāṣpâmbhaḥ-saṃbhāra-bhajyamāna-dhairyârdra-locanaḥ kiṃ-cit parāvṛtta-nayano dīrghaṃ niḥśaśvāsa. sthitvā ca kṣaṇam ekaṃ pradarśita-praśrayo mṛdu-vādī madhurayā vācā vyājahāra: "kalyāṇa-rāśe! alaṃ ruditvā na ciram āste. rāja-loko nâdyâpi rodanān nivartate. kriyatām avaśya-karaṇīyaḥ snāna-vidhiḥ. snātvā ca gamyatāṃ tām eva bhūyo bhuvam" iti.
body.translated_text: The teacher, gradually learning that this was <s>Harṣa</s>, his respect greatly increased, after what seemed but a moment, took with his own hands the water for washing the face, brought by a disciple directed through a quiet signal, upon lotus-leaves, and bowing, presented it for the washing of the face. And the king, accepting it with respect, first washed his sister's eye—crimson from incessant weeping, a flood of long-flowing tear-water, like a red lotus—and then his own. And when the king's face-moon had been washed, everywhere the entire assembly became utterly silent, as if painted. Then the king spoke gently to his sister: 'Child, bow to the venerable teacher here. He is the second heart of your husband, and our <s>guru</s>.' But when the princess, at the king's word, bowed—her tears brought forth anew by the opening of the gate of memories of her husband—the teacher, his composure breaking as the reservoir of tears that had come from afar was carefully guarded and restrained, his eyes moist, turning his gaze slightly away, heaved a long sigh. And standing for a single moment, having shown his courtesy, the soft-spoken one said in a sweet voice: 'O treasury of auspiciousness! Enough of weeping—it does not last long. The assembly of kings has still not ceased from tears. Let the necessary rite of bathing be performed. And after bathing, let us return to that same place.'

body.translated_text: Then the king, conforming to worldly custom and the teacher's words, rose, and having bathed with his sister in the mountain river, returned to that same spot. And there, having first attended to his sister's retinue, sitting nearby with focused attention, he fed his sister—who was beyond comfort from grief and had been brought to accept food only through the demonstration of effort with the offering of the husband's funeral rice-ball. And immediately afterward, he himself took his meal. And after eating, he heard from the attendants the full account of his sister's ordeal in detail—from the time of her imprisonment onward: the <s>Gauḍa</s> panic at <s>Kānyakubja</s>, her secret removal by the nobleman named <s>Gupta</s>; and after her escape, her hearing of the news of <s>Rājyavardhana</s>'s death, and upon hearing it, her—

body.text: ayaṃ hi yauvanônmādāt paribhūya bhūyasīr bhāryā yauvanâvatāra-tarala-tarās tārā-rājo rajanī-karṇapūraḥ purā puru-hūta-purodhaso dhiṣaṇasya puraṃdhrīṃ dharma-patnīṃ patnīyann ati-taralas Tārāṃ nāmâpajahāra. nākataś ca palāyāṃ-cakre. cakita-cakora-locanayā ca tayā sahâti-kāmayā sarvâkārâbhirāmayā ramamāṇo ramaṇīyeṣu deśeṣu cacāra. cirāc ca kathaṃ-cit sarva-gīrvāṇa-vāṇī-gauravād girāṃ patyuḥ punar ipa pratyarpayām āsa tām. hṛdaye tv an-indhanam adahyata virahād varârohāyās tasyāḥ satatam.
body.translated_text: 'For in the past, this moon—the ear-ornament of the night—intoxicated by the madness of youth, disdaining his many wives, exceedingly fickle in the descent of youth, courting the lawful wife of <s>Dhiṣaṇa</s> (<s>Bṛhaspati</s>), the chaplain of the lord of the gods (<s>Indra</s>)—being exceedingly restless, he abducted the one named <s>Tārā</s>. And he fled from heaven. And with her—wide-eyed as a frightened <s>cakora</s> bird, yet deeply in love, charming in every aspect—he wandered delighting in delightful places. And after a long time, somehow, out of reverence for the speech of all the gods, he returned her to the lord of speech (<s>Bṛhaspati</s>). But in his heart, without fuel, the fire of separation from that beautiful woman burned ceaselessly.

body.text: ekadā tu śailād udayād udayamāno vimale vāriṇi Varuṇâlayasya saṃkrāntam ātmanaḥ pratibimbaṃ vilokitavān. dṛṣṭvā ca tat tadā sa-smaraḥ sasmāra smera-gaṇḍa-sthalasya Tārāyā mukhasya. mumoca sa manmathônmāda-mathyamāna-mānasaḥ svaḥ-stho 'py a-svasthaḥ sthavīyasaḥ pīta-sakala-kumuda-vana-prabhā-pravāha-dhavala-tārābhyām iva locanābhyāṃ bāṣpa-vāri-bindūn. atha patatas tān udanvati samastān evâcemur muktā-śuktayaḥ. tāsāṃ ca kukṣi-koṣeṣu muktā-phalī-bhūtān avāpa tān katham api rasā-tala-nivāsī Vāsukir nāma viṣamucām īśaḥ. sa ca tair muktā-phalaiḥ pātāla-tale 'pi tārā-gaṇam iva darśayadbhir ekâvalīm akalpayat. cakāra ca Mandākinîti nāma tasyāḥ. sā ca bhagavataḥ somasya sarvāsām oṣadhīnām adhipateḥ prabhāvād aty-anta-viṣaghnī himâ-mṛtasaṃbhavatvāc ca sparśena sarva-sattva-saṃtāpa-hāriṇī babhūva. yataḥ sa tāṃ sarvadā viṣôṣma-śāntaye Vāsukiḥ paryadhatta.
body.translated_text: One day, rising from the eastern mountain, he saw his own reflection transmitted into the clear water of <s>Varuṇa</s>'s abode (the ocean). And seeing it, lovesick, he remembered the face of <s>Tārā</s> with her smiling cheek-surface. He—though dwelling in heaven yet not at ease, his mind churned by the madness of love—released tear-drops from his two eyes, which were white with the swallowed radiance-stream of all the groves of night-lilies, as if from stars. And as those drops fell, pearl-oysters in the ocean drank them all. And the one named <s>Vāsuki</s>, lord of serpents, dwelling in the netherworld, somehow obtained those drops that had become pearls within the hollow shells of the oysters. And with those pearls—which displayed a constellation of stars even on the floor of the netherworld—he fashioned a single-strand necklace. And he named it <s>Mandākinī</s>. And by the power of the blessed <s>Soma</s> (Moon), lord of all herbs, it became supremely effective against poison; and because of its origin from the frost and nectar [of the moon], its touch removed the anguish of all beings. Therefore <s>Vāsuki</s> always wore it for the cooling of the heat of his venom.

children.translated_text: —obtained the single-strand necklace. And having emerged from the netherworld, he gave it to his friend, the king named <s>Sātavāhana</s>, lord of the three oceans. And by the course of time, through our succession of teachers, it has somehow come into our hands. 'And although for those such as you an offered gift is almost like an insult, yet with the understanding that it is a medicine, by one of wisdom who is devoted to the protection of all living beings, whose body must be preserved, and in consideration of protection against poison—let the long-lived one accept it.' Having said this, from the hem of the monk's robe of the disciple standing nearby, he released that single-strand necklace, the <s>Mandākinī</s>.

body.translated_text: And when some time had elapsed, once, a monk named <s>Nāgārjuna</s>, brought by serpents themselves to the floor of the netherworld, from that king of serpents—

body.text: unmucyamānāyā eva yasyāḥ prabhā-lepini labdhâvakāśe viśada-mahasi mahīyasi visarpati raśmi-maṇḍale yugapad-dhavalāyamāneṣu diṅ-mukeṣu mukulita-latā-vadhûtkaṇṭhitair ā-mūlād vikasitam iva tarubhiḥ, abhinava-mṛṇāla-lubdhair dhāvitam iva dhuta-pakṣa-puṭa-paṭala-dhavalita-gaganaṃ vana-sarasī-haṃsa-yūthaiḥ, sphuṭitam iva bhara-vaśa-viśīryamāṇa-dhūli-dhavalair garbha-bheda-sūcita-sūcī-saṃcaya-śucibhiḥ ketakī-vāṭeḥ, uddalita-danturābiḥ prabuddham iva kumudinībhiḥ, vidhuta-sita-saṭā-bhāra-bharita-dik-cakraiś calitam iva kesari-kulaiḥ, prahasitam iva sita-daśanâṃśu-mālâloka-lipyamāna-vanaṃ vana-devatābhiḥ, vikasitam iva śithilita-kusuma-kośa-kesarâṭṭahāsa-nir-aṅkuśaṃ kāśa-kānanaiḥ, bhrāntam iva saṃbhrama-bhramita-bāla-pallava-pariveṣa-śvetāyamānaiś camarī-kadambakaiḥ, prasṛtam iva sphāyamāna-phenila-taralatara-taraṅgôdgāriṇā giri-nadī-pūreṇa, a-para-tārā-gaṇa-lobha-muditenôditam iva vikaca-marīci-cakrâkrānta-kakubhā pūrṇa-candreṇa, prakṣālita iva dāvânala-dhūli-dhūsarita-dig-anto divasaḥ, punar iva dhautāny aśru-jala-kliṣṭāni nārīṇāṃ mukhāni.
body.translated_text: Even as it was being released, as the lustre-spreading great radiance, having gained scope, spread its ray-circle—when all the directions simultaneously turned white—the trees seemed to bloom from root to top, with their creeper-brides eagerly opening their buds; the flocks of swans at the forest-lake seemed to fly, greedy for fresh lotus-fibers, whitening the sky by the fluttering of their wing-feathers; the <s>ketakī</s> (screw-pine) groves seemed to burst open, their bursting indicated by the needle-clusters, their dust turning white from the weight of splitting; the night-lily beds seemed to awaken, tearing open their jagged petals; the lion-prides seemed to stir, filling the circle of the directions by shaking the burden of their white manes; the forest-deities seemed to laugh, the forest being smeared with the light of their garlands of white tooth-rays; the <s>kāśa</s>-grass forests seemed to bloom, their loosened flower-sheath pollen-laughter unrestrained; the <s>camarī</s> (yak) herds seemed to whirl, turning white with the halos of their confused, rapidly swirling young tail-sprouts; the mountain-river flood seemed to spread, disgorging ever-more-restless foaming waves; the full moon seemed to rise—delighted by the greed for further starry hosts—its blossoming ray-circle conquering the quarters; the day seemed washed—the horizons grey with the dust of forest-fire now cleansed; the faces of women, tear-stained, seemed washed anew.

children.text: -bhuvana-bhūṣaṇa-bhūti-prabhāvām ivâiśānīṃ śaśi-kalām, dhavalatā-guṇa-parigṛhītāṃ kāntim iva nirgatāṃ kṣīra-rāśeḥ, an-eka-mahā-mahī-bhṛt-paramparâgatāṃ Gaṅgām iva durgati-harām, an-avarata-sphurita-taralâṃśukāṃ puraḥ-sara-patākām iva mahêśvara-bhāvâgamasya, ghana-sāra-śuklāṃ danta-paṅktim ivâbhimukhasyêśvarasya, vara-mano-ratha-pūraṇa-samarthāṃ svayaṃ-vara-srajam iva bhuvana-śriyaḥ, nija-kara-pallavâvaraṇa-dur-lakṣyāṃ cakṣū-rāga-vihasatikām iva vasudhāyāḥ, mantra-kośa-sādhana-pravṛttasyâkṣa-mālām iva rāja-dharmasya, samudrâlaṃ-kāra-bhūtāṃ saṃkhyâlekhya-paṭṭikām iva Kubera-kośasya. paśyaṃś câitāṃ vismayam ājagāma manasā su-ciram. ācāryas tu tām uddhṛtya babandha bandhure skandha-bhāge bhū-pateḥ. atha nara-patir api pratiprītim upadarśayan pratyavādīt: "ārya! ratnānām īdṛśānām an-arhāḥ prāyeṇa puruṣāḥ. tapaḥ-siddhir iyam āryasya devatā-prasādo vā. ke ca vayam idānīm ātmano 'pi kim uta grahaṇasya pratyākhyānasya vā. darśanāt prabhṛti prabhūta-guru-guṇa-gaṇa-hṛtena hṛdayena paravanto vayam. saṃkalpitam idam ā-maraṇād āryôpayogāya śarīram. atra kāma-cāro vaḥ kartavyānām" iti. samatikrānte ca kiyaty api kāle gate câikâvalī-varṇanâlāpe lokasyân-antaraṃ labdha-viśrambhā rājya-śrīs tāmbūla-vāhinīṃ patra-latām āhūyôpāṃśu kim api karṇa-mūle śanair ādideśa. darśita-vinayā ca patra-latā pārthivaṃ vyajñāpayat: "deva! devī vijñāpayati na smarāmy āryasya puraḥ kadā-cid uccair vacanam api. kuto vijñāpanam. iyaṃ hi
children.translated_text: ornaments of the entire world—like the crescent of <s>Śiva</s>; like beauty itself emerged from the milk-ocean, taken up by the quality of whiteness; like the <s>Gaṅgā</s>, descended through many great mountain-ranges, remover of misfortune; like a forerunner-banner of the approach of the <s>Māheśvara</s> doctrine, with its shimmering, restless folds; like the row of teeth of the lord facing toward one—white as condensed camphor; like a garland of self-choice for the beauty of the world, capable of fulfilling the finest wishes; like the playful sidelong glance of the earth—hard to discern through the screen of her own hand-sprout; like the rosary of royal <s>dharma</s>, engaged in accomplishing the treasury of <s>mantras</s>; like an inventory-record of <s>Kubera</s>'s treasury—an ornament of the ocean, bearing a tally of enumeration. And gazing at this, he was filled with wonder in his mind for a long time. The master then, lifting it up, bound it upon the handsome shoulder of the king. And the king, displaying his reciprocal pleasure, replied: 'Venerable sir! For such jewels, people are generally unworthy. This is the fruit of your austerities, or the grace of the deities. And who are we now, to ourselves—let alone to the acceptance or refusal [of such a gift]? From the moment of seeing you, with a heart seized by your abundant weighty virtues, we are in your power. This body has been resolved upon, until death, for the venerable one's use. Here you may act as you please.' And when some time had passed and the topic of describing the <s>ekāvalī</s> (pearl necklace) had given way, the royal fortune [<s>Rājyaśrī</s>], having gained confidence, called the betel-bearer <s>Patralatā</s> and whispered something softly in her ear. And <s>Patralatā</s>, showing her deference, reported to the king: 'Your Majesty! The queen informs you: I do not recall having ever spoken a loud word in the presence of my noble [brother]. How much less a formal request. But this

children.text: śucām a-sahyatāṃ vyāpārayantī hata-daiva-dattā ca daśā śithilayati vinayam. a-balānāṃ hi prāyaśaḥ patir apatyaṃ vâvalambanam. Ubhaya-vikalānāṃ tu duḥkhânalêndhanāyamānaṃ prāṇitam a-śālīnatvam eva kevalam. āryâgamanena ca kṛto 'pi pratihato maraṇa-prayatnaḥ. yataḥ kāṣāya-grahaṇâbhyanujñayânugṛhyatām ayam a-puṇya-bhājanaṃ janaḥ" iti. janâdhipas tu tad ākarṇya tūṣṇīm

body.text: athâcāryaḥ su-dhīram abhyadhāt: "āyuṣmati! śoko hi nāma paryāyaḥ piśācasya, rūpântaram ākṣepasya, tāruṇyaṃ tamaso viśeṣaṇaṃ. viṣasyân-antakaḥ preta-nagara-nāyakaḥ, ayam a-nirvṛti-dharmā dahanaḥ, ayam a-kṣayo rājayakṣmā, ayam a-lakṣmī-nivāso Janārdanaḥ, ayam a-puṇya-pravṛttaḥ kṣapaṇakaḥ, ayam a-pratibodho nidrā-prakāraḥ, ayam an-alasa-dharmā saṃnipātaḥ, ayam a-śiva-sahacaro vināyakaḥ, ayam a-budha-sevito graha-vargaḥ, ayam a-yoga-samuttho jyotiḥ-prakāraḥ, ayaṃ snehād vāyu-prakopaḥ, mānasād agni-saṃbhavaḥ, ārdra-bhāvād rajaḥ-kṣobhaḥ, rasād abhiśoṣaḥ, rāgāt kāla-pariṇāmaḥ. tad asyâ-jasrâsra-srāviṇo hṛdaya-mahā-vraṇasya bahala-doṣândha-kāra-labdha-praveśa-prasarasya prāṇa-taskarasya śūnyatā-hetor mahā-bhūta-grāma-ghātakasya sakala-vigraha-kṣapaṇa-dakṣasya doṣa-cakra-

children.text: -vartinaḥ kārśya-śvāsa-pralāpôpadrava-bahalasya dīrgha-rogasyâ-sad-grahasya sakala-loka-kṣaya-dhūma-ketor jīvitâpahāra-dakṣasyâkṣaṇa-rucer an-abhra-vajra-pātasya sphurad-an-a-vadya-vidyā-vidyud-vidyotamānāni gahana-grantha-gūḍha-garbha-grahaṇa-gambhīrāṇi bhūri-kāvya-kathā-kaṭhorāṇi bahu-śāstrôdvahana-bṛhanti viduṣām api hṛdayāni nâlaṃ soḍhum āpātaṃ kim uta nava-mālikā-kusuma-komalānāṃ sarasa-bisa-tantu-dur-balakam a-balānāṃ hṛdayam.
children.translated_text: rife with the afflictions of emaciation, labored breathing, and delirious rambling, a long disease, an evil planetary seizure, the comet heralding the destruction of all the world, skilled at robbing life, inimical at every moment, a thunderbolt from a cloudless sky—even the hearts of the learned, flashing with the lightning of brilliant blameless knowledge, deep in their grasp of the hidden meanings of profound texts, hardened by abundant poetry and narrative, weighty from bearing many scriptures, cannot endure the onslaught—how much less the hearts of weak women, tender as fresh jasmine blossoms, fragile as the fibers of juicy lotus-stalks?

body.translated_text: Then the master spoke with great composure: 'O long-lived one! Grief indeed is another name for a demon, another form of a curse, the youth of darkness, the epithet of poison. This unending lord of the city of the dead, this fire whose nature is non-joy, this incurable royal consumption, this dwelling-place of misfortune which is <s>Janārdana</s>, this ascetic whose career is in the non-meritorious, this form of sleep without awakening, this seizure whose nature is never idle, this <s>Vināyaka</s> (obstacle-deity) whose companion is the inauspicious, this planetary host served by the unwise, this form of luminosity not born of <s>yoga</s>, this aggravation of wind from affection, this fire born of the mind, this disturbance of <s>rajas</s> from tenderness, this desiccation from <s>rasa</s> (sentiment), this transformation of time from passion—therefore, of this great wound of the heart that incessantly bleeds tears, into which the darkness of accumulated humors has found entrance and spread, which is a thief of life, a cause of emptiness, a slayer of the assemblage of great elements, skilled at wasting the entire body, revolving in the cycle of humors,

body.text: evaṃ sati satya-vrate! vada kim atra kriyate, katama upālabhyate, kasya pura uccair ākrandyate, hṛdaya-dāhi duḥkhaṃ vā khyāpyate? sarvam akṣiṇī nimīlya soḍhavyam a-mūḍhena martya-dharmaṇā. puṇyavati! purātanyaḥ sthitaya etāḥ kena śakyante 'nyathā-kartum. saṃsarantyo naktaṃ-divaṃ drāghīyasyo janma-jarā-maraṇa-ghaṭana-ghaṭī-yantra-rāji-rajjavaḥ sarva-pañca-janānām. pañca-mahā-bhūta-pañca-kulâdhiṣṭhitântaḥ-karaṇa-vyavahāra-darśana-nipuṇāḥ sarvaṃkaṣā viṣamā dharma-rāja-sthitayaḥ. kṣaṇam api kṣamamāṇā galanty āyuṣ-kalā-kalana-kuśalā nilaye nilaye kāla-nālikāḥ. jagati sarva-jantu-jīvitôpahāra-pātinī saṃcarati jhaṭiti caṇḍikā Yamâjñā. raṭanty an-avaratam akhila-prāṇi-prayāṇa-prakaṭana-paṭavaḥ preta-pati-paṭahāḥ. prati-diśaṃ paryaṭanti peṭakaiḥ prati-puraṃ pratapta-loha-lohitâkṣāḥ kāla-kūṭa-

children.text: -kānti-kāla-kāyāḥ kāla-pāśa-pāṇayaḥ kāla-puruṣāḥ. prati-bhavanaṃ bhramanti bhīṣaṇa-kiṃkara-kara-ghaṭṭita-Yama-ghaṇṭā-puṭa-paṭu-ṭāṃkāra-bhayaṃ-karāḥ sarva-sattva-saṃgha-saṃharaṇāya ghorâghāta-ghoṣaṇāḥ. diśi diśi vahanti bahu-citā-dhūma-dhūsarita-preta-pati-patākā-paṭu-patita-gṛdhra-dṛṣṭayaḥ śoka-kṛta-kolāhala-kula-kuṭumbinī-vikīrṇa-keśa-kalāpa-śabala-śava-śibikā-sahasra-saṃkulāḥ kila-kilāyamāna-śmaśāna-śibira-śivā-śāvakāḥ para-lokâvasatha-pathika-sârtha-prasthāna-viśikhā vīthayaḥ. sakala-loka-kavalâvaleha-lampaṭā bahalā vahaṃ-lihā leḍhi lohitâcitā citâṅgāra-kālī kāla-rātri-jihvā jīvitāni jīvinām. tṛptam a-śikṣitā ca bhagavataḥ sarva-bhūta-bhujo bubhukṣā mṛtyoḥ. ati-druta-vāhinī câ-nityatā-nadī. kṣaṇikāś ca mahā-bhūta-grāma-goṣṭhyaḥ. rātriṣu bhahgurāṇi gātra-yantra-pañjara-dārūṇi dehinām. a-śubha-śubhâveśa-vivaśā viśarāravaḥ śarīra-nirmāṇa-paramâṇavaḥ. chidurā jīva-bandhana-pāśa-tantrī-tantavaḥ. sarvam ātmano 'n-īśvaraṃ viśvaṃ naśvaram. evam avadhṛtya nâty-artham evârhasi medhāvini mṛduni manasi tamasaḥ prasaraṃ dātum. eko 'pi pratisaṃkhyāna-kṣaṇa ādhārī-bhavati dhṛteḥ. api ca dūra-gate 'pi hi śoke nanv idānīm apekṣaṇīya evâyaṃ jyeṣṭhaḥ pitṛ-kalpo bhrātā bhavatyā guruḥ. itarathā ko na bahu-manyeta kalyāṇa-rūpam īdṛsaṃ saṃkalpam atra-bhavatyāḥ kāṣāya-grahaṇa-kṛtam. akhila-mano-jvara-praśamana-kāraṇaṃ hi bhagavatī pravrajyā. jyāyaḥ khalv idaṃ paramâtmavatām. mahā-bhāgas tu bhinatti mano-ratha-madhunā. yad ayam ādiśati tad evânuṣṭheyam. yadi bhrātêti yadi jyeṣṭha iti yadi vatsa iti yadi guṇavān iti yadi rājêti sarvathā sthātavyam asya niyoge" ity uktvā vyaraṃsīt.
children.translated_text: bearing the nooses of Death in their hands. In every house, there sound the terrifyingly sharp clangs of <s>Yama</s>'s bells struck by the hands of fearful servants—proclamations of terrible blows for the annihilation of all beings. In every direction, the streets—through which pass the caravans of travelers to the abode of the next world—are thronged with thousands of biers strewn with scattered tresses of wailing family-women, grief-stricken and clamorous, with the jackals of the cremation-camp shrieking with their young, their vulture-gazes fixed upon the falling of the deft banners of the Lord of the Dead, grey with the smoke of many funeral pyres. The tongue of Death's night—black with funeral-pyre embers, red with blood-smears, greedy for the mouthful-licking of the swallowing of all people—licks the lives of the living in an abundant, sweeping, lapping flame. And the hunger of the blessed Lord Death, devourer of all beings, is untrained [insatiable] and satisfied [only temporarily]. And the river of impermanence flows exceedingly swiftly. And the gatherings of the assemblage of great elements are momentary. In the nights, the wooden cage-frames of the body-machines of embodied beings are fragile. The atoms that construct the body are uncontrollable, subject to the possession of the auspicious and inauspicious. The threads of the rope-nooses that bind life are easily cut. Everything in this impermanent universe is beyond one's own control. Having understood this, O wise one, O tender-hearted one, you should not allow the spreading of darkness too much in your mind. Even a single moment of analytical reflection becomes a foundation for fortitude. Moreover, even though grief has gone far, surely this elder brother, who is like a father, must now be your authority. Otherwise, who would not greatly esteem such a beautiful resolve of yours to take the ochre robe? For the blessed life of renunciation is indeed the cause of quenching every fever of the mind. This is indeed the higher [path] for those of supreme self-mastery. But the great fortunate one [your brother] shatters desires with the honey of his wishes. What he commands, that alone should be done. Whether he is a brother, or an elder, or calls you 'dear child,' or is virtuous, or is a king—in every case, one must abide by his authority.' Having spoken thus, he fell silent.

body.translated_text: This being so, O one true to your vow! Tell me—what can be done here, whom can one blame, before whose door can one cry aloud, or to whom can one declare the heart-burning sorrow? Everything must be endured with eyes closed by one who is not deluded by the mortal condition. O blessed one! These are ancient laws—who has the power to alter them? Revolving day and night, the exceedingly long rope-chains of the bucket-wheel rows that produce the sequence of birth, old-age, and death [rotate] for all five peoples. The decrees of the King of <s>Dharma</s> (<s>Yama</s>)—penetrating, expert at perceiving the workings of the inner faculties governed by the five families of the five great elements—are all-pervasive and uneven. The water-clocks of time, skilled at measuring the dripping moments of lifespan, not tolerating even an instant, flow in every dwelling. In the world, the fierce decree of <s>Yama</s>, falling as an offering upon the lives of all creatures, moves swiftly like <s>Caṇḍikā</s>. The drums of the Lord of the Dead, skilled at announcing the departure of all living beings, beat unceasingly. In every direction, in every city, the agents of <s>Kāla</s> (Death) roam about with their receptacles—red-eyed as heated iron, bodies black as the hue of the <s>kālakūṭa</s> (deadly) poison,

children.text: uparata-vacasi ca tasmin nijagāda nara-patiḥ: "āryam apahāya ko 'nya evam abhidadhyāt. an-abhyarthita-daiva-nirmitā hi viṣama-vipad-avalambana-stambhā bhavanto lokasya. snehârdra-mūrtayo mohândha-kāra-dhvaṃsinaś ca dharma-pradīpāḥ. kiṃ tu praṇaya-pradāna-dur-lalitā dur-labham api mano-ratham ati-prītir abhilaṣati. dhīrasyâpi dhārṣṭyam āropayati hṛdaya-laghima-laṅghitam ati-vallabhatvam. yuktâ-yukta-vicāra-śūnyatvāc ca śālīnam api śikṣayanti svârtha-tṛṣṇāḥ prāgalbhyam. abhyarthanāyā rakṣanti ca jala-nidhaya iva maryādām āryāḥ. dattam eva ca śarīram idam an-abhyarthitena prathamam evâtithyāya mānanīyena bhavatā mahyam. ataḥ kiṃ-cid arthaye bhadantam iyaṃ naḥ svasā bālā ca bahu-duḥkha-kheditā ca sarva-kāryâvadhīraṇôparodhenâpi yāval lālanīyā nityam. asmābhiś ca bhrātṛvadhâpakāri-ripu-kula-pralaya-karaṇôdyatasya bāhor vidheyair bhūtvā sakala-loka-pratyakṣaṃ pratijñā kṛtā. pūrvâvamāna-nābhi-bhavam a-sahamānair arpita ātmā kopasya. ato niyuktāṃ kiyantam api kālam ātmānam āryo 'pi kārye madīye. dīyatām atithaye śarīram idam. adya-prabhṛti yāvad ayaṃ jano laghayati pratijñā-bhāram, āśvāsayati ca tāta-vināśa-duḥkha-viklavāḥ prajāḥ, tāvad imām atra-bhavataḥ kathābhiś ca dharmyābhiḥ, kuśala-pratibodha-vidhāyibhir upadeśaiś ca dūrâpasārita-rajobhiḥ, śīlôpaśama-dāyinībhiś ca deśanābhiḥ, kleśa-prahāṇa-hetu-bhūtaiś ca tathā-gatair darśanaiḥ, asmat-pārśvôpayāyinīm eva pratibodhyamānām icchāmi. iyaṃ tu grahīṣyati mayâiva samaṃ samāpta-kṛtyena kāṣāyāṇi. arthi-jane ca kim-iva nâtisṛjanti mahāntaḥ. sura-nātham ātmâsthibhir api yāvat kṛtârtham akarod dhairyôdadhir Dadhīcaḥ. muni-nātho 'py an-apekṣitâtma-sthitir anukampêti kṛtvā kṛpāvān ātmānaṃ vaṭhara-sattvebhyaḥ katikṛtvo na dattavān. ataḥ paraṃ bhavanta eva bahutaraṃ jānanti." ity uktvā tūṣṇīṃ babhūva bhū-patiḥ.
children.translated_text: When he had ceased speaking, the king said: 'Who else but the venerable one could speak thus? For you are the world's pillars of support in dire calamity—created by fate itself unsolicited, your forms moist with affection, lamps of <s>dharma</s> that destroy the darkness of delusion. But excessive love, rendered wayward by the gift of intimacy, longs for even an unattainable desire. Excessive dearness, overleaping the lightness of the heart, imposes boldness even upon the steadfast. And thirsts for one's own ends, being devoid of discrimination between the proper and improper, teach even the self-respecting to be presumptuous. But the noble maintain the boundaries of entreaty, like the oceans their bounds. And this body has already been given, without being asked, at the very first, as hospitality by you, the honored one, to me. Therefore, I request something of the venerable one: this sister of ours, being young and exhausted by much suffering, must be always cherished, even at the cost of obstructing all other duties. And we, having become obedient to the arm that is eager to bring about the annihilation of the enemy clan that murdered our brother, have made a vow in the sight of all the world. Unable to endure the humiliation inflicted before, we have surrendered ourselves to wrath. Therefore, let the venerable one also devote himself to my cause for however long it takes. Let this body be given to the guest [i.e., to duty]. From this day forth, until this person [myself] lightens the burden of my vow and consoles the subjects, distraught with grief at the destruction of our father, I wish her to remain near you, being gradually awakened—by your <s>dharmic</s> narratives, by your instructions that produce the awakening of well-being and keep <s>rajas</s> at a distance, by your teachings that bestow calm and good conduct, and by the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s (the <s>Buddha</s>'s) philosophical views that are the cause of the abandonment of affliction. And she shall take the ochre robe together with me, when my duties are completed. And what indeed would the great not bestow upon the needy? Patient as the ocean of fortitude, <s>Dadhīca</s> made even the lord of the gods content with his own bones. And the lord of sages too, out of compassion, saying "It is compassion," without regard for his own condition, gave himself how many times to wretched creatures? Beyond this, you know far more than I.' Having spoken thus, the king fell silent.

children.text: bhūyas tu babhāṣe bhadantaḥ: "bhavyā na dvir uccārayanti vācam. cetasā prathamam eva pratigrāhitā guṇās tāvakāḥ kāya-balim imām. amunā janenôpayogas tu nir-upayogasyâsya laghuni guruṇi vā kṛtye guṇavad āyattaḥ" iti. atha tathā tasminn abhinandita-praṇaye prīyamāṇaḥ pārthivas tatra tām uṣitvā vibhāvarīm uṣasi ca vasanâlaṃ-kārâdi-pradāna-paritoṣitaṃ visarjya Nirghātam ācāryeṇa saha svasāram ādāya prayāṇakaiḥ katipayair eva kaṭakam anu-Jāhnavi niviṣṭaṃ pratyājagāma.
children.translated_text: But the venerable monk spoke again: "The noble-minded do not repeat their words. Your virtues have already at first been accepted by the mind as this bodily tribute. But the usefulness of this person, who is otherwise useless, in any task whether light or weighty, depends on a man of virtues." Then the king, pleased by such warmly welcomed affection, having spent that night there, and at dawn having dismissed <s>Nirghāta</s> satisfied with gifts of garments, ornaments, and the like, taking his sister along with the preceptor, returned in just a few marches to the camp situated on the <s>Jāhnavī</s> (Ganges).

body.text: tatra ca Rājyaśrī-prāpti-vyatikara-kathāṃ kathayata eva praṇayibhyo ravir api tatāra gagana-talam. bahala-madhu-paṅka-piṅgalaḥ paṅgajâkara iva saṃcukoca cakra-vāka-vallabho vāsaraḥ. prakīrṇāni nava-rudhira-rasâruṇa-varṇāni lokâloka-jūṃṣi yajūṃṣîva kupita-Yājñavalkya-vaktra-vāntāni nija-vapuṣi pūṣā pāpa-mūṃṣi punar api saṃjahāra jālakāni rociṣām. krameṇa ca samupohyamāna-māṃsala-rāga-rociṣṇur uṣṇâṃśur uṣṇīṣa-bandha-sahaja-cūḍā-maṇir iva Vṛkodara-kara-puṭôtpāṭitaḥ, pratyagra-śoṇita-śoṇâṅga-rāga-raudro Drauṇāyanasya, rudra-bhikṣā-dāna-śauṇḍa-pura-mathana-mukta-muṇḍa-sirā-nāḍi-rudhira-pūraṇa-śoṇita-kapilaḥ kapāla-karpara iva ca paitāmahaḥ, pitṛ-vadha-ruṣita-Rāma-rāga-racitaḥ, pṛthu-vikaṭa-Kārtavīryâṃsa-kūṭa-kuṭṭāka-kuṭhāra-tuṇḍa-taṣṭa-

children.text: -duṣṭa-kṣatriya-kaṇṭha-kuhara-rudhira-kulyā-praṇāla-sahasra-pūrito hrada iva dūra-rodhī raudhiro bhaya-nigūḍha-kara-caraṇa-muṇḍa-maṇḍalâkṛtir guru-Garuḍa-nakha-pañjarâkṣepa-kṣapaṇa-kṣipta-kṣatajôkṣito vy-asur Vibhāvasuḥ, kaṇṭha iva ca loṭhyamānaḥ, nabhasy Aruṇa-garbha-māṃsa-piṇḍa iva ca khaṇḍimānam ānītaḥ, niyata-kālâtipāta-dūyamāna-dākṣāyaṇī-kṣiptaḥ, dhātu-taṭa iva ca Sumeror a-sura-vadhâbhicāra-caru-pacana-piśunaḥ, śoṇita-kvātha-kaṣāyita-kukṣir ati-visaṃkaṭaḥ kaṭāha iva ca Bārhaspatyaḥ, sadyo-galita-gaja-dānava-deha-lohitôpalepa-bhīṣaṇaḥ mukha-maṇḍalâbhoga iva Mahābhairavasya muhūrtam adṛśyata. jala-nidhi-jala-pratibimbita-ravi-bimbā-rāji-bhāsvarâbhrâvalambinī gṛhītârdra-māṃsa-bhārêva câbabhāse vāsarâvasāna-velā vetāla-nibhā. jvalat-saṃdhyā-rāga-rajyamāna-jala-pravāhaḥ punar iva purāṇa-puruṣa-pīvarôru-saṃpuṭa-piṣṭa-Madhu-Kaiṭabha-rudhira-paṭala-pāṭala-vapur abhavad adhipatir arṇasām. Samavasite ca saṃdhyā-samaye saman-antaram a-parimita-yaśaḥ-pāna-tṛṣitāya muktā-śaila-śilā-caṣaka iva nija-kula-kīrtyā, kṛta-yuga-karaṇôdyatāyâdi-rāja-rājata-śāsana-mudrā-niveśa iva rājya-śriyā, sakala-dvīpa-jigīṣā-calitāya śveta-dvīpa-dūta iva câyatyā, śveta-bhānur upānīyata niśayā narêndrāyêti bhadram om.
children.translated_text: like a far-reaching blood-lake filled by thousands of canal-channels of blood from the throat-hollows of wicked <s>Kṣatriyas</s>; with the appearance of a sphere whose hands and feet were hidden in fear; sprinkled with blood thrown off by the fierce tearing claws of mighty <s>Garuḍa</s>, the lifeless demon; as if being rolled like a severed head in the sky; like the lump of flesh that was the embryo of <s>Aruṇa</s>, brought to destruction; thrown by <s>Dākṣāyaṇī</s> (Satī), anguished that the appointed time had passed; like the mineral slope of <s>Sumeru</s>, betraying the cooking of a ritual offering for the sorcery of slaying demons; like the exceedingly dreadful cauldron of <s>Bṛhaspati</s>, its belly stained with a decoction of blood; like the terrifying orb of the face of <s>Mahābhairava</s>, smeared with the blood from the freshly fallen body of the elephant-demon. The close of day appeared like a <s>vetāla</s>, hanging from clouds that shone with rows of sun-reflections in the ocean's waters, as if holding a load of wet flesh. The lord of waters, its flowing stream colored by the blazing twilight glow, assumed a pinkish body as if reddened again by the layers of blood of <s>Madhu</s> and <s>Kaiṭabha</s> crushed between the massive thighs of the Primordial Man. When the twilight hour had ended, immediately—like a goblet of pearl-mountain stone offered by his own family's glory to one thirsting for the drink of immeasurable fame, like the impression of the silver seal of the primordial king's edict by the royal splendor eager to bring about the Golden Age, like an envoy from the White Continent by the future set in motion by the desire to conquer all continents—the white-rayed moon was brought by the night to the king. Thus, may there be well-being. <s>Oṃ</s>.

body.translated_text: There, while he was narrating to his dear ones the tale of the adventure of finding <s>Rājyaśrī</s>, the sun too crossed the vault of the sky. The day, dear to the <s>cakravāka</s>, contracted like a lotus pond tawny with thick honey-mud. The sun again gathered into his own body the scattered nets of his rays, red as fresh blood in color, like the world-illuminating <s>Yajus</s> mantras vomited from the mouth of angry <s>Yājñavalkya</s>—rays that remove sins. And gradually, the hot-rayed sun, glowing with intensifying deep crimson, appeared for a moment—like the natural crest-jewel of the turban-knot torn out by the cupped hand of <s>Vṛkodara</s> (Bhīma), terrible with the body-paint of fresh blood of <s>Aśvatthāman</s>; tawny with blood like the skull-bowl of <s>Brahmā</s> filled with blood from the severed head-vein released during the destruction of the Triple City, given as alms to <s>Rudra</s>; fashioned by the fury of <s>Paraśurāma</s> enraged at his father's murder; hewn by the axe-blade used to hack at the broad and massive shoulder-joints of <s>Kārtavīrya</s>—

body.text: iti śrī-mahā-kavi-Bāṇa-bhaṭṭa-kṛtau Harṣacarite 'ṣṭama ucchvāsaḥ
body.translated_text: Thus ends the eighth <s>ucchvāsa</s> (chapter) of the <s>Harṣacarita</s> composed by the illustrious great poet <s>Bāṇabhaṭṭa</s>.
